papers.abstract: Camera-controlled video generation re-renders a video along a target camera trajectory, yet moving the camera around an object, the most natural way to change the viewpoint of an object-centric scene, remains difficult. Existing methods condition either on camera parameters, which are scale-ambiguous in monocular video, or on explicit geometry such as warped point clouds or depth, which breaks down under large viewpoint changes. We present AnyCam, a method that represents the camera with an anchor object in the scene: we reconstruct it in 3D and render it along the target trajectory, a camera signal that is scale-aware, view-complete and easy to specify relative to the object. A video diffusion model transfers the content and dynamics of the source video to the new viewpoint. Its H-Concat layout aligns source and target frames in time, so the model can be distilled into AnyCam-AR, a streaming few-step generator for on-the-fly camera control. Both models are trained on paired videos with pixel-aligned anchor renderings from multi-camera videos and static-scene captures. Experiments on diverse datasets and trajectories show that AnyCam performs favorably against camera-controlled video generation and 3D reconstruction methods in camera control and visual quality.
authors: Weijie Lyu, Zhixin Shu, Yuntian Ke, Ming-Hsuan Yang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of changing viewpoints around objects, where camera parameters are scale-ambiguous and explicit geometry can fail under large viewpoint changes.
Reconstructs an anchor object in 3D and renders it along a target trajectory to represent the camera relative to the scene.
Uses a video diffusion model with H-Concat temporal alignment to transfer source-video content and dynamics to the new viewpoint.
Introduces AnyCam-AR, a streaming few-step generator for on-the-fly camera control.
Experiments across diverse datasets and trajectories show favorable camera control and visual quality compared with existing camera-controlled generation and 3D reconstruction methods.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of AnyCam. (a) The user selects an anchor object in the source video. SAM 2 [37] tracks it to give the source camera representation (the anchor cut-out), and SAM 3D [8] reconstructs it; the reconstruction is aligned to the source cameras and rendered along the target trajectory to give the target camera representation. The noisy target latent and the source latent are concatenated along the height (H-Concat), each half receives its camera representation through channel concatenation, and the diffusion transformer denoises the target half, which the VAE decodes into the target video. (b) The numbers under the tokens are their RoPE positions (t, h), with the role ID as a third entry in the fourth layout. The grids mark which source frames each target frame attends to. Frame concatenation [1, 7, 28] places the whole source after the target, so the first target frame needs the complete source video and therefore the generation cannot stream. Channel concatenation [15] merges the two frames into one token, which loses information and lowers fidelity to the source video [1]. Frame interleaving [52] doubles the length of the temporal axis. A shared position with a role phase [49] needs an additional positional encoding to tell the two streams apart. Our H-Concat keeps the source and target as separate tokens at the same temporal index and offsets the source in height, so the base model is used without new parameters or a custom attention mask.

Figure 10. Video-to-video comparison on CO3D. Each case takes two rows with the source frame (Input), the ground-truth frame and the frame of every method at the same time. 3DGS [20] is optimized per scene on the 81 source frames. AnyCam-AR, HY-WorldPlay [41] and InSpatio-World [40] are autoregressive models. On the sides of the objects that the source video does not show, AnyCam and AnyCam-AR match the ground truth, while 3DGS and DepthDirector [7] break down and most other baselines show the object from a wrong angle or lose it. For the television (bottom), ReDirector [30] and DepthDirector show only the floor and HY-WorldPlay shows its back.

Figure 6. Visual comparison on DAVIS. AnyCam follows every trajectory and keeps the scene intact, since the anchor rendering fixes the scale of the motion relative to the anchor and covers it from every side. Methods that warp estimated geometry show holes and stretched content at new viewpoints: TrajectoryCrafter [56] tears the airplane apart during rotation (rows 1 and 2), GEN3C [39] leaves stripes (row 2), and DepthDirector [7] breaks down under zoom-in and rise (rows 3 to 6). Methods conditioned on camera parameters guess the scale of the motion: ReCamMaster [1] loses the airplane after the orbit (row 2), Wan-Fun-Cam [44] zooms far past the train into the tree (row 4), ReDirector [30] and Wan-Fun-Cam collapse into noise under large orbit and rise (rows 2 and 6).

Figure 11. Single-image comparison on CO3D. Each block shows one case with the input image (Input), the ground-truth frame and the frame generated by each method of Tab. 3 from the same target camera. The 3D reconstruction methods render only the object and often distort its shape, e.g., LGM [42] for three of the four objects and TRELLIS [48] for the handbag and the bench. Most video generation baselines move to an incorrect viewpoint. GEN3C [39], TrajectoryCrafter [56], ReDirector [30] and Wan-Fun-Cam [44] lose the banana (top right). GEN3C, TrajectoryCrafter, DepthDirector [7], ReCamMaster [1] and ReDirector shift the sandwich (bottom right) to the right. AnyCam and AnyCam-AR match the viewpoint and the appearance of the ground truth.
Figure 21. Anchor selection prompt. System prompt given to Qwen3-VL-32B together with 8 frames of the video.

Figure 8. Long-video comparison on CO3D (left) and RealEstate10K (right). The anchor rendering gives every chunk a reference to the object, so AnyCam-AR stays registered to the scene over hundreds of frames. The baselines drift as their errors accumulate over the chunks: both lose the cellphone (left, rows 5, 6), and both turn away from the house (right, rows 1, 2) and the deck (right, rows 5, 6).

Figure 7. Single-image to video comparison on Mip-NeRF 360. Since the anchor rendering is object-relative and view-complete, AnyCam always reaches the target viewpoints. Wan-Fun-Cam [44] and ReCamMaster [1] are conditioned on camera parameters, whose scale a single photo cannot determine, and barely move away from the input view (rows 1 to 3). GEN3C [39], TrajectoryCrafter [56] and DepthDirector [7] warp a depth map that covers only the visible surface, which leaves distorted or missing content (rows 1 to 3).

Figure 4. Anchor rendering as a camera signal only. The anchor (center console) is poorly reconstructed with no texture (column 3), compared with its cut-out in the source video (column 2). AnyCam still recovers the appearance of the console and the cabin from the source video and controls the camera movement correctly, showing that the rendering only provides a camera signal and the model is robust to poor reconstructions.

Figure 12. Additional visual comparison on DAVIS (same layout as Fig. 6). The camera zooms out from the swing (rows 1 and 2) and rises by 60◦ over the display shelf, the skate bowl and the railway crossing (rows 3 to 8). AnyCam shows the whole swing frame after the zoom-out and looks down on the other three scenes. DepthDirector [7] breaks apart on the swing (rows 1 and 2) and the crossing (rows 7 and 8) and turns toward the sky above the skate bowl (rows 5 and 6). Wan-Fun-Cam [44] moves closer to the swing instead of away from it (rows 1 and 2), stays at the height of the input at the shelf (rows 3 and 4) and turns into noise on the skate bowl and the crossing (rows 6 and 8).

Figure 13. Comparison with the Plücker-ray models. Wan-Fun-Cam† and Wan-Fun-Cam-AR† are trained on our data with our recipe and receive the camera as Plücker rays instead of the anchor rendering. Top: DAVIS [32, 34] with a 60◦ rise, AnyCam and Wan-Fun-Cam†; the numbers on the input frames give the frame index. Middle: a 333-frame CO3D [38] video (166 frames out and back) generated from an 81-frame source video; bottom: a 165-frame RealEstate10K [63] video generated from a single image; AnyCam-AR and Wan-Fun-CamAR†; the labels on the ground-truth frames give the frame index and the video length. Wan-Fun-Cam† distorts the street in the last frames of the rise. Wan-Fun-Cam-AR† drifts off the bench, which the frame border cuts off from frame 94 on. On RealEstate10K, it moves into the armchair instead of toward the coffee table. AnyCam and AnyCam-AR follow the target views.

Figure 15. Failure case: small anchors. When the anchor covers only about 1% of the frame, its rendering gives little information about the rotation of the camera. For the agave plant (row 1, 0.7% of the frame), the output camera barely moves, and for the garden stool (row 2, 1.2%) it turns much less than the target orbit. Both rows show AnyCam.

Figure 2. Camera representations. Yellow represents the input camera. (a) Camera parameters are scale-ambiguous: a small object near the input camera and a large object farther away give the same input image, but the same target camera parameters (blue and red camera) see them at a different size, position and angle (blue and red boxes), so the target view is not determined. (b) A point cloud or depth warp of the input image only covers the surface seen from the input camera. Under a large viewpoint change, views are often heavily distorted (red box). The points in the target view sometimes come from the inside of the object or from the back of the image (blue box). The renderings are wrong and mislead the subsequent video generation. (c) Our anchor rendering uses the complete reconstructed object, so target cameras at any angle (green) see the whole anchor with the correct size and pose.
Figure 5. Training samples. Top: MultiCamVideo [1], a dynamic scene captured by two synchronized cameras. Bottom: DL3DV [24], two clips of a static capture.

Figure 9. CO3D target trajectories of the three difficulty levels for one sequence (hydrant), seen from above. Positions are normalized by the median radius of the source cameras. The target camera moves from source frame 0 to the first real target camera (dotted) and then follows real CO3D cameras, with ground truth at the dots.

Figure 14. Moving and deforming anchors. The anchor need not be static or rigid: a swimming swan (DAVIS [32, 34], row 1), a walking dinosaur (row 2), and a person from the DyCheck dataset [9] (bottom left: holding a teddy bear; bottom right: sitting in a chair). The condition renders the anchor reconstructed from one frame, while the generated video keeps the motion of the source, e.g., the swimming swan, the walking legs, and the moving hands and arms. Row 2 shows AnyCam-AR; all other examples show AnyCam.

Figure 16. Different anchors in the same video. For each source video, the user picks two or three objects as anchors and a target trajectory around each of them. The tags above each example name the anchors and their trajectories. Each anchor has its own trajectory, so the rows show camera control through different objects of one video, not one camera applied to several anchors. Each condition renders only its anchor. The numbers on the source frames give the frame index. All outputs are from AnyCam. In the first video, the camera pushes in toward the mirrorless camera or the instant camera on the table, or pulls back and rises over the armchair. In the second video, it orbits around the food truck toward its front or pushes in to the sandwich board.

Figure 17. Different anchors in the same video (continued). Same setting as Fig. 16. All outputs are from AnyCam. In the gaming room, the output orbits around the gaming chair or moves toward the PC tower. In the second video, it orbits around the carved armchair or rises over the side table.

Figure 18. Different anchors in the same video (continued). Same setting as Fig. 16. All outputs are from AnyCam. The output moves toward the telephone or the perfume bottle while the person keeps moving as in the source. In the studio, it rises over the writing desk or turns toward the stool.

Figure 19. The anchor leaves the frame. The camera moves past anchor A until A leaves the view; starting at the switch frame, the condition renders anchor B, a second object reconstructed from the first source frame, and the camera continues toward it. The numbers on the source frames give the frame index; tags A and B mark the anchor in the condition. All rows show AnyCam. The output keeps moving after A has left and approaches anchor B (the sports car, the red car, the white SUV and the PC tower in rows 1 to 4).

Figure 20. Switching the anchor during a video. The target camera follows one continuous trajectory. The condition renders anchor A up to frame 32 and anchor B from frame 33 (tags A and B), and both anchors are reconstructed from the first source frame. The numbers on the source frames give the frame index. Rows 1 to 3 show AnyCam, row 4 shows AnyCam-AR. After the switch, the output moves toward the side table, the perfume bottle, the bentwood chair and the PC tower.

Table 5. Long-video comparison on RealEstate10K. AnyCamAR’s rotation error is less than half that of InSpatio-World [40].

Table 4. Single-image comparison on Mip-NeRF 360. AnyCam is best on all ground-truth metrics and FID.

Table 8. Long videos on CO3D, all metrics. 30 sequences; the source is an 81-frame clip played forward and backward to the target length, and the target follows the real CO3D cameras around the object for 165 or 249 frames, or for 166 frames and back (333 frames). PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS compare each generated frame with the ground-truth frame of the same camera, and oPSNR, oSSIM and oLPIPS do so inside the object mask. Unseen views are the ground-truth frames whose camera is at least 45◦ in azimuth away from the arc covered by the source clip, i.e. sides of the object the input never shows; the way back is the second half of the 333-frame videos. Anchor IoU compares the anchor tracked in the generated video with the object mask, and Lost is the fraction of frames where the track is lost. Best in bold, second underlined, ranked within each group.

Table 7. Attention fine-tuning versus LoRA. LoRA [16] of rank 32 on the attention and feed-forward layers, trained with a learning rate of 10−4, versus fine-tuning the self-attention layers and the patch embedding with a learning rate of 5 × 10−5. Both are trained on the same data for 10K steps with a batch size of 32. The attention fine-tuning row is AnyCam; the cases and metrics are those of its DAVIS and CO3D comparisons (Tabs. 1 and 2). Better in bold.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a method for camera-controlled video generation using 3D reconstruction of an anchor object, fitting Video Diffusion and 3D Foundation Models.
papers.title: AnyCam: Anything Can Represent Camera for Video Generation
papers.tldr: AnyCam enables camera-controlled video generation by using a reconstructed 3D anchor object to specify scale-aware, view-complete camera motion.

papers.abstract: A general-purpose Vision-Language Model (VLM) has surpassed expert vision models in many domains such as object detection and video recognition. However, point correspondence is known to be challenging for VLMs since it goes beyond object-level recognition: it requires pixel-level localization of the same physical surface point across observations, even when appearance changes or the point disappears and later reappears. In this paper, we introduce AgenTAP, a VLM-based agent that directly predicts point coordinates and visibility and actively reasons over videos. Starting from its own estimate, the agent autonomously chooses what to inspect and uses the resulting evidence to verify point identity and refine its predictions. With GPT-6 Astra, it surpasses expert vision models in both point localization and visibility prediction, without correspondence-specific fine-tuning. We further use AgenTAP to re-identify physical points after disappearance and reconnect fragmented tracks, constructing EgoTAP-4D, a dataset of 3D point trajectories in long real-world egocentric videos. On sampled reappearing points, its predictions approach human agreement, and adding EgoTAP-4D to D4RT training improves average 3D tracking performance.
authors: Xuweiyi Chen, Jin Yao, Linzhan Mou, Lei Gong, Di Liu, Cheng Zhang, Ziqiao Ma, Sihan Xu, Adam W. Harley, Shengyi Qian, Zezhou Cheng
bullets: Addresses VLM difficulty with pixel-level point correspondence under appearance changes and occlusions.
Predicts point coordinates and visibility, then actively selects video evidence to verify identity and refine estimates.
Outperforms expert vision models on localization and visibility without correspondence-specific fine-tuning.
Uses re-identified points to build EgoTAP-4D, a dataset of 3D trajectories from long egocentric videos.
Its reappearing-point predictions approach human agreement, and EgoTAP-4D improves D4RT’s average 3D tracking performance when used for training.

figures.caption: Figure 6 EgoTAP-4D annotation pipeline. From a stereo egocentric video with camera poses and hand motion capture, we recover metric depth and camera poses, label each region as static (blue), moving (orange), or hand (green), and build 2D trajectories from the fused scene geometry, AllTracker, and MANO. When an object returns after leaving the view, AGENTAP with GPT-6 Astra locates its query points again (Fig. 9, first row). All trajectories are then lifted to 3D in one world frame.

Figure 4 Analysis of VLM correspondence. Direct prediction improves with model size (a), transfers to held-out videos (b), and trails trackers on synthetic videos (e). AGENTAP’s lead over trackers grows with frame gap (c), its improvement over direct prediction is largest at strict thresholds (d), and its verification is robust (f). Agent results use GPT-6 Astra. Red: linear fit. Shading: 95% CIs. †: video input.

Figure 3 AgenTAP. (1) Initial prediction: the VLM agent inspects both views and records its own prediction. (2) Optional expert consultation: expert vision models propose candidate locations. (3) Iterative visual verification: the agent selects visual tools to test its hypothesis, revises the point’s location and visibility, and re-checks as needed.

Figure 8 EgoTAP-4D trajectories. Each panel shows one recording. The main view shows 3D trajectories in world coordinates together with the reconstructed scene, and the inset shows the corresponding video frame with the 2D trajectories. The same color marks the same track in both views. The white frustum shows the current camera pose, and the dashed white line shows the camera trajectory.

Figure 9 Point reconnection after reappearance. Two Xperience-10M sequences in which an object or a person exits the field of view and later re-enters it. From left to right, the columns show the query points, their tracks shortly before the exit, a frame in which they are out of view (dimmed), and the predictions of AGENTAP and AllTracker after the return. Colors denote point identity. Points predicted invisible are omitted, and each prediction panel reports how many of the ten query points are predicted visible. The arrow gives the time between exit and re-entry. Supplementary Fig. S14 shows two more sequences.

Figure 7 AgenTAP and AllTracker on DAVIS. Trails show each point from frame 0 to the shown frame. Each answer uses only that frame and frame 0, and AGENTAP also receives the RoMa v2 and AllTracker answers. A point predicted invisible has no dot.
Figure 5 Visibility and localization. In direct prediction, VLMs that localize better also judge visibility better. †: video input.
Figure 1 Tracking Any Point with Agentic Visual Reasoning.

Table 1 Main results on TrackingBench. Direct prediction, AGENTAP, and expert vision models answer the same 2,000 queries. Overall columns evaluate all queries together rather than averaging the six domains, and domain columns omit EPE. Higher is better except for EPE. HR: high resolution. Subscripts give each agent’s change from the same VLM’s two-image direct prediction, which is also the reference

papers.tldr: AgenTAP uses agentic visual reasoning to track physical points through video, including periods when they disappear and reappear.

papers.abstract: Image editing models can follow a wide range of instructions, but video editing models still lag behind, limited in part by the difficulty of collecting paired source and edited videos. Is it possible to transfer advanced image editing capabilities to video editors without new paired videos? We introduce Image-to-Video Transfer (I2VT), which improves pretrained video editors and expands them to new editing tasks using an image editor. It enables efficient post-training with no architectural changes and no new videos, using only individual images. Our key idea is to let the video editor role-play as an image editor: it edits an image as a one-frame video, with the image editor guiding the video editor's predictions at each denoising step. Although the video editor sees only single images during training, at test time it applies the improved and expanded capabilities to whole video clips while preserving temporal consistency. To push the boundaries of video editing, we introduce OpenVE++, an extension of OpenVE-Bench that adds four new editing tasks useful for video production, including action changes, expression changes, body movements, and scene relighting. Our experiments across three different video editors show that I2VT improves existing editing capabilities and expands them to new tasks, and our models achieve state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on both OpenVE-Bench and OpenVE++.
authors: Ji Xie, Yanhao Jia, Xiangpeng Yang, Martin Q. Ma, Sihan Xu, Erik Cambria, Louis-Philippe Morency
bullets: Addresses the lack of paired source–edited videos for training video editors.
Uses an image editor to guide a video editor’s frame-level predictions during denoising, with no architectural changes or new videos.
Applies the resulting capabilities to full video clips at test time while maintaining temporal consistency.
Introduces OpenVE++, extending OpenVE-Bench with action, expression, body-movement, and scene-relighting edits.
Experiments across three video editors report improved existing capabilities, broader task coverage, and SOTA performance on OpenVE-Bench and OpenVE++.

Figure 3. I2VT and the offline distillation baseline. Left: offline distillation fine-tunes on teacher-edited images. Middle: I2VT supervises the student along its own rollout. The cross marks stop-gradient. Right: at inference, the student edits whole video clips.

Figure 5. Offline versus online distillation with I2VT. Bernini-R-1.3B on a basic edit from OpenVE-Bench (left) and a body-movement edit from OpenVE++ (right), showing three frames sampled from each video.

Figure 2. Motivation and intuition. Left: image editors handle complex edits such as actions and relighting on single frames, whereas video editors lack the paired data to learn them. Our goal is a video editor that makes these edits while keeping the video temporally consistent. Middle: can a video editor learn to edit images by treating each image as a one-frame video? Right: video editing ability improves while temporal quality remains comparable.

papers.abstract: We present LuxAvatar, a feed-forward framework for real-time head avatar animation and relighting from a single portrait. To achieve both 3D controllability and complex facial light transport, we factorize avatar synthesis into an animatable 3D intrinsic Gaussian proxy and a causal autoregressive neural shader. This proxy disentangles canonical geometry and reflectance attributes, rapidly rasterizing deformed Gaussians into view- and motion-consistent PBR buffers. Conditioned on these buffers, our neural shader formulates forward rendering as a conditional video diffusion process, bypassing explicit PBR computation to synthesize realistic shading effects under target illumination. We achieve real-time streaming through heterogeneous distillation from a pretrained multi-step bidirectional relighting teacher to a two-step causal autoregressive neural shader, inheriting broad synthetic lighting priors while minimizing conditioning and decoding latency. To further specialize these priors to human heads, we construct a hybrid relighting dataset for domain-specific fine-tuning, capturing authentic facial dynamics and physically grounded light transport. Extensive experiments show that our framework enables 3D-controllable, real-time portrait animation and relighting, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in visual fidelity, motion control, and lighting accuracy.
authors: Yipengjing Sun, Chenyang Wang, Boyao Zhou, Jiapeng Zhu, Ka Leong Cheng, Shengping Zhang
bullets: Factorizes synthesis into an animatable 3D proxy for geometry and reflectance and a neural shader for complex facial light transport.
Renders view- and motion-consistent physically based buffers from deformed Gaussians to condition relighting.
Uses a two-step causal autoregressive shader distilled from a multi-step bidirectional video-diffusion teacher for low-latency streaming.
Fine-tunes on a hybrid relighting dataset designed to capture realistic facial dynamics and physically grounded lighting.
Experiments report improved visual fidelity, motion control, and lighting accuracy over prior methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of LuxAvatar. (a) Intrinsic Gaussian Head Proxy: Given a single reference image I , our feed-forward network predicts decoupled geometry and material attributes on a canonical UV manifold. Driven by target FLAME and camera parameters, the canonical Gaussians are deformed and rasterized into 4D-consistent PBR buffers {Ct}. (b) Causal Neural Shader: Conditioned on {Ct}, the reference image, and target scene illumination, our distilled causal neural shader autoregressively streams photorealistic relit video chunks in just two denoising steps, while reusing KV caches across chunks to maintain temporal coherence.

Figure 4. Environment-map relighting comparison. Rows 1–2 show self- and cross-reenactment on VFHQ, while Rows 3–4 show self-reenactment on FaceOLAT and novel-view cross-reenactment on NeRSemble, respectively. The last column displays the relit ground truth for Row 3 and driving frames for other rows. Target illumination is visualized via diffuse (top) and mirror (bottom) spheres.

Figure 3. Hybrid relighting data curation. Three complementary data sources provide (a) intrinsic and relit appearance supervision, (b) real video targets preserving facial details and natural motion, and (c) physically grounded supervision under continuously varying illumination.

Figure 5. Background harmonization comparison. We show cross-reenactment results on (a) VFHQ and (b) NeRSemble, with reference images and target backgrounds shown at the top. The last column displays the driving frames.
Figure 6. Effect of the causal neural shader. On the unseen NeRSemble dataset, our shader synthesizes expression-dependent wrinkles and reduces eyeglass distortion.
Figure 7. Effect of hybrid training data. Top: relighting comparison under the same target lighting. Bottom: head animation under dynamic lighting.

papers.title: LuxAvatar: Real-Time Relightable Head Avatars via Causal Neural Shading of 3D Intrinsic Proxies
papers.tldr: LuxAvatar enables real-time, controllable head animation and relighting from a single portrait by combining an intrinsic 3D Gaussian proxy with a distilled causal neural shader.

papers.abstract: We present MEMO (a Mesh for Every MOment), a method that reconstructs the geometry of complete dynamic scenes, captured by multiple synchronized cameras, and extracts a mesh at every frame. Existing dynamic Gaussian splatting methods either model appearance alone or target isolated objects segmented by foreground masks, and all of them recover meshes by TSDF fusion or Poisson reconstruction, whose fixed grids limit the detail they can capture. At the core of MEMO is a per-Gaussian motion model inspired by Gaussian processes, which represents each Gaussian's position and rotation over time as a combination of temporal Gaussian kernels. The model keeps every Gaussian a valid surface element throughout the sequence and carries an implicit representation of the dynamic geometry, so a mesh can be derived at any time from a field defined by the Gaussians. Although common in real captures, large and fast motion poses a challenge that dynamic Gaussian splatting methods usually overlook. To account for it, we design a track-based initialization scheme that fits each Gaussian's initial trajectory to point tracks in closed form. We evaluate MEMO on Blender-Moments, a new benchmark of nine animated scenes with ground-truth meshes at every frame, and on two real-world datasets. MEMO reconstructs the most accurate geometry among state-of-the-art methods, and remains competitive in novel-view synthesis and training time. Project page: https://memo-4d.github.io
authors: Roy Or-El, Jeong Joon Park, Ira Kemelmacher-Shlizerman
bullets: Addresses limitations of dynamic Gaussian splatting methods that focus on appearance or isolated objects and derive meshes through detail-limited TSDF/Poisson fusion.
Models each Gaussian’s position and rotation over time using temporal Gaussian kernels inspired by Gaussian processes.
Maintains Gaussians as valid surface elements throughout the sequence, enabling mesh extraction at any frame from an implicit geometry field.
Uses track-based initialization to fit Gaussian trajectories in closed form for large and fast motion.
On Blender-Moments and two real-world datasets, achieves the most accurate geometry among compared methods while remaining competitive in novel-view synthesis and training time.

papers.abstract: Synthesizing diverse dexterous manipulation policies is challenging: existing simulation-based approaches rely on human demonstrations which are difficult to scale, or use generic reward functions, which provide limited control over the hand-object interactions. We propose DexLink, which addresses these limitations by synthesizing diverse dexterous behaviors from sparse, reusable hand-object interaction templates. Given key task waypoints, DexLink retargets static interaction templates to target objects using an optimization that preserves spatial hand-object relationships. It then links the retargeted poses into an approximate reference trajectory and uses residual reinforcement learning to refine this reference into a closed-loop policy in simulation. Experiments spanning single-hand, bimanual, articulated, and dynamic tasks demonstrate that DexLink provides fine-grained control over task timing, grasp types, and high-level execution. The modular interaction templates transfer reliably across object scales, instances, and categories; without object-specific human demonstrations, the framework also matches the performance of dense reference-tracking methods. Finally, zero-shot deployment of policies trained purely in simulation shows promise for the simulation-based framework.

papers.abstract: Language models think in words; then multimodal models might think in images. We test whether a generated helper improves the answer to a visual question. A model describes the helper it needs and then answers using the original and generated images together. Across 13 vision-language model and generator pairs, generation lowers mean accuracy by 3.7 percentage points, with declines on nine of ten tasks. Two unified models, BAGEL and Janus-Pro-7B, each lose accuracy on eight tasks. On VSTAR, adding a generated image to the same planning hint lowers accuracy by 10.47 points. Repeated image edits yield different outcomes across tasks. ChartQAPro and MathVista stay below their no-generation baselines, while ERQA gains three points after ten edits.
authors: Xueyang Yu, Yifan Jing, Taiming Lu, Linrong Cai, Zhipeng Cai, Yunyang Xiong, Gabriel Sarch, Zhuang Liu

papers.abstract: Robots operating in previously mapped spaces must localize accurately despite moving people and rearranged objects. Most localization pipelines match the query against a sparse set of captured reference images retrieved by appearance, which is brittle under scene change and repeating structures. We present MERLoc, which turns a single metric 3D Gaussian Splatting scan into a dense Functional Reference Memory. Reference views are sampled over the navigable space for the robot's morphology and sensors at a target density and rendered offline. Pre-encoding them for the chosen off-the-shelf localizer removes the reference encoder from inference. A pose-based retrieval strategy then selects references by spatial proximity and viewing direction rather than appearance, sidestepping visual ambiguities whenever a prior exists. Across one classical and four learned localizers in simulated and real dynamic scenes, pose-based retrieval matches or outperforms appearance retrieval in most cases, even when the latter is gated by the same prior. On real data, it lowers position RMSE by 15-60 % in nine of ten backend/split combinations, and the rendered memory outperforms real-image caches posed by Structure-from-Motion. The system runs onboard a Jetson Orin NX at 5 Hz, enabling a navigation policy to successfully traverse a hallway with people roaming and rearranging objects.
authors: Michael Baumgartner, Dario Mylonopoulos, Sammy Christen, Markus Gross, Moritz Bacher
bullets: Builds a dense reference memory by sampling and offline-rendering views from a single metric 3D Gaussian Splatting scan.

On real data, reduces position RMSE by 15–60% in nine of ten backend/split combinations.
Runs onboard a Jetson Orin NX at 5 Hz and supports hallway navigation amid people and rearranged objects.

papers.abstract: A single casual video leaves a moving scene under-determined: a point seen once from each place can slide toward or away from the camera and still match every frame. We constrain the reconstruction with the structure of the motion itself. Building on DynMF, we model a scene's motion as a handful of SE(3) trajectories, each rigid, and let every point follow one of them alone, never a blend. DynMF2 computes this factorization directly from 3D point trajectories, with no rendering, by Expectation-Maximization (EM). Its M-step fits, in closed form, every rigid motion to the points assigned to it, and its E-step reassigns every point to the motion that explains it with the least error. The background is simply one more motion, the camera's, so no masks are needed. Three tools then revise the factorization: requery adds trajectories where the rendering shows parts the tracker missed, merge joins motions that move together, and split separates those that do not. Thus the number of motions follows the scene. Without masks, DynMF2 clearly outperforms the mask-based baselines in view synthesis on iPhone and NVIDIA and in 3D tracking on iPhone. It recovers what masks leave out, from thin parts and details to small movers far in the background. Its motions segment the moving parts of MOVi-F and iTACO scenes competitively, although DynMF2 is never trained to segment. What moves in a scene is not decided in advance: it emerges from the rigid motions themselves.
authors: Agelos Kratimenos, Yile Hua, Kostas Daniilidis
bullets: Addresses the under-determined nature of reconstructing moving scenes from a single casual video.

Requery, merge, and split operations adapt the number of motions to missed, shared, or distinct movements.
Outperforms mask-based baselines in view synthesis and 3D tracking, while producing competitive unsupervised motion segmentation.

papers.abstract: Post-training large language models (LLMs) for mathematical reasoning often relies on accepted traces whose final answers pass a verifier. For hard math problems, however, such traces can be rare under independent Monte Carlo (MC) sampling. To address this, we propose Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces (DART), a trace-mining method that starts from a rejected trace, decomposes it into reasoning steps, and ranks them by position-weighted uncertainty. It then generates deliberately distinct alternative candidates for highly ranked steps using reference-answer guidance and a meta-thought before completing the resulting traces. On greedy-unsolved DeepMath-103K problems, DART recovers 37% more problems than MC sampling at a matched number of generated traces. Its estimated generation cost per recovered problem is nearly identical, while its cost per accepted trace is 30% lower. Post-training Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on traces mined by DART achieves the highest point estimate in five of six evaluations across MATH-500 and AIME benchmarks. These results demonstrate that revisiting rejected traces with DART can expand problem coverage and provide effective post-training data.
authors: Lukas Aichberger, Adam Golinski, Arno Blaas, Arwen Bradley, Jacob Springer, Mehrdad Farajtabar, Michael Kirchhof, Sinead Williamson
bullets: Hard math problems often have few accepted reasoning traces under independent sampling, limiting post-training data.

papers.abstract: Simulation is essential for marine robotics, yet existing platforms often trade off between visually realistic worlds, high-throughput experimentation, and ocean-condition realism grounded in real data. We present OneOcean, a data-grounded simulation suite and benchmark built around a unified spatiotemporal ocean-environment product that harmonizes bathymetry with data-driven currents and tides, with optional pollution fields for cleanup-related evaluation. On top of this environment representation, OneOcean defines a task ladder spanning navigation and station-keeping under currents, waypoint and route following, depth-profile tracking, area scanning, pipeline inspection, and multi-agent coordination, including formation transit, fish protection and patrol (herding), and surface pollution localization, containment, and cleanup. The suite supports multi-agent settings with 2-10 vehicles. Our simulator supports three to six Degrees of Freedom (DoF) and produces standardized metrics and reproducible run manifests, enabling consistent aggregation across tasks, difficulties, and scaling settings. Experiments across dataset variants and scenes systematically stress planning and control under data-grounded disturbances and reveal trade-offs among heuristic baselines, Behavior Cloning (BC), and a Large Language Model (LLM)-based planner.
authors: Shuaijun Liu, Qifu Wen, Xingwei Chen, Xinwen Hu, Feiyang You, Sijia Chen, Ningxin Su
bullets: Combines bathymetry with data-driven currents and tides, with optional pollution fields.
Provides a task ladder from station-keeping and route following to inspection, multi-agent coordination, and cleanup.
Supports 2–10 vehicles and vehicle models with three to six degrees of freedom.
Uses standardized metrics and reproducible run manifests across tasks, difficulty levels, and scaling settings.
Experiments compare heuristic, Behavior Cloning, and LLM-based planning under data-grounded disturbances, exposing planning–control trade-offs.

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers boost expressivity by reusing shared layers across loops, yet at the cost of efficiency. Pushing their expressivity-efficiency frontier requires rethinking the core mechanism connecting adjacent loops: What should be passed as a Transformer loops? We introduce Mixture-of-Loops Transformer (MoLT), whose Mixture-of-Loops Attention (MoLA) uses keys and values (KV) as memory for selective reuse across depths and loops. Under loop residual, MoLT-R retains the residual stream and reads local KV across loops for expressivity. Under loop KV, MoLT-KV instead restarts from embeddings and reads current-loop local KV with preceding-loop memory KV at earlier positions for efficiency. MoLT-KV eliminates same-position cross-loop dependence and, paired with loop forcing for parallel training, unlocks single-traversal Mixture-of-Loops (MoL) decoding beyond the training loop horizon. To balance efficiency and quality, we introduce U-shaped MoLT (U-MoLT), which separates memory construction from prediction readout and skips unused decoder traversals without changing predictions. In 400B-token pretraining, U-MoLT outperforms OLMo3 across 700M/1.5B dense and 3B MoE models, achieving 1.7x validation cross-entropy (CE) token efficiency at 700M while improving 3B MoE 10-domain perplexity by 0.75 and 10-task accuracy by 2.1 percentage points. In 100B-token continued pretraining of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base, our U-MoLT adaptation lowers CE on all 11 domains over the matched baseline with 1.4x mean token efficiency. At inference, U-MoLT with MoL-Hybrid-2 matches non-looped OLMo3 latency at 996.6 vs. 1,000.6 ms on S-size (~113M) models. Code is available at https://github.com/hustvl/MoLT
authors: Lianghui Zhu, Shijie Wang, Xinggang Wang, Jinze Bai, Bo Wang, Xiang Bai
bullets: Introduces Mixture-of-Loops Attention, which uses keys and values as reusable memory across depths and loops.
MoLT-KV removes same-position cross-loop dependence and supports single-traversal decoding beyond the training loop horizon through loop forcing.
U-MoLT separates memory construction from prediction readout, skipping unnecessary decoder traversals without changing predictions.
Across multiple model scales and settings, U-MoLT improves token efficiency, perplexity, and task accuracy while matching non-looped inference latency in one evaluation.

papers.selection_reason: Looped transformer with KV memory reuse directly targets LLM architecture efficiency and inference memory.
papers.title: Mixture-of-Loops Transformer
papers.tldr: MoLT improves the efficiency–expressivity trade-off of looped Transformers by selectively reusing key-value memories across loops, enabling efficient training and decoding without sacrificing quality.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) enable robots to reason about semantic and spatio-temporal context, verify task-relevant objects, and guide sensing and navigation. Persistent memory can reduce redundant search for field robots, but when should a memory continue to guide behavior? Repeated misses may suggest that a memory is stale. Our experiments show why this evidence can remain ambiguous under VLM-based perception. Using a Boston Dynamics Spot with four fixed cameras and a persistent spatio-temporal visual memory, we measure negative-verification behavior across targets, viewpoints, language queries, and repeated revisits. False-negative rates vary substantially across objects, nearby revisits often reproduce the same detector outcome, and some matched target-present and target-removed experiments yield identical miss histories. This ambiguity persists under changed observation geometry, identity-preserving query reformulation, and conditioning on a previously verified target image. These findings raise two questions: is the object still there, and is this memory still useful for navigation? We introduce a dependence-aware, reversible memory-update mechanism that avoids double-counting correlated misses and stops using unsupported memories as direct navigation goals without claiming that the object is absent. Later positive evidence can restore a memory's use for navigation. One resident onboard VLM is shared across memory verification, semantic frontier reasoning, and in-motion perception. In three matched real-robot decision contexts, an episode-local baseline selected a stale memory as its navigation objective in every case, whereas our method selected semantic frontiers in all three. A complementary trial re-verified the target during motion and promoted fresh memory. These results support revising memory actionability rather than interpreting failed detection as object absence.
authors: Sumukh Shrote, Shenbagaraj Kannapiran, Eric Eaton, Camillo Jose Taylor
bullets: VLM-based negative detections are ambiguous: false-negative rates vary, repeated nearby views can reproduce misses, and target-present and target-removed scenes may look identical.
The proposed dependence-aware, reversible updates avoid double-counting correlated misses and stop unsupported memories from serving as direct navigation goals.
Semantic frontiers become alternatives when memory confidence is insufficient; later positive evidence can restore navigation use.
On a Spot robot in three matched decision contexts, the baseline chose a stale memory every time, while the proposed method chose semantic frontiers in all three.
A motion-time recheck demonstrated that fresh positive evidence can promote memory again.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Persistent semantic-navigation system architecture. The robot combines four fixed cameras, persistent CLIP/FAISS visual memory, semantic frontier exploration, and a shared resident VLM. Historical observations are retrieved and strictly reverified before they can influence navigation. Negative evidence updates memory actionability from VERIFIED ACTIVE to SUSPECT and eventually DORMANT UNTRUSTED, while later strict positive evidence can restore navigation authority. When no trusted memory remains, the system selects a semantic frontier instead. A single resident Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct instance is shared across target verification, memory verification, frontier reasoning, and asynchronous perception during motion.

Fig. 1. Memory is not ground truth. A previously verified object can fail current VLM verification either because the environment has changed or because perception has failed. An episode-local policy forgets earlier failed verification and can repeatedly revisit the same remembered location. Our method instead revises the memory’s navigation authority without asserting that the object is absent, redirects search toward a semantically selected frontier, and preserves the memory for future positive evidence. The inset in (c) shows frontier candidates in the deployed 2-D navigation representation.

Fig. 3. Repeated VLM misses are redundant and can be ambiguous with respect to physical object state. In E2, Spot repeatedly leaves and returns to human-visible target viewpoints; nearby revisits frequently preserve the previous verifier outcome, with 90.0% of adjacent observations producing the same result. In E3, the corresponding objects are physically removed and the same anchor regions are revisited. For the three blue-chair anchors C1-C3, both target-present and target-removed conditions produce the identical six-observation history MMMMMM. Thus, the deployed detector observations alone cannot distinguish the two physical states.

papers.selection_reason: Persistent spatio-temporal memory for semantic navigation with VLM-based verification, fitting embodied memory and vision-language navigation.
papers.title: Memory Is Not Ground Truth: Revising Navigation Authority under Unreliable VLM Evidence for Persistent Semantic Navigation
papers.tldr: Robots should reduce a memory’s navigation authority after correlated detection failures without assuming the remembered object is absent.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) are capable low-level controllers, but they tie where objects go to the layouts they were trained on: when objects are moved or obstacles block the way, they carry them to the wrong place or into collisions. Fine-tuning on new layouts needs robot data for each one and erodes skills the model already has. We introduce Cairn, which keeps the VLA frozen and steers it at test time along learned 3D trajectories of the object in its gripper. A small prior reads point clouds of the scene and the held object, along with its pose when grasped and the instruction, and samples SE(3) trajectories up to its release that lead it around obstacles and turn it to fit through gaps. The prior and the VLA form the two levels of a hierarchical planner in which feedback runs both ways: the VLA's intended motion chooses and reshapes the trajectories, and the chosen one guides the VLA's denoising. Its predicted actions, mapped to the held object's poses through the grasp, are pulled toward the next waypoint, while the VLA's weights stay untouched. Across 1,941 held-out LIBERO scenes with displaced objects and obstacles, Cairn raises the success rate of a frozen {\pi}0.5 from 24.5% to 95.1%, above that of a {\pi}0.5 fine-tuned on our training layouts, without hurting standard LIBERO. On the third-party LIBERO-PRO benchmark, it raises success from 27.3% to 38.0%, and from 54.4% to 81.1% on the episodes it steers. On a real Franka, with a prior trained purely in simulation, it guides the frozen DROID {\pi}0.5 around an obstacle and to a placement at the limit of the arm's reach, where it otherwise fails. All code, models and data will be made public.
authors: Agelos Kratimenos, Kostas Daniilidis, Evangelos Chatzipantazis
bullets: Addresses VLA failures when object locations differ from training layouts or obstacles block direct motion.
Uses a scene-and-object point-cloud prior conditioned on the grasp pose and instruction to sample obstacle-avoiding SE(3) trajectories through release.
Hierarchically couples the prior and frozen VLA: the VLA shapes trajectory selection, while trajectory waypoints guide action denoising.
Improves frozen π0.5 success from 24.5% to 95.1% across 1,941 held-out LIBERO scenes, without hurting standard LIBERO performance.

Also improves results on LIBERO-PRO and demonstrates simulated-prior guidance on a real Franka robot; scope includes scenarios where object motion and placement are constrained by obstacles or reachability.

papers.title: Cairn: Object-Centric 3D Trajectory Priors for Steering Frozen VLAs
papers.tldr: Cairn steers frozen vision-language-action models through displaced-object and obstacle scenarios using learned object-centric 3D trajectory priors, substantially improving manipulation success without fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: While video diffusion models have grown faster and increasingly streamable, the video VAE remains a primary latency bottleneck across interactive generation and editing pipelines. Existing VAEs and their acceleration methods rely mainly on heavy convolutions or full frame attention, and most focus only on decoding, leaving encoding costly for streaming conditional generation and editing. This raises a natural question: Do video VAE encoding and decoding actually require such global spatiotemporal modeling? By analyzing the effective receptive fields of pretrained video VAEs, we find that both encoding and decoding a patch rely almost entirely on its spatial and temporal neighbors. To exploit this strong locality, we introduce LiveVAE, a streaming encoder and decoder built on causal window attention, which cuts per frame compute while keeping the temporal KV cache bounded for streaming. Decoupled encoder/decoder distillation followed by joint finetuning preserves the pretrained latent space, making LiveVAE a drop-in replacement for the original VAE. On MiniMax-H3, LiveVAE achieves 5.2-6.2x faster encoding and 3.0-3.3x faster decoding than the official VAE with higher PSNR. Paired with our dedicated inference infrastructure, LiveVAE pushes the speedup to 13.4x with almost no quality loss. Code and models will be released.
authors: Jiachen An, Sijie Zhao, Le Li, Hongyu Liu, Zhiyuan Li, Tianyu Yang, Xiaoyu Kong, Xunliang Cai, Yong Zhang, Chi-Man Pun, Xiaoming Wei, Xiaodong Cun
bullets: Existing video VAEs are latency bottlenecks, especially for encoding, due to heavy convolutions or global spatiotemporal attention.
Effective receptive-field analysis shows that VAE patches depend mainly on nearby spatial and temporal neighbors.
Causal window attention reduces per-frame computation and keeps the temporal KV cache bounded for streaming.
Decoupled encoder/decoder distillation and joint finetuning enable drop-in replacement with the original VAE.
On MiniMax-H3, LiveVAE delivers 5.2–6.2× faster encoding and 3.0–3.3× faster decoding with higher PSNR; infrastructure raises speedup to 13.4× with nearly no quality loss.

papers.abstract: Real-time autoregressive video generators stream minutes of video and accept new prompts on the fly, but struggle to keep people, objects, and places consistent over a long interactive story. Agent systems provide such memory for offline multi-shot generation, yet they read the whole script in advance, plan each shot before generating it, and regenerate failed shots, which a live stream does not allow. We present Agentic LongLive, an asynchronous agentic memory for long video generation. A memory agent on separate GPUs reads only the prompts revealed so far, never the generated video, and keeps a text state and evolving images for every person, object, and scene. From this entity memory it composes a global image and a per-shot memory image, which an auxiliary GPU prefills into the generator's attention sink before the next shot starts, and writes entity cards for the prompts that name them, so the video never waits for memory and video errors are not written back. A small language model, trained with reinforcement learning and an image reward calibrated using downstream video outcomes, decides what to remember before the next prompt is known. On LongStory-Online, a new benchmark of 25 stories (857 shots) revealed one shot at a time, Agentic LongLive improves persistent-state accuracy of LongLive-2.0, its base generator, by 26.3 points, protagonist identity by 44.9, and revisited-place consistency by 40.4, at about 1% extra generation time on H100. The full system streams faster than real time on one 8xB200 node with the generator in BF16 (34.3 FPS), keeps image quality stable over 14-minute stories, and improves identity on two MiniMax-H3 generators, one of which, LongLive-H3, also runs in real time with it. To our knowledge, it is the first real-time video generator with text and image memory kept by an LLM agent.
authors: Shaoteng Liu, Shuai Yang, Wei Huang, Luozhou Wang, Song Han, Yukang Chen
bullets: Targets identity and scene consistency in interactive, multi-minute video where future prompts and generated video are unavailable in advance.
A memory agent processes only revealed prompts, maintains entity and scene state, and prepares global and per-shot memory images before generation.
An RL-trained language model selects what to remember using an image reward calibrated to downstream video quality.
On LongStory-Online, it improves persistent-state accuracy by 26.3 points, protagonist identity by 44.9, and revisited-place consistency by 40.4.
Adds about 1% generation time, supports real-time streaming, and maintains image quality over 14-minute stories.

papers.abstract: Processing long videos with multimodal large language models (MLLMs) is prohibitively expensive, making informative frame selection essential for accurate video understanding. The default uniform sampling often misses task-relevant keyframes, while recent training-free selectors instead pick frames by how well each one matches the question under an image-text alignment (ITA) score. However, we show that ITA signals correspond poorly with the MLLM's true needs: their rankings correlate weakly with downstream accuracy and are even negatively correlated on over 40% of questions, whereas the MLLM's internal yes/no judgment yields a much stronger signal. We present ProbFaS, a training- and label-free probabilistic pipeline that fuses both signals for key frame selection. ProbFaS treats dense ITA scores as cheap, biased measurements and sparse MLLM judgments as accurate, costly ones, unifying them via co-kriging, a multi-fidelity Gaussian process, to calibrate relevance across all frames. A temporal determinantal point process then selects frames capturing relevance peaks while preserving temporal coverage. Across Video-MME, MLVU and LongVideoBench, ProbFaS is the most accurate among fourteen state-of-the-art training-free selectors and uniform sampling in 13 of 15 settings (8-128 frames), outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 3.1 percentage points. On MLVU and LongVideoBench, 32 ProbFaS frames match or surpass the top baseline at 128 frames and uniform sampling with up to 768 frames.
authors: Tianru Zhang, Mayank Nautiyal, Hugo Eidmann, Prashant Singh, Ekta Vats
bullets: Uniform sampling can miss keyframes, while image-text alignment rankings often poorly reflect the MLLM’s actual needs.
The training- and label-free method fuses dense ITA scores with sparse, more accurate MLLM yes/no judgments using co-kriging.
A temporal determinantal point process selects relevance peaks while maintaining temporal coverage.
Across Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench, ProbFaS leads training-free selectors and uniform sampling in 13 of 15 settings.
Using 32 frames, it matches or surpasses top-baseline performance obtained with 128 frames on MLVU and LongVideoBench.

papers.abstract: How an object deforms when it hits the ground reveals what it is made of. From a single real video of a drop, we estimate a deformable object's density-normalized stiffness $E/\rho$, and its yield stress $\sigma_Y/\rho$ when the impact causes plastic deformation, with a feed-forward predictor trained only in simulation. Real videos carry no material labels, so such predictors are developed and validated on synthetic data alone. We show that synthetic validation ranks their geometric inputs in the wrong order. Material acts through 3D deformation, and tracklets lifted to 3D with estimated depth are indeed the most accurate input in simulation. However, on real drops they are the least accurate, and better depth does not repair them: the failure persists with simulator depth in training, LiDAR depth at test time, and exact depth on rendered replays of the real drops. Short 2D optical-flow tracklets do the opposite: they improve nothing in simulation, yet they transfer best. Material is therefore better read from what perception measures consistently in both domains than from what is most informative in simulation. Our predictor, PhysReader, reads the video and 2D tracklets and learns the lift to 3D in simulation by matching a teacher that sees exact 3D deformation. To measure transfer, we introduce PhysReader-Real: 16 everyday objects dropped five times each, with reference materials fit jointly to each object's drops and checked against tensile tests. On PhysReader-Real, PhysReader is closer to the reference materials than every other input and baseline. The one exception is a per-scene optimizer started from PhysReader's prediction, which ends slightly closer but takes 49 minutes per video instead of 12 seconds.
authors: Ziyue Peng, Yanxi Hu, Junyoung Kim, Andrew Chen, Jin Yang, Chandrajit L. Bajaj, Etienne Vouga, William T. Freeman, Qixing Huang, Brandon Y. Feng
bullets: The task is to estimate density-normalized stiffness and, for plastic impacts, yield stress from how an object deforms when dropped.
Synthetic experiments misleadingly favor 3D tracklets, while real-world transfer favors short 2D optical-flow tracklets.
PhysReader learns to infer 3D deformation from video and 2D tracks by matching a teacher trained with exact simulated 3D deformation.
On 16 everyday objects dropped five times each, PhysReader was closer to reference materials than other inputs and baselines.
A scene optimizer improved accuracy slightly but required 49 minutes per video versus 12 seconds for PhysReader.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of PhysReader. Training in simulation (left): ❶ a teacher encodes exact 3D deformation, available only in simulation, into a feature fT , from which material heads predict E/ρ and σY /ρ (loss ℓ against the GT material). ❷ PhysReader sees only inputs that real video also provides: the RGB clip (V-JEPA 2 with LoRA), 2D optical-flow tracklets, and temporal and scale context. It maps them to f̂T and is trained to match fT (loss d) and the material through a frozen copy of the teacher’s heads (ℓ; Eq. 4). Inference in real (right): PhysReader alone predicts the material, without depth. For evaluation, the prediction re-simulates the drop with density ρ and Poisson’s ratio ν, and we report the replay loss and the parameter distance to the plausible region of reference materials (Sec. 4).

Figure 4. Simulation ranks the inputs backwards: stiffness error on synthetic validation and on real drops. Left: arrows connect each model with 2D flow tracklets to the same model with tracklets lifted to 3D (tracklets only, RGB + tracklets, and the two students). Every arrow leads to a lower error in simulation and a higher error on real videos. The feed-forward baselines (gray) are less accurate than PhysReader in both. Right: lifted tracklets, under each geometry condition of Table S7, beat 2D flow tracklets in simulation and lose to them on real videos.

Figure 3. PhysReader-Real. Left: the 16 objects, each dropped five times in different orientations. Right: for the 8 objects we cut specimens from, the reference stiffness fit jointly to the five drops (dot) and its plausible region (blue) against the measured stiffness of tensile specimens (gray).

Real: distance to the plausible region, relative increases in total and deformation replay loss, and direct simulation difference (Sec. 4).

Synthetic rows use the 10,202 validation videos on which every row is defined; real rows use the 80 PhysReader-Real drops, scored against the reference materials. Exact geometry comes from the simulator; flow tracks from WAFT [76]; estimated depth from 4RC [51].

papers.title: What a Drop Reveals: Sim-to-Real Material Estimation for Deformable Objects from Video

papers.abstract: Dexterity is, at its core, finger-level control, yet existing dexterous manipulation and human-object interaction (HOI) generation methods rarely let one specify how an interaction is performed: five-fingered hands are often reduced to grippers, or finger usage is copied from individual human demonstrations. We present FineDex, a framework that makes finger-level intent both expressible and executable. FineDex learns coordinated human body, hand, and object motions that follow fine-grained instructions on hand selection, individual fingers, and contacts with articulated objects. To bridge generation and execution, FineDex leverages generated interactions as actionable priors for an agent that discovers physically feasible contact strategies through practice in a physics-based digital twin. By adapting at test time without per-instance retraining, FineDex generalizes across fine-grained instructions and object configurations. Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art HOI generation quality and fine-grained controllability, substantial improvements in dexterous manipulation success, and successful deployment on a real dexterous humanoid robot.
authors: Yujia Zeng, Yuxin Chen, Yuzhen Song, Runhan Huang, Chensheng Peng, Yiyang Shao, Koushil Sreenath, Masayoshi Tomizuka, Yilun Du
bullets: Addresses the lack of explicit control over hand choice, individual fingers, and contacts in existing HOI generation and manipulation methods.
Jointly generates coordinated human body, hand, and articulated-object motions conditioned on fine-grained interaction instructions.
Uses generated interactions as actionable priors for physics-based practice to discover feasible contact strategies.
Adapts at test time across instructions and object configurations without per-instance retraining.
Reports state-of-the-art HOI generation and controllability, improved manipulation success, and real humanoid-robot deployment.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Architecture of the FineDex generator. The generator supports all articulated objects in ARCTIC, integrating language conditioning, articulated object geometry, and anatomical hand features within a diffusion-based framework. A finger-specific adapter injects control signals into anatomical anchor tokens while the pretrained backbone stays frozen. At inference, dual-trajectory sampling edits the commanded fingers while preserving the rest of the motion.

Figure 2. Overview of FineDex. A language-conditioned generator synthesizes fine-grained human–object interactions. The generated interaction x serves as a prior for an agent that proposes contact programs π and refines them through feedback from a physics-based digital twin. The most reliable program, π⋆, is then executed on a dexterous humanoid robot.
Figure 6. Real-world humanoid robot dexterous manipulation. G1 humanoid manipulation with different hand and finger instructions across articulated objects.
Figure 4. Qualitative comparison on ARCTIC. FineDex generates coordinated hand–object motion.

Figure 5. Qualitative comparison of fine-grained control. Top: finger-specific manipulation using different instructed fingers. Bottom: hand selection and designated contact control of an articulated object.

papers.abstract: Visual context is a powerful cue for object recognition: scenes inform what, where, and at what scale objects are likely to appear. Yet over-reliance on context becomes a failure mode when models predict objects based on their typical neighbors rather than the objects' own visual features, which we call typicality bias. While extensively studied in the pre-Transformer era, it has often been assumed that architectural and scale improvements would naturally solve it, and a systematic diagnostic across the modern vision stack remains absent. We provide such a diagnostic framework. We measure typicality bias via normalized pointwise mutual information (NPMI) over object pairs, and introduce STRANGE-Bench (Synthetic Typicality-RANked Grounded Evaluation Benchmark): a photorealistic, layout-controlled benchmark spanning 17 sub-tiers from typical to never-co-occurring object pairs. Across five model families (specialist detectors, open-vocabulary detectors, self-supervised, vision-language, and multimodal large language models) and three recognition tasks (supervised detection, open-vocabulary detection, and classification), the bias is prevalent: gaps of 5-11 p.p. persist when objects appear outside their typical company, and do not consistently shrink with scale. To mitigate it, we turn to data augmentation: existing augmentations are designed for visual diversity, not for breaking co-occurrence shortcuts, and sample from the very distribution that produces typicality bias. We propose Anchor-Atypicality Sampling (AAS), a simple sampling rule for paste-based augmentations that uses the NPMI signal to tilt the training-time co-occurrence distribution toward atypical partners. AAS reduces the typicality gap by up to 1.6 p.p. on natural-image COCO splits and 23.0 p.p. on synthetic STRANGE-Bench across three model families, without sacrificing overall performance.
authors: Siddhartha Gairola, Jiahao Xie, Anna Kukleva, Francesco Locatello, Bernt Schiele
bullets: Introduces a diagnostic framework for measuring typicality bias using normalized pointwise mutual information (NPMI) over object pairs.
Presents STRANGE-Bench, a photorealistic, layout-controlled benchmark with 17 tiers ranging from typical to never-co-occurring object pairs.
Finds persistent 5–11 percentage-point recognition gaps for atypical object contexts across five model families and three tasks; scaling does not consistently resolve the bias.
Proposes Anchor-Atypicality Sampling (AAS), which uses NPMI to pair objects with atypical partners during paste-based augmentation.
AAS reduces the typicality gap by up to 1.6 points on COCO splits and 23.0 points on STRANGE-Bench without sacrificing overall performance.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of the STRANGE-Bench generation pipeline, illustrated with outputs of the actual build. (1) Typicality-based sampling: partners are drawn by their COCO NPMI with the anchor, high for the typical arm and low or never co-occurring for the atypical arm. (2) Layout and caption: a planner places the categories in a layout and writes a caption from it; each category keeps its color in panels 2 and 3. (3) Rendering and annotation: SD 3.5 Large renders the caption up to three times until SAM3 finds every category, and the boxes of the SAM3 masks are the annotations. (4) Audit: Grounding DINO rejects scenes with unintended objects (here, a laptop), and SAM3 and OWLv2 turn the remaining ones into ignore regions or drop the scene. (5) Assembly: typical and atypical sub-tiers at each contextual load k, plus Tnever, form STRANGE-Bench.

Figure 1: Typicality bias across the modern vision stack. Left: Three anchor classes (target object categories we examine): skateboard, dog, and cow, shown in their typical company (top row: with a person, with a frisbee, with a bird) and in atypical surroundings (bottom row: with a cat, with a spoon, with a clock). Right: Each model’s score on the anchor classes in COCO val images where they appear with typical vs. atypical partners (NPMI quintile splits, §3.1). The performance gap ∆ = (Typical – Atypical) persists across all five model families and three tasks we examine, ranging from ∆ = 5.4 p.p. (Co-DINO Swin-L) to ∆ = 11.0 p.p. (OpenCLIP).

Figure 5: Per-tier typicality gap including T6. Fig. 4 with the five-partner tier T6 and an Avg group (each model’s mean over T1 to T6) added. T6 layouts come from a rule-based layout solver, while those of T1 to T5 mostly come from Qwen, so T6 differs from the other tiers in layout source as well as in k.

papers.selection_reason: Diagnostic of typicality bias across vision-language and multimodal LLMs; introduces benchmark and co-occurrence-aware augmentation.
papers.title: Stranger Things: When Objects Appear Without Their Typical Neighbors
papers.tldr: Modern vision models rely on objects’ typical neighbors, but NPMI-guided atypical sampling substantially reduces this context bias without hurting overall performance.

papers.abstract: Cross-modal place recognition (CMPR) matches natural language descriptions against databases of geo-tagged reference images, enabling localization without visual queries. Despite its potential for language-guided navigation, existing vision-language models lag far behind visual place recognition (VPR) baselines, even after task adaptation. Unlike general-purpose text-to-image retrieval, place recognition relies on subtle local cues to distinguish visually similar locations. We therefore hypothesize that a primary bottleneck in CMPR is capturing fine-grained correspondences between image regions and text details, which requires higher visual token granularity, strong text representation capacity, and local cross-modal matching. To address this challenge, we propose CrossPlace, a two-stage CMPR framework. Stage 1 performs global retrieval by pairing a jointly aligned DINOv2-B/14 visual backbone with a progressively fine-tuned BGE-Large text encoder, while Stage 2 refines top candidates using a lightweight token-level cross-attention reranker. Through systematic analysis, we isolate the drivers of retrieval accuracy and show that visual token density provides the largest performance improvement, while text encoder capacity and task fine-tuning offer complementary gains. To evaluate robustness under realistic conditions, we also extend CMPR evaluation to city-scale and severe weather and illumination settings. Across all existing and new benchmarks, CrossPlace achieves double-digit Recall@1 improvements over prior cross-modal methods, closes the gap to unimodal text retrieval, and narrows it to unimodal VPR. Code and benchmarks are available at https://github.com/oferidan1/CrossPlace
authors: Ofer Idan, Dan Badur, Yoli Shavit
bullets: CMPR matches natural-language descriptions to geo-tagged reference images, but trails visual place recognition because subtle local details are difficult to align.
A two-stage pipeline first performs global retrieval with DINOv2-B/14 and a fine-tuned BGE-Large text encoder, then reranks candidates with lightweight token-level cross-attention.
Analysis identifies visual token density as the largest accuracy driver, with text capacity and task fine-tuning providing complementary gains.
Evaluation includes existing benchmarks plus city-scale and severe weather/illumination conditions.
CrossPlace reports double-digit Recall@1 gains over prior cross-modal methods and narrows the gap to unimodal VPR.

figures.caption: Figure 5. Overview of our two-stage pipeline. Stage 1 retrieves a top-K shortlist via cosine similarity between LoRA-tuned BGE and DINOv2 global embeddings. Stage 2 re-ranks the shortlist with a lightweight cross-attention module operating on raw text tokens and image patch tokens from the frozen Stage 1 encoders, bypassing the projection heads, and fuses the local score with the global score.

Figure 3. Cross-modal encoder ablation across AmsterTime, MSLS-val, and Pittsburgh30k. All models (including the CLIP floor baselines) are fine-tuned using LoRA and Multi-Similarity (MS) loss. Visual encoders vary in token granularity and pretraining initialization (CLIP vs. DINOv2). Textual encoders differ by parameter scale and domain fine-tuning. DINOv2-B/14 paired with fine-tuned BGE-Lft achieves top performance across datasets (Ours).

Figure 1. Cross-modal place recognition performance (Recall@1) on the MSLS Val and Pitts30k benchmarks. Bars depict cross-modal models: LaVPR denotes the LaVPR crossmodal model (its best-performing variant, using BLIP). CrossPlace Stage 1 (CP-S1) is our global retrieval model, and CrossPlace Stage 2 (CP-S2) adds cross-attention reranking. Horizontal reference lines contextualize cross-modal retrieval relative to unimodal performance: the dotted cyan line marks unimodal text-to-text retrieval using BGE-Large, while the dashed orange line gives the performance of visual (image-to-image) place recognition using CricaVPR.

Figure 2. Qualitative comparison on an AmsterTime query (“dark double doors... arched windows...”). LaVPR (a) retrieves an incorrect candidate (red), whereas CrossPlace (b) retrieves the correct location (green). Grad-CAM visualizations show that LaVPR activates on unrelated regions (c), while CrossPlace focuses on the architectural landmarks described in the query (d).

Figure 4. Score fusion weight α on Pitts30k-val. Recall@1 peaks at α∗=0.2 (65.0%), outperforming the reranker-only baseline (α=0, 62.9%, dashed line), and declines monotonically toward Stage 1 retrieval at larger α.

Figure 6. Qualitative R@1 comparison between LaVPR and CrossPlace Stage 1 retrieval. For the query text (a), LaVPR (b) retrieves an incorrect place, whereas CrossPlace (c) retrieves the correct location, matching distinctive cues such as the “PETRUS CLOPPENBORG” signage.

Figure 7. Qualitative R@1 comparison between LaVPR, CrossPlace Stage 1 retrieval, and CrossPlace Stage 2 re-ranking. For the query text (a), both LaVPR (b) and Stage 1 retrieval (c) return incorrect places, whereas Stage 2 re-ranking (d) recovers the correct location by matching fine-grained cues such as the dark double doors and the arched windows.

Table 2. Cross-modal reranking of top-20 candidates obtained with CrossPlace Stage 1. All methods are evaluated as standalone scores (α=0). Best results per dataset in bold. †Reranks the top-10 candidates only, thus R@10 is omitted.

Table 10. Text-to-text retrieval diagnostic. In the uni-modal rows, both query and database entries are textual descriptions, which removes cross-modal alignment entirely. LoRA adaptation matters more than model size, and the best text-to-text result (BGELarge, LoRA-MS All r=64) serves as the reference for cross-modal (text-to-image) retrieval. Cross-modal scores that exceed this reference are shown in blue. LoRA-MS denotes LoRA fine-tuning with the multi-similarity loss, applied either to the query and value projections (QV) or to all linear layers (All). LLP denotes Learned Language Pooling [13].

papers.selection_reason: Cross-modal place recognition for language-guided localization; fine-grained image-text spatial matching.
papers.title: Towards Closing the Performance Gap in Cross-Modal Place Recognition
papers.tldr: CrossPlace improves cross-modal place recognition by combining high-resolution visual tokens, a stronger text encoder, and token-level reranking to better match fine-grained image–text cues.

papers.abstract: Since vision-language-action (VLA) policies can inherit the slow pace of human demonstrations, accelerating these demonstrations before fine-tuning can lead to faster VLA policies without an additional speed-selection module at deployment. Several offline speedup methods have focused on identifying segments that require less precision and assigning predefined speedup factors to the segments. However, even within a single segment, a speedup factor suitable for steady motion may be too high when precise alignment is required. To this end, this paper presents RePace, an offline reasoning framework that determines how much to accelerate each part of a demonstration. For the same recorded movement, RePace measures how much each candidate speedup factor shortens the sequence and compares the resulting observation-action pairs used for training. Given the task instruction, a pretrained language model uses the visual context and original motion of successive windows to interpret these candidate retiming effects and select a speedup profile for the complete episode. Experimental results demonstrate that RePace outperforms the baselines in overall task execution efficiency on both LIBERO and RoboCasa-Kitchen. On all three tasks with a gripper-equipped Franka Research 3 arm, RePace matches or exceeds the acceleration baselines in success rate and completes successful trials faster.

bullets: Targets slow VLA policies caused by the pace of human demonstrations.
Evaluates multiple speedup factors per successive motion window by comparing their retimed observation-action pairs.
Uses task instructions, visual context, and original motion with a pretrained language model to select an episode-level speed profile.
Outperforms baselines in overall task execution efficiency on LIBERO and RoboCasa-Kitchen.
On three gripper-equipped Franka Research 3 tasks, matches or exceeds baseline success rates while completing successful trials faster.
