papers.selection_reason: Method to speed up demonstrations for VLA policies, directly relevant to embodied AI.
papers.title: RePace: Reasoning about Demonstration Speedup for Faster Vision-Language-Action Policies
papers.tldr: RePace uses language-model reasoning to adaptively speed up different parts of vision-language-action demonstrations, producing faster policies without deployment-time speed selection.

papers.abstract: Vision transformers are strong but costly image encoders for video object segmentation. Training-free token merging cuts compute uniformly across the frame, including on tracked objects. We give a frozen DINOv3 ViT inside a trained Cutie head a training-free focus map: full resolution where the segmenter expects its objects and coarser merging elsewhere. Protecting only the previous frame's mask works on short clips but fails on long videos, where fast motion pushes targets outside the margin and into background merging, locking in loss. Our policy instead takes the union of velocity-shifted and block-matched masks, runs a camera-compensated surprise check, delegates uncertain regions to the compared merger, and falls back to it when all objects are lost. On long videos (LVOS V2 valid, pre-specified protocol, three ViT-S seeds), it beats ALGM 0.98 by +2.76 J&F (95% object CI [+1.22,+4.44]; video-cluster [+0.99,+4.52]) at 16% fewer counted encoder FLOPs (0.385 vs. 0.459), sitting 1.0 J&F point below the dense-encoder baseline; at ViT-B the gain over ALGM 0.95 is +3.89 [+2.03,+5.87]. On DAVIS 2017 val it stays within -0.19 J&F of the dense encoder at ViT-S (-0.12 at ViT-B). Controls qualify the result: protecting only the previous mask under ALGM matches or exceeds accuracy at higher FLOPs (0.486), so expectation and surprise mainly reduce counted encoder compute. Practically, lower counted encoder compute did not reduce startup-inclusive mean Cutie step time on a 12-video LVOS sample (3%-8% lower in steady state; an equally engineered ALGM is faster at ViT-S and ViT-B). Section 5.2 separately examines a Cutie permanent-memory schedule and its latency and memory trade-offs. Code: https://github.com/boletoms/focused-cv
authors: Harsha Karipineni, Rajesh Reddy Chintha
bullets: Addresses object loss in long videos when uniform token merging accidentally coarsens fast-moving targets.
Uses velocity-shifted and block-matched mask unions, camera-compensated surprise checks, uncertainty delegation, and an all-objects-lost fallback.
On LVOS V2, improves J&F over ALGM by 2.76 points at ViT-S and 3.89 points at ViT-B, with 16% fewer counted encoder FLOPs at ViT-S.
Remains close to dense-encoder accuracy on DAVIS 2017 validation, within 0.19 J&F points at ViT-S.
Reduced counted encoder FLOPs did not translate into lower startup-inclusive mean Cutie step time; latency depends on implementation and regime.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free focus-map token merging for efficient long-video object segmentation.
papers.title: Focus Only on What's Important: Training-Free Focus Maps for Frozen Vision Transformers in Long-Video Object Segmentation
papers.tldr: A training-free focus-map policy for frozen ViTs preserves high-resolution processing around likely objects, improving long-video segmentation accuracy while reducing counted encoder FLOPs, though not necessarily end-to-end latency.

papers.abstract: We introduce BOP-Refer, the first benchmark for monocular 3D and 2D grounding of everyday and industrial objects sourced from 9 diverse BOP datasets. We pair images from these datasets with VLM-generated and human-verified referring expressions, and derive accurate ground-truth 3D and 2D bounding boxes of the referred objects from their 3D models and 6DoF pose annotations. Our systematic evaluation of 17 frontier VLMs across the major proprietary and open-weight families (Gemini, GPT, Claude, Qwen, Gemma) shows that the best model, Gemini 4 Carbon, reaches 72.6% AP_IoU2D in 2D but only 12.4% AP_IoU3D in 3D, despite the more lenient IoU thresholds in 3D. The predicted 3D boxes are usually centered on the target objects in the image but often off in depth by more than the object's size, suggesting that metric scale estimation, which needs reliable object size priors, is currently by far the main source of error.
authors: Tomas Hodan, Vineet Bhat, Martin Sundermeyer, Jonathan Tremblay, Yash Patel, M\'ed\'eric Fourmy, Stephen Tyree, Junwen Huang, Varun Burde, Martin C\'ifka, Eric Brachmann, Vincent Lepetit, Stan Birchfield, Jiri Matas, Carsten Rother
bullets: Introduces a benchmark covering everyday and industrial objects from 9 diverse BOP datasets.
Pairs images with VLM-generated, human-verified referring expressions and derives 2D/3D ground-truth boxes from object models and 6DoF poses.
Evaluates 17 proprietary and open-weight VLMs across Gemini, GPT, Claude, Qwen, and Gemma families.
The best reported model achieves 72.6% 2D AP but only 12.4% 3D AP, even with more lenient 3D IoU thresholds.
3D predictions are generally image-centered but often have large depth errors, indicating metric scale and object-size priors as the main limitation.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for 3D object grounding, directly relevant to spatial intelligence in multimodal models.
papers.title: BOP-Refer: Benchmark for Monocular 3D and 2D Object Grounding
papers.tldr: BOP-Refer benchmarks monocular 2D and 3D object grounding and finds that VLMs localize objects well in images but struggle substantially with metric-depth estimation.

papers.abstract: Spike cameras capture high-speed motion through an integrate-and-fire mechanism, providing fine-grained temporal observations without exposure blur. However, their binary streams encode accumulated illumination rather than instantaneous intensity, making reliable motion estimation challenging. Existing spike-based methods exploit temporal aggregation to construct motion representations, but this process may weaken fine-grained firing patterns. Meanwhile, correlation-based estimators often rely on learned matching features without explicitly characterizing the spatial distribution and ambiguity of candidate displacements. To address these challenges, we propose TIDE-Flow, a spike-based optical flow estimation framework that jointly exploits Temporal Integration Evidence (TIE) and Displacement Evidence Encoding (DEE). TIE combines raw spike patterns, multi-scale firing statistics, temporal moments, and boundary-aware interval cues, preserving complementary temporal information before spatial feature compression. DEE further integrates structured candidate-grid features with explicit displacement statistics to characterize matching geometry and competing correspondences. Both components are incorporated into a difference-correlation recurrent refinement framework, enabling effective temporal motion modeling and correspondence estimation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of TIDE-Flow, with controlled ablations validating the contributions of temporal and displacement evidence modeling.
authors: Hanwen Liang, Wenxuan Liu, Wenxin Huang, Jingling Yuan, Zhaofei Yu, Xian Zhong, Tiejun Huang
bullets: Spike cameras provide blur-free temporal observations, but binary accumulated-illumination streams make motion estimation difficult.
Temporal Integration Evidence (TIE) combines raw spikes, multi-scale firing statistics, temporal moments, and boundary-aware interval cues.
Displacement Evidence Encoding (DEE) models candidate-grid structure, displacement statistics, and correspondence ambiguity.
Both components are integrated into a difference-correlation recurrent refinement framework for temporal motion modeling and flow estimation.
Experiments and controlled ablations demonstrate the effectiveness of the temporal and displacement evidence designs.

papers.abstract: Real-to-simulation transfer, which builds simulations from real-world observations, has long been studied in research and industry. Recently, coding agents have become capable of generating simulation programs from video recordings, and several benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate them. However, each individual benchmark defines its own inputs, deliverables, and scoring pipeline. This leads to $N \times M$ integrations when evaluating $N$ methods on $M$ benchmarks. To this end, we present Real2SimLab, a unified platform for real-to-simulation transfer. It evaluates a method by running its written program and scoring the output simulation with the original scorer of each benchmark. Moreover, Real2SimLab provides a pipeline to create training data and reward annotations for real-to-simulation methods. Our pipeline carefully avoids data contamination by filtering out the video recordings that exist in benchmarks. For each video recording, a program is first produced, and then our pipeline computes its reward with the same code that Real2SimLab uses for evaluation. So far, it supports 47 coding agents and 5 non-agent methods on 6 benchmarks. Both the platform and Awesome-Real2Sim, our research map of nearly 300 real-to-simulation papers, are open source, and we invite the Real2SimHub community to build them together.
authors: Yongchang Zhang, Jie Huang, Yunhe Ni, Ningyu Zhou, Guangyu Zhao, Ruixun Liu, Rui Huang, Yidi Wu, TianZe Zhang, Zixiang Jiang, Xiang Li, Kevin Shen, Yiwu Zhong
bullets: Addresses fragmented benchmark interfaces that otherwise require separate integrations for every method–benchmark pair.
Runs each method’s generated program and scores its simulation using each benchmark’s original evaluator.
Provides contamination-aware pipelines for generating programs and reward annotations from non-benchmark videos.
Currently supports 47 coding agents, 5 non-agent methods, and 6 benchmarks.
Open-sources the platform and Awesome-Real2Sim, a research map covering nearly 300 papers.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of this work. (1) The new paradigm: a coding agent turns a recording of a real event into a program that simulates it. Every simulation frame here is rendered by re-running a program that the Codex agent wrote for the input video recording.(2) Real2SimLab runs the program that a method writes, scores its output with the scorer of the benchmark, and creates training data and reward annotations. (3) Awesome-Real2Sim organizes nearly 300 real-to-simulation papers according to what they deliver or ask for.

Figure 6: The training data pipeline. (1) Training tasks come from recordings of users, from a released training split when a benchmark has one, or from our generator of synthetic scenes, and they use the format of evaluation tasks. (2) The overlap check removes every task that shows the recording of an evaluation task, by comparing thumbnails of the frames in which something moves, at every time offset. In the example, a PhysCodeGym clip, treated here as a candidate for training, contains the hidden test video of a Physics-IQ evaluation task, starting 3 s into the clip. (3) The dataset holds the tasks and the runs on them, and each run holds a program, its reward, and the log of the agent. (4) A trainer of the user’s choice trains a method offline on the dataset, or online with rewards from the evaluation code. (5) Real2SimLab evaluates the trained method as in Section 3, but skips the evaluation tasks that overlap its training tasks. Real2SimLab provides all steps but the trainer; we have not yet trained a model with them.

Figure 4: Architecture of Real2SimLab. A method-wise adapter (left) passes the visible part of a task to a method and collects its deliverable, and a benchmark-wise adapter (right) turns the data of a benchmark into tasks. In between (center), Real2SimLab fixes one task format. It builds each deliverable in a sandbox, freezes it, re-runs it offline, and scores it with the protocol of the benchmark. All results are stored in one record format and reported in one scorecard. Training tasks use the same format as evaluation tasks, and their rewards are computed by the scoring code of evaluation (Section 5).

Figure 3: A roadmap of real-to-simulation, from Awesome-Real2Sim. Selected methods (gray) and benchmarks (violet) are placed by the month of their first arXiv version (for Galileo, which has none, by the month of its conference). Each card names the institution and what the paper delivers or asks for. The methods deliver many kinds of results, such as physical twins (fitted or assigned), simulation-ready assets, scene twins, learned simulators, and simulation programs. One recent trend is that coding agents write simulation programs, and recent benchmarks such as 4DCodeBench, PhysCodeGym, and Video2World are proposed to evaluate these agents.

Figure 5: The benchmarks that Real2SimLab adapts so far. Each card shows what a method sees, what it delivers, and how the deliverable is scored. Of the 6 existing benchmarks, 5 keep their official scorers, while IRIS (marked Lab) and our synthetic suite (marked exact truth) use the reproduction skill of Real2SimLab. New benchmarks and recordings of users are added by converting them into tasks of the shared format (Section 3.1).

Figure 2: Why a shared platform helps. (a) Without a shared platform, benchmarks differ in what they provide to a method, what they ask the method to deliver, and how they score the output. Every pair of a method and a benchmark thus requires its own adapter to run. (b) Real2SimLab makes the delivered program into the interface between methods and benchmarks. So each method and each benchmark is integrated only once.

Table 1: Real2SimLab among the evaluation platforms of other fields. Each platform contributes to a research field by offering a shared way to evaluate many methods or systems. Real2SimLab aims to play this role for real-to-simulation, where the method to be tested delivers a simulation program.

papers.selection_reason: Unified platform for real-to-simulation transfer and simulation generation from video, relevant to embodied AI and world-model evaluation infrastructure.
papers.title: Real2SimLab: A Unified Platform for Real-to-Simulation Transfer
papers.tldr: Real2SimLab unifies evaluation and training-data generation for methods that convert real-world videos into executable simulations.

papers.abstract: We consider the problem of constructing knowledge bases for applications based on large language models, in which the structure of a knowledge base determines how an application can retrieve and connect the information needed to answer a question. We study Self-Structuring Learning, a setting in which questions and expected answers guide the construction of a persistent knowledge base whose editable structure can be a graph schema or the organization of linked knowledge documents. We propose Knowledge-Base Gradient Descent, which diagnoses discrepancies between expected answers and responses obtained through the current knowledge base. At each round, the method proposes a structural edit, rebuilds the knowledge base, and adopts the edit when the learning loss decreases. The retained structure is evaluated on other questions about the same sources. By randomizing over candidate edits, we express the loss change of an edit as a derivative with respect to the probability of selecting it, and we evaluate joint edits as single candidates because their changes interact. Schema Descent instantiates the method for graph schemas. In experiments on large documents, each a bundle of research papers, the updated knowledge cards and graph schemas obtain higher mean Answer F1 on held-out generated questions than their initial structures, with schema gains in every document. On human questions, mean F1 rises for schemas and falls for cards: the updated structures serve the kind of question they were learned from.
authors: Masahiro Kato
bullets: Targets self-structuring knowledge bases whose organization controls information retrieval and connections.
Diagnoses answer discrepancies, proposes structural edits, rebuilds the knowledge base, and retains edits that reduce learning loss.
Models candidate-edit loss changes via selection probabilities and evaluates interacting edits jointly.
On document-based experiments, updated cards and graph schemas improved mean Answer F1 on held-out generated questions.
Performance on human questions improved for schemas but declined for cards, indicating question-type-specific effects.

papers.abstract: We study risk-sensitive reinforcement learning in finite discounted infinite-horizon Markov Decision Processes with recursive entropic risk measures (ERM), parameterized by $\beta\neq 0$. We consider both risk-averse ($\beta>0$) and risk-seeking ($\beta<0$) settings. We consider the offline RL setting, where the agent is provided with a fixed dataset and wishes to learn a near-optimal policy using this dataset. We introduce a model-based algorithm, called ERM Value Iteration Lower Confidence Bound (ERM-VI-LCB) and derive a PAC-type bound on its sample complexity. We also establish a corresponding lower bound, demonstrating that exponential dependence on $|\beta|/(1-\gamma)$ asserted by the upper bound is unavoidable in the worst case. The presented bounds provide the first rigorous sample complexity guarantees for offline RL under recursive ERM across both risk-averse and risk-seeking regimes.
authors: Amirparsa Bahrami, Oliver Mortensen, Mohammad Sadegh Talebi
bullets: Studies finite discounted infinite-horizon MDPs under recursive entropic risk measures with parameter β ≠ 0.
Introduces the model-based ERM-VI-LCB algorithm for learning near-optimal policies from a fixed offline dataset.
Derives a PAC-type sample-complexity upper bound and a corresponding lower bound.
Shows that worst-case exponential dependence on |β|/(1−γ) is unavoidable.
Provides the first rigorous offline RL guarantees for recursive entropic risk across both risk regimes.
papers.selection_reason: Offline risk-sensitive RL with sample-complexity guarantees is transferable to safe robot policy learning from fixed datasets.
papers.title: Provably Efficient Offline Discounted Reinforcement Learning under Recursive Entropic Risk
papers.tldr: This work gives matching-style sample-complexity guarantees for offline RL with recursive entropic risk in both risk-averse and risk-seeking settings.

papers.abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models can generate images that satisfy complex prompts, yet often produce images that omit requested objects, attributes, or relationships. We ask if models can more reliably generate text-aligned images by redistributing probability toward their more successful outcomes. We propose TrailMix, a training-free method that uses the base model's distribution of possible outcomes to adaptively guide generation toward better text alignment. During denoising, TrailMix generates inexpensive lookahead images from parallel trajectories (trails) and scores their alignment with the prompt using an external judge. The resulting distribution of reward scores allows us to estimate how strongly to steer generation toward a desired alignment level. We use these estimates to reweight and resample trajectories, favoring more promising outcomes. Across three text-to-image benchmarks, TrailMix outperforms existing baselines, with particularly strong gains on rare multi-object compositions. We further extend TrailMix to targeted image editing and introduce SEAM-Bench (Semantic Editing and Attribute Maintenance), a systematic benchmark evaluating whether semantic edits preserve other image content. Experiments on SEAM-Bench and existing benchmark PIE-Bench demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach for controlled image editing. Our results show how a model's own possible outcomes can inform reliable and controllable generation.
authors: Abinitha Gourabathina, Sana Tonekaboni, Marzyeh Ghassemi, Akbar Rafiey
bullets: Addresses missing objects, attributes, and relationships in diffusion-generated images.
Generates inexpensive lookahead images from parallel denoising trajectories and scores prompt alignment with an external judge.
Adaptively estimates steering strength, then reweights and resamples trajectories toward better-aligned outcomes.
Outperforms existing baselines across three text-to-image benchmarks, with especially strong gains on rare multi-object compositions.
Extends to image editing and introduces SEAM-Bench to evaluate semantic edits while preserving other content; also performs effectively on SEAM-Bench and PIE-Bench.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free reward-guided diffusion steering for text-to-image alignment; transferable to video and world generative models.
papers.title: Diffusion Steering via Adaptive Reward Estimation and Resampling
papers.tldr: TrailMix improves text-aligned text-to-image generation and controlled editing by using reward-guided lookahead, trajectory reweighting, and resampling without training the base model.

papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation enables the deployment of large language models through smaller student models, but the compression process can introduce regressions in trustworthiness even when downstream performance is preserved. Repairing such failures is challenging because the original distillation corpus is often unavailable, while direct preference optimization may alter capabilities inherited from the teacher. We propose a targeted repair framework based on the proximal Bregman response function (PBRF) that addresses both limitations. We estimate the curvature required for PBRF using a surrogate proxy dataset, removing dependence on the original transfer corpus, and extend the framework to preference-based supervision through an odds-ratio objective. This enables the use of preferred and dispreferred response pairs while constraining changes to the distilled model. Our results show that the proposed approach improves targeted trustworthiness behaviors for both pre-training and post-training models while largely preserving downstream performance, providing a practical alternative to re-distillation or unconstrained preference optimization. Our experiment results show that across different distilled models, the trustworthy regression can be improved by up to 8% with less than 1% decrement in perplexity.
authors: Kumar Shubham, Devendra Vyas, Vidushi Agarwal, Jayin Khanna, Prathosh AP
bullets: Distillation can cause trustworthiness regressions even when downstream capabilities remain intact.
The framework estimates PBRF curvature from a surrogate proxy dataset, avoiding reliance on the original transfer corpus.
An odds-ratio objective incorporates preferred and dispreferred responses while constraining model changes.
It improves targeted trustworthiness behaviors by up to 8% with less than a 1% perplexity increase across distilled models.
The approach applies to both pre-training and post-training models as an alternative to re-distillation or unconstrained preference optimization.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of post-hoc trustworthiness repair. Left: the shipped student is produced by a distillation process the practitioner does not observe; the distillation corpus Ddistill is unavailable after deployment (dashed), and the student inherits the teacher’s task performance but degraded trustworthiness. Right: our method repairs the shipped student without access to Ddistill, using a generic proxy corpus Dproxy to preserve capability and trustworthiness dataset Dtrust to restore the preferential behaviour, yielding a repaired student that improves trustworthiness at negligible cost to distillation performance.

Table 2: Trustworthiness and capability evaluation before and after repair for pre-training models using FineWeb and OpenWebText (OWT) as proxy datasets. Positive values indicate improvement, while negative values indicate degradation.

papers.title: Repairing the Trustworthiness of Distilled Language Models
papers.tldr: A targeted PBRF-based repair method improves trustworthiness in distilled language models without requiring the original distillation data or substantially harming performance.

papers.abstract: World models predict how an environment responds to actions, so that candidate actions can be evaluated before execution. Executed actions, or decisions, taken in this manner are only as reliable as the model's predictive capabilities, and predictions in turn are only reliable within the model's experience. Epistemic uncertainty (EU) is the signal that marks where that experience ends. In this work we offer an extensive empirical study on how training objectives and architectures shape epistemic uncertainty of world models. More precisely, we present a controlled comparison of post-hoc EU (last-layer Laplace and ensembles) between two dominant models of different paradigms: 1) LeWorldModel (LeWM): A joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA), which predicts the next embedding without a decoder, and 2) DreamerV3: A recurrent state-space model (RSSM), which reconstructs the observation from a recurrent latent state. In ten simulated visual-control environments, we follow a controlled state perturbation of the environment state through every stage of the models up to the final EU estimate. We find that the RSSM attenuates the state perturbation through two mechanisms before it reaches an estimator on the predictor feature. Its recurrent update averages over context, so a change in a single frame reaches the state at a fraction of its size and recovers only as the change persists. Its reconstruction objective weights an entity by the pixels it covers, so a small object can be lost due to the training objective. The JEPA has neither mechanism and passes the change through all stages to the uncertainty. We further show that this translates to gaps in five uncertainty related downstream tasks, from unfamiliar-state detection to uncertainty-penalised planning: the RSSM uncertainty misses deviations that its own posterior registers, whereas the JEPA uncertainty reports what its model sees.
authors: Simon Baur, Wojciech Samek, Jackie Ma
bullets: Epistemic uncertainty should indicate when a world model encounters states beyond its experience.
The study compares post-hoc Laplace and ensemble uncertainty in a JEPA model (LeWM) and an RSSM model (DreamerV3).
Across ten simulated visual-control environments, controlled state perturbations are traced through each model to its uncertainty estimate.
RSSM recurrence can dilute transient changes, while its pixel-based reconstruction objective can overlook small objects; JEPA lacks these attenuation mechanisms.

These differences affect downstream tasks including unfamiliar-state detection and uncertainty-penalized planning: RSSM uncertainty can miss deviations recorded by its posterior, whereas JEPA uncertainty better reflects model-visible changes.

papers.selection_reason: Empirical study of epistemic uncertainty in JEPA and RSSM world models, directly relevant to world models.
papers.title: Not all world models can doubt: how training objective and architecture shape epistemic uncertainty in JEPA and RSSM world models
papers.tldr: Training objective and architecture strongly shape whether world models detect epistemic uncertainty: JEPA-based uncertainty preserves state deviations better than RSSM-based uncertainty in the studied tasks.

papers.abstract: Underexposure weakens object details, and overexposure obscures boundaries. Spike cameras encode light into high-frequency binary streams. Long-window spike counts give stable appearance cues, while short observations reveal changes in firing rates from sparse measurements. We propose SPIRE, a sensor-grounded semantic-spiking framework for illumination-robust object detection from a single spike stream. SPIRE builds an appearance view from the full packet through detection-oriented illumination adaptation and constructs a sequence of cumulative views from progressively longer prefixes. Each prefix supplies a rate map, an edge map, and a rate difference that tracks changes as spikes accumulate. At selected scales, ANN features and spike-derived initialization jointly set the initial membrane potentials and firing thresholds, allowing semantic cues to shape the responses during temporal encoding. Local spike-count contrasts supervise both branches during training. The residual between measured and ANN-predicted contrasts combines with the spiking features to produce a bounded correction to the fused feature pyramid. On simulated VOC and COCO, SPIRE-D outperforms the strongest baseline by 4.00-5.50 AP50 points across the four under- and overexposure settings. On real PKU-Vidar-DVS recordings, it achieves 67.07 AP50 and 40.10 AP75. SPIRE-D also uses 50.4% fewer MACs than SPFD.
authors: Hanwen Liang, Wenxuan Liu, Wenxin Huang, Jingling Yuan, Zhaofei Yu, Xian Zhong, Tiejun Huang
bullets: Addresses object-detail loss under underexposure and boundary loss under overexposure.
Builds an appearance view plus progressively accumulated views containing rate, edge, and rate-difference maps.
Uses ANN features and spike-derived signals to initialize membrane potentials and firing thresholds during temporal encoding.
Applies contrast supervision and a residual correction to refine the fused feature pyramid.
Outperforms the strongest baseline by 4.00–5.50 AP50 points in simulated settings, reaches 67.07 AP50 and 40.10 AP75 on real recordings, and uses 50.4% fewer MACs than SPFD.

papers.abstract: Temporal difference (TD) learning is central to reinforcement learning. Many methods use semi-gradient TD, which may diverge, or develop algorithms with mean-squared Bellman or TD-error objectives that are difficult to analyze. Gradient TD algorithms overcome these challenges by using projection of the value function and present convergent off-policy algorithms. However, the algorithm for $\lambda$-return was limited to linear function approximation. Here, we extend the same to non-linear function approximation, which is desirable since many strong modern function approximators are complex and non-linear. Recent works have derived similar algorithms with a generalized projected Bellman error objective. Alternatively, we continue working with the projected Bellman error.
authors: Sujeet Lahane
bullets: Semi-gradient TD methods can diverge, especially in off-policy settings.
Existing convergent gradient TD methods for $\lambda$-returns were limited to linear approximators.
The work develops a gradient TD($\lambda$) algorithm for non-linear function approximation.
It continues to optimize the projected Bellman error rather than adopting a generalized projected Bellman error objective.
The abstract does not report specific experiments or quantitative results.
papers.selection_reason: Gradient TD for nonlinear function approximation is a meaningful RL contribution transferable to robot policy learning.
papers.title: Gradient TD($\lambda$) for Non-Linear Function Approximation
papers.tldr: Extends gradient TD($\lambda$) learning from linear to non-linear function approximation while retaining a projected Bellman error objective.

papers.abstract: LLM routing aims to choose, for each prompt, which model in a portfolio is most likely to answer correctly. This only makes sense when the benchmark contains enough prompt-specific variation for different models to be best on different inputs. On coarse-scored LLM benchmarks, however, many models often tie for the best score, and the single best model may already leave little room for improvement. We therefore propose a routeability-first audit, instantiated as RAP and RouteabilityBench, a runnable claim-verification package. The audit is retrospective: it runs once the benchmark-portfolio score matrix exists and before router comparisons are interpreted as general evidence, rather than certifying a portfolio that has not yet been evaluated. Across four benchmarks and 66 LLMs, generic routing enhancements such as larger embedding sets, dimensionality reduction, selective abstention, clustering, and stronger regressors do not consistently outperform the single best model. The clearest positive evidence is concentrated in portfolio-dependent Omni-MATH settings, while GPQA, MMLU-Pro, and IFEval show different ways in which routing can remain hard or predictor-sensitive. Our practical recommendation is that routing gains should be reported together with routeability diagnostics, tied-best analysis, portfolio construction details, and family-corrected statistical tests.
authors: Yihang Lu, Denica Kjorvezir, Ana Gjorgjevikj, Carola Doerr, Tome Eftimov
bullets: Motivation: coarse-scored benchmarks often produce many tied best models, leaving limited headroom for routing.
Method: retrospectively analyze the benchmark–portfolio score matrix using routeability diagnostics, tied-best analysis, portfolio details, and family-corrected tests.
Finding: across four benchmarks and 66 LLMs, common routing enhancements do not consistently beat the single best model.
Positive evidence is strongest in portfolio-dependent Omni-MATH settings, while GPQA, MMLU-Pro, and IFEval expose different routing difficulties.
Scope: RAP audits already-evaluated benchmark portfolios; it does not certify routeability before portfolio evaluation.

papers.abstract: Looped Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures revisit layer parameters across depths. This design increases effective depth without adding parameters. Recent looped MoE studies report substantial gains over the standard MoE at matched budgets (parameters, FLOPs and KV cache). However, the reported gains still confound parameter revisit with other design choices, e.g., network shape and residual scale. We ask, what does parameter revisit itself buy? Using matched non-revisit controls, we find that parameter revisit itself buys almost nothing. We argue that revisit only offers a freedom an MoE already has, i.e., trading experts for depth (more layers, fewer experts each) at fixed parameters. First, at matched budgets, we decompose the state-of-the-art looped recipe, with revisit last. A non-revisit control retains all the gain. Most comes from network shape, and the rest from residual scale. We prove this scale acts as a lower learning rate on revisited layers. This helps under AdamW's uneven layer step sizes, but disappears under Muon, which keeps them nearly equal. Second, beyond matched budgets, we evaluate revisit by adding compute at fixed parameters. One extra visit gains more than doubling the experts. Yet without revisit, a deeper standard MoE at equal parameters and compute obtains 90.2% of that gain under Muon. Overall, gains come from network shape, the optimizer and added compute, which a standard MoE can adopt. Accordingly, we propose LoopTitan-Base as a stronger MoE baseline. Under Muon, it matches the strongest looped recipe without revisit or residual scale. We open-source LoopTitan and release 17 pretrained models (including LoopTitan-Base and the control). Our experiment record is public as GitHub issues, with predictions pre-registered and the full exploration history kept. This is our Phase 1 technical report, laying the foundation for follow-up studies.
authors: Zichen Tian, Yudong Lu, Xuansheng Wu, Na Zou, Xia Hu, Guanchu Wang, Qianru Sun
bullets: Looped MoEs revisit parameters across depth to increase effective depth without increasing parameter count.
Matched non-revisit controls retain nearly all reported gains, implicating network shape and residual scaling rather than revisit itself.
Residual scaling behaves like a lower learning rate on revisited layers under AdamW; this effect largely disappears with Muon.
With extra compute at fixed parameters, revisiting outperforms doubling experts, but deeper standard MoEs recover 90.2% of the gain under Muon.
LoopTitan-Base is proposed as a stronger non-revisit MoE baseline; the authors release 17 pretrained models and public experiment records.

papers.abstract: Collecting data from wireless sensors can be challenging when limited communication infrastructure prevents them from offloading their measurements. In such settings, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) can exploit their mobility to harvest data locally, while coordinated UAV teams can provide efficient and redundant coverage of remote areas. Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) enables such teams to learn decentralized coordination policies. However, training separate policies for different team and sensor populations is costly, and fixed-population policies may be vulnerable to agent failures. This work proposes F-MADDPG, a flexible variant of Multi-Agent Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (MADDPG) that supports data harvesting with varying numbers of wireless sensors and UAVs. The framework also accommodates unexpected catastrophic failures that permanently remove agents during a mission. We compare F-MADDPG with a MADDPG baseline that uses multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) and evaluate training strategies based on team-size sampling and exposure to agent terminations. The results show that F-MADDPG learns across the evaluated population sizes, completes missions faster than the baseline on average, benefits from inverse-cardinality team-size sampling compared with uniform sampling, remains effective after permanent agent losses, and gains no consistent benefit from exposure to failures during training.
authors: Thiago de Souza Lamenza, Bruno Jos\'e Olivieri de Souza, Markus Endler
bullets: Addresses the cost and fragility of training separate policies for fixed UAV and sensor populations.
Extends MADDPG to support variable numbers of UAVs and wireless sensors during missions.
Evaluates team-size sampling strategies and training with or without agent-failure exposure.
Learns across evaluated population sizes and completes missions faster on average than an MLP-based MADDPG baseline.
Inverse-cardinality sampling helps, while failure exposure provides no consistent training benefit.

papers.abstract: World-action models jointly predict future observations and actions, yet visual corruption can disrupt the resulting policies. We introduce HOG-WAM, which adds future Histograms of Oriented Gradients (HOG) as structural supervision derived directly from demonstration images. An auxiliary HOG diffusion transformer (DiT) module reads RGB features through asymmetric attention, allowing its objective to shape the visual representation used for control. The module is used only during training and removed at inference, preserving FastWAM's RGB-to-action architecture. We evaluate four controlled observation corruptions through a visual-corruption extension of RoboTwin, termed RoboTwin-Plus; HOG-WAM achieves the highest success among the compared policies under all four. Mixed-noise success increases from 78.86% to 82.86% relative to FastWAM, with comparable performance on clean scenes. On LIBERO Plus, overall success increases from 74.49% to 75.26%, with the largest gain under sensor noise, from 74.14% to 78.89%. Across four Franka tasks, average success increases from 40% to 59% under clean observations and from 17% to 24% under noisy observations. A representation ablation favors combining RGB observations with auxiliary HOG prediction over replacing RGB with HOG. These findings support future-gradient prediction as complementary supervision for visually robust control, with larger absolute gains on physical tasks than in simulation. Code is available at https://github.com/iPPLab/HOG-WAM.
authors: Boxuan Dong, Yupeng Qian, Ying Wu, Heshuai Li, Junhao Tan, Zhenxiong Tan, Weijia Wu, Weihao Yu
bullets: Addresses policy degradation caused by visual corruptions in jointly predictive world-action models.
Adds a training-only HOG diffusion transformer that predicts future image structure from RGB features via asymmetric attention.
Outperforms compared policies across four corruption types in RoboTwin-Plus, while maintaining comparable clean-scene performance.
Improves mixed-noise RoboTwin-Plus success from 78.86% to 82.86% and LIBERO Plus overall success from 74.49% to 75.26%.
Physical Franka-task gains are larger than simulated gains; an ablation favors combining RGB with HOG supervision rather than replacing RGB with HOG.

papers.abstract: Constructing complete 3D worlds from a single panorama is challenging because large portions of the scene remain unobserved. Existing panoramic-video methods expand spatial coverage through dense sequential generation, but neighboring frames contain substantial redundancy, long trajectories accumulate errors, and independently generated directions may be inconsistent. We present WorldExpand, which formulates single-panorama world expansion as the generation of sparse, complementary, and high-resolution panoramic observations. This representation concentrates the generation budget on informative scene regions and preserves the fine-grained details required for 3D construction. WorldExpand addresses two key challenges: where to observe and how to synthesize. Our Coverage-Guided View Selection identifies informative target locations using scene-adaptive quadrants and warp-based coverage scores, while our Joint Panoramic Diffusion uses Gaussian-splatting-based geometric warps to jointly synthesize four pose-grounded and cross-view-consistent panoramas. A diagnostic-guided global--local attention schedule retains global attention only in sensitive layers, reducing the training and inference costs of high-resolution joint generation. The resulting posed panoramas can be directly fed into an existing reconstruction pipeline to build an explicit 3D representation. Experiments show that WorldExpand recovers content behind occluders and around distant corners, improves both novel-view synthesis and downstream 3D reconstruction metrics across various datasets, and generalizes robustly to diverse in-the-wild scenes. WorldExpand runs significantly faster than the state-of-the-art panoramic-video method while producing higher-resolution observations with stronger cross-view consistency.
authors: Yuyang Yin, Chenjie Cao, Xuhui Zuo, Yuning Gong, Pengfei Wang, Junta Wu, Zhenwei Wang, Yao Zhao, Tengfei Wang, Yunchao Wei, Chunchao Guo
bullets: Targets the challenge of unobserved regions, redundant dense video generation, error accumulation, and inconsistent independently generated views.
Selects informative target locations with scene-adaptive quadrants and warp-based coverage scores.
Jointly synthesizes four pose-grounded panoramas using Gaussian-splatting-based geometric warps and panoramic diffusion.
Uses a diagnostic-guided global–local attention schedule to reduce high-resolution generation costs.
Recovers occluded and distant-corner content, improves novel-view synthesis and 3D reconstruction, and runs faster than a state-of-the-art panoramic-video method.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of WorldExpand. Given one panorama, we select four viewpoints that expose complementary unseen regions, jointly synthesize their panoramic observations with selective crossview communication, and align multi-view depths to reconstruct an expanded Gaussian scene.

Figure 8: Additional in-the-wild comparisons. The four groups are arranged on one page; method headers are shared at the top. WorldExpand remains robust across diverse styles, while independent video generation is more susceptible to distortion, exposure shifts, and structural degradation.

In contrast, Matrix-3D exhibits local point-cloud collapse and distorted geometric details, reflecting inconsistencies in its generated observations.

A single video trajectory cannot reach all four directional target viewpoints, so GenEx (Lu et al., 2025) and Matrix-3D (Yang et al., 2025b) each generate four independent clips. Their results exhibit ERP distortions, content collapse on diverse wild inputs, and abnormal overexposure, whereas WorldExpand preserves coherent structure and geometric cues across different visual styles. Additional comparisons and analysis are provided in Supplementary Sections B, G and H.

Each run reports its own best checkpoint (⋆: 20.49 vs. 20.16 dB, a ∼0.33 dB gap), so localizing 30 layers costs little quality while saving substantial memory and time (Table 6).

papers.abstract: Guidance repels the prediction of a diffusion model away from a weaker reference prediction. It substantially improves sample quality, but its mechanism remains poorly understood. We first find that, at the scales used in practice, guidance does not improve the prediction of the posterior mean (the model's training target); it makes the prediction worse, while samples improve. Second, posterior-mean predictions have less variance than the data, and we find that guidance restores it. We introduce variance-matched guidance: a closed-form rule that picks the guidance scale by matching the variance of the guided predictions to that of the data. Without tuning, it recovers the hand-picked scales of eleven widely used models across image, video, audio, motion, and world generation; to our knowledge, no previous explanation of guidance predicts them. Applied per noise level, it yields a schedule without tuned hyperparameters that users prefer to hand-crafted ones on SD 3.5 Medium. Third, we offer an interpretation of the mechanism behind guidance: each model makes a random error in predicting the posterior mean, and guidance rescales the difference of these errors into a sample with the posterior's covariance, which improves sampling. This view also suggests two new hypotheses that our experiments support: guidance can work with negative scales, and guiding a model with its own checkpoint needs a larger scale than guiding it with an independently trained model.
authors: Ali Backour, Artem Lukoianov, Frank Permenter, Tommi Jaakkola, Justin Solomon, Vincent Sitzmann
bullets: Guidance can worsen posterior-mean prediction even as it improves generated samples.

The rule recovers hand-tuned scales across image, video, audio, motion, and world-generation models.
Applied across noise levels, it produces an untuned schedule preferred over handcrafted schedules on SD 3.5 Medium.
The error-based interpretation supports guidance with negative scales and explains why self-guidance needs larger scales.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) policies are often trained by mixing contradictory feedback that is localized in space and time. For example, a robot may prioritize speed in open areas versus precision in tight gaps. We introduce Split-RL, a Gradient Boosting Trees (GBT) algorithm that uses guidance labels to locally isolate these conflicting signals. Standard neural networks (NNs) lack the structural mechanism to do this, as their parameters share feedback from all sources. While GBT provides the inductive bias to explicitly partition the state-space per objective, standard tree-fitting procedures aggregate contradictory gradient signals before they reach the leaves. Split-RL leverages this bias to integrate guidance labels into tree construction, routing these updates into disjoint state-space regions and preventing signal interference. Such labels can arise from heuristics, sensor-derived events, or existing rule-based systems, allowing Split-RL to incorporate rule-derived structure while retaining a learned policy. We theoretically show how early gradient aggregation loses objective-specific information and characterize when the Split-RL score isolates conflicting updates. We focus on constrained RL and offline RL with mixed datasets, each balancing two objectives that conflict locally. Across domains with spatial, rare-event, and temporal conflicts, Split-RL consistently outperforms existing methods by meeting the episodic cost budget while maintaining competitive rewards. In offline settings, Split-RL localizes the tradeoff between imitation and policy improvement, outperforming other methods and achieving near-expert performance across varying dataset sizes.
authors: Benjamin Fuhrer, Chen Tessler, Gal Dalal
bullets: Addresses locally conflicting objectives in constrained and offline RL, such as speed versus precision or imitation versus policy improvement.

Theoretically characterizes information loss from early gradient aggregation and when its scoring isolates conflicting updates.
Across spatial, rare-event, and temporal conflicts, meets episodic cost budgets and achieves near-expert offline performance across dataset sizes.

papers.abstract: Existing Knowledge Distillation (KD) methods for semantic segmentation often guide the student to mimic the teacher's structured information generated from an individual image. However, they ignore the global semantic relations across various images that are valuable for KD. This paper proposes Cross-Image Relational KD V2 (CIRKDV2), which focuses on transferring structured pixel-to-pixel, pixel-to-region, and channel-to-channel relations modeled from global images in the dataset. A large teacher network often constructs a well-structured feature space in terms of global contextual dependencies. CIRKDV2 makes the student mimic the better structured semantic relations of the teacher, thus improving the feature representational capability. Beyond relational distillation, we further propose contextual feature distillation by using context aggregation to augment student pixel embeddings to match the semantic level with the teacher. This avoids the semantic gap problem between the teacher and student occurred in traditional feature distillation studies. Experimental results on Cityscapes, ADE20K, Pascal VOC, and COCO-Stuff-164K demonstrate that CIRKDV2 outperforms the state-of-the-art semantic segmentation distillation methods by large margins across various network architectures. Our code and pre-trained models are publicly available at https://github.com/winycg/CIRKD.
authors: Chuanguang Yang, Yu Wang, Chengqing Yu, Xinqiang Yu, Weilun Feng, Yuqi Li, Zhulin An, Libo Huang, Boyu Diao, Fei Wang, Fuzhen Zhuang, Yongjun Xu, Yingli Tian, Tingwen Huang, Yongduan Song
bullets: Addresses the limitation of image-wise knowledge distillation, which overlooks global semantic relations across images.
Transfers teacher-modeled pixel-to-pixel, pixel-to-region, and channel-to-channel relations across the dataset.
Uses contextual feature distillation to augment student pixel embeddings and reduce the teacher–student semantic gap.
Experiments on Cityscapes, ADE20K, Pascal VOC, and COCO-Stuff-164K show large-margin improvements over state-of-the-art distillation methods across architectures.
Code and pretrained models are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Scene rearrangement is an essential task for 3D content creation applications, requiring generation of diverse, aesthetic and functional scene rearrangements. We present SceneDesigner3D, an agentic evolutionary search method for 3D indoor scene rearrangement that systematically explores the design space of 3D scenes and generates multiple solutions according to common interior design principles. Given an input scene and a text prompt, SceneDesigner3D represents the rearrangement as an editable program and evolves a population of candidate layouts. Starting from distinct design ideas, a VLM agent mutates the programs by refining promising candidates, exploring new rearrangement strategies or redesigning from scratch, while verifying the layouts for physical validity. Proposals are scored by a VLM judge for adherence to the input prompt and satisfaction of design principles such as balance, zoning and emphasis, as well as numerically computed principles such as circulation and clutter. An archive of top-performing, structurally varied candidates further increases diversity of rearrangements. Experiments on the SAGE-10k and SceneSmith datasets show that SceneDesigner3D improves prompt adherence and computed design principle scores over baselines by up to 5.1% and 15.2%, respectively. Code will be made publicly available.
authors: Chandan Yeshwanth, Angela Dai
bullets: Represents scene rearrangements as editable programs and evolves populations of candidate layouts.
A VLM agent mutates candidates through refinement, exploration, or redesign from scratch, with physical-validity checks.
A VLM judge scores prompt adherence and qualitative principles, while numerical metrics assess circulation and clutter.
An archive preserves high-performing, structurally diverse solutions.
Experiments on SAGE-10k and SceneSmith report up to 5.1% better prompt adherence and 15.2% better computed design-principle scores than baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Method overview. Given an input 3D scene and a text prompt, SceneDesigner3D evolves a population of programs that rearrange its objects. The prompt is decomposed into requirements, design seeds are initialized and objects are described by a VLM. An agentic evolutionary search explores the design space through various strategies (colored paths: object movement relative to parent). Each candidate is judged by a VLM against its parent on the prompt requirements and design principles, and combined with numerically computed principles into its fitness. An archive keeps diverse candidates as inspiration for future iterations, giving diverse layouts that follow the prompt and design principles.

papers.abstract: Recent vision-language models (VLMs) can act as robot-use agents that understand diverse scenes and control robots through policy code and tools. However, they predict 3D gripper poses poorly even with extended reasoning, struggling with precise manipulation. Vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action (WAM) models are the opposite: they execute fast, smooth control on trained tasks, yet fail under domain shifts or when tasks require long-horizon memory and reasoning. Agentic robots therefore combine VLM reasoning and perception with precise VLA/WAM control through a policy harness. Yet harness design spans thousands of configurations, shifting success by tens of points with the same models. Moreover, testing even one design takes thousands of rollouts at high API and GPU cost, so prior works often commit to a single design chosen from few alternatives. To guide harness design, we evaluate over 470,000 rollouts across eight simulation benchmarks, six VLMs, and 15 VLA/WAM checkpoints. Seven controlled studies show effective harnesses must adapt to both VLM and VLA/WAM capabilities. Our findings specify what structure the VLM's policy code needs, where VLA manipulation needs help from tools and policy code, and when to involve the VLM at test time. The reference recipe X-Harness shows that these findings compose without weight updates, lifting base policies up to $+42.8$ points across memory, reasoning, and domain shifts.
authors: Yuxiang Lai, Jike Zhong, Yu-Jhe Li, Lan Wang, Chengzhi Liu, Youbao Tang, Ming Li, Xi Xiao, Xiaofeng Yang, Liang Zhao, Zheda Mai, Ruixi Fan
bullets: VLMs provide broad perception and reasoning but struggle with precise 3D manipulation, while VLA/WAM models control trained tasks well but lack robustness and long-horizon reasoning.
Harness design can substantially change performance, making systematic evaluation important despite its high rollout and compute cost.
The study evaluates over 470,000 rollouts across eight simulation benchmarks, six VLMs, and 15 VLA/WAM checkpoints.
Seven controlled studies identify how policy code, tools, and test-time VLM involvement should adapt to the capabilities of each model.
The proposed X-Harness combines these findings without weight updates and improves base policies by up to 42.8 points across memory, reasoning, and domain-shift settings.

papers.abstract: To avoid the quadratic cost of dense attention over long contexts, models such as DeepSeek-V4 and Hy4 have turned natively sparse, and speculative decoding, which matters most where decoding is slowest, increasingly runs on them. Their drafters, however, still keep a context cache of their own, over the whole prompt or a sliding window. Beyond memory, such a cache costs prefill time, prefix-cache hits and decode concurrency. Drafters that read the target's cache avoid one of their own, but settle only which cache, not which positions, and still read everything or a recent window. Neither rule is made for the query at hand, and computing a selection per query in the drafter would cost more as the context grows. Yet a natively sparse target already picks positions for each query, over a cache it keeps anyway. Both of the drafter's choices are therefore already made, and paid for, by the target: its cache and its selection. We measure how far one selection carries: made a step early, it still covers close to nine tenths of what each later token selects on DS-V4.1-Flash. We present DFly2, a block-parallel drafter that shares the target's sparsity. Each draft layer reads the KV its paired target layer cached (KV sharing), at the positions that layer's indexer selected, a fixed number anywhere in the context (Index sharing). DFly2 thus runs no scoring pass and keeps no cache of its own. On DS-V4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash and Hy4~flash, whose sparse attention and architecture differ, it accepts more tokens per step than DFlash and DSpark trained on the same recipe, over general, long-context and agentic benchmarks. Its margin over the stronger baseline widens from 3.9%-10.5% on general workloads to 10.0%-31.5% on long-context and agentic ones. At high concurrency on DS-V4.1-Flash, at matched per-user decode speed, its throughput is 62% and 81% higher on two 64K sets.
authors: Hong Liu, Rui Cen, Junhan Shi, Lin Niu, Runzhi Fan, Zhaojing Zhou, Haodi Lei, Jiebin Zhang, Saiyong Yang, Junqiang Zheng, Zhenghai Xue, Guanghua Yu, Jianchen Zhu
bullets: Targets the memory, prefill, cache-hit, and concurrency costs of maintaining a drafter-side context cache.
Shares each target layer’s cached KV states and selected context positions with its paired drafter layer.
Uses block-parallel drafting without independently scoring or caching context positions.
Across DS-V4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash, and Hy4~flash, accepts more tokens per step than same-recipe DFlash and DSpark.
Reported gains are larger on long-context and agentic workloads; at high concurrency on two 64K DS-V4.1-Flash sets, throughput is 62% and 81% higher at matched per-user decode speed.

papers.selection_reason: Shares the target's sparse attention selection and cache to speed up speculative decoding, directly addressing token selection and KV cache efficiency.
papers.title: DFly2: Turbocharging Long-Context Speculative Decoding by Sharing the Target's Sparsity
papers.tldr: DFly2 accelerates speculative decoding for sparse long-context models by reusing the target model’s KV cache and query-specific sparse attention selections, avoiding a separate drafter cache and scoring pass.

papers.abstract: When a robot navigates an unfamiliar grid, noisy sensor readings can make it hard to tell whether the cells along its next move are free. Additional scans can reduce that uncertainty, but a fixed scan count spends the same sensing effort at every position. In a static-grid simulation, a sequential rule uses a Gaussian likelihood ratio to determine when the cells newly covered by the robot's footprint have enough evidence of free space. On 324 held-out scenarios from 18 public maps, the sequential gate and a four-scan reference chosen on validation data both completed every mission without an observed collision. With their respective validation-selected routing weights, the gate averaged 123.15 scans per episode versus 224.13 for the reference, a reduction of 45.05% (95% map-stratified bootstrap interval: 42.21--48.95%). In a retrospective check on the same scenarios with routing weights held equal, the reductions were 43.91% and 43.37% at the two tested weights, with all missions completed. On 216 scenarios from 12 previously unused maps, allocating more of the same certification error budget near the initial start--goal rectangle cut the sequential gate's scan count by a further 11.58%. The spatial variant completed 206 missions versus 208 for the original gate and increased computation time. The collision bound depends on the assumed observation model and footprint geometry. In a stress test with persistent per-cell bias, the original gate completed 0 of 54 missions.
authors: Saad Korchi, Abderrahim Waga
bullets: Problem: Fixed scan counts waste sensing effort because perception uncertainty varies across positions during navigation.
Method: A Gaussian likelihood-ratio rule adaptively scans newly covered footprint cells until evidence supports that they are free.
Result: Across 324 scenarios on 18 maps, the gate used 123.15 versus 224.13 scans per episode—a 45.05% reduction—with no observed collisions.

Extension: Reallocating the certification error budget near the initial start–goal region reduced scans by a further 11.58% on previously unused maps, but slightly reduced mission completions and increased computation time.
Limitation: Collision guarantees rely on the observation model and footprint geometry; persistent per-cell bias caused the original gate to complete 0 of 54 missions.

papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on external memory, yet they still hallucinate about what they remember. Often the correct memory is retrieved and placed in the prompt, but the answer contradicts it or the memory is applied to the wrong question. We call these use-time memory hallucinations. Across five open models, we find that they arise from the conflict between parametric knowledge and external memory and take three forms: memory-ignoring, where the model returns to a stale fact in its weights (up to 46% of queries); memory-misapplying, where it attributes the memory to unrelated entities (up to 24%, and 49% when retrieval is combined with weight editing); and version confusion, where 53% of answers about revised facts assert the superseded value when both versions remain stored. We propose TASK memory, which goes beyond text-only memory by combining a Text note with Activation Steering and Knowledge editing that share one in-model address. The text holds the content. A removable knowledge edit supplies the address through its subject key and supports multi-hop composition. A pair of steering vectors decides, query by query, whether the model adopts the memory or keeps its own answer; the vectors store no content and control how the text memory is used. On frozen models under a pre-registered, test-once protocol, TASK reduces memory-ignoring hallucinations to at most 1.5% in all ten model-dataset cells and cuts neighbour misuse from 39.2% to 7.5% (+10.8 pp composite on CounterFact). It improves a 300-memory library over BM25 RAG by 16.4 pp, an advantage that holds at 3,000 memories, resolves fact revisions without fact IDs, and adds 7.5 pp of multi-hop accuracy on MQuAKE. 21 of 23 cross-model comparisons (8B-27B, four families) are significant, and TASK beats three recent context-steering methods in 9 of 10 model-dataset cells.
authors: Jinkun Zhao, Wenjun Wu
bullets: Memory hallucinations stem from conflicts between parametric knowledge and external memory, causing memory-ignoring, misapplication, and version confusion.
TASK stores content in text, uses a knowledge edit as an in-model address, and applies query-dependent steering to control memory use.
On frozen models, it reduced memory-ignoring errors to at most 1.5% across all tested model-dataset cells.
It improved over BM25 RAG by 16.4 percentage points on a 300-memory library, with gains persisting at 3,000 memories, and added 7.5 points on multi-hop accuracy.
The method resolved revised facts without fact IDs and outperformed three context-steering methods in 9 of 10 model-dataset cells.

figures.caption: Figure 3: TASK memory overview. (a) Write. A visible observation (s, p, o∗) is compiled into a memory object bound to the model hash, scope and version. The object contains a text record T, an address key km at layer ℓE with a threshold τm calibrated at write time, a closed-form, low-rank and removable patch E keyed on the same address, and steering vectors S = (v+m, v−m) trained on the frozen model; these are kept in a text store, a patch library and a steering bank. (b) Read, against memory-ignoring (Type I) and memory-misapplying (Type II) hallucination. Candidates are retrieved by BM25 or semantic search, and one partial forward pass to layer ℓE computes each candidate’s address response rm. The shared gate gm = ⊮[rm ≥ τm] decides whether the note is shown, whether the patch is loaded as W +BA, and whether v+m or v−m is added at the decision positions of layer ℓS ; multi-hop composition uses v+ only. All hooks and patches are unloaded after generation. (c) Revise, against version confusion (Type III). A new observation is matched to the top-2 active records by BM25, checked with the address and judged by the agent’s own model. On UPDATE the old version’s T, E and S are retired together; on DIFFERENT the existing record stays active. No fact IDs are used.

Figure 1: Memory hallucination: the memory is correct, the answer is not. (a) Text-only memory or RAG puts the retrieved note into the prompt and leaves the rest to the frozen model, where the note in the context conflicts with the stale fact in the weights. On a question about the memory, the weights win and the model answers with the stale fact (Type I, memory-ignoring). On a question about another entity, the note wins and the model assigns the memory to the wrong entity (Type II, memory-misapplying). Across our five models these rates reach 46% and 24%, and Type II reaches 49% when retrieval is combined with weight editing. (b) TASK memory goes beyond text-only memory. Each memory object holds Text content, a Knowledge edit ∆Wm whose key ûm serves as the in-model address, and a pair of Activation-Steering vectors (v+, v−) that carry no content. For a query x, the address response rm(x) is compared with the threshold τm. A relevant query shows T, loads E and adds v+, so the model adopts the memory; an unrelated query leaves T and E off and adds v−, so the model keeps its own answer.

Figure 4: TASK reduces both types of use-time memory hallucination on five models and two datasets (test). (a) Type I, memoryignoring: reversion to the stale parametric answer on queries whose stale fact is in the weights. (b) Type II, memory-misapplying: misuse on neighbour questions that the no-memory model answers correctly. This subset is why the values differ from the misuse over all neighbours in Table 3 (e.g. 24.3% vs. 39.2% for Qwen3-8B with T). Bars give values in %. Per-cell bootstrap CIs are in Section A.

(a) Type I, memory-ignoring: adoption of the memory’s answer on paraphrased questions. Filled markers: queries on which the no-memory model states the stale fact, i.e. the old fact is in the weights. Hollow markers: all other queries. The gap is in percentage points; ∗ marks a paired world-level bootstrap 95% CI that excludes 0. (b) Type II, memory-misapplying: on neighbour questions (same relation, different subject) that the no-memory model answers correctly, the rate at which the model instead states the memory’s answer. Without memory this is ≤0.9%. With text memory it rises on every model, and with text memory plus a weight edit (T+E) it rises further on four of the five models. All numbers come from frozen predictions (Section A).

Figure 5: Scaling the library to 3,000 memories (CounterFact test queries; distractors are training-split memories written by the same writer). Dashed: BM25 retrieval; solid: address-verified reading. Colours follow the carriers as in Figures 2 and 4. At 300 memories, address-verified T and T +S have the same locality (96.9%), so their markers coincide in (b). The full configuration with gated E (address-verified T + gated E + S, Table 4) scores 0.946 / 0.928 / 0.916 and lies between the two upper curves in (a); it is omitted for legibility.

Bold and ∗: 95% CI excludes 0, in either direction (full CIs in Section D). n/a: not run for Gemma-3-27B, as fixed in advance for compute reasons.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses use-time memory hallucinations in LLM agents via activation steering and knowledge editing; fits LLM memory.
papers.title: TASK Memory: Beyond Text-Only Memory with Activation Steering and Knowledge Editing against Memory Hallucination
papers.tldr: TASK memory combines text notes, removable knowledge edits, and activation steering to substantially reduce use-time memory hallucinations in LLM agents.

papers.abstract: LLM agents have made remarkable progress in robot manipulation, yet they suffer from expensive inference, dense step-by-step control, and tool bottlenecks. We introduce SOLVE, a training-free, versatile and efficient agent policy: a multimodal LLM agent writes a sparse, ordered sequence of 6-DoF end-effector keyposes per call, observes the result, and writes the next, while a motion planner interpolates between them. The agent decides the number and spacing of keyposes for both fast long-range motion and fine-grained manipulation. This granularity matches the sparsity of teleoperated manipulation: most demonstrations in DROID can be compressed into a few keyposes instead of dense actions. SOLVE grounds keyposes with sparse depth queries answered by noisy sources, such as multi-view triangulation, stereo, or monocular depth, and copes with that noise itself. It also improves from execution feedback, reflecting on its own rollouts and distilling a few rules per task. SOLVE reaches state-of-the-art performance of 74.5% on RoboDojo and 84.5% on RoboLab, with only $1.7 per episode on average, 12x less than previous dense-control agent policies. On a real robot, the same agent achieves an 88% success rate (75 of 85 episodes) over 16 challenging zero-shot tasks. Our project page is at https://serenos.github.io/solve-website.
authors: Xiang Li, Hongyu Zhou, Ya-Li Li, Tao Li, Rui Zhang, Junjie Lai, Weihua Zhang, Shengjin Wang
bullets: A multimodal LLM outputs a sparse sequence of end-effector keyposes, observes execution, and iteratively plans the next sequence.
A motion planner interpolates between keyposes, supporting both fast long-range movement and fine-grained manipulation.
The agent grounds keyposes using sparse, potentially noisy depth information and improves through execution feedback and task-specific rule distillation.
It achieves 74.5% on RoboDojo, 84.5% on RoboLab, and 88% success across 85 real-robot episodes, while costing $1.7 per episode on average.
The approach is training-free and targets lower inference cost than dense-control agent policies.

papers.selection_reason: Multimodal LLM agent for robot manipulation using sparse keyposes and execution feedback, directly fitting vision-language-action and robot learning.
papers.title: SOLVE: Sparse, Ordered Keyposes Make LLM Agents Versatile and Efficient Robot Manipulator
papers.tldr: SOLVE makes LLM-based robot manipulation more efficient and versatile by planning sparse, ordered 6-DoF keyposes instead of dense step-by-step actions.

papers.abstract: Robot trajectories naturally decompose into variable-length phases with distinct semantic intents, such as reaching, grasping, and lifting. However, training policies to minimize MSE treats all actions as equal, obscuring their semantic structure. While latent action models attempt to create a structured prediction target by compressing action chunks into latent representations, existing approaches rely on two-stage training and context-blind decoders. Consequently, their representations are context-agnostic motion codes (e.g., "move down") which fail to capture behavioural intent (e.g., "pick up the block"). To overcome these bottlenecks, we introduce the Emergent Latent-action MOdel (ELMO), an end-to-end framework that encodes robot trajectories as grounded semantic codes -- representations that ground task-level behavioural intent in the current environment. ELMO jointly trains a VLA planner and an observation-conditioned decoder over dynamically chunked trajectories, learning a semantically grounded action space without separate pretraining. Across standard benchmarks, ELMO outperforms comparable prior methods by 9.6 percentage points on LIBERO-Plus and by 0.75 in average task length on CALVIN. Furthermore, on Blocks -- our shortcut-free simulation and real-world generalization benchmark -- ELMO reaches a 38.6% success rate while all baselines remain below 5%, demonstrating its ability to capture the semantic structure of demonstrations. Produces grounded codes that link task-level intent, such as picking up an object, to the current environment.

papers.abstract: World models are evaluated by predicting future observations from actions. These evaluations assume that actions are prepared the same way as during training, but an unchecked mismatch can make a model appear less accurate than it is. We audit this assumption in Navigation World Models (NWM) and find three interacting differences between its training and rollout code. Correcting the inputs, without retraining, reduces mean visual prediction error by 42%, measured with DreamSim on the RECON navigation dataset. The correction also changes the ranking of NWM checkpoints in an exploratory analysis and removes or reduces two alternative models' measured advantages. Correcting only the normalization offset instead increases error, showing why interacting mismatches must be checked together. To test whether sensitivity to input preparation extends beyond NWM, we deliberately introduce encoding errors into two alternative models; both become less accurate. We introduce ActRosetta, a tool that checks whether action encoding matches training, identifies supported causes of disagreement, and repairs inputs when sufficient information is available. Repair helps little where predictions barely respond to actions, the tool's diagnosis has limited coverage, and improved control remains unproven. For any action-conditioned world model, the lesson is the same: before reporting rollout error, verify that evaluation encodes actions exactly as training did.
authors: Ajmain Istiak Apon, Md Mehedi Hasan, Sejuti Rahman
bullets: Auditing NWM rollout code revealed three interacting differences from training-time action preparation.
Fixing the mismatches reduced mean visual prediction error by 42% on the RECON navigation dataset, measured with DreamSim.
Repairs changed checkpoint rankings and removed or reduced apparent advantages of two alternative models.
ActRosetta diagnoses supported action-encoding mismatches and repairs inputs when sufficient information is available.
Scope: repair helps little when predictions are weakly action-sensitive; diagnostic coverage is limited, and improved control is unproven.

papers.abstract: Video world models aim to create interactive physical worlds that capture how diverse materials move and interact. Yet material-dependent dynamics remain underexplored in controllable video generation, limiting reliable control in scenes with different materials. We present WorldInteract, a streaming video generation framework that decomposes cross-material interaction into material-dependent behavior generation and contact response computation. External pushes and contact impulses are expressed through a shared velocity-increment interface, allowing material behaviors learned from interaction-free videos to be reused in interacting scenes. A physics controller predicts contacts and computes velocity increments from estimated masses and restitution coefficients, while a causal generator executes these increments using learned material behaviors. This separation enables cross-material interaction without supervised contact videos spanning diverse material pairings and contact configurations. We train the generator on 30k simulated interaction-free videos spanning 22 material classes and introduce Material-Aware RL, using verifiable physical rewards to refine material behavior and control execution. WorldInteract substantially outperforms state-of-the-art methods on Physics-IQ and delivers more reliable push control on real-world images.
authors: Ahmed Hatem, Caoliwen Wang, Robert Hoang, Siyuan Chen, Spencer Szabados, Zike Wu, Xiyang Tan, Shenyifan Lu, Rafael Bischof, Bernd Bickel, Renjie Liao, Peter Yichen Chen
bullets: Targets reliable control of scenes containing different interacting materials.
Decomposes interactions into material-dependent behavior generation and contact-response computation.
Uses a shared velocity-increment interface so behaviors learned from interaction-free videos can handle contacts and external pushes.
Combines a physics controller with a causal video generator and refines control using Material-Aware RL.
Reports substantially better Physics-IQ performance and more reliable push control on real-world images.

papers.abstract: We ask how much of a transformer's backbone the Chorus N-gram module replaces. Chorus adds hashed tables of token bigrams and trigrams to its input and attention. We train models of 16M to 349M parameters on 1.34 billion tokens of Polish printed before 1918 and find the size of a plain model with the same held-out loss. A separate learning-rate search for each kind of model cuts Chorus's gain at 47M by about a third. With tables about as large as the backbone, Chorus then matches a plain model 1.34 times its size at 16M and 1.16 to 1.20 times from 107M to 349M. With these tables, each added parameter replaces at most 0.31 backbone parameters. Chorus trains slower than a plain model of its size and faster than one of the same loss. On a fact quiz the two differ about as much as two seeds of one model. The results rest on one corpus, one 8,000-token vocabulary and a fifth of an epoch.
authors: Szymon Kocur
bullets: Chorus augments transformer inputs and attention with hashed bigram and trigram tables.
On Polish pre-1918 text, similarly performing Chorus models match plain models 1.34× larger at 16M parameters and 1.16–1.20× larger at 107M–349M.
With tables roughly the backbone’s size, each added table parameter replaces at most 0.31 backbone parameters.
Separate learning-rate tuning reduces Chorus’s gain at 47M parameters by about one third.
Chorus trains slower than an equally sized plain model, while quiz differences are comparable to variation across random seeds.
