papers.abstract: Mixed-task reinforcement learning (MixRL) directly trains a unified policy across domains to continually expand agent capabilities without training separate specialists or requiring an extra distillation stage. Despite its appeal, scaling MixRL poses significant challenges in achieving stable and efficient mixed-task learning, effectively allocating rollout compute, and supporting continual domain expansion. To address these challenges, we propose Maco-RL, an approach that effectively scales MixRL. Specifically, Maco-RL employs a quota-based scheduler for asynchronous rollouts across multiple task domains, thereby stabilizing training by balancing gradient contributions and mitigating off-policy effects. Along an orthogonal axis, Maco-RL further introduces Tri-Buffer Sampling (TBS) to allocate compute among samples with varying levels of mastery, promoting sustained frontier exploration while preserving acquired capabilities. Experiments on five benchmarks show Maco-RL raises Qwen3.5-27B's overall score from 43.6 to 54.2 and then to 60.1 with continual expansion, reaching the frontier held by Qwen3.8-27B, which is further pushed outward by +5.7. Maco-RL also outperforms single-task RL with less compute for policy updates. These results support MixRL as a practical and compute-efficient post-training approach with substantial potential to strengthen general agent capabilities.
authors: Jiacheng Zhang, Qixing Zhou, Haiyang Wang, Qipeng Gu, Shuzhe Wu, Feiyang Pan, Lue Fan, Dandan Tu, Zhaoxiang Zhang
bullets: Addresses unstable mixed-task learning, inefficient rollout allocation, and continual domain expansion without separate specialists or distillation.

Across five benchmarks, Qwen3.5-27B improves from 43.6 to 54.2 and then 60.1 with continual expansion, reaching the frontier of Qwen3.8-27B.
Outperforms single-task RL while using less compute for policy updates, supporting MixRL as a compute-efficient post-training approach.

papers.abstract: Remote sensing scene understanding requires multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to interpret queried targets in relation to nearby objects and surrounding structures, which serve as spatial references or define the scope of an answer. However, standard answers and bounding boxes often leave these contextual relationships implicit. Thus, we construct GeoContext-5K to make them explicit in 5,394 training pairs for visual question answering (VQA), with spatial cues, visual facts, and supporting regions. GeOPD uses these annotations for on-policy distillation, guiding a frozen teacher with region marks on the full image and a visual fact while preserving surrounding spatial references. It prioritizes teacher corrections that agree with the shift in the student's next token distribution when evidence is restored. A complementary objective weights the contrast between the student's scores on the two views by how much masking lowers the teacher's log probability for the same sampled token. Experiments on five remote sensing VQA benchmarks show that GeOPD outperforms the evaluated open-source MLLMs and matched post-training baselines, improving over the 4B and 9B base models by 5.81 and 2.97 percentage points on average. The dataset and code will be publicly released at https://github.com/YeeCharm/GeOPD.
authors: Yichang Luo, Hourun Zhu, Shixiong Liu, Kan Wei, Shi Liang, Yidan Zhang, Lei Wang
bullets: GeoContext-5K contains 5,394 VQA training pairs with spatial cues, visual facts, and supporting regions.
GeOPD performs on-policy distillation with region-marked full images and visual facts while preserving spatial references.
It prioritizes teacher corrections supported by changes in the student’s next-token distribution when evidence is restored.
A contrastive objective uses how masking affects the teacher’s token likelihood to weight student-view comparisons.
Across five remote-sensing VQA benchmarks, GeOPD improves over 4B and 9B base models by 5.81 and 2.97 percentage points on average, respectively.

papers.abstract: Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models rarely satisfy all behavioral requirements of a new platform, and teams without a large deployed fleet lack the data to address the resulting failures. We propose a failure-driven data flywheel for post-training such models. It constructs target scenarios absent from the available data by inserting task-relevant entities into reconstructed real-world scenes, and evaluates the model against each behavioral requirement of the target task. Failure rates form a failure map across task conditions and difficulty levels, which is re-evaluated after each round and assigns larger data generation quotas to conditions where the model still fails. We instantiate the framework in autonomous driving for occluded-pedestrian emergence and yielding at stop-sign-controlled intersections, and evaluate it on two VLA models and one non-VLA planner in simulation and on a real vehicle. For occluded-pedestrian emergence, five rounds of post-training improve the critical-phase collision-free rate on the sealed test set from 0.261 to 0.579 for AutoVLA and from 0.390 to 0.765 for ReCogDrive, while the unnecessary braking rate in paired control scenarios never exceeds 0.013. On a full-scale vehicle without real-world training, post-trained ReCogDrive achieves 4 of 5 safe passages, versus 1 of 5 for the base model. Fine-grained evaluation reveals a pattern obscured by the collision-free rate alone: both VLA models learn anticipatory deceleration before reaching the occluding vehicle, while braking after pedestrian emergence remains limited. For stop-sign yielding, the stop-before-line rate rises from 0.100 to 0.897 for AutoVLA and from 0.000 to 0.667 for ReCogDrive. With sequential training from the pedestrian-capability models, it reaches 0.599 and 0.358, respectively, while the pedestrian collision-free rate decreases by at most 0.032.

papers.abstract: Interactive world models must generate video continuously while responding promptly to user actions. Real-time throughput alone leaves input latency unresolved: coarse generation blocks delay action updates, and generation after input adds work to the response path. We introduce ShowNow, a fine-grained speculative streaming framework that uses computation available during playback to prepare action-conditioned futures before input arrives. Single-latent commitment enables frequent decisions, while configurable preparation covers one to eight actions. We construct a matched multi-future dataset to train alternative continuations from a common state; shared-history tree execution and fused commitment make their preparation efficient. On a single H100, our 5B model sustains 480p generation at 16 fps with eight prepared futures. In ViZDoom, the complete ShowNow deployment reduces median input-to-display latency from 620 to 208 ms relative to the native-block SolarWM-FT deployment. Matched-policy experiments reduce restart empty ticks from 1.56% to 0.09% (94%) and improve on-time responses to action changes. These results establish complementary roles for fine-grained commitment and advance preparation, with measured trade-offs in visual fidelity and long-horizon consistency. ShowNow turns playback-time computation into responsive visual interaction. Project: https://github.com/showlab/ShowNow.
authors: Yiren Song, Guian Fang, Mike Zheng Shou
bullets: Targets input latency caused by coarse, blocking video generation and post-input computation.

On a single H100, a 5B model generates 480p video at 16 fps with eight prepared futures.
In ViZDoom, latency falls from 620 ms to 208 ms, while restart empty ticks decrease from 1.56% to 0.09%; trade-offs remain in visual fidelity and long-horizon consistency.

papers.abstract: Poetry-to-video generation requires more than translating text into visual scenes. Poetic language is highly compressed, often depends on historical and cultural knowledge, and frequently conveys meaning through metaphor, imagery, and other non-literal expressions. We introduce PoVi, a benchmark and agentic framework for grounded poetry-to-video generation, evaluating semantic grounding, discourse coherence, and audiovisual realization. PoVi reconstructs poem semantics into an evidence-bounded representation and progressively transforms them into narration, interpretation, character assets, and shot-level visual plans, followed by narration-aligned video generation. Across three planning backbones and four video generators, PoVi consistently improves over single-call generation, with the largest gains on implicit background knowledge and metaphorical relations. PoVi provides a testbed for studying knowledge-grounded, long-horizon multimodal generation beyond direct text-to-video synthesis.

Across three planning backbones and four video generators, consistently outperforms single-call generation, especially for implicit knowledge and metaphorical relations.
Provides a testbed for long-horizon, knowledge-grounded multimodal generation beyond direct text-to-video synthesis.

papers.abstract: Non-invasive brain-to-text seeks to recover language from brain activity without surgery. A central challenge is turning learned brain-language representations into accurate word predictions. We present MEG2text, a decoding system that combines corrected training and evaluation, brain-text alignment, a class-balanced word readout, and target-word language-model fusion. On LibriBrain100's word-ranking task, MEG2text reaches 64.12% mean Top-10 balanced accuracy, improving on published MEG-XL by 16.92 percentage points across four corpora, with gains on each corpus. Controlled comparisons show that both implementation corrections and a learned readout contribute to this improvement. Candidate-level analysis reveals that some words receive informative scores yet consistently lose to competing candidates, while an identical-feature comparison shows that learning the classification rule improves decoding without changing the representation. These findings identify the decoding rule as a consequential part of non-invasive brain-to-text and show how system improvements can make better use of aligned neural features.

bullets: Addresses the challenge of converting aligned brain-language representations into accurate word predictions.

papers.abstract: Answering a knowledge-based visual question requires first recognizing the entity in the image and then recalling knowledge about it. Thinking vision-language models (VLMs) reason for thousands of tokens before answering, yet it remains underexplored how well such thinking VLMs perform each of these two steps. We therefore analyze thinking VLMs on this task and make two key observations. (1) Recognition is the bottleneck, since 76.3% of errors across four models on ViQuAE stem from misrecognizing the entity, and 84.9% of these failures are resolved once the entity name is provided in the question. (2) Recognition is driven by entity-recall clues rather than by general descriptions of the image. An entity-recall clue is a distinctive visual detail that helps the model recall the entity, such as keys, a traditional attribute of Saint Peter. Based on these findings, we propose ClueRL, a reinforcement learning approach that extends Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with an advantage localized to the entity-recall clue in the thinking trace. Rather than injecting new entity knowledge, ClueRL changes how VLMs think: it leads them to attend more closely to visual details and spot these clues, helping them use the knowledge they already have. Consequently, it outperforms both GRPO and a perception-reward baseline on three entity recognition benchmarks. Moreover, this clue-seeking behavior generalizes beyond entity recognition, the only task used for training. Since recognition is the bottleneck, the gains carry over to knowledge-based visual question answering. They even extend to general multimodal reasoning, raising Qwen3.5-4B by 4.4 and 4.0 points on the ScienceQA and MMMU subsets of MMStar, respectively.
authors: Kyungmin Min, Soyeon Kim, Junseok Kim, Kyomin Jung
bullets: Entity recognition is the main bottleneck: 76.3% of errors across four models on ViQuAE come from misidentifying the entity.
Most recognition failures are resolved when the entity name is supplied, indicating that models often possess the needed knowledge but fail to identify the visual entity.
Recognition depends on entity-recall clues—distinctive details such as Saint Peter’s keys—rather than generic image descriptions.
ClueRL extends GRPO with an advantage focused on entity-recall clues in the reasoning trace, without adding entity knowledge.
It outperforms GRPO and a perception-reward baseline on three entity-recognition benchmarks and improves knowledge-based VQA and broader multimodal reasoning.

papers.abstract: Generative video models are becoming powerful renderers, yet lack the predictable control interfaces of conventional systems such as HTML/CSS engines or Blender. Their capabilities emerge implicitly from training, making it difficult to determine what they can reliably execute. We present Neural Rendering Compiler (NeurCo), which automatically probes frozen video models to construct model-specific capability manuals describing which semantic requirements they can reliably satisfy. NeurCo represents user intent in a model-agnostic intermediate representation of objects, constraints, events, and cameras, then compiles it into model-specific execution strategies. Reliable requirements remain unchanged, while unreliable ones are selectively rewritten or compiled into alternative execution strategies. We introduce VComBench, a benchmark of 380 compositional, multi-requirement tasks spanning text-to-video, image-to-video, and reference-to-video generation. NeurCo improves requirement satisfaction from 46.8% to 52.3% on Wan and from 66.5% to 69.3% on Minimax H3, and achieves further gains when combined with prompt enhancers, including on Seedance 2.5. Our analysis reveals model-specific differences in control capabilities and trade-offs between controllability and photorealism, highlighting capability-guided compilation as a promising approach to programmable generative video rendering.
authors: Yuxia Zhu, Xinglong Xu, Hao Liang, Linzhuang Sun, Caijun Jia, Qifeng Cai, Jincen Luo, Lei Li, Alden Cai, Asher Qin, Wentao Zhang, Cheng Tan
bullets: Addresses the lack of reliable control interfaces in generative video models.
Represents intent using objects, constraints, events, and cameras in a model-agnostic intermediate representation.
Automatically builds capability manuals, preserving reliable requirements while rewriting or recompiling unreliable ones.
Introduces VComBench, a 380-task benchmark covering text-, image-, and reference-to-video generation.
Improves requirement satisfaction on Wan and Minimax H3, with additional gains when combined with prompt enhancers; results expose controllability–photorealism trade-offs.

papers.abstract: Robots should adapt to unfamiliar environments and acquire new skills through interaction, then execute those skills efficiently with practice. Vision-language-action policies provide efficient control, but often need additional human demonstrations to handle unfamiliar settings; reasoning agents can discover solutions using broad prior knowledge and robot-control APIs, but repeated deliberation and repair are costly. Inspired by human learning through reasoning and practice, we propose RoboEvo$^2$, a framework for recursive harness-policy co-evolution. In Policy-to-Harness (P2H) evolution, policy failures guide a coding agent to search complementary Code, Code+ICL, and Code+Policy routes, consolidating verified solutions into reusable skills, routing strategies, and experience memory. In Harness-to-Policy (H2P) evolution, verified trajectories provide supervised training, while Counterfactual Preference Distillation (CPD) teaches the policy to favor successful corrections over failures from the same starting state. The improved policy provides stronger motor skills for subsequent search, while its remaining failures redirect harness evolution, closing the reciprocal loop. Through recursive co-evolution without additional human demonstrations, RoboEvo$^2$ improves standalone success from 11.0% to 84.1% and hybrid success from 30.4% to 90.5% on LIBERO-PRO, with similar gains and reduced agentic costs on RoboTwin C2R. Further experiments demonstrate autonomous task acquisition, cross-embodiment harness transfer, and 95.0% hybrid success on the Unitree G1-D. Our models and code will be publicly released.

Reported success improves from 11.0% to 84.1% standalone and from 30.4% to 90.5% hybrid on LIBERO-PRO; similar gains and lower agentic costs are reported on RoboTwin C2R.
Demonstrations include autonomous task acquisition, cross-embodiment harness transfer, and 95.0% hybrid success on Unitree G1-D.

papers.abstract: Scaling robot learning requires demonstrations that combine realistic visual observations with reliable action supervision. Simulation-based synthesis faces a substantial visual gap relative to real environments, while video-only generation struggles to maintain physically consistent interactions and provide aligned action labels. We present DemoFoundry, an automated framework that couples coding agents with generative rendering to synthesize photorealistic and physically grounded robot demonstrations. Coding agents both construct aligned real--proxy video pairs from existing robot episodes to train a video renderer and write executable interaction programs to generate new demonstrations. Given a scene reference and task instruction, an agent reconstructs task-relevant geometry and writes a control program without requiring target-task human demonstrations. Program execution in a physics simulator produces proxy videos with aligned robot states and actions. The video renderer translates these proxy videos into scene-consistent, photorealistic observations, reducing the need for detailed appearance modeling in each scene. Automated task-execution checks select successful trajectories for rendering and policy learning. Experiments show improved visual quality and action--video consistency. Policies trained on the generated demonstrations outperform raw-simulation training and approach the performance of training on an equal number of real demonstrations.

Generated-data policies outperform raw-simulation training and approach training with an equal number of real demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Autonomous robotic palpation offers repeatable, quantitative estimates of tissue properties for stiff inclusion localization. However, existing methods often rely on prior mesh models or planar surface assumptions that do not generalize to complex human anatomy. We propose an ergodic palpation framework that operates directly on curved soft surfaces using point cloud data. Central to our approach is the Laplace--Beltrami operator, which grounds both online estimation and exploration in the surface intrinsic geometry. We estimate local viscoelastic parameters using an Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF) and fuse them into a surface-aware Gaussian Process (GP). This probabilistic model drives a diffusion-based ergodic motion planner, generating a continuous exploration trajectory that feeds the new informative samples back to the GP in a closed loop. Throughout this process, a hybrid force-impedance controller regulates interaction forces to maintain contact. We evaluate the approach against existing methods in simulation and validate it in physical experiments on tissue-mimicking silicone phantoms with varying geometries and viscoelastic properties, demonstrating geometry-consistent mapping and stiff inclusion localization under contact-rich conditions.
authors: Luca Beber, Cem Bilaloglu, Edoardo Lamon, Matteo Saveriano, Daniele Fontanelli, Luigi Palopoli, Sylvain Calinon
bullets: Addresses the limitations of mesh-dependent and planar-surface palpation methods for complex anatomy.
Uses point clouds and the Laplace–Beltrami operator to represent intrinsic surface geometry.
Combines UKF-based local viscoelastic estimation with a surface-aware Gaussian Process.
Plans continuous diffusion-based ergodic exploration in a closed loop, while regulating contact forces with hybrid force-impedance control.
Simulation and silicone-phantom experiments demonstrate geometry-consistent mapping and stiff-inclusion localization under contact-rich conditions.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Detailed architecture of the proposed framework. An offline preprocessing stage acquires a point cloud representation of the workspace and performs a Laplace-Beltrami decomposition to initialize both the Gaussian Process (GP) model and the ergodic exploration basis. During online operation, a tactile ergodic control policy generates desired end-effector trajectories and interaction forces based on the current ergodic information density (EID). A Cartesian force-impedance controller ensures stable and compliant physical interaction with the environment, while an Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF) estimates local viscoelastic parameters from measured end-effector states and contact forces. The GP model and the EID are continuously updated, closing the perception-action loop and enabling adaptive, information-driven exploration.

papers.abstract: Compression based on singular value decomposition (SVD) often requires subsequent fine-tuning or weight correction to mitigate performance degradation. Budget-specific optimization must be repeated for different compression ratios. We introduce LLift, which prepares a pretrained model for SVD compression across ratios without further fine-tuning. LLift fine-tunes a low-rank approximation at a single ratio using the original model as a teacher. We merge the learned updates into the original weights while preserving the complementary components excluded from the training forward pass. We apply SVD to the prepared model's target matrices and reuse the decompositions at different truncation ranks. On LLaMA-7B, we demonstrate accuracy gains across three compression ratios using a single prepared model. The gains extend across model families, model sizes, and SVD compression operators. We analyze gradients and an early training update to provide local evidence that updates learned at one ratio can benefit compression at other ratios. These results show that LLift can improve compression across deployment budgets without fine-tuning each compressed model separately.
authors: Chenyue Fang, Danila Mishin, Babak Falsafi
bullets: SVD compression can degrade performance and typically requires ratio-specific fine-tuning or weight correction.

Experiments report accuracy gains across three ratios, model families, model sizes, and SVD operators; the method’s scope is evaluated through local gradient and early-update analyses.

papers.abstract: Generative driving planners may produce trajectories that appear feasible at their reference points but violate environmental constraints over the full vehicle body. We propose FeaXDrive2, an end-to-end generative planning framework that enhances vehicle-embodied spatial feasibility (VESF) through body-scene spatial grounding. The proposed method constructs spatial queries from actual vehicle-body corners and dynamically updates visual sampling locations using evolving trajectory estimates across Flow steps. Retrieved local visual features condition subsequent Action Flow-DiT velocity predictions, allowing trajectory generation to guide spatial information retrieval. Rollout-Consistent Safety Fine-Tuning (RC-F) combines high-risk trajectory supervision with reference behavior preservation, followed by planning-supervised VLM-Action Alignment. Vehicle-geometry counterfactual analysis reveals safety differences under identical trajectories but varying vehicle geometry. On NAVSIM, FeaXDrive2 reduces at-fault collisions by 36.5% relative to the base planner and improves PDMS from 87.0 to 88.8. Under NAVSIM v2 evaluation, EPDMS increases from 86.5 to 88.3. Ablation and body-clearance analyses further demonstrate the safety benefits of body-scene spatial grounding.
authors: Bo Leng, Baoyun Wang, Wenxin Wen, Ming Liu, Weiqi Zhang, Ran Yu, Chongfeng Wei, Zhuoren Li, Lu Xiong

Adds Rollout-Consistent Safety Fine-Tuning and planning-supervised VLM–Action Alignment.
On NAVSIM, reduces at-fault collisions by 36.5% and improves PDMS from 87.0 to 88.8; NAVSIM v2 EPDMS rises from 86.5 to 88.3.

papers.abstract: Counting how many times something happens is among the simplest questions about a video and among the hardest for video-language models, autoregressive and diffusion alike. The difficulty lies between the frames: a model samples only a few of them, while each repetition unfolds as movement in between. Video codecs already record this movement densely as block displacements, and codec-based video models use it to shape their visual input. We are the first to show that this motion provides direct evidence for the count: a candidate count is a testable motion hypothesis, and unwinding the cycles it implies measures how strongly the observed directions support it. We present CoDiCount, a unified training-free framework that turns this test into a count potential and applies it while a frozen diffusion vision-language model (dVLM) denoises its answer. At every denoising step, structured count messages map each option letter, or each grammar-valid edit of an open integer, to the count it expresses and reweight the model's own probabilities within that set. Consistent gains over the official decoders on MotionBench, TOMATO, and SVCBench demonstrate the broad generalization of CoDiCount across diffusion models, datasets, and diverse counting tasks. With CoDiCount, a 7B dVLM outperforms GPT-5.1 and Gemini-2.5-Pro on MotionBench, surpasses GPT-4o and much larger open models on TOMATO, and matches GPT-5.4 on SVCBench.
authors: Zhuoqin Li, Jiayu Ding, Ge Li
bullets: Video counting is difficult because sparse frames miss repetitions occurring between them.
Codec motion vectors provide dense evidence about the direction and cycles of movement.
CoDiCount is a training-free framework that converts motion consistency into a count potential during diffusion denoising.
Structured count messages reweight probabilities for multiple-choice options or grammar-valid edits of open-ended integer answers.
It consistently improves official decoders across MotionBench, TOMATO, and SVCBench, with reported comparisons to leading proprietary and open models.

papers.abstract: Dexterous mobile manipulation is essential for robots to perform useful tasks in complex, unstructured environments. However, existing systems face two challenges. First, navigation remains too coarse for downstream manipulation, which often requires a precise base position and approach orientation rather than merely reaching a meter-scale goal region. Second, navigation and manipulation are commonly trained in isolation, lacking a feedback loop that enables the two capabilities to co-evolve. These limitations prevent current systems from reliably executing long-horizon dexterous mobile-manipulation tasks in real-world environments. To address them, we introduce Nav4Manip, a bidirectionally coupled co-evolution system for long-horizon dexterous mobile manipulation. It comprises two complementary architectures: Nav4Manip-N learns long-horizon navigation and refines its policy through manipulation feedback, while Nav4Manip-M trains a world-action model (WAM) for downstream dexterous manipulation. We train Nav4Manip-N in three stages: multi-task co-tuning learns navigation behavior and manipulation-aware affordance prediction; rejection sampling fine-tuning (RFT) rejects low-quality policy-generated paths and fine-tunes the model on retained trajectories; and reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF) uses counterfactual preferences to further improve navigation decisions. To support this framework, we establish the Nav-N-Manip benchmark and construct Nav4Manip-Pairs from benchmark rollouts, providing large-scale paired navigation--manipulation trajectories and affordance supervision. Extensive experiments on public vision-language navigation (VLN) benchmarks and Nav-N-Manip demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, while real-world evaluations show that Nav4Manip completes diverse dexterous mobile-manipulation tasks. Project website: https://nav4manip.github.io/.
authors: Yusen Feng, Zixi Kang, Zhijun Yin, Changxiao Liu, Tianhong Gao, Jiazhao Zhang, Jiahang Liu, Libin Liu, Zhizheng Zhang, He Wang
bullets: Targets navigation that must achieve manipulation-ready base positions and orientations, not just coarse goal regions.
Uses two coupled components: Nav4Manip-N for manipulation-aware navigation and Nav4Manip-M with a world-action model for dexterous manipulation.
Trains navigation through multi-task co-tuning, rejection-sampling fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning from AI feedback.
Introduces the Nav-N-Manip benchmark and paired navigation–manipulation trajectories with affordance supervision.
Reports state-of-the-art results on public VLN benchmarks and Nav-N-Manip, plus successful real-world task execution.

papers.abstract: Many embodied world models predict future states in latent spaces optimized for RGB reconstruction, which do not explicitly prioritize object-level semantics and geometry relevant to motion generation. We present MotionRep, a visual representation world model that jointly generates future DINO representations and 3D object flow, coupling semantic and geometric information with object-centric dynamics. To make high-dimensional DINO features amenable to generative modeling, we introduce DINO-VAE, which combines temporal and channel compression with latent regularization to produce compact latents while preserving semantic and geometric information. Conditioned on an initial observation, object query points, and a language instruction, a unified diffusion transformer predicts future visual representations and 3D object flow through joint attention. MotionRep employs asymmetric modality-specific noise schedules to keep the visual stream ahead of 3D object flow during joint denoising, allowing progressively refined future visual representations to guide flow generation. Experiments on simulated and real-world manipulation benchmarks demonstrate that MotionRep outperforms pixel-based baselines in 3D object flow accuracy and generalization to unseen scenes, while requiring only three denoising steps for inference. These results support predictive visual representations as an effective future-state space for object-centric dynamics modeling.
authors: Chengzhi Zhao, Juelin Li, Zhennan Wang, Sheng Wang, Zhuoman Liu, Yuhao Lu, Jiongxu Chen, Haitang Feng, Yanjie Li, Lin Shao
bullets: Targets the weak object-level semantics and geometry of RGB-reconstruction world models.
Introduces DINO-VAE to compress DINO features while preserving semantic and geometric information.
Uses a diffusion transformer conditioned on observations, object query points, and language instructions to jointly predict future representations and 3D object flow.
Applies asymmetric denoising schedules so refined visual representations guide flow generation.
Outperforms pixel-based baselines in 3D flow accuracy and unseen-scene generalization on simulated and real manipulation benchmarks, using three denoising steps.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of DINO-VAE. DINO-VAE compresses high-dimensional DINO features through temporal attention pooling and a causal ViT encoder, achieving 4× temporal and 8× channel compression. Figure 2. Overview of MotionRep. Given an initial RGB observation, 3D object query points, and a language instruction, MotionRep jointly generates future DINO representations and 3D object flow within a unified diffusion transformer. papers.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) promises data efficiency and generalization, but typical reconstruction-based objectives encourage models to waste representational capacity on task-irrelevant distractors. We introduce VIBES (Variational Inference for Bisimulation-based Encoded States), a new objective that replaces pixel reconstruction with an adversarial term, which enforces that latent states suffice to predict both rewards and the next latent state. We show that this objective measures how far the encoder is from reward and dynamics sufficiency, and that whenever exact sufficiency is attainable, its global optima induce bisimulation relations on histories. Combined with a fixed-capacity latent bottleneck, this encourages latent states to retain task-relevant information while discarding irrelevant variation. Our method serves as a drop-in replacement for Dreamer's model-learning component, achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Distracting Control Suite, and extends to visually complex manipulation in Realistic ManiSkill. Unlike prior approaches, it does not rely on image-specific augmentations and applies equally well to high-dimensional vector-state tasks, demonstrated on a 100-link swimmer robot. Finally, latent-space analyses (UMAP embeddings and nearest-neighbor probes) confirm that the learned representations are sensitive to task-relevant structure while invariant to distractors.
authors: Benjamin Freed, Vivaan Singh, Dean Zadok, Roberto Calandra, Jeff Schneider, Howie Choset
bullets: Addresses reconstruction objectives that waste capacity modeling irrelevant distractors.
Uses an adversarial variational bisimulation objective to enforce reward and next-latent-state sufficiency.
A fixed-capacity bottleneck promotes task-relevant, distractor-invariant representations.
Works as a drop-in replacement for Dreamer’s model learning and does not require image-specific augmentations.
Reports state-of-the-art results on Distracting Control Suite, plus applicability to Realistic ManiSkill and high-dimensional vector-state tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Latent-space analyses on Reacher-easy. (a) UMAP projections of 9 encoded trajectories in a 3 × 3 grid; rows share task states and columns share background distractors. Latent states change with the task state but not with the background. (b) Five nearest latent neighbors for six query observations (top of each column). Neighbors differ in background but match the query’s arm pose relative to the goal, sometimes rotated about the origin, showing that the representation is task-relevant and invariant to joint rotations of the arm and goal.

Figure 6: Adversary–dynamics likelihood gap on Cheetah-run. (Left) ∆̂ = dynamics NLL − adversary NLL; positive values mean the history-conditioned adversary predicts the next latent better than the dynamics model. (Right) The two NLLs separately; spikes at 125K and 187.5K steps are scheduled model resets (Table 3). NLLs are summed over latent dimensions and averaged over batch and time. Lines show the mean over 5 seeds and shading the 95% CI; curves are smoothed with a 20-episode rolling mean.

Figure 2: Model diagram and objective. Our model comprises an encoder (CNN+GRU) that maps history (o≤t, a<t) to a stochastic latent s̃t; a dynamics model that predicts s̃t+1 from (s̃t, at); a reward model p(rt | s̃t, at); and an adversary network that predicts s̃t+1 from the history and current action, (o≤t, a≤t). Our objective has two parts: a reward sufficiency term, maximized when the latent state contains all information needed to predict the current reward, and a dynamics sufficiency term, maximized when the latent state is as informative as the full history for predicting the next latent state.

Figure 1: Side-by-side comparison of graphical model assumptions. These Probabilistic Graphical Models (PGMs) model environment dynamics, where the latent state s̃t represents the true, underlying hidden state from which observations and rewards arise. Actions may be either fixed exogenously or depend on observations through a policy. Left (Dreamer): the observation at time t is conditionally independent of prior observations and actions given the current latent state, i.e., ot ⊥⊥ o<t, a<t | s̃t. Right (Ours): we allow ot to depend on the full history of observations (and, in general, on the history of states/actions). Under Dreamer’s assumption, any information in o<t needed to predict ot must be encoded into st; in our formulation this pressure is removed from st because past observations can inform ot directly.

Figure 3: 100-link swimmer (vector states): learning curves. Mean episode return over 4 runs versus environment steps, with 95% confidence intervals shaded, for VIBES, Recon. Obj. papers.abstract: The behavior of memory systems for long-running AI assistants is governed by a harness, which consists of the code, prompts, and configurations for memory construction, maintenance, retrieval, and answer generation. However, optimizing the harness of a memory system remains largely manual, and unrestricted editing alone does not ensure structural improvements. In this paper, we introduce HoMe, an evaluation-driven framework that iteratively evaluates candidate harnesses and derives each new candidate from any previously evaluated harness by editing any part of it. HoMe combines session-level memory versioning with execution traces to identify shared failure mechanisms across cases and localize them to the responsible sessions and harness components. It encourages early structural exploration through candidate gating and reduces evaluation cost through smoke tests, adaptive sampling, and the reuse of constructed memory. We validate HoMe with the open-source memory system ReMe on two large-scale long-horizon memory benchmarks, LongMemEval-S and BEAM. With six formal candidate evaluations per benchmark, after a full initial evaluation, HoMe discovers harnesses that improve end-task performance over the originally strong harness while consuming far fewer query-time tokens. The code is available at https://github.com/agentscope-ai/ReMe.
authors: Yifei Xu, Li Yu, Zhaoyang Liu, Ce Wang, Sen Huang, Yanyan Shen, Yun Lin, Linpeng Huang, Hong Mei
bullets: Targets the largely manual optimization of memory-system code, prompts, and configurations.

Validated with ReMe on LongMemEval-S and BEAM; after six formal evaluations per benchmark, it found harnesses with better end-task performance and fewer query-time tokens than the original harness.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models introduce language reasoning into end-to-end autonomous driving. They output a language decision together with a trajectory, which makes the planner more interpretable. However, in existing methods the language decision is either an independent output or an index that selects among similar candidate trajectories, and its annotations are not verified against the trajectory. As a result, the language decision and the trajectory are often inconsistent in closed-loop driving. To address this, we propose Commit2Drive, a framework that imposes the language decision as a consistency constraint on trajectory planning. The decision is a commitment, a maneuver class with a continuous parameter that one deterministic rule reads from any trajectory, and it is grounded in facts reported by the perception of the model itself. A Maneuver Bank maps the commitment to a code with a kinematic meaning, and consistency losses train the planner to execute every admissible decision of a scene, so that the trajectory follows the decision. An automatic data pipeline supplies the supervision. Decisions are labeled from the future motion of the expert, counterfactual executions train the decision and the trajectory together, and rule-based functions with a Vision-Language Model (VLM) generate, review and refine the language annotations. The code is a lookup that involves no hidden state of the language model, so Commit2Drive is extensible to rule-based decisions, which the same planner executes without retraining. Commit2Drive uses a 0.5B language model and runs closed-loop inference online on a single consumer graphics card. On Bench2Drive, Commit2Drive reaches a Driving Score (DS) of 78.50 and a Success Rate (SR) of 55.91% with a lightweight model, which is competitive with the state of the art, and greatly reduces the language-action inconsistency. Code will be released soon.
authors: Zikai Zhang, Hubert P. Shum, Toby Breckon
bullets: Addresses inconsistencies between language decisions and trajectories in vision-language-action driving models.
Represents each decision as a maneuver class plus a continuous parameter grounded in the model’s perceived scene facts.
Uses a Maneuver Bank and consistency losses so trajectories execute every admissible decision in a scene.
Automatically generates supervision from expert motion, counterfactual execution, rule-based checks, and VLM-refined annotations.
With a 0.5B language model, it runs online on a single consumer GPU and substantially reduces language-action inconsistency on Bench2Drive.

papers.abstract: Recent work on Weight-Space Programming uses LLMs to edit neural weights with forward passes only, conflating LLM scripting with the underlying algebra of forward-only editing. We show that for core structured editing regimes, an LLM optimizer is unnecessary, and introduce Forward Weight-Space Programming (FWSP): a deterministic pipeline combining probing, localization, stratified operators (O1-O4), automatic blind routing (83.3% vs. 33.3% for a 27B LLM with the same tool library), and paired verification with zero additional per-token computation. For reasoning LLMs, we propose Protected FisherGate, a closed-form covariance-whitened readout edit orthogonal to normal-reasoning states: on DeepSeek-R1-0528-8B, a single frozen math-calibrated patch achieves 84.2% HumanEval pass@1 (1K budget; 75.4 +/- 9.4% across 3/5 Stage-4-passing subsets), beating 512-token-reserved budget forcing by +14.6 pp (-23.4% tokens) while transferring across HF-to-vLLM backends on full GSM8K and MATH-500. Across five modalities and thirteen models (50K to 27B dense and FP8 MoE), we further prove and verify two operator boundaries, subspace entanglement and frozen representation span, where FWSP-localized LoRA bridges forward-only and gradient adaptation.
authors: Lin Yao
bullets: LLM optimizers are unnecessary for core weight-space programming regimes.
FWSP combines probing, localization, stratified operators, blind routing, and paired verification without extra per-token computation.
Protected FisherGate enables a closed-form, reasoning-state-orthogonal readout edit for math-calibrated reasoning models.
On DeepSeek-R1-0528-8B, one frozen patch reaches 84.2% HumanEval pass@1 and improves over 512-token budget forcing by 14.6 percentage points with fewer tokens.
Across five modalities and thirteen models, FWSP identifies subspace entanglement and frozen representation span as operator boundaries; localized LoRA can bridge these limits.

papers.title: Do We Really Need an LLM for Weight-Space Programming? A Deterministic Forward-Only Paradigm and Its Capability Boundaries

papers.abstract: Dense global attention is crucial for capturing cross-view geometry in visual geometry foundation models, yet its quadratic complexity limits efficient inference on long image sequences. Existing sparse attention methods primarily select entries of the global attention matrix based on attention probabilities and construct masks independently across layers, overlooking value redundancy and cross-layer information reuse. By analyzing attention distributions and clustering value representations across layers, we reveal two forms of \emph{cross-layer consistency}, characterized by highly similar attention probability distributions and localized changes in value redundancy structures. Building on these observations, we propose \textbf{DuCo}, a training-free sparse attention framework that exploits historical attention information and value redundancy for efficient geometric inference. Specifically, DuCo leverages historical attention information to estimate current-layer dense attention probabilities and introduces value clustering to exploit redundancy, with clusters efficiently refined through local updates across layers. Both factors are integrated through probability-weighted value distortion to jointly optimize four cluster representation states under an attention budget for sparse mask construction. Experiments across three visual geometry foundation models and five benchmarks demonstrate favorable accuracy--efficiency trade-offs.
authors: Liangyu Xiang, Junyu Gao, Xiaofeng Wang, Changsheng Xu
bullets: Dense global attention captures cross-view geometry but has quadratic cost on long image sequences.
DuCo estimates current attention from historical layers and reuses clustered value representations with efficient local updates.
Probability-weighted value distortion jointly optimizes cluster states under an attention budget to construct sparse masks.
Experiments on three visual geometry foundation models and five benchmarks show favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of DuCo. The resulting probabilities and clusters are jointly used to optimize cluster representation states based on probability-weighted value distortion, constructing sparse attention masks. Updated attention information and value clusters are propagated to subsequent layers as historical priors.

papers.abstract: We introduce a new model for real-time streaming captioning on a single GPU. YoloMT is a 449.8M-parameter streaming captioner that provides Pareto-frontier performance among generative vision models in its class. Distilled from a 27B teacher by SFT and GRPO, it leads every model under 1B parameters on OVO-Bench, MVBench, StreamingBench and Video-MME, answered from its captions, and beats LFM2.5-VL-1.6B and SmolVLM2-2.2B. YoloMT is designed to read more frames cheaply and make them informative, encoding each frame once and caching it as 16 tokens. This allows the model to incorporate and infer from past frames without additional vision passes, making it efficient and effective. We also provide a detailed recipe for training YoloMT, with its stages and data, as well as ablations that demonstrate the contribution of each component.
authors: Nessim Ben Abbes, Duc Han Le, Sabri Mtibaa, Van-Tam Nguyen
bullets: Targets efficient real-time streaming captioning with a single GPU.
Encodes each frame once and caches it as 16 tokens, enabling inference over past frames without repeated vision passes.
Distilled from a 27B teacher using supervised fine-tuning and GRPO.
Leads sub-1B-parameter models on OVO-Bench, MVBench, StreamingBench, and Video-MME when evaluated from captions.
Provides a training recipe and ablations covering its stages, data, and components.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Accuracy against time, memory and size: Tab. 1 in three plots. The mean accuracy of the four benchmarks (caption then answer, L=min(t, 16) past frames) against (a) the median T4 time of a 50-token caption at L=16, eager PyTorch FP16 (cream: one caption a second or faster; hatched: models whose weights alone exceed the T4’s memory), (b) the T4 process memory while captioning at L=16 (cream: the 2 GB budget; arrow: a lower bound, the weights alone), and (c) the parameters. A marker is a model family and its tag the model’s size; ∗: under 30 words per caption; Tab. 1 also reports the lead of YoloMT after deliberately truncating its captions to the three small baselines’ word counts. Qwen3.8-27B is the teacher.

Figure 3. Distilling a larger teacher into YoloMT in three stages. The teacher labels the student’s own view: a greedy caption for SFT, and sampled captions that yield claims and questions for RL. SFT starts with shorter captions on 2 s windows at L=1, then uses the sandwich rule up to L=5 and finally L=16 (shown). The last SFT phase trains all weights; GRPO shares one L in each group, and a KL penalty toward the SFT model keeps captions from ending in fact-free closers. On held-out OpenVid the result reaches 83.8% (L=0) to 92.6% (L=16) of the teacher ceiling in fact-F1, from one engine with p99 12.66–12.69 ms per frame on a T4.

Figure 2. Look once, read many. (a) Each sampled frame (one per second) passes the vision encoder once. Its 64 tokens enter the prompt as the present and, pooled to 16, a ring of the last 16 frames that later captions read; a caption reads L of these blocks, its lookback, 0 ≤ L ≤ 16, chosen at run time with one set of weights. (b) The pooler. Each 2×2 block of the projected 8×8 grid becomes one mean token (highlighted: one block followed through the pooler). A linear residual shared by the 16 positions transforms each mean without mixing positions; with zero-initialized weights and bias, the pooler starts as average pooling.

Figure 5. One second on the T4. Each frame carries one kind of work, so p99 per frame is 12.66–12.69 ms at every measured L; a larger L adds prefill frames and caption lag, not frame time. Bars: the p99 GPU time of each kind of frame at L=16, among the 30 frames of 33 ms in a second; dashed: the 16 ms budget per frame. Frame counts follow the engine’s prefill schedule and the mean caption lag. The schedule is new in YoloMT.

Fig. 5. Its output head is cut to 16,575 token ids, which cover 99.9% of the tokens of the teacher’s SFT labels, plus byte-level and special tokens. A caption still open at the next second would be abandoned (Tab. S1). Where FP16 captions differ from the float32 reference, they differ in wording at near-ties.

Every timed model with the same script on a T4. ‡: vLLM with weight-only INT8 or INT4, peak device memory. †: the weights alone (FP16; the teacher FP8). Fact-F1 as a percentage of the teacher ceiling (judge: phi-4) on held-out OpenVid (a training source of YoloMT, held out by video) and LLaVA-Video test (test), without a test-time word-limit penalty. Parentheses give the original score with the 60-word rule where the rounded values differ. This rule was part of YoloMT’s RL reward; the baselines were only prompted for 30–50 words. papers.title: You Only Look Multiple Times: YoloMT, a Real-Time Streaming Model on a T4

papers.abstract: We present $\mu$MPC, a fast model predictive control (MPC) framework that reduces online computation using learned Koopman-linearized dynamics. By precomputing finite-horizon control-to-output maps, $\mu$MPC eliminates lifted-state trajectories, yielding an action-only Koopman-Compiled QP (KC-QP) with $Hn_u$ decision variables, independent of lifted dimension. A fixed, precomputed primal operator enables efficient primal-dual iterations using only matrix-vector products and projections, accommodating changing goals and constraints without refactorization. This efficiency also enables control-aware dynamics learning through differentiable KC-QPs in the training loop and batched DAgger-style data aggregation. $\mu$MPC achieves solve times as low as $23\mu$s on a desktop CPU and 24 ms onboard a 168 MHz Crazyflie microcontroller. It scales to 4096D quadruped control in under 5 ms, visual planning with 2048D world models in 0.4 ms, and collision-aware planning for 200 quadrotors at over 30 Hz on the GPU. Across these benchmarks, $\mu$MPC achieves up to $108\times$ faster constrained MPC and $1907\times$ faster visuomotor planning than competing methods.
authors: Devesh Nath, Glen Chou
bullets: Precomputes finite-horizon control-to-output maps, removing lifted-state trajectories and making optimization size depend only on the control horizon and input dimension.
Uses a fixed primal operator for fast primal-dual iterations with matrix-vector products and projections, while supporting changing goals and constraints without refactorization.
Enables differentiable KC-QPs for control-aware dynamics learning and batched DAgger-style data aggregation.
Reports solve times from 23 μs on a desktop CPU to 24 ms on a 168 MHz Crazyflie, with scaling to high-dimensional quadruped, visual-planning, and multi-robot tasks.
The abstract reports up to 108× faster constrained MPC and 1907× faster visuomotor planning than competing methods.

papers.abstract: Catastrophic forgetting, the drastic loss of previously acquired capabilities when learning new ones, is a central challenge in language model fine-tuning. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is widely believed to be prone to such forgetting. Recent works have attributed this to the off-policy nature of SFT, arguing that on-policy learning is key to continual learning. In this paper, we challenge this premise. We show that while maximizing new-task performance can induce catastrophic forgetting, alternative hyperparameter choices (lower learning rate and batch size) can yield similar gains with little to no forgetting. With hyperparameters selected jointly for gain and retention, vanilla SFT retains prior capabilities far better than previously suggested and can be competitive with Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (SDFT), an on-policy approach designed to mitigate forgetting. While SDFT can be more robust to hyperparameter choices, it also requires a retention-aware criterion to identify hyperparameter configurations that avoid catastrophic forgetting. Our results challenge the view that on-policy training is what enables learning with retention and raise broader questions about what drives catastrophic forgetting during fine-tuning.
authors: Nirmit Joshi, Nathan Srebro, Eran Malach
bullets: SFT can forget substantially when hyperparameters are chosen solely to maximize new-task performance.
Lower learning rates and batch sizes can achieve similar gains while greatly reducing forgetting.
Jointly tuning for gain and retention makes vanilla SFT more retention-friendly than previously believed.
SFT can be competitive with Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning, though SDFT is more robust to hyperparameter choices.
Both approaches require retention-aware evaluation to avoid configurations that cause catastrophic forgetting.

papers.selection_reason: Challenges catastrophic forgetting assumptions in SFT, relevant to continual learning and retention.
papers.title: Tune for Retention, Not Just Gain: SFT Forgets Far Less than You Think
papers.tldr: Catastrophic forgetting in SFT is often a hyperparameter problem: tuning for both task gains and retention can preserve prior capabilities with little forgetting, sometimes matching on-policy SDFT.

papers.abstract: Multi-session hiring assistants must infer evolving recruiter preferences and decision patterns across projects and time. We introduce Open Knowledge Format (OKF)-indexed episodic memory to organize interactions and retrieve related events through their lineage. We also introduce Procedure Memory, which learns reusable decision procedures from these episodes through prompted reflection or reinforcement learning. We compare these approaches with no memory, full-history context, and conversation search, and evaluate Jev-class models for index navigation and GPT-5.6 Luna as a lower-cost alternative to GPT-5.4. In our evaluation, OKF-indexed retrieval achieves low-priority preference F1 scores of 0.93-0.95 at medium and high preference overlap between hiring projects. It significantly outperforms full-history context and conversation search in both settings, and no memory at high overlap, while using 69% fewer context tokens than full history. Procedure Memory reduces conversational turns by up to 39% relative to no memory. Qualitative and long-horizon evaluations provide evidence of temporal reasoning, with RL-learned procedures achieving 60% on both correct abstention and exact-field identification. Jev-class models improve conversational efficiency but more frequently miss temporally relevant evidence, highlighting the importance of evidence selection. On PersonaMem-v2, Procedure Memory with OKF retrieval achieves 50.2% accuracy versus 48.6% for full-history context and 29.0% for no memory, using 90.5% fewer reader input tokens than full history. GPT-5.6 Luna performs comparably to GPT-5.4 at lower cost. These findings highlight the value of structured episodic memory and learned decision procedures for efficient personalization and temporal reasoning.
authors: Praveen Kumar Bodigutla, Yizhi Zhang, Sai Vivek Kanaparthy, Arup De
bullets: OKF-indexed memory organizes interactions by lineage to retrieve temporally and project-relevant episodes.
Procedure Memory learns reusable hiring decision procedures through prompted reflection or reinforcement learning.
OKF retrieval reaches 0.93–0.95 low-priority preference F1 and uses 69% fewer context tokens than full-history context.
Procedure Memory reduces conversational turns by up to 39%; on PersonaMem-v2, the combined approach reaches 50.2% accuracy with 90.5% fewer reader input tokens than full history.
Smaller Jev-class models improve efficiency but more often miss temporally relevant evidence, emphasizing evidence selection.

papers.title: Procedure Inference as Memory: Learning Recruiter Decision Procedures from OKF-Structured Episodes in Multi-Session Hiring Assistants
papers.tldr: Structured episodic memory and learned decision procedures help multi-session hiring assistants track evolving recruiter preferences while reducing context use and conversation length.

papers.abstract: Establishing effective scaling laws for medical multimodal large language models (MLLMs) remains a persistent and fundamental challenge. Our systematic evaluation shows that existing medical MLLMs tend to underperform frontier general-purpose MLLMs across a range of medical tasks, while scaling model size primarily improves text capabilities rather than multimodal perception, and enabling reasoning modes fails to close this visual gap. To investigate how medical multimodal intelligence scales in practice, we introduce Sage-Med-Preview, a 35B-parameter medical multimodal model with 3B activated parameters, built by combining stage-specific curation over 322.7 million candidate records with a progressive training curriculum spanning medical pretraining, staged supervised fine-tuning, and adaptive reinforcement learning. Across this curriculum, progressive supervised refinement and adaptive reinforcement learning yield consistent stage-wise gains, substantially advancing both specialized visual understanding and medical language capabilities. Evaluated against 77 competing models across 238 clinical tasks spanning 61 public and 13 private multi-center benchmarks in more than 40 modalities, Sage-Med-Preview achieves an average score of 58.26% on the 31 public multimodal benchmarks. It outperforms the state-of-the-art open-source medical model Hulu-Med-235B-A22B at 50.99% and the general scientific model Intern-S2-Preview at 52.24%, and approaches the advanced proprietary model GPT-6.2-Sol across multiple tasks such as comprehensive multimodal understanding, report generation, and visual grounding. Although substantial challenges remain in complex medical reasoning and multi-step clinical workflows, this report provides empirical evidence, actionable data and training recipes, and a rigorous benchmark toward scalable clinical multimodal intelligence.

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots on deformable elastic terrains face a surface whose position and motion are coupled in space and time: deflection and rebound persist between contacts, and load at one foothold alters the support at others, so training must capture how each contact changes the support that follows. We present RIPPLE (Robust Interaction via Proprioceptive Policies on Large-deformation Elastic terrain), a simulation-to-real learning framework for humanoid control on such terrains. RIPPLE integrates ElasticMembrane, a pretensioned mass-spring mesh that models spatially coupled deflection, energy storage, and rebound, together with deformable contact into MJLab for GPU-parallel policy learning. Staged training then transfers rigid-ground skills to balance and jumping on these terrains using only proprioception, without vision or force sensing. Deployed zero-shot, the policies enable a MagicBot Z1 humanoid to balance, jump consecutively, and enter a trampoline from a rigid platform. In simulation, ElasticMembrane training holds standing success of at least 98.7% (mean over three seeds) on ElasticMembrane, IndependentSprings, and BouncyPlate under 0.3 m/s perturbations, whereas rigid-ground or contact-compliance training transfers poorly to the first two. A fixed policy tolerates stiffness from 0.35 to 2.8 times the training value, beds up to 7 m wide, and seven further simulated support scenarios, so transfer needs no calibration to the trampoline's stiffness. papers.abstract: Instruction-following robots need navigation policies that reach high accuracy and remain inexpensive to train and to run on a single graphics processing unit (GPU). The most accurate vision-language navigation policies for continuous environments rely on language models with 4 to 8 billion parameters, long observation histories, and large auxiliary corpora. Two properties of the standard training setup limit smaller policies. Imitation labels cover the states that an expert visits, whereas the running policy reaches states that its own errors produce. In addition, an image-plane waypoint exists only while the route lies inside the camera view. We present \textbf{\paper}, a monocular red-green-blue (RGB) policy with 2 billion (2B) parameters that addresses both limitations. \paper adapts Qwen3-VL-2B with low-rank adapters and processes an eight-frame memory and the current view in one forward pass. The policy predicts the route direction as a bearing in the body frame of the agent, which remains defined for every heading, and a deterministic controller converts this bearing into motion. This design allows training to relabel the states that the policy itself visits. On-policy correction improves success, while bearing decoding outperforms image-plane waypoint scanning across all evaluated start headings with identical weights. On the \valunseen split, \paper achieves \rFinSR\% success on Room-to-Room in Continuous Environments (\rtor), averaged over three seeds, and \rRxFinSR\% on its Room-Across-Room counterpart (\rxr). Inference requires \rDecMs\,ms and \rInferGB\,GiB of memory, while training takes \rCostTrainTyp\ GPU-hours on one 12\,GB consumer GPU.

papers.abstract: Effective robotic manipulation calls for multimodal memory and rapid adaptation to shifts in contact dynamics. However, many existing policies, which retain either visual or wrench history, may miss key cues from the other modality. Moreover, even with wrench memory, fixed policies can struggle when contact conditions shift at deployment. To this end, we introduce M$^{2}$AdaptVLA, a vision-language-action model that integrates visual and wrench memories with predictive test-time adaptation. For visual memory, the model uses test-time training (TTT) to encode observation history in fast weights. Each entry in the bounded TTT bank combines the corresponding frame's features with a readout from these weights, preserving cues that predate the oldest retained frame. For wrench memory, a context gate controls how much the action expert draws on wrench history as it jointly denoises future actions and wrenches. For predictive test-time adaptation, the auxiliary wrench prediction loss also provides online self-supervision. Using measured wrenches as targets, we update low-rank policy adapters by backpropagating only through the final denoising step. Real-world experiments show that the TTT bank outperforms visual memory baselines on progress tracking, scene recall, and demonstration following. On contact-sensitive tasks, the context gate yields higher success rates than direct injection or gated cross-attention. Predictive test-time adaptation improves robustness to shifts in contact dynamics. On eight tasks requiring visual and wrench memory, M$^{2}$AdaptVLA achieves a mean success rate of 82.71%, a 31.46% absolute gain over the strongest baseline. The project page is available at https://tlf-tlf.github.io/M2AdaptVLAPage/.

papers.abstract: Collaborative reconstruction with consumer phones promises faster and more complete indoor maps. However, heterogeneous devices introduce degraded observations and unreliable cross-device associations, so a single poor contributor or incorrect match can corrupt the shared Gaussian map. To address this, we propose \textbf{CADENCE}, a collaborative Gaussian simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) system that separates finding cross-device matches from deciding whether and how peer observations update the map. To find matches, a sensor-grounded regional memory summarizes committed observations and ranks candidate peer regions using appearance, relative pose, gravity, barometric altitude, and observation quality. Deterministic geometric verification and optional physical checks then decide which of the proposed matches are accepted. Once a match is accepted, separate cue-based confidences control how its observations contribute to pose constraints, geometry, appearance, and memory. As a result, useful depth can still contribute even when color is unreliable. Throughout this process, local tracking remains isolated from mapping, verification, and networking. We evaluate CADENCE on eight Matterport3D houses that were not used to train the memory. On these houses, regional memory achieves an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of $0.95$ to $0.97$ and thus outperforms appearance retrieval, while verification keeps false-link rates below $0.5\,\%$. Furthermore, soft confidence weighting reduces the mean receiver peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) loss from $2.66$ to $1.05$\,dB across eight degradations while retaining useful peer depth. Finally, using inertial and platform motion, CADENCE tracks all twelve held-out iPhone scans with a mean absolute trajectory error of $6.98$\,cm, and its refined maps achieve better average rendering quality than the baselines.

On eight held-out Matterport3D houses, memory reached 0.95–0.97 AUROC, verification kept false-link rates below 0.5%, and confidence weighting reduced mean PSNR loss from 2.66 to 1.05 dB; all twelve held-out iPhone scans were tracked with 6.98 cm mean absolute trajectory error.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in video understanding, yet existing video question answering (VQA) benchmarks mainly evaluate models in offline settings. Real-world streaming scenarios instead require models to answer context-dependent queries by retrieving and reasoning over evidence distributed across the video history. We introduce StreamRecall, a benchmark for context-aware Multi evidence reasoning in streaming video QA. StreamRecall requires models to retrieve, associate, and reason over temporally scattered evidence to answer queries at the appropriate moment. It contains 4,983 questions over 462 videos, with context-aligned query times and fine-grained temporal evidence annotations. We further propose the Evidence Utilization Cascade to diagnose model reasoning through evidence localization, grounding, chain completion, and answer derivation. To enable efficient long-term streaming reasoning, we present EviStream, a training-free causal visual memory mechanism that preserves reasoning-critical evidence under a fixed KV budget. Experiments reveal substantial gaps between current VLMs and realistic streaming requirements, establishing StreamRecall as a foundation for developing evidence-aware streaming video intelligence.
authors: Cui Yakun, Tiantian Geng, Huixiang Kong, Xingqun Qi, Sirui Han, Yike Guo

Presents EviStream, a causal visual memory mechanism that preserves reasoning-critical evidence under a fixed KV budget.
Experiments show current VLMs remain substantially short of realistic streaming video reasoning requirements.

papers.abstract: Due to context-length constraints, most MLLMs cannot process full-length videos and therefore rely on sampling a subset of frames as input. However, existing sampling methods, ranging from uniform sampling to relevance-based selection, are often driven by a single sampling principle and thus struggle to accommodate the heterogeneous evidential requirements of different queries: some demand a holistic understanding of how the video unfolds over time, while others hinge on fine-grained events within a short temporal window. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{Hierarchical Adaptive Frame Sampling (HAS)}, a two-stage frame sampling framework. In the first stage, \emph{Backbone Frame Construction}, we apply a Determinantal Point Process (DPP) to sample frames that are both query-relevant and non-redundant. These selected frames capture key moments across the video and form the backbone of the sampling set, providing a foundation for subsequent enrichment. In the second stage, \emph{Adaptive Contextual Enrichment}, we analyze the temporal distribution of the backbone frames to infer the query's requirements and adaptively allocate the remaining frame budget between Local and Global Context. The Local Context enriches the backbone with fine-grained temporal dynamics and short-range causal relations, whereas the Global Context connects temporally isolated evidence and provides a holistic view of the entire video to support global understanding. Through such a hierarchical two-stage process, HAS effectively addresses diverse query requirements. Incorporated into three leading MLLMs, it demonstrates consistently superior performance across the Video-MME, LongVideoBench, and MLVU benchmarks.
authors: Yuyao Sun, Daiqi Shi, Shuang Li, Liao Zhang, Yang Cai, Deqing Wang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of sampling frames for queries requiring either holistic video understanding or fine-grained local evidence.
Uses a Determinantal Point Process to select relevant, non-redundant backbone frames spanning key moments.
Infers query needs from the backbone’s temporal distribution and allocates remaining budget to local or global context.
Local enrichment captures short-range dynamics and causal relations, while global enrichment connects isolated evidence across the video.
Shows consistently superior performance when integrated with three leading MLLMs on Video-MME, LongVideoBench, and MLVU.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies perform well on fixed-instruction robotic manipulation benchmarks, but their ability to adapt to instruction changes during execution remains understudied. We introduce the Dynamic Task Update Benchmark (DTU-Bench), evaluating 40 task revisions across seven update types and three execution stages using LIBERO, a simulated robotic manipulation benchmark. We compare performance when a new instruction is given before execution starts versus during execution, and examine whether the new task instructions are followed. Across 13 representative VLA configurations, average task success is 95.8% on the original object-manipulation tasks, compared with only 1.6% when the instruction changes which object to manipulate during execution. Controlled diagnostics show that policies often complete the original task before the updated one, and that their responses depend on the robot's physical state. We further test whether a simple scripted controller that releases the grasped object and moves the arm back helps robots respond to instruction changes. This improves success from 2% to 38% for {\pi}0.5 and from 8% to 48% for DM0.5, but can cause unwanted object motion. These findings reveal limitations that fixed-instruction benchmarks and task-success metrics alone can overlook in evaluating robotic manipulation. Project page: https://dtu-bench.github.io/

papers.abstract: We present AliceAI-Foundation-80B-A3B-Base, a mixture-of-experts language model with 80 billion total parameters and approximately 3 billion active parameters per token, trained from scratch at Yandex and released under the Apache 2.0 license. The model combines Kimi Delta Attention with full attention, uses Attention Residuals, and is trained with Muon. Training comprises general pretraining on 17.5 trillion tokens, two context-extension stages, and a dedicated stage for reasoning and agentic interaction. We describe the data collection and augmentation pipelines, evaluation protocols, architectural ablations, and scaling-law experiments. We identify the limitations of held-out training loss as a proxy for downstream performance and introduce an auxiliary loss on mixture-of-experts outputs to stabilize training at the predicted learning rate. Domain-specific data selection and augmentation improve factual knowledge, mathematics, and programming skills, while agent trajectories introduced during pretraining improve performance on agentic benchmarks after supervised fine-tuning. In zero-shot reasoning evaluation, the model achieves leading results among open base models of comparable size, with 88.7% pass@8 on IMO-AnswerBench and 82.9% pass@8 on LiveCodeBench v5-v6. To evaluate Russian-language factual knowledge, we introduce and release two benchmarks with their evaluation protocols: WikiWebFacts, which tests short factual questions drawn from encyclopedic sources and search queries, and HardMultiQA, which tests more demanding factual questions inspired by user interactions. Our model scores 86.5% on WikiWebFacts and 67.9% on HardMultiQA, compared with 83.2% and 65.4% for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base (284B total and 13B active parameters) and 72.8% and 54.5% for Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B-Base (120B total and 12B active parameters), outperforming both larger models on these benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Classifying a whole-slide image requires encoding thousands of high-resolution tiles with a pathology foundation model, which accounts for most of the inference cost. Existing efficient methods reduce this cost by selecting fewer tiles, but typically train a new model around their selection strategy. A largely unexplored alternative is to keep an existing full-bag model frozen and run it on selected tiles at the same encoder cost. We introduce this comparison, alongside random tile sampling at matched cost. To select tiles, we fit a lightweight selector with 3.3K parameters to the attention of a frozen model, without additional slide labels. The selector ranks regions from a slide thumbnail, encodes the top K regions at 5x magnification, and selects b for processing at 20x. We evaluate seven frozen MIL aggregators on six tasks and compare them with nine efficient methods trained on the same features and splits. At a budget of (K,b)=(1000,10), encoding costs about 6.6% of the full bag and is 10-14x faster, excluding tiling. The AUROC drop is no more than 0.005 in 33 of 36 aggregator-task pairs. At (500,10), the cost falls to about 4% and inference is 13-22x faster, but AUROC drops by up to 0.035 on CAMELYON17, where small metastases are easily missed. Selection improves over random sampling by about 0.10 AUROC on tasks with focal lesions, while random sampling performs well on diffuse tasks. In our comparisons, the frozen model at (500,10) is ahead of nine efficient methods in 55 of 60 paired comparisons. Giving an existing WSI model fewer tiles is thus a baseline that a new efficient model should be compared with at matched encoder cost.
authors: Haoyu He, Mahdi S. Hosseini
bullets: Motivation: Whole-slide classification is dominated by encoding thousands of high-resolution tiles.
Method: A 3.3K-parameter selector ranks regions from a slide thumbnail using a frozen model’s attention, then encodes only the top regions at higher magnification.
Evaluation: Seven frozen MIL aggregators were tested on six tasks against random sampling and nine efficient methods at matched feature and split settings.
Results: Encoding 10 selected tiles from 1,000 candidates costs about 6.6% of a full bag and is 10–14× faster, with AUROC loss ≤0.005 in 33/36 aggregator-task pairs.
Scope: More aggressive selection can miss small focal lesions; at 500 candidates, AUROC dropped by up to 0.035 on CAMELYON17, while random sampling worked well for diffuse tasks.

papers.abstract: Video large language models incur substantial inference costs from long visual token sequences. Existing video token compression methods mitigate these costs by exploiting spatial redundancy within frames and temporal redundancy across frames. However, many approaches impose predefined processing orders or fixed allocation ratios for spatial and temporal compression, limiting their ability to adapt to the varying balance of spatiotemporal redundancy across videos. To address this limitation, we propose PURA, a training-free method that prunes visual tokens through unified spatiotemporal redundancy assessment. For each token, PURA constructs spatial and temporal reference candidates and selects the reference with the lowest representation error across the two dimensions. The representation error is combined with token importance to determine each token's removal cost. To avoid the time overhead of removing the lowest-cost token one by one, we introduce Coordinated Pruning, which iteratively groups mutually compatible low-cost removals into batches for simultaneous execution and updates the pruning state after each batch until the target budget is reached. Extensive experiments on three video large language models and five video understanding benchmarks demonstrate that PURA achieves a favorable trade-off between task performance and inference efficiency.
authors: Yuyao Sun, Hongli Yuan, Shuang Li, Tao Deng, Deqing Wang
bullets: Addresses the high cost of long visual token sequences in video large language models.
Builds spatial and temporal reference candidates for each token and selects the one with lower representation error.
Combines representation error with token importance to estimate each token’s removal cost.
Uses Coordinated Pruning to batch compatible low-cost removals instead of pruning tokens individually.
Experiments across three video large language models and five video understanding benchmarks show a favorable performance–efficiency trade-off.
