papers.abstract: It is commonly accepted that high-level concepts are represented linearly in the representation space of large neural networks. For Large Vision Language Models (LVLMs), finding those interpretable directions in visual representations is important for interpretability. To find them, the classical approach is to train a linear classifier on the representations, but it needs a large amount of labels and only recovers what can be read from the representations, not what the model actually uses. In this paper we start from the following insight: The LLM Decoder of an LVLM is also a classifier whose classes are the possible next tokens. So we use its first-order Taylor expansion as a linear classifier. Hence, we introduce Decoder-as-a-Probe (DaP), which significantly outperforms classical probing and steering baselines especially when training data is sparse. (1) It verbalizes what an LVLM perceives in a given image. (2) It can surgically change the perception of the LVLM about specific attributes (e.g. change only the color, the clothes worn or the action done). Due to its simplicity and data efficiency, we believe DaP can serve as a plug-and-play tool for LVLM research, such as interpretability, hallucination mitigation or instruction tuning.
authors: Adhemar de Senneville, Xavier Bou, J\'er\'emy Anger, Rafael Grompone, Gabriele Facciolo
bullets: Addresses the need to identify interpretable directions in LVLM visual representations without large labeled datasets.
Approximates the decoder with a first-order Taylor expansion, treating it as a linear classifier over next-token classes.
Can verbalize what an LVLM perceives in an image and surgically alter specific attributes such as color, clothing, or action.
Outperforms classical probing and steering baselines, particularly when training data is sparse.
Proposed as a plug-and-play tool for interpretability, hallucination mitigation, and instruction tuning.

papers.abstract: Latent world models plan in a compact latent space by predicting the outcomes of actions. Their planners judge a plan by the latent distance between its predicted end state and the goal image. We show that this distance fails in two distinct ways. First, it loses directional signal a few steps from the goal, causing distant goals to fail. Second, it weighs the robot arm over the manipulated object, causing manipulation to fail at contact. We measure both failures directly on recorded data by asking whether a lower latent distance corresponds to true progress toward the goal. Across five environments, six visual representations (including raw pixels and V-JEPA 2), and nine Meta-World tasks, this ranking test cleanly separates the two failures, and the graph distance to a goal predicts where closed-loop planning breaks down. Both failures share a single remedy: replacing the distant goal with a nearby target that lies on a recorded trajectory. We realize this principle with Graph Anchors, a training-free planner for frozen latent world models. It builds a sparse graph once over the model's own training frames and aims each planning step at a node a few moves ahead along the shortest path to the goal, keeping paths on recorded transitions wherever contact matters. On goals up to 400 steps away, Graph Anchors raise LeWM's success from 13% to 85% on PointMaze-Medium, from 8% to 87% on PointMaze-Large, and from 5% to 71% on Push-T, where stronger search toward the goal fails and where prior training-free planners break down under missing step horizons, subsampling shortcuts, or fragmented contact.
authors: Syed Nazmus Sakib, Abdul Monaf Chowdhury, Peizhen Li, Nafiul Haque, Chandak Chakma, Md Mehedi Hasan, Zehong Cao, Shifat E. Arman
bullets: Latent goal-distance planning fails because it loses directional guidance near distant goals and overweights the robot arm during object contact.
A ranking test on recorded data diagnoses these failures across five environments, six visual representations, and nine Meta-World tasks.
Graph Anchors build a sparse graph over training frames and guide each step toward a nearby node on a shortest recorded path to the goal.
The training-free method raises LeWM success from 13% to 85% on PointMaze-Medium, 8% to 87% on PointMaze-Large, and 5% to 71% on Push-T.
The approach targets goals up to 400 steps away and preserves recorded transitions where contact dynamics matter.

papers.abstract: A watermark lets the provider of a language model recognise the text its model wrote, which matters more as generated text becomes hard to tell from human writing: provenance underpins academic integrity, the fight against misinformation and new regulation. Providers have started to watermark the text of their models, and to explain how their watermarks work. Explaining a watermark, however, also tells an attacker how to break it, and there are two ways to do so: reword the text to erase the mark, or learn the mark and copy it onto text the model never wrote. Each attack has been studied on its own. We study an attacker that reads the published design to choose between them: it erases the watermarks that are hard to learn and forges the ones that survive rewording. Against it, every existing watermark we compare fails. We propose KeyedLex, which reads its secret key from the grammar of the previous sentence, which rewording changes little, and whose detector does not need to recover the key exactly. It outperforms every watermark we compare on both models we test, losing about half of its signal where the best alternative loses two thirds, at no extra cost in text quality over the best-known watermarks.
authors: Jon Carmona, Jon Irureta, Jon Imaz, Aizea Lojo, Juan Mart\'inez-Romo, Lourdes Araujo
bullets: Published watermark designs enable two attacks: rewording to erase the signal or learning it to copy the signal onto ungenerated text.
The proposed attacker selects whichever attack is more effective for each known watermark, defeating all compared existing methods.
KeyedLex derives its secret key from the previous sentence’s grammar, which tends to remain stable under rewording.
Its detector does not need to recover the key exactly, improving robustness to attacks.
On both tested models, KeyedLex retains about half its signal versus two thirds lost by the best alternative, with no additional text-quality cost.

papers.abstract: Recurrent-depth language models generate each token by iterating a shared block of layers until its hidden state converges. Inference methods for these models decide when to stop the iteration, yet every token still starts from random noise and pays the full cost of converging. We show that where the iteration starts is a second, independent lever. A token's fixed point is predictable from the state at which the previous token stopped, after a learned change of coordinates, and we introduce FlyingStart, a linear warm start that is fitted in closed form on the frozen model and costs under 5% of one loop. The iteration and its stopping rule are unchanged, so the exit criterion certifies the same distance to the fixed point from any start: a better start removes loops at unchanged accuracy. On Huginn-0125, FlyingStart matches the accuracy of the strongest training-free baseline with 14--19% fewer decoding layers, raises batched throughput by 16--18% in two serving engines, and adds a further 10--14% on top of self-speculative decoding. A contraction analysis predicts the number of loops saved on all four models we study, including one where the prediction was recorded before any evaluation, and token by token on Huginn, and it identifies when a warm start pays off: the saving grows with the number of loops a model needs to converge.
authors: Runguo Li, Dezhen Lu, Zixiang Ni
bullets: Targets recurrent-depth language models where each token repeatedly applies shared layers until convergence.
Uses a learned linear change-of-coordinates warm start fitted in closed form on the frozen model, costing under 5% of one loop.
On Huginn-0125, matches the strongest training-free baseline with 14–19% fewer decoding layers.
Improves batched throughput by 16–18% in two serving engines and adds 10–14% gains alongside self-speculative decoding.
A contraction analysis predicts loop savings and indicates warm starts help most when convergence normally requires more loops.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a warm-start method to reduce decoding loops in recurrent-depth LLMs, directly improving inference efficiency.
papers.title: FlyingStart: Learned Cross-Token Warm Starts for Fixed-Point Decoding in Recurrent-Depth Language Models
papers.tldr: FlyingStart accelerates fixed-point decoding by predicting each token’s converged state from the previous token, reducing iteration cost without changing accuracy or stopping criteria.

papers.abstract: Almost every short-video upload now passes through a classifier that fuses video, speech, and on-screen text into one decision about whether it may be seen. It moderates every language community on the platform at once, and fairness across them is judged, if at all, from one accuracy score. That score is compatible with error falling almost entirely on one language group. An audit that goes looking reads the model's decisions, the last stage of a long pipeline and the one whose test has the fewest items. We ask where in a fused pipeline a subgroup asymmetry can be detected at all: in what the classifier may read, in what its branches encode, or in what it decides. We answer this with a post-hoc audit of a published TikTok classifier, holding all three stages to one significance standard using only its logged decisions, labels, and pre-fusion features, with source language as the subgroup axis. The asymmetry is significant at the stage deciding what the model may read, and again in what the text branch encodes. At the earlier stage, a language-blind cap admits less of a Vietnamese clip than an English one, for reasons of segmentation, not verbosity. The asymmetry is undetectable at the decision, where the smallest subgroup leaves twelve items to test. An audit reading only decisions looks where its evidence is thinnest; the same test staged upstream recovers a disparity the decision-level view returns as noise.
authors: Kardelen Subasi, Jaros{\l}aw A. Chudziak
bullets: Audits a fused video, speech, and text moderation pipeline using logged decisions, labels, and pre-fusion features.
Tests three stages under one significance standard, with source language as the subgroup axis.
Finds significant asymmetry in what content the model may read and in the text branch’s representations.
A language-blind cap admits less of a Vietnamese clip than an English clip due to segmentation, not verbosity.
Decision-level asymmetry is undetectable because the smallest subgroup provides only twelve test items.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The audited pipeline and the three stages at which we test it. A clip enters MTikGuard as a raw video file; extraction yields sampled frames, a Whisper transcript, and an EasyOCR string concatenated into one text field, a language-blind cap decides how much of that field survives, two encoders represent what is left, and a fusion layer emits one label. The audit taps three of these links and holds all three to the same significance standard. The item counts show why they are not equally testable. The cap and the encoders can be tested over every clip, while a false-positive rate exists only over a subgroup’s true-PASS items, which leaves twelve in the smallest subgroup.

Figure 3: What a language-blind token cap does to each subgroup. (a) Fused-text length per clip (log scale) against the pipeline’s 64-word-piece cap, where everything above the line is discarded before the classifier reads it, with the median share each subgroup keeps printed above. (b) The cause is segmentation: median word pieces per character with bootstrap 95% intervals, Vietnamese separated from English while the volume of text extracted does not differ. Tests (Holmadjusted within the four-test family): truncated at all, Fisher p = 0.21; retained fraction, Mann–Whitney p = 0.014, padj = 0.042; word pieces per character, p = 3 × 10−4, padj = 0.001; extracted volume, p = 0.18. The undetected-language subgroup is the most fragmented and most truncated, and its wide interval is the same small-subgroup problem that defeats the comparison in Section 5.1.

Figure 1: The case the audit is built to surface. Two creators upload near-identical borderline clips, one narrated in English and one in Vietnamese, to the same classifier and receive opposite outcomes. One aggregate accuracy score is reported whichever way the errors fall, whether they are spread evenly across the language groups or concentrated almost entirely on one, so only disaggregation separates the two situations.

Table 2: The two attribution instruments at the representation stage. Gaps are percentage points. Nulling audio or on-screen text leaves both gaps unchanged and is omitted. Removing video zeroes the gap only by collapsing the classifier to always-flag, which is what the accuracy column shows. Each probe branch is scored against its own permuted-label null, since a branch’s chance level depends on its own feature geometry; ≤0.02 is the floor attainable with 50 permutations.

Table 1: Disaggregated error rates by source-language subgroup on the 790-item held-out test split. Unknown = items with no confidently detected language (Section 3.3). The 95% Wilson intervals are computed over each subgroup’s true-PASS items, which number 142, 46 and 12 respectively; the unknown subgroup’s interval therefore spans 5–45%. All three overlap, which is why the 7.97-point point-estimate gap does not survive Fisher’s exact test (p = 0.59; Vietnamese-vs-unknown FNR p = 0.15; all six pairwise tests Holm-adjusted p ≥ 0.44).

papers.selection_reason: Conducts a fairness audit of a fused multimodal moderation pipeline (video, speech, text), identifying where subgroup asymmetry enters the decision-making process.
papers.title: Where Does the Asymmetry Enter? Staging a Fairness Audit Across a Fused Multimodal Moderation Pipeline
papers.tldr: A staged fairness audit finds that language-based asymmetry enters upstream—in content access and text encoding—while decision-only audits miss it because their evidence is too sparse.

papers.abstract: A first-person (ego) image reveals what a camera sees, but not who or what carries it. Given a synchronized third-person (exo) image, camera wearer identification asks who is ego: which candidate carries the ego camera? We extend this task beyond humans to robots, vehicles, animals, and drones, and broaden its spatial scope (where is ego) from selecting a provided candidate mask to wearer segmentation with absence prediction and mutual camera localization across ego-exo views. We introduce FindEgo-1M, comprising 1.16M real and simulated ego-exo pairs across 12 wearer types, 17 domains, and 111 test settings. Our approach exploits a geometric relation: the ego camera's projection into the exo image, i.e., the epipole, lies on or near its wearer. We introduce EgoRay-ZS, the first method to turn a frozen feed-forward 3D reconstruction model, VGGT-$\Omega$, into a training-free solution for wearer identification and segmentation. Its geometric readout ranks candidate masks or segmentation proposals by angular offset and distance to the ego camera, while the relative pose provides mutual camera directions. We then develop the full EgoRay model through pose-supervised training on FindEgo-1M and label-free test-time adaptation constrained by candidate masks. Without task-specific training, EgoRay-ZS achieves 78.0% identification accuracy on TF2023's original labels, versus 52.9% reported for the dataset-trained PEN. On FindEgo-1M, EgoRay achieves state-of-the-art chance-corrected accuracy of 87.1 and 77.7 on seen and unseen settings. On matched queries, EgoRay also outperforms GPT-6 Astra by 31.6 and 21.3 points on seen and unseen settings, respectively, while running $18\times$ faster. Data, code, and models will be released.
authors: Yifan Jin, Zheng Zhang, Tianwen Qian, Dong Wang, Bo Zhao, Yanwei Fu, Yuqian Fu
bullets: Extends camera-wearer identification from humans to robots, vehicles, animals, and drones, while adding wearer segmentation, absence prediction, and mutual camera localization.

EgoRay reaches 87.1% and 77.7% chance-corrected accuracy on seen and unseen settings, respectively, and is faster and more accurate than the reported baselines in the abstract.

papers.selection_reason: Ego-exo camera wearer identification and segmentation using feed-forward 3D reconstruction; relevant to egocentric video learning and 3D vision.
papers.title: Who Is Ego? Scaling Cross-View Camera Wearer Identification and Segmentation beyond Humans
papers.tldr: EgoRay uses cross-view geometry from 3D reconstruction to identify and segment the wearer of an ego camera—including nonhuman carriers—without requiring task-specific training.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have improved semantic and visual reasoning, enabling UAVs to search for open-vocabulary queries in unstructured environments at high altitude. However, existing systems mainly follow low-altitude strategies, focusing on close-range iterative exploration, requiring storage-intensive dense 3D metric-semantic reconstructions or relying on large cloud-serviced VLMs assuming constant internet access. We propose SkySearcher, an aerial semantic search navigation method designed for large outdoor scenes. SkySearcher integrates onboard VLM reasoning with a lightweight probabilistic representation that guides an information-driven exploration. The VLM extracts semantic information at high altitude about the target or cues informing about its location. This information is projected to the ground using the camera frustum instead of limited-depth sensors, actively exploiting the expansive field of view offered by elevated sensing. The information regarding the presence or absence of semantic cues is then integrated into a probabilistic map by modeling the spatial belief of the query, maintaining a task-driven memory for the mission and guiding the exploration towards semantically promising regions. Extensive simulations for Aerial Object Goal Navigation on public benchmarks demonstrate that SkySearcher significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in success rate, flight time, and navigation precision, while a deployment of SkySercher running fully onboard a drone demonstrates the applicability of our approach.
authors: Giacomo Vianello, David Morilla-Cabello, Juan Dendarieta Serrano, Ruggero Carli, Eduardo Montijano

papers.abstract: Upgrading feed-forward geometry to metric scale with visual-inertial odometry (VIO) raises the question of which correction should align dense feed-forward prediction with sparse metric VIO anchors. Existing methods use either a similarity transformation, which cannot represent depth-dependent distortion, or a projective transformation, which alters pre-calibrated intrinsics. We prove that the transformations compatible with pre-calibrated intrinsics form a ten-dimensional manifold. Beyond Sim(3), this manifold contains three degrees of freedom (DoF) that locate the plane at infinity and leave residuals growing quadratically with depth range after any similarity alignment. These DoF are invisible in the image and can be resolved only by metric depth along viewing rays or by multi-view constraints. To estimate them, we propose ProManO, a probabilistic manifold optimization framework in which every anchor is weighted by its along-ray uncertainty and inlier probability within a single expectation-maximization (EM) procedure. ProManO certifies the similarity synchronization and refines the plane at infinity only where it is observable, which guarantees an objective value no worse than that of the optimal similarity alignment. Experiments on EuRoC, CID-SIMS, Oxford Spires, and KITTI-360 demonstrate that ProManO achieves the highest mean F1 and outperforms Sim(3) alignment on all four datasets. The project page is available at https://h0xg.github.io/ProManO/.
authors: Lingxiang Hu, Zhenjun Zhao, Qi Shao, Naima Ait Oufroukh, Fabien Bonardi, Raymond Ghandour, Shenghai Yuan, Javier Civera, Baoru Huang
bullets: Existing Sim(3) alignment cannot model depth-dependent distortion, while unrestricted projective alignment changes pre-calibrated intrinsics.
The valid intrinsic-preserving transformations form a ten-dimensional manifold with three additional degrees of freedom beyond Sim(3).
ProManO estimates these degrees of freedom using probabilistic manifold optimization and EM, weighting anchors by along-ray uncertainty and inlier probability.
The method refines the plane at infinity only when observable and guarantees an objective no worse than optimal similarity alignment.
Experiments on EuRoC, CID-SIMS, Oxford Spires, and KITTI-360 report the highest mean F1 and improvement over Sim(3) on all four datasets.

papers.abstract: Path-traced rendering shows CT and MR volumes with realistic lighting, but it restarts after every change of view, clipping plane or transfer function (TF), the map from voxel intensity to colour and opacity, which limits the frame rate. Feed-forward Gaussian splatting models such as RenderFM predict the Gaussians directly from the volume instead of fitting them to each scan, and are fast. RenderFM, however, handles only CT, runs its network again after every TF edit, has no clipping operator, and places its Gaussians on a uniform 3-mm grid that blurs organ boundaries and cut faces. We present RenderFM-Next, a feed-forward model that addresses these limits. One network handles both CT and MR. Its Gaussians are predicted once per volume: a new TF needs no pass of this network, and a clipping plane cuts them exactly, using operators from prior work. The model predicts coarse 3-mm Gaussians for the whole volume and refines them to 1.5 mm only where refinement improves the image. A small score head ranks the coarse Gaussians by how much refining them would reduce the rendering error; at render time the user chooses how many are refined, and those next to a clipping plane are always refined, which sharpens cut faces. We build a benchmark of about 2,000 CT and MR scans with path-traced references under clinical presets, TF edits and clipping. Our RenderFM-Next improves over RenderFM retrained on this benchmark by 2.8 dB on CT and 2.4 dB on MR and renders a 1600x1600 view in 4-6 ms. Refinement adds 0.30 / 0.69 dB over the same model trained without it (0.51 / 1.17 dB on cut faces), and refining a learned 10% of the coarse Gaussians matches a random 50% with 2.4x fewer Gaussians. Project page: https://gaozhongpai.github.io/renderfmnext/
authors: Zhongpai Gao, Benjamin Planche, Meng Zheng, Anwesa Choudhuri, Chaoyi Zhou, Terrence Chen, Ziyan Wu
bullets: Addresses RenderFM’s single-modality support, repeated inference after transfer-function edits, lack of clipping, and blurred boundaries from a uniform 3-mm grid.
Predicts coarse Gaussians once per volume, supports both CT and MR, applies new transfer functions without network reruns, and clips splats exactly.
Uses a score head to selectively refine Gaussians from 3 mm to 1.5 mm, prioritizing regions where refinement improves quality and areas near clipping planes.
On a benchmark of about 2,000 CT and MR scans, it improves over retrained RenderFM by 2.8 dB on CT and 2.4 dB on MR, rendering 1600×1600 views in 4–6 ms.
Refining 10% of learned coarse Gaussians matches random refinement of 50% using 2.4× fewer Gaussians; gains are especially strong on cut faces.

papers.abstract: Recent feed-forward approaches mark a paradigm shift in novel view synthesis by eliminating the reliance on per-scene optimization, directly inferring 3D representations from input views. However, their reliance on global scene-token context incurs substantial memory and latency overhead, constraining their ability to handle increasingly dense source-view contexts. Compressing source representations offers an intuitive way to limit this token budget. Prior general-purpose compression methods are not tailored for novel view synthesis, as their fixed, target-agnostic nature fails to adapt evidence allocation to individual target views. To overcome this, we introduce TACC, a target-aware compression module tailored for feed-forward latent NVS. Specifically, TACC organizes each source view into a progressive carrier hierarchy. Driven by source-target geometric relevance, it adaptively retrieves tokens to dynamically allocate exact computational quotas. This selective retrieval directly yields a compact, target-conditioned representation. Extensive experiments on the RE10K demonstrate that under dense input settings, TACC achieves $9.23\times$ and $64\times$ higher Effective FPS than Full Context on LagerNVS and LVSM, respectively. Effective FPS excludes one-time source encoding and Carrier construction.

papers.abstract: AI wearables, such as smart glasses, extend the context available to agents beyond digital environments to users' physical surroundings. With these devices, computer tasks can originate from users' ongoing activities rather than solely from explicit instructions. Through first-person observations, agents can identify objects and activities relevant to user requests and ground digital tasks in the surrounding context. We call this interaction paradigm Ego Use. However, first-person observations are limited by the wearer's viewpoint and may provide incomplete or ambiguous evidence of ongoing activities. As new observations arrive, agents may need to revise their understanding of the physical context and user intent, and reassess whether prior digital actions remain valid. Whether current agents can reliably handle these changes remains insufficiently evaluated. We introduce EgoUseBench, a benchmark for evaluating Ego Use across three interaction settings with different levels of first-person context. Computer-Use relies on explicit instructions, Offline Ego Use provides prerecorded first-person context before execution, and Online Ego Use provides continuous observations as user intent evolves. Based on over 74 hours of real-world first-person recordings, we construct 693 tasks across the three interaction settings. To capture task evolution, we track first-person observations, user requirements, and website state separately. We further group tasks by how information changes during execution, resulting in three types: Graft (revised user requirements), Refresh (new first-person observations), and Clarify (agent-initiated information seeking). We evaluate advanced models and find that average success rates in Online Ego Use are 26.3% lower than in Computer-Use. This result reveals the difficulty of keeping task execution aligned with evolving first-person context and user intent.

papers.abstract: Recent video generators produce realistic videos, yet controlling how scenes unfold remains challenging. Structural proxies, such as animated 3D blockouts, guide generation by specifying scene layout, motion, camera behavior, and event order. However, these coarse inputs leave details unspecified and may contain artifacts that should not be reproduced. Successful proxy-guided generation must therefore Preserve intended structure, Complete missing content and correct proxy artifacts, and Bind text, image, and audio conditions to the right entities and events. We introduce ProxyGenBench to study these interacting requirements, with 312 evaluation cases from 60 scenes across three scene tasks and controlled variations in proxy fidelity, text detail, and multimodal inputs. We evaluate five video generators using verified, case-specific checklists. Experiments show that proxies improve spatiotemporal control, but greater proxy detail can coincide with poorer completion, while strong structural adherence does not ensure correct binding.

papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) captures neural activity associated with human perception and decision-making. It provides human-robot collaboration (HRC) systems with measurable evidence for event recognition, situation assessment, and action preparation. External sensing cannot easily provide such evidence. However, the quality and complementarity of this evidence vary across samples, and existing EEG fusion methods do not explicitly determine when EEG improves a prediction. We therefore framed selective EEG use as a sample-wise incremental-value estimation problem and proposed Value Estimation and Constraint-Aware Triage for Adoption (VECTA). VECTA separates the generation of an EEG-informed Fusion prediction from the decision about whether it should replace the existing Base prediction. The framework uses system gain to quantify the loss reduction from Base to Fusion and matching gain to assess whether benefits arise from sample-matched EEG. A signed-value learner estimates system gain from decision-time evidence and prioritizes high-value Fusion outputs under budget constraints. Cross-subject evaluations on three HRC datasets showed that matched Fusion outperformed shuffled controls. Estimated gains tracked realized gains, with Spearman correlations of 0.347-0.612 and positive-gain areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) of 0.708-0.842. Under budget constraints, VECTA reduced Brier loss and harmful Fusion adoption and achieved the highest mean normalized AUBC across three datasets among the selective-decision methods evaluated. Validation on three external multi-modal datasets showed that VECTA could be applied directly as a post-hoc decision layer to task-specific predictors without retraining. These results show that selective Fusion adoption can translate the uneven utility of EEG into system-level gains.

papers.abstract: We present HoloBrain-0.5, a family of vision-language-action (VLA) models for manipulation across robot embodiments. The policies plan in a shared action space using robot state, kinematic structure, and calibrated camera observations. We standardize joint axes, coordinate frames, and tool-center points in robot descriptions (URDFs) and encode their kinematic graphs in a shared 3D representation. HoloBrain-0.5-Continuous generates action chunks by diffusion, while HoloBrain-0.5-Discrete uses residual finite scalar quantization (FSQ) and delayed autoregression. We pretrain both policies on over 10,000 hours of real-robot, simulation, and human-manipulation data spanning 15 embodiment categories. Across six closed-loop simulation settings, the discrete policy converges faster and reaches a higher mean success rate than the continuous policy (56.77% vs. 49.71%). On seven real-robot tasks, it achieves a mean progress score of 87.76% without task-specific post-training. After post-training, the continuous policy outperforms $\pi_{0.5}$ on the seven-task benchmark (94.52% vs. 86.25%) and an 11-task dual-arm benchmark (79.07% vs. 69.41%). The discrete-initialized continuous policy transfers five tasks zero-shot from Piper to Piper-X, scoring 63.28% on average. With target-robot demonstrations, the continuous policy scores 89.2% on Franka Panda and 92.94% on a mobile dual-arm platform. Although pretraining includes no Unitree G1 data, post-training with limited G1 demonstrations yields a mean progress score of 70.24% across three humanoid tasks, compared with 11.00% for $\pi_{0.5}$.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly improved via agentic reinforcement learning, which can be on-policy but suffers from expensive rollouts and sparse rewards, limiting its application at test time. In this paper, we present a verbally Supervised Fine-Tuning (vSFT) framework that enables the conjunction of dense feedback in natural language and weight updates at test time. Specifically, our vSFT forms a closed loop between an agent and a supervisor via a hypernetwork, in which the supervisor generates verbal supervision from the agent's failed trajectories, and the hypernetwork converts that supervision into low-rank weight updates to tune the agent. We validate that this test-time in-parameter evolving process outperforms both its in-context counterparts and prevalent reinforcement learning methods. In particular, our vSFT using Qwen3-4B outperforms GRPO and Reflexion by 8.7% and 13.9% in success rate on ALFWorld, and by 4.8% and 18.2% on WebShop, respectively. We believe that learning how to adapt a model, rather than an adapted model, offers a promising path towards more capable agents that improve themselves.
authors: Qishuai Wen, Rui Chen, Haiwen Li, Zhiyuan Huang, Qiwen Gu, Bingjie Gao, Geng Li, Jing Tang, Xiangxiang Chu, Chun-Guang Li
bullets: Addresses the high rollout costs and sparse rewards of agentic reinforcement learning at test time.
Creates a closed loop where a supervisor provides natural-language feedback and a hypernetwork converts it into parameter updates.
Combines dense verbal supervision with in-parameter adaptation rather than relying only on in-context learning.
On ALFWorld and WebShop, Qwen3-4B vSFT achieves higher success rates than GRPO and Reflexion.
The approach is evaluated for self-improving agents, with scope limited to the reported benchmark tasks and comparisons.

figures.caption: Figure 1 Overview of our proposed vSFT. This design trains the hypernetwork to convert verbal feedback into LoRA adapters that effectively steer the agent’s behavior (left panel).

The textual content to be internalized is first processed by the base model in a single forward pass to collect its key-value states in attention layers. The hypernetwork then uses these states to generate LoRA adapters, which are applied to the down-projection weight matrices of the FFN layers.

papers.abstract: Modern video generators excel at producing visually plausible futures guided by text and image prompts. Yet their emphasis on semantic plausibility does not guarantee fidelity to the physical consequences of specific actions. Action-conditioned world models (ACWMs), in contrast, aim to simulate how the world responds to robot actions, enabling scalable policy evaluation and improvement without costly real-world rollouts. The challenge is not merely to generate a plausible future, but to predict what follows from a specific physical action. As video priors grow stronger, we ask how little adaptation is truly needed to bridge this gap. We introduce Dianjing, a minimal recipe that preserves and unlocks the capabilities of strong video priors through unified physical action conditioning, training concentrated at the high noise levels where motion and layout, and thus the consequences of actions, are decided, and native history conditioning. Built upon MiniMax H3, a 33B video foundation model, Dianjing freezes the pretrained backbone and trains only 0.34% of its parameters using approximately 65 hours of robot video across two embodiments, without additional robot-specific pretraining or camera calibration. Controlled ablations show that where training is allocated across noise levels matters more than how actions enter the network. On WorldOracle, which evaluates predictions against paired real-world executions, Dianjing achieves the best scores on four of the five evaluation tracks and ranks second on AgiBot-Long. Our findings suggest that strong video priors already bring us most of the way to world modeling; lightweight physical action grounding can unlock their potential for real-world prediction.
authors: Zanyi Wang, Xia Chen, Liu Liu, Xianglong Guo, Dengyang Jiang, Haodong Li, Tingyang Xiao, Wenhao Hu, Zhizhong Su
bullets: Addresses the gap between visually plausible video generation and predicting the physical consequences of specific robot actions.
Freezes the MiniMax H3 backbone and trains only 0.34% of parameters using about 65 hours of robot video from two embodiments.
Uses unified physical-action conditioning, high-noise-focused training, and native history conditioning.

Achieves the best WorldOracle scores on four of five tracks and ranks second on AgiBot-Long.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Dianjing: minimal adaptation of a strong video prior for action-conditioned world modeling. Starting from an initial observation and native text conditioning, we retain the frozen video prior and introduce only 0.34% trainable parameters for actionconditioned rollout. (a) Shared EEF30: robot commands across embodiments are converted to a common, temporally aligned end-effector representation and injected through additive AdaLN residuals. (b) High-noise sampling: training emphasizes high noise levels to improve action-conditioned adaptation. (c) Native references: the clean latent tail of the generated past is passed to the next chunk through the pretrained reference pathway, without a specialized memory module.

Figure 4. Additional predictions on WorldOracle validation episodes. Top: AgiBot G2 policy rollout (pick fruit). Bottom: humanoperated YAM episode (pick fruit). In each block, the top row shows the real execution and the bottom row shows Dianjing’s prediction.

Figure 1. Most of the way there: from rich video priors to action-grounded prediction. (a) Modern video generators exhibit rich visual and semantic capabilities acquired through large-scale pretraining. (b) Yet visually plausible interactions can still exhibit physical inconsistencies and do not guarantee faithful prediction of specific executions. (c) The zero-shot TI2V prior generates a visually plausible but action-inconsistent future, whereas Dianjing grounds its predictions in temporally aligned robot actions with only 0.34% trainable parameters, improving the episode-level SV from 31.99 to 76.74 and producing a prediction more faithful to the paired real-world execution.

Figure 3. Qualitative comparison on a WorldOracle validation episode (AgiBot Core, hang towel), in which the robot hangs the yellow towel and then the pink one. GE-Sim 2.0 is run with its released WorldOracle checkpoint and inference script. It moves the arms as commanded but leaves the yellow towel on the table; Dianjing reproduces both hanging events.

papers.abstract: Background: Large language models produce hallucinations in medical question answering (QA). Verify-and-revise pipelines that check atomic claims against retrieved guideline evidence are a standard mitigation, but evaluations almost universally treat the verifier's output as ground truth, an assumption rarely tested. Objective: To measure, claim by claim against human judgement, how such a pipeline fails in a guideline-grounded clinical setting. Methods: We built a dataset of 160 questions (100 patient vignettes from 89 de-identified cases, 60 fact-based) over four recent ESC cardiology guidelines, all approved by a practising internist, and a retrieval corpus of 627 hand-verified guideline records at two chunk granularities. A five-stage pipeline was run under four retrieval configurations and three independent runs (1920 arm-runs); all 606 first-pass refuted claims were manually audited, an independent judge re-judged 906 decisions, and the expert blindly reviewed 100 accepted claims. Results: Only 44.7-50.6% of flagged claims were true hallucinations. Correction loops converged in 85.2-95.1% of cases, yet 35% of genuine final errors were introduced by correction. Single-run true-hallucination recall was 35.6-41.2%, the three-run union 71-80%; verifier agreement was moderate (kappa = 0.505). The blind probe estimated the accepted-claim miss rate at 3.2% (95% CI 0.7-6.7%). Final genuine-error rate: 1.7% of answers. Conclusion: Claim-level verification reduces hallucinated content by an order of magnitude, but verifier reliability, not generation, is the limiting factor and must be measured, not assumed.
authors: Ilkin Masimov, Rufana Baghirli, Muhammad Rashid
bullets: Only 44.7–50.6% of claims flagged by the verifier were confirmed hallucinations by human review.
Correction loops converged in 85.2–95.1% of cases, but introduced 35% of genuine final errors.
Three independent runs improved true-hallucination recall from 35.6–41.2% to 71–80%.
The verifier showed moderate agreement (κ=0.505), while the final genuine-error rate was 1.7%.
The study supports measuring verifier reliability rather than treating verifier output as ground truth.

papers.abstract: Robots executing tasks in partially observed environments must resolve uncertainty while operating with incomplete skills. Inspired by human curiosity, we investigate how robots can formulate task-relevant hypotheses, seek evidence, and acquire missing skills during task execution. We propose CHASE, a Curiosity-guided Harness for Acquiring Skills from Evidence, which operationalizes curiosity as selecting investigations that resolve task uncertainty and expand executable capabilities. Four modules connect dynamic scene understanding, hypothesis-driven planning, on-demand skill acquisition, and verified execution. The planner balances information value, skill reuse, and acquisition/execution cost. Missing skills trigger bounded exploration, learning from verified segments, and held-out admission during acquisition; separate checks verify physical effects and acquired evidence. Newly admitted skills expand the executable investigation set, closing the loop between resolving uncertainty and acquiring capabilities. Simulation and real-robot experiments evaluate investigation, skill acquisition, and task execution. CHASE achieves 50-80% task success under combined information and capability gaps, with 70-90% evidence resolution.
authors: Zixuan Wang, Wei Zhang, Chenlei Zhu, Naiyu Chen, Xihua Wang, Jie Chen
bullets: Targets task execution when robots face both incomplete information and missing capabilities.
Combines scene understanding, hypothesis-driven planning, skill acquisition, and verified execution.
Selects investigations by balancing information value, skill reuse, and acquisition or execution cost.

Simulation and real-robot experiments report 50–80% task success and 70–90% evidence resolution under combined gaps.

papers.abstract: We formalize Agentic Waterfall Feed, a new problem of personalized information discovery in which users actively direct recommendations and the system adapts to evolving needs inferred from both explicit requests and browsing behavior. We address this problem with the Agentic Waterfall framework, whose language-model controller maintains persistent user state and coordinates content retrieval, ranking, and state updates. To evaluate systems on this task, we contribute the Agentic Waterfall Dataset and a replay-based evaluation protocol. The dataset combines real content metadata with simulated interaction histories. The protocol compares systems under shared histories using relevance scores and blind judgments of how well recommendations satisfy current user goals and constraints. Agentic Waterfall remains competitive with strong baselines on conventional recommendation tasks across five public benchmarks. On the Agentic Waterfall Dataset, it outperforms the strongest baseline in both evaluations, with relative improvements of up to 16.1%.
authors: Yige Luo, Shining Zhang, Jikun Liu, Hongjiao Qiang, Ran Guan
bullets: Targets personalized discovery where users actively steer recommendations rather than passively receiving feeds.
Uses a language-model controller to coordinate retrieval, ranking, and updates to persistent user state.
Introduces the Agentic Waterfall Dataset and a replay-based evaluation protocol with relevance scores and blind goal-satisfaction judgments.
Remains competitive on conventional recommendation tasks across five public benchmarks.
Outperforms the strongest baseline on its dataset by up to 16.1% in the reported evaluations.

papers.abstract: Autonomous driving powered by neural network models lacks safety guarantees. We propose a state-level policy editing technique that guarantees closed-loop safety under recoverable disturbances while reusing the model's existing driving capabilities. Closed-loop safety means that the vehicle remains free of collisions at all future times. We introduce the concept of policy recoverability to characterize whether a vehicle can safely return to the original policy's feasible set in finite time. Our method identifies states that are unsafe in the long term under the original policy but recoverable, and selectively edits policy outputs within this region. The vehicle corrects its actions upon entering this region and resumes the original policy upon recovery. Closed-loop simulations on nuPlan urban driving scenarios show a 48% reduction in safety incidents under the original policy while largely preserving its driving performance.
authors: Yang Guan, Shengbo Eben Li
bullets: Targets the lack of safety guarantees in neural-network autonomous driving.
Defines policy recoverability as the ability to return safely to the original policy’s feasible set in finite time.
Edits actions only in states that are unsafe under the original policy but still recoverable.
Resumes the original policy after recovery, retaining existing driving capabilities.
Closed-loop nuPlan simulations report 48% fewer safety incidents while largely preserving driving performance.

figures.caption: Figure 1. The concept of a policy's recoverable set. The feasible set of a given neural policy (blue region) guarantees the vehicle's closed-loop safety. However, disturbances whose evolution differs from the training environment, such as an unexpected vehicle running a red light, can force the vehicle outside this set. Without policy intervention, the vehicle will eventually enter an unsafe state (red region). While preserving the original policy's capabilities, our method first identifies the set of states that are recoverable to the original policy's feasible set (yellow region) and those that are not (grey region). It then incrementally edits the original policy's outputs in recoverable states, guiding the vehicle back into the original policy's range of capabilities and thereby ensuring closed-loop safety.

papers.abstract: Nested multi-precision quantization derives multiple precisions from a single checkpoint by reading only the leading bits of each weight, which makes it attractive for on-device deployment under varying memory and energy budgets. However, existing methods offer only integer bits, leaving large accuracy gaps between adjacent precisions and severe degradation at 2 bits. To address this, we propose Any-Rate, which serves 2-8 bits from one checkpoint, in half-bit steps over 2-4 bits. Any-Rate restricts some bit-planes to extended Hamming codewords in 8-weight blocks (0.5 bits per weight), shares one LUT per row across precisions, and encodes all precisions jointly with a separate target for each, reducing the loss from sharing bit-planes. Across four LLMs, Any-Rate achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among multi-precision methods at 2 and 3 bits, keeping 69% of FP16 accuracy at 2 bits, and is within one point of the best at 4 bits. It decodes about as fast as existing kernels, and an LPDDR energy model estimates up to 27% less energy at equal accuracy. Code is available at https://github.com/hoonki2002/Any-Rate.
authors: Hoonki Lee, Haechan Shin, Hyuntaek Jung, Yeonu Choi, Sangyeob Kim

Across four LLMs, retains 69% of FP16 accuracy at 2 bits, achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among multi-precision methods at 2 and 3 bits, and is within one point of the best at 4 bits.
Decoding speed is comparable to existing kernels; an LPDDR energy model estimates up to 27% lower energy at equal accuracy.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are evolving from passive chatbots into autonomous systems that operate continuously in dynamic environments. Such agents need not only solve current tasks but also learn from past interactions to improve future performance. However, existing streaming benchmarks often rely on short task sequences or largely independent tasks, providing limited evidence of whether agents can effectively reuse experience when later tasks depend on earlier outcomes. To address this gap, we introduce \textbf{EvoLink-Bench}, a benchmark for evaluating self-evolving agents in long-horizon, interdependent task streams. It covers daily office work, multi-turn dialogue, and AutoResearch-style workflows, with persistent workspaces and dependencies across tasks. The benchmark includes two complementary levels: \textbf{L1}, which evaluates the acquisition and revision of language-expressible knowledge, and \textbf{L2}, which assesses the development of task-level capabilities through execution and feedback. Its evaluation further distinguishes within-task recovery, persistent-state updates, and experience reuse in later tasks. We evaluate five agent frameworks across three backbone configurations under three persistence conditions, covering 19,635 scored task slots from selected evaluation cohorts. Results show that no framework consistently performs best across both levels, retries recover only a limited proportion of failed tasks, and persistent-state updates do not necessarily improve subsequent performance. Furthermore, the effects of evolution differ between knowledge- and capability-level tasks, suggesting that these two forms of evolution require different learning mechanisms. Performance gains also vary across domains and task streams, with improvements on some tasks not necessarily extending to others.
authors: Wei Chen, Xiaodong Lu, Weihao Shen, Gongxun Li, Xingyu Guo, Qihang Sun, Fuwei Zhang, Zhao Zhang, Yikun Ban, Shuang Li, Deqing Wang, Fuzhen Zhuang
bullets: Targets limitations of streaming benchmarks with short or mostly independent task sequences.
Covers office work, multi-turn dialogue, and AutoResearch-style workflows with persistent workspaces and task dependencies.

Analyzes within-task recovery, persistent-state updates, and reuse of experience in later tasks.
Findings show inconsistent framework performance, limited retry recovery, and that persistence or improvement on one task does not reliably transfer to others.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces EvoLink-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating self-evolving agents in long-horizon, interdependent task streams, a critical area for research in continual and online learning.
papers.title: EvoLink-Bench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Self-Evolving Agents in Long-Horizon Interdependent Task Streams
papers.tldr: EvoLink-Bench evaluates whether LLM agents can learn and reuse experience across long-horizon task streams where later tasks depend on earlier outcomes.

papers.abstract: Skill acquisition alone does not establish a reusable skill library: task proficiency does not specify a compositional interface. Motivated by agents that acquire and refine skills, we study independently learned soft-prompt skills on frozen language models, with skill identities and execution order supplied. Across four digit-task bases and three record-editing models, mean composition accuracy in one call is at most 7.6%, compared with 88.2% to 100% over two calls that add computation and an explicit intermediate output. Neutral-insertion training improves robustness but leaves substantial interference, which block length and per-token norm alone cannot explain on two of four digit bases. Blocks of the same operation need not be interchangeable: after training next to frozen learned partners, a post hoc test on two Qwen bases shows that replacing those partners with independently learned blocks of the same operations lowers median composition accuracy from 98.0% and 95.3% to 12.7% and 0.5%, although every replacement scores at least 90% alone. Repair can improve a composition while impairing the original skill, and rehearsal improves retention while transfer remains limited on Qwen2.5-0.5B. Internal interventions constrain explanations without identifying a shared failure mechanism. These findings motivate evaluating compatibility, retention and transfer alongside acquisition when building skill libraries for self-evolving agents. Code is available at https://github.com/YanLin-Quinne/SkillCompatibility.
authors: Yan Lin, Zhongliang Guo, Jingyu Sun, Qiyan Zhao, Ruihong Zeng, Ying Chen, Zhengtao Yao, Yan Wen, Kunyu Peng, Yuxia Wang
bullets: One-call composition is poor: mean accuracy is at most 7.6%, versus 88.2%–100% when using two calls with an explicit intermediate output.
Neutral-insertion training improves robustness but does not eliminate interference, which is not explained by block length or per-token norm alone.
Skills with the same operation are not interchangeable: replacing learned partner blocks sharply reduces composition accuracy despite strong standalone performance.
Repair can harm the original skill, while rehearsal improves retention but provides limited transfer on Qwen2.5-0.5B.
The findings support evaluating compatibility, retention, and transfer—not acquisition alone—when building reusable skill libraries.

papers.selection_reason: Studies skill composition and retention in language models, relevant to continual learning and adaptation.
papers.title: When Skills Fail to Compose: Compatibility and Retention in Language Models
papers.tldr: Independently learned soft-prompt skills often fail to compose or transfer reliably, even when each skill works well alone.

papers.abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) integrates separately trained domain specialists into a single unified model. Existing methods focus on refining the distillation procedure while initializing the student from a base model or a multi-domain SFT checkpoint, which leaves capability integration largely to distillation itself. Instead, we treat the starting point as a design variable and propose Unified MOPD (Uni-MOPD), which pairs a strong start with a simple recipe: a training-free uniform merge of specialists from the same base model initializes the student, and short MOPD with uniform domain sampling and full-vocabulary reverse KL refines it. Across five multimodal domains and 19 benchmarks, our study establishes three findings. (1) The starting point matters more than subsequent training choices: before any training, the uniform merge already matches the score that the base model reaches after 200 MOPD updates, and after short distillation it matches higher-scoring, search-based starts. (2) Short MOPD recovers most of the capabilities the merge leaves unintegrated; it improves every domain, with the largest gains where the domain teacher still leads. (3) From a strong start, uniform domain sampling and full-vocabulary reverse KL match or exceed every evaluated sampling strategy and divergence, without schedules, per-token weighting, or truncation hyperparameters. Uni-MOPD outperforms Open-MOPD at the same training budget while training 3.3 times faster than its released code. We will release the training framework, specialist checkpoints, and unified student.
authors: Wenzheng Chang, Taiqiang Wu, Yuqi Xu, Yongfu Zhu, Zelin Peng, Ji Zhao, Shuai Dong, Wenpu Liu, Caoyuan Ma, Xuehui Wang, Ziyue Wang, Weichu Xie, Haiyuan Wan, Ngai Wong, Tong He, Wenqi Shao, Jiaqi Wang
bullets: A training-free uniform merge of specialists from the same base model provides a strong initialization.
Short MOPD with uniform domain sampling and full-vocabulary reverse KL recovers capabilities left unintegrated by the merge.
The approach improves performance across all five multimodal domains and 19 benchmarks, especially where teachers remain stronger.
From a strong initialization, simple uniform sampling and reverse KL match or exceed evaluated alternatives without extra schedules or weighting hyperparameters.
Uni-MOPD outperforms Open-MOPD at the same training budget and trains 3.3× faster than its released implementation.

Merging and short MOPD thus combine the five specialists into one unified model.

papers.selection_reason: Unifies multimodal domain specialists via multi-teacher distillation and model merging, directly relevant to multimodal foundation model research.
papers.title: Strong Starts, Simple Recipes: Unified Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation from Multimodal Specialists
papers.tldr: Uni-MOPD shows that merging multimodal specialists before simple on-policy distillation is more important than complex distillation choices for efficiently building a unified model.

papers.abstract: Biological intelligence thrives on minimal power despite its noisy, imperfect components, with neurons that communicate through voltage spikes. Brain-inspired computing seeks to bring such efficiency to real devices, which requires training methods tailored to them. The standard way to train spiking neural networks, backpropagation through time, computes weight updates through every step of a simulated device, so faithful or long simulations can make training costly and unstable. Here we show that spiking networks can learn reliably and efficiently by decoupling the clock of learning from that of computing. Our method, ChronoProp, calculates weight updates from each neuron's spike counts in fixed time bins using its measured input-output function. Compared with backpropagation through time, ChronoProp reaches similar accuracy in image classification, with about 3 times less training time and 20 times less memory at the finest timestep tested, and up to 10 times fewer spikes. On spoken-word benchmarks, ChronoProp is far more accurate in recurrent networks at fine timesteps, and with simple, hardware-compatible techniques it approaches the best published models. These networks also tolerate simulated hardware defects and limitations better than those trained with backpropagation through time. Therefore, ChronoProp enables stable and efficient training in simulations close to the continuous time of analog hardware.
authors: Michalis Pagkalos, Panayiota Poirazi
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost and instability of backpropagation through time for long or faithful spiking-neural simulations.
Computes updates from neuron spike counts in fixed time bins and measured input–output functions.
Matches image-classification accuracy with about 3× less training time and 20× less memory, while using up to 10× fewer spikes.
Performs especially well on spoken-word benchmarks, including improved recurrent-network accuracy at fine timesteps.
Improves tolerance to simulated hardware defects and limitations, supporting near-continuous-time analog hardware simulations.
papers.selection_reason: Decouples learning and computing clocks in spiking networks, reducing training time, memory, and spikes; fits efficient AI.
papers.title: Decoupling the clocks of learning and computing in spiking neural networks
papers.tldr: ChronoProp decouples learning from simulation time in spiking neural networks, achieving comparable or better accuracy with substantially lower training cost and greater hardware robustness than backpropagation through time.

papers.abstract: Robotic tasks combine object relations, logical dependencies, and temporal requirements, which robot planning and industrial control commonly specify in temporal logic (TL). We introduce TL-VLA, a vision--language--action framework that replaces natural-language task instructions with temporal logic, making this spatiotemporal structure explicit. A typed graph encoder and visual--logical fusion condition continuous actions on the task specification and the current observations. To prepare a general vision--language backbone for this interface, we develop TL-aware robot pretraining with separate semantic and structural readouts: a frozen language teacher aligns task semantics, the structural readout encodes TL syntax to support complex, long-horizon tasks, and autoregressive action prediction connects the graph representation to robot behavior. Downstream policies inherit the pretrained backbone and TL encoder and learn new fusion and action modules. On CALVIN ABC$\rightarrow$D, our TL-aware initializer reaches \textbf{3.800} average chain length and \textbf{62.3\%} five-task success, compared with 3.578 and 54.5\% for a FAST initializer pretrained on the same data and 3.485 average chain length for a Qwen+NL baseline. On LIBERO-10, TL-aware initialization improves success from \textbf{91.2\% to 95.8\%}. On LIBERO-Mem, our policy reaches \textbf{65.0\%} success without observation history, compared with 45.0\% for a Qwen+NL reference. On held-out Panda planning specifications, it reaches \textbf{59.6\%} at Success@256 over three generation seeds, versus 48.4\% for Qwen+TL and 37.0\% for Qwen+NL. These results support explicit logical task conditioning and transferable TL-aware representations for robot action learning.
authors: Zezhi Liu, Jingwen Sun, Hongjin Chen, Shaojie Ren, Peiyan Tu, Xin Jin, Zhibo Chen
bullets: Targets robotic tasks involving object relations, logical dependencies, and temporal requirements.
Encodes temporal-logic specifications with a typed graph encoder and fuses them with visual observations to condition continuous actions.
Pretrains a vision-language backbone with separate semantic and structural readouts, using a language teacher for task meaning and autoregressive action prediction for behavior.
Reports improvements across CALVIN, LIBERO-10, LIBERO-Mem, and held-out Panda planning specifications, including 95.8% success on LIBERO-10 and 65.0% on LIBERO-Mem without observation history.
The abstract supports the approach’s scope on the reported benchmarks and planning specifications; broader generalization is not established.

papers.selection_reason: Temporal logic as task language for VLA models with visual-logical fusion.
papers.title: Beyond Natural-Language Instructions: Temporal Logic as a Task Language for VLA Models with Visual-Logical Fusion
papers.tldr: TL-VLA uses temporal logic instead of natural-language instructions to give vision-language-action robots explicit spatiotemporal task structure, improving long-horizon and memory-dependent performance.

papers.abstract: Robust image-text retrieval aims to maintain accurate cross-modal matching when image or text queries are incomplete, supporting reliable information access in real-world applications. However, existing methods typically focus on adapting to distribution shifts, without adequately addressing candidate discrimination for incomplete queries and ranking instability. To this end, we propose semantic projection and alignment with relational constraints (SPARC), which elicits latent multimodal knowledge from frozen encoders to improve candidate discrimination and ranking stability. Specifically, we first devise a semantic calibration module on a product of spheres that refines incomplete visual and textual features through tangent-space updates, maintaining the unit-sphere structure used for cosine similarity. Second, we introduce a robust semantic guidance module that combines latent multimodal knowledge encoded in complete image-text features with cross-modal semantic anchors to promote semantic alignment of the calibrated features. Finally, we introduce a matching relation constraint module that fuses original query features with their calibrated counterparts and applies a soft ranking constraint to penalize reductions in initially positive matching margins, thereby limiting ranking perturbations. Extensive experiments on Flickr30K and COCO demonstrate that SPARC outperforms competing methods under various image occlusion and word deletion settings, while achieving consistent gains across different pretrained backbones.
authors: Zhongkuan Mao, Wenzhuo Zhao, Haidong Chen, Shangze Li, Yidong Wang, Jinhe Bi, Yunpu Ma, Junfeng Fang, Fei Shen, Tat-Seng Chua
bullets: Targets candidate discrimination and ranking instability caused by image occlusion and word deletion.
Refines incomplete visual and textual features with tangent-space updates on a product of spheres.
Uses complete image-text features and cross-modal anchors to guide semantic alignment.
Applies a soft matching-relation constraint to preserve initially positive ranking margins.
Outperforms competing methods on Flickr30K and COCO across corruption settings and pretrained backbones.

papers.abstract: Even a correct operator reply can be an unreliable training target for a customer-support agent. About a quarter of the factual claims in these replies lacked full support in the agent's knowledge base and tool records. We treat operator replies as claims to verify rather than answers to imitate. Unverified claims guide revisions to the knowledge base and tools. Verified claims serve as coverage targets in a claim-level GRPO reward that scores factual precision against the evidence the agent retrieved for its answer. On an offline benchmark, 8.6% of the GRPO agent's text answers were flagged for hallucinations, compared with 13.6% for the supervised fine-tuning baseline. In a randomized A/B test against the existing procedural bot, the deployed system increased the share of conversations closed without a human operator from 63.3% to 80.8%.
authors: Dmitrii Stoianov, Olga Tsymboi, Danil Taranets, Daniil Strizhakov, Ilya Buryak, Almaz Dautov, Dmitry Fatnev, Arthur Babkin, Aleksandr Fida, Daniil Dryabin, Maksim Shilenko, Nikita Surnachev, Anatolii Potapov
bullets: Operator replies are treated as claims to verify, not answers to imitate, because some lack support in available evidence.
Unverified claims guide updates to the knowledge base and tools.
Verified claims become coverage targets for a GRPO reward measuring factual precision against retrieved evidence.

papers.abstract: We introduce Puzzling-Bench, a benchmark of 23,777 puzzles with community-verified answers drawn from the Puzzling Stack Exchange archive (2014-2026): riddles, ciphers, logic grids, lateral-thinking problems, wordplay and recreational mathematics, a third of them with images. Every puzzle carries the answer accepted by its author, a short reference answer taken from it (LLM-extracted for the evaluation sets and checked on a 50-puzzle human review), the author's own hints, community tags and a creation date, so that the benchmark supports hint ablations, category analysis and a rolling post-cutoff slice (254 puzzles posted after the training cutoff of six of the nine models we evaluate, including the best one) as a contamination check. We evaluate nine frontier and open models with a two-tier scorer (normalized exact match, then an LLM judge) and validate the judge with three judges from two model families: they agree on 95-97% of verdicts (kappa 0.82-0.96), move no model by more than 1.6 points, and show no own-family preference. The best model, GPT-6.1, reaches 74.8% on a shared 255-puzzle set; a hard core of 17 puzzles defeats all nine models; model failures are strongly correlated, and the second-best model contributes a single puzzle to a greedy ensemble, yet an oracle over all nine reaches 91%. On a 100-puzzle multimodal pilot, withholding the question's image costs the two best models 24 and 35 points. We release the dataset, the scoring pipeline and all per-row provenance.
authors: Abhinav Sharma, Li Li, Chien Van Nguyen, Sai Karthik Navuluru, Bo Ni, Xiangbo Gao, Xiaolei Huang, Yue Zhao, Nesreen K. Ahmed, Tyler Derr, Yu Wang, Hongjie Chen, Zhengzhong Tu, Thien Huu Nguyen, Ryan A. Rossi, Franck Dernoncourt
bullets: The benchmark contains 23,777 community-verified puzzles spanning riddles, ciphers, logic, wordplay, mathematics, and image-based tasks.
It supports analysis by hints, categories, dates, and a post-training-cutoff contamination check, with released data, scoring, and provenance.
Nine evaluated models were scored using normalized exact match plus an LLM judge validated across model families.
GPT-6.1 achieved 74.8% on a shared 255-puzzle set, while 17 puzzles stumped every model and failures were strongly correlated.
In a 100-puzzle multimodal pilot, removing images reduced the two best models’ scores by 24 and 35 points; an oracle combining all models reached 91%.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for evaluating language models on puzzles.
papers.title: Puzzling-Bench: Evaluating Language Models on 23,777 Human-Written Puzzles with Community-Verified Answers

papers.abstract: Social intelligence in a robot requires interpreting a situation from the perspectives of the people involved and using that understanding to decide when and how to act. We introduce LUDIUS, a benchmark for evaluating how vision-language models exercise this judgment through a robot's verbal responses and actions, organized around 15 social intelligence skills drawn from social psychology, sociology, and cognitive science. LUDIUS comprises six editions, each a collection of episodes spanning one simulated week. Three editions each cover all 15 skills in a different household. The other three focus on interactions involving multiple people, safety, and context-specific norms, respectively. We evaluate frontier models and a smaller model finetuned on social-interaction data we generated, using a common evaluation harness. The harness supplies each model with the robot's camera views and residents' reactions, retrieves relevant interaction history, and converts the model's tool calls into robot verbal responses and actions. Models tend to perform worse when they must reason about what a resident saw or heard earlier, reconcile competing interests, or fulfill a request within safety constraints and household rules. Beyond the home setting, LUDIUS's design pipeline offers a way to construct social intelligence benchmarks by translating social intelligence skills into context-specific judgments and observable robot behavior.
authors: Chaewon Kim, Sangheon Lee, Seyeon Choi, Kangwook Lee, Yea Seul Kim
bullets: Covers 15 social-intelligence skills across six simulated-week editions and varied household scenarios.
Tests how models use camera views, residents’ reactions, interaction history, and tool calls to produce robot speech and actions.
Models struggle most with recalling what residents previously saw or heard, balancing competing interests, and respecting safety constraints and household norms.
Includes evaluations of frontier models and a smaller model fine-tuned on generated social-interaction data.
The benchmark design pipeline can extend to other settings by linking social skills to context-specific judgments and observable behavior.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs) outperform single-agent systems, but inter-agent communication incurs substantial token overhead. While assigning a large LLM to every agent is common, it results in inefficient resource utilization, leaving the system far from the Pareto frontier. The cost of answering a query is set jointly by how many agents are recruited, the role and LLM assigned to each, and communication topology among them. Most existing routers treat cost only implicitly rather than as an explicit optimization constraint. A fixed accuracy-cost preference also cannot express how much a caller is willing to pay for a particular query. We introduce MeterRouter, a budget-aware dynamic router that incrementally synthesizes a collaboration graph by selecting each agent's role, LLM, incoming connections, and termination conditioned on the query and a per-query monetary budget. We initialize the router by imitating successful execution graphs, then jointly refine its decisions with a variant of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) whose reward favors correct answers and penalizes spending and budget overruns. Across five benchmarks and a three-tier LLM pool, MeterRouter is (1) accurate, achieving performance comparable to the strongest MAS; (2) economical, reaching that accuracy at 82% lower cost than the strongest MAS router and extending the accuracy-cost frontier beyond the ceiling of single-agent systems; and (3) controllable, adapting its spending to the specified budget while rarely exceeding it.
authors: Yue Xu, Leikun Yin, Ruiming Min, Yufeng Lai, Justin Andrew Johnson, Sitao Luan, Xiaotong Shen
bullets: Targets inefficient LLM assignment and communication overhead in multi-agent systems.
Selects agent roles, LLMs, incoming connections, and termination decisions conditioned on the query and monetary budget.
Initializes from successful execution graphs and refines routing with a GRPO variant rewarding correctness while penalizing cost and budget overruns.
Evaluated on five benchmarks with a three-tier LLM pool, it matches the strongest MAS while using 82% lower cost.
Adapts spending to specified budgets, rarely exceeds them, and extends the accuracy–cost frontier beyond single-agent systems.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses token overhead in LLM-based multi-agent systems by proposing a budget-aware dynamic router that optimizes resource utilization and cost, directly contributing to efficiency in AI systems.
papers.title: MeterRouter: Budget-Aware Dynamic Routing for Multi-Agent Systems
papers.tldr: MeterRouter dynamically builds cost-aware multi-agent collaboration graphs to achieve strong accuracy while adapting spending to each query’s budget.

papers.abstract: Artistic mesh generators turn a dense 3D object into an artist mesh: a compact, quad-dominant mesh that is easy to edit. Most of current models are auto-regressive methods which decode a mesh token by token, take tens to hundreds of seconds per mesh. Diffusion- and flow-based generators are much faster, but their meshes still fall short of artist quality. To our knowledge, PostMesh is the first post-training method for a diffusion- or flow-based artist mesh generator, and it needs no expensive artist-made ground truth: the generator is trained on its own samples, scored by a reward computed from the dense input and the output. We propose an artistic mesh reward that keeps the output consistent with the dense input while making the mesh structure into artistic. We also propose a multi-negative flow preference optimisation that transfers the reward to the generator. After a short LoRA post-training, PostMesh is comparable to or better than slow autoregressive generators on most artist-mesh quality metrics and in a blind VLM preference test, at a fraction of their time.
authors: Gihyun Kwon
bullets: Targets fast diffusion- and flow-based generators whose meshes lag in artist quality.
Uses self-generated meshes scored by a reward based on the dense input and output, avoiding expensive artist-made ground truth.
Introduces an artistic mesh reward balancing input consistency with artist-friendly mesh structure.
Applies multi-negative flow preference optimisation through short LoRA post-training.
Reports comparable or better quality than slow autoregressive generators on most metrics and in a blind VLM preference test, with much lower generation time.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Training Overview. For each dense input I , the current model (MeshFlow with LoRA) draws a group of samples then the artistic mesh reward scores them. The gating algorithm keeps a winning sample w and weighted losing samples lj . With those samples, a DPO and RPO step updates only the LoRA adapters, and the next round samples fresh inputs with the updated model.

Figure 5. Qualitative Results. In this figure, we show the input dense mesh and the generated artist mesh outputs from autoregressive baselines and flow-based models. For the outputs from baselines, they are broken or incomplete, irregular, or filled with very small faces, which makes them hard for an artist to use, while the PostMesh outputs are complete and more evenly laid out. The output shows our proposed model have superior performance compared to baselines.
Figure 9. Further comparisons on test objects: the dense input, shaded, and the output of each method with its mesh grid.

Figure 6. The prompt of the VLM judge. The lines ===SYSTEM=== to ===QUESTION=== separate the parts of one call: the system prompt, the introduction, the labels of the three images and the question. The images are sent as image blocks between the labels.

Figure 2. Artistic Mesh Rewards. Each row shows the dense input I and the winning and a losing sample of the same input. In each row the named term favours the winning sample. Silhouette IoU and depth agreement compare renders of the output with renders of I: they penalise missing or extra parts (filled silhouettes with the outline of I) and surfaces pushed in or out (depth maps). Quad strips and tessellation reward quads laid out in rings and strips. The sliver term penalises needle-like triangles (red edges). Vertex valence, the number of edges at a vertex, penalises poles and fans: a vertex with 10 or more edges (red dots) is typically the hub of a fan of thin triangles, and a vertex with at most 2 edges (blue dots) belongs to a single triangle, a loose corner. Both break the edge loops of a regular layout. Tiny and stray components penalises specks and floating pieces (red).
Figure 7. Failure cases of PostMesh. Our model can improve the shape consistency and mesh structure, but still some of the defects can remain.

Figure 4. Training Group Examples. The dense input I and six of its 16 samples are shown. Green frame: the winning sample w. Red: gate-passing losing samples with their preference weight ω. Grey: a sample that failed a gate, which counts as a losing sample with ω = 1. r: artistic mesh reward.

Its DFF is lower than that of every baseline except Mesh Silksong, which it approaches, and its fragmentation is lower than that of MeshFlow, though above most autoregressive baselines. Its CD and HD are the lowest. Its ECD is higher than that of Mesh Silksong and FastMesh, likely because they use several times more faces. Above all, PostMesh runs almost as fast as MeshFlow (2.53 vs. 2.17 s per mesh), one to two orders of magnitude faster than the autoregressive models, while matching or exceeding them on most metrics.
