papers.selection_reason: Addresses the generation of artist-quality meshes using flow-based models and self-rewarded preference post-training. This is a significant contribution to 3D generation and foundation models.
papers.title: PostMesh: Self-Rewarded Preference Post-Training for Flow-Based Artist Mesh Generation
papers.tldr: PostMesh self-improves fast flow-based artist mesh generators using reward-based preference post-training, achieving quality comparable to slower autoregressive methods without artist-labeled ground truth.

papers.abstract: As LLM agents increasingly learn from their own experience, the tasks they learn from and are evaluated on are almost always in English. We ask whether self-evolution transfers from English to Urdu, and release IRTIQA, a benchmark of aligned English, Urdu-translated, and Urdu code-switched variants of DROP, SNIPS, AppWorld, and SkillsBench, built with a matrix-language code-switching pipeline and human verification. Using IRTIQA, we evaluate three self-evolving frameworks, Tool-R0 (self-play RL), AgentEvolver (experience-guided RL), and Autogenesis (protocol-level evolution), against their unevolved backbones. Self-evolution often raises capability: AgentEvolver lifts AppWorld goal completion from near zero to 20-36% across all conditions, and Autogenesis improves SkillsBench pass rate from 16.48% to 22.22%. But it rarely closes the language gap. Evolved systems remain stronger in English, by up to 0.26 DROP F1, the gap is largest on multi-step tasks, and code-switching behaves as a distinct condition rather than degraded translation. On a shared Gemma-4 31B backbone, the gap exists before evolution, and RL-based evolution can hurt Urdu reasoning more than English. Language parity must therefore be an explicit design target, as it does not emerge from self-improvement alone.
authors: Abdullah Hashmat, Danish Javed, Usman Naseem, Agha Ali Raza
bullets: IRTIQA benchmarks aligned English, Urdu, and Urdu code-switched versions of DROP, SNIPS, AppWorld, and SkillsBench.
It evaluates Tool-R0, AgentEvolver, and Autogenesis against their unevolved backbones.
Self-evolution improves some capabilities, including AppWorld goal completion and SkillsBench pass rate.
English performance remains stronger—especially on multi-step tasks—and code-switching is a distinct evaluation condition.
RL-based evolution can worsen Urdu reasoning, indicating that language parity must be designed explicitly.

papers.abstract: Human videos are abundant and cheap to obtain, whereas robot trajectories remain scarce and costly, making zero-shot skill transfer from a single human demonstration an appealing route to scalable robot learning. Existing methods, however, either retarget human-specific geometry or match only static visual goals, and thus stumble over the cross-embodiment dynamics mismatch and the ungrounded action execution. We present the Co-World Model (CoWM), a predictive framework jointly optimized from paired yet unsynchronized human and robot streams. To bridge the cross-embodiment dynamics gap, CoWM disentangles each observation into a shared object-relation state and embodiment-specific context. It aligns latent actions across embodiments using effect-swap and action-sensitivity objectives,such that actions are matched by their predicted effects on the manipulated objects rather than by embodimentdependent kinematics. For grounded execution, a phase-aware receding-horizon controller estimates demonstration progress, projects the inferred human action prior onto the robot action-support density, and translates the resulting latent dynamics into executable robot commands. Extensive experiments in simulation and on two physical robot platforms demonstrate the effectiveness of CoWM, its cross-platform generalizability, and the contribution of each component. See the demo video in the supporting information for details.
authors: Xuetao Li, Xuan Jiang, Chen Liu, Zhongrui Rao, Yu Ling, Hui Wang, Sheng Liu, Miao Li
bullets: Addresses scarce robot data and cross-embodiment dynamics mismatch in human-video-to-robot transfer.
Jointly learns from paired but unsynchronized human and robot streams.
Disentangles shared object-relation states from embodiment-specific context.
Aligns actions by their predicted effects on manipulated objects, rather than kinematic similarity.
Experiments in simulation and on two physical robot platforms show effectiveness, cross-platform generalizability, and contributions from its components.

papers.selection_reason: Co-constructed shared latent dynamics for human-video-to-robot transfer.
papers.title: Co-World Model for Human-Video-to-Robot Transfer via Co-Constructed Shared Latent Dynamics

papers.abstract: Random projection is a basic compression primitive for Euclidean representation learning, with the Johnson--Lindenstrauss lemma giving a target dimension $k=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log n)$ independent of the ambient dimension. As hyperbolic representations gain increasing attention in modern Transformers, vision-language models, and large language models, the same need for oblivious dimensionality reduction arises, but no analogous primitive yet exists for hyperbolic representations. We study this gap. Two natural attempts fail in dual ways: a tangent-space scheme gives a clean local guarantee but is chart-bound and pays a curvature penalty, while a fully hyperbolic projection in the hyperboloid model is geometrically native but mixes radial and angular error before feeding them into the conditioning of $\operatorname{arcosh}$. We propose radial-angular random projection (RAP), which preserves the radial coordinate exactly and applies a Euclidean random projection only to the angular direction, lifting the result back to the target hyperboloid. RAP is hyperbolic-to-hyperbolic by construction, costs one Gaussian matrix-vector product, and reduces hyperbolic compression to a normalized angular JL question on $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$. We prove a finite-set RAP guarantee with explicit $\sinh(\sqrt{c}\,r_x)\sinh(\sqrt{c}\,r_y)$ conditioning, complemented by a local tangent-space JL theorem and an arcosh-conditioning lemma for the fully hyperbolic comparator. Across an origin-centered broad-radius point cloud, a balanced tree, a clustered Gaussian, and the WordNet noun hierarchy, RAP attains the lowest mean relative distortion in every $(n,k)$ cell, reducing distortion over the strongest hyperbolic baseline by approximately $48\%$--$49\%$ on broad-radius data. RAP also scales to million-point datasets and improves retrieval on vision--language representations over hyperbolic projection baselines.
authors: Jiahong Liu, Wenhao Yu, Yifan Li, Yanyu Chen, Rex Ying, Menglin Yang, Irwin King
bullets: Addresses the lack of a Johnson–Lindenstrauss-style dimensionality reduction primitive for hyperbolic representations.
Preserves each point’s radial coordinate while applying a Euclidean random projection to its angular direction.
Provides finite-set guarantees with explicit curvature- and radius-dependent conditioning, plus analyses of tangent-space and fully hyperbolic alternatives.
Achieves the lowest mean relative distortion across all tested settings and reduces distortion by approximately 48%–49% over the strongest baseline on broad-radius data.
Scales to million-point datasets and improves retrieval for vision–language representations over hyperbolic projection baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Unified schematic of the three hyperbolic random projection paradigms studied in this paper. Panel (a) shows the tangent-space baseline: points are sent to a Euclidean tangent chart by loga, sketched by a Gaussian JL matrix, and mapped back by an exponential map. Panel (b) shows the fully hyperbolic baseline: spatial coordinates are projected in the hyperboloid model and the time coordinate is recomputed, which keeps the output on the hyperboloid but couples radial and angular perturbations. Panel (c) shows RAP, our proposed radial-angular projection: the radius rx is preserved exactly while only the angular direction ux is projected and renormalized. This separation keeps hierarchy-carrying radial depth unchanged and confines compression error to angular information.

papers.selection_reason: Random projection for hyperbolic representations, transferable to efficient AI.
papers.title: RAP: Radial-Angular Random Projection for Hyperbolic Representations
papers.tldr: RAP is a hyperbolic-to-hyperbolic random projection that preserves radial distance exactly and compresses only angular information, achieving strong theoretical guarantees and lower distortion than prior hyperbolic projections.

papers.abstract: Modern video foundation models generate high-quality short clips, but preserving long-video consistency and correctly depicting event-driven state changes remain challenging. Existing agentic workflows face these challenges because continual planning and repair accumulate context, while reference updates remain limited. We introduce StateWeaver, which combines Active States and Hierarchical Collaboration to connect review-driven visual reference updates with cross-shot state inheritance. Active States translate state discrepancies identified during review into concrete visual asset requirements that guide reference construction, validation, and regeneration, preserving identity and already-correct content while repairing target attributes. Confirmed generation results are linked to the corresponding asset states, story time, and reference versions for verification and reuse by subsequent shots. Hierarchical Collaboration isolates execution contexts by task, clip, and repair round, and uses hierarchical memory to organize this process across multiple sets. Across multiple benchmarks, StateWeaver outperforms existing methods and produces long videos with sustained cross-shot consistency under predefined and autonomously planned storyboards.
authors: Modi Jin, Xuying Zhang, Yijing Guo, Haoran Li, Yanwen Ma, Jing Wang, Chenyu Ge, Ming-Ming Cheng, Haoyang Huang

Uses Hierarchical Collaboration and hierarchical memory to isolate and organize task, clip, and repair-round contexts.
Outperforms existing methods across multiple benchmarks, sustaining cross-shot consistency for predefined and autonomously planned storyboards.

papers.abstract: Embodied world models aim to predict future interactions that are both visually realistic and physically consistent. Yet explicit 3D motion prediction alone does not guarantee that object structure and contact relationships are preserved. Beyond motion prediction, 3D representations provide an explicit state space for imposing structural and physical constraints. Building on this insight, we introduce RehearsalWorld, an editable robot world model driven by 3D Interaction Rehearsal (3DIR). Given an initial RGB-D observation and robot actions, Interaction-Consistent Rehearsal (ICR) uses a pretrained 3D point-flow model as a motion prior. It refines the predicted trajectories through response-aware object grouping, persistent grasp memory, and contact structure refiner, preserving scene stability, object structure, and grasp attachments. Rehearsal-Aligned Video Generation (RAVG) then uses geometric projections of the rehearsal as temporal conditioning. We fine-tune a video generator on projection-video pairs to synthesize realistic interaction videos. Thanks to the decoupling of physical response from visual synthesis, RehearsalWorld also supports independent editing of material properties and camera viewpoints. Compared with PointWorld on real DROID grasping sequences, RehearsalWorld reduces gripper-relative offset by approximately 79% to 84% across deformable, articulated, and rigid objects and lowers reference motion error. For video prediction, it achieves a PSNR of 23.92 dB and an FVD of 149.
authors: Guangyu Liu, Hanzhang Wang, Huijia Zhang, Hanbei Zhan, Linjie Hu, Bin Xiao, Xuan Zhou, Dong Zhang, Hanwei Liu
bullets: Addresses the gap between explicit 3D motion prediction and preserving object structure, contacts, and grasp relationships.
Uses 3D Interaction Rehearsal: a point-flow motion prior refined with object grouping, grasp memory, and contact-structure constraints.
Conditions video generation on geometric projections of the refined 3D rehearsal, separating physical response from visual synthesis.
Supports independent editing of material properties and camera viewpoints.
On real DROID grasping sequences, reduces gripper-relative offset by approximately 79–84% versus PointWorld and reports 23.92 dB PSNR and 149 FVD for video prediction.

papers.abstract: We present a dataset of 340 fully synthetic manipulation demonstrations generated from real seed data for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) training. The corpus contains 32,340 frames with synchronized RGB and actions across eight object categories, represented as LeRobot v2.1 episodes with H.264 video, per-frame robot states and pose-valued action labels, language task annotations, summary statistics and quality decisions. Each synthetic demonstration is produced without additional teleoperation: a LoRA-fine-tuned Cosmos-3 model generates a manipulation video, and RoboHaMeR recovers the corresponding robot trajectory from RGB. Quality screening accepted 300 of 340 episodes for policy fine-tuning. As preliminary evidence of feasibility, a pretrained GR00T N1.6 policy fine-tuned exclusively on the 300 accepted episodes reaches 16/20 (80%) real-world pick-and-place success on the Oreo-package task. A policy fine-tuned on 105 real teleoperated episodes achieved 18/20 (90%) under the same protocol. These results are based on one object and 20 trials per policy and are therefore reported as preliminary evidence rather than a general performance claim.
authors: Sergei Kurchev, Iaroslav Kolomiets, Filipp Maksimov, Elizaveta Semenyakina, Miguel Altamirano Cabrera, Artem Lykov, Dzmitry Tsetserukou
bullets: Motivation: reduce reliance on costly real teleoperation data for vision-language-action policy training.
Method: generate manipulation videos with a LoRA-fine-tuned Cosmos-3 model, then recover robot trajectories from RGB using RoboHaMeR.
Dataset: 340 synthetic demonstrations across eight object categories, with 32,340 synchronized RGB-action frames and language annotations; 300 episodes passed quality screening.
Result: a GR00T N1.6 policy trained only on the accepted synthetic data achieved 16/20 (80%) real-world Oreo-package pick-and-place success, versus 18/20 (90%) using 105 real teleoperated episodes.
Scope: evidence is preliminary, based on one object and 20 trials per policy; broad performance conclusions are not established.

papers.abstract: Physically based rendering (PBR) material estimation facilitates relighting, material editing, and 3D content creation. As the reflectance of a surface heavily depends on whether it is a metal or a dielectric, producing any map that determines albedo involves a decision on metalness, which we call the "intended metalness" of the map. Rendering maps with mismatched intended metalness yields physically implausible or misinterpreted materials. The metallic--roughness workflow makes metalness explicit and thus encourages base color to match it, but does not enforce this match, especially for automated methods directly predicting each map. Therefore, we propose ReMeDi, which enforces the match through two components. First, we reparameterize base color as a metalness-weighted blend of its two variants, estimated under the all-metal and all-dielectric hypothesis, respectively. Second, as available supervision cannot teach a single network both hypotheses at every pixel, we restrict each of two separate networks to one hypothesis, so that each variant is ensured to follow its hypothesis. Besides enforcing the match, this also improves each estimated material map. Experiments show that ReMeDi outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both material accuracy and relighting fidelity.
authors: Fan Fei, Xin Huang, Yixin Zhu, Jiawei Lu, Xin Yang, Jinglin Liang, Ruining Tang, Yifei Feng, Boxin Shi, Chunchao Guo
bullets: Addresses physically implausible or misinterpreted materials caused by mismatched intended metalness in automated map prediction.
Reparameterizes base color as a metalness-weighted blend of all-metal and all-dielectric variants.
Uses two separate networks, each dedicated to one material hypothesis, because supervision cannot cover both hypotheses in one network.
Experiments report better material accuracy and relighting fidelity than state-of-the-art methods.

papers.selection_reason: Focuses on PBR material estimation for relighting, a fundamental task in 3D vision. The reparameterization technique for metal/dielectric hypotheses is a technical contribution to 3D perception and generation.
papers.title: ReMeDi: Single-Image PBR Material Estimation via Reparameterization between Metal and Dielectric Hypotheses

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies are trained to follow a fixed instruction, yet people change their minds while the robot acts. We identify the instruction black hole: once a VLA policy commits to a task, new instructions are absorbed and the robot completes the old task or freezes. We quantify it with a transmission ratio and an event horizon and prove it is a blind spot of static imitation, which cannot distinguish a policy that listens from a deaf one once the execution state reveals the task. We propose Wormhole, a training-free plug-in that relocates the robot instead of re-instructing it: optimal transport selects an approach-phase state of the new task, a rate-limited traversal carries the robot there, and the unmodified policy takes over. On LIBERO,Wormhole raises committed-switch success of pi to and pi0.5 from at most 1.2% to 93.1%, matching or exceeding scripted retreat-and-restart with one fifth of its action discontinuity.
authors: Xuetao Li, Chen Liu, Jing Wu, Sheng Liu, Miao Li
bullets: VLA policies can ignore changed instructions after committing to an initial task, creating an “instruction black hole.”
The work quantifies this failure using a transmission ratio and event horizon, and argues that static imitation cannot distinguish attentive from nonresponsive policies in this setting.
Wormhole is a training-free plug-in: optimal transport selects an approach-phase state for the new task, then rate-limited motion moves the robot there before the original policy resumes.
On LIBERO, committed-switch success increases from at most 1.2% to 93.1%, with one fifth of the action discontinuity of scripted retreat-and-restart.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free plug-in to handle instruction changes in VLA policies via optimal transport.
papers.title: Escapingthe instruction blackhole of vision-language-action policies via optimal-transport wormholes
papers.tldr: Wormhole lets vision-language-action policies recover from mid-execution instruction changes by transporting the robot into a suitable state for the new task.

papers.abstract: Pretrained visual representations improve diffusion-transformer training, yet exploiting both global context and local spatial structure requires deciding which semantic states to model and how to access them. We introduce Semantic State Reading (SSR), which jointly denoises image latents, a global CLS token encoding image-level context, and a compact patch state preserving spatial correspondence. SSR couples this global-local modeling with distinct reading paths: local states are fused with corresponding image tokens at the input, while independent projections inject the current global state into every transformer block. Both semantic scopes thus remain accessible throughout denoising. Ablations show complementary benefits from local-state modeling and repeated global reading, and semantic-trajectory interventions alter image layout under a fixed class label. On ImageNet $256 \times 256$, SiT-XL/2 with SSR reaches or surpasses the reference FIDs of SiT, REPA, and Representation Entanglement for Generation (REG) with $100\times$, $40\times$, and $2\times$ fewer training iterations, respectively. SSR achieves unguided FID 1.78 at 2M iterations and FID 1.34 with classifier-free guidance alone. Combining classifier-free guidance with autoguidance yields FID 1.31 at 1M iterations, achieving the best FID in our main comparison table.
authors: Guanxi Lai, Zixuan Li, Zhiwei Li, Qi Li
bullets: Jointly denoises image latents, a global CLS state, and compact spatially aligned patch states.
Fuses local semantic states with corresponding image tokens and injects global context into every transformer block.
Ablations show complementary gains from local-state modeling and repeated global-state reading.
Semantic-trajectory interventions can change image layout while keeping the class label fixed.

On ImageNet 256×256, it reports FID 1.78 unguided, 1.34 with classifier-free guidance, and 1.31 with combined classifier-free guidance and autoguidance, using fewer training iterations than cited baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Comparison between REG and our Semantic State Reading (SSR). (a) During training, REG jointly denoises image latents and a global CLS token from a pretrained visual encoder, while aligning intermediate features with clean teacher representations. (b) During inference, REG jointly generates image latents and global semantics from random noise. (c) SSR additionally models PCA-compressed spatial patch features as a local semantic state, which is fused with spatially corresponding image tokens at the input. Each transformer block also directly reads the current noisy CLS state through an independent projection Eℓ, providing global context throughout the network. (d) During inference, SSR jointly generates image, local and global states from random noise, retaining spatial input fusion and per-layer CLS injection at every sampling step. No reference image or visual encoder is required during sampling.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Semantic State Reading (SSR) for diffusion transformers, combining image latents with global and local semantic states. This advances the architecture of multimodal generative models.
papers.title: Semantic State Reading for Joint Image-Semantic Diffusion Transformers
papers.tldr: Semantic State Reading improves diffusion-transformer image generation by jointly modeling global and local semantic states and repeatedly injecting them during denoising.

papers.abstract: Beat and downbeat tracking have seen multiple improvements through recent deep learning approaches, but most target an offline setting, precluding their use in real-time scenarios. We adapt a recent offline beat tracking model, Beat This, for online, low-latency operation and propose Beat This! Live, a causal variant designed for real-time beat and downbeat tracking. We present the architectural modifications required to obtain a causal system suitable for streaming inference and measure their impact on accuracy. By training our model with temporally shifted labels, it produces predictions slightly ahead of the current frame, which not only reduces latency, but enables much more effective peak-picking. Evaluation on the GTZAN dataset shows the F1-score improves from 80.6 to 86.7 for beats and 56.5 to 74.1 for downbeats compared to BeatNet+, the current state of the art in online beat tracking.
authors: B\'ank Juh\'asz, Gerhard Widmer, Jan Schl\"uter
bullets: Targets the gap between accurate offline tracking and real-time streaming requirements.
Introduces causal architectural modifications for online beat and downbeat tracking.
Uses temporally shifted labels to predict slightly ahead of the current frame, reducing latency and improving peak-picking.
On GTZAN, F1 improves from 80.6 to 86.7 for beats and from 56.5 to 74.1 for downbeats versus BeatNet+.

At frame 11 (red line), the shifted model (c) produces its estimate for frame 14 (3-frame lookahead). This provides additional time for computational latency as the model must only emit this prediction at frame 14 – potentially allowing for zero- or negative-latency predictions.

Figure 2: Comparison of postprocessing strategies. Offline Beat This! picks local maxima above a threshold (a), which requires access to future predictions. Causal thresholding reports the first activation above a threshold (b, c). A low threshold reports events too early (b). Raising the threshold reports events later (c), but may miss events completely. Training with shifted labels moves all predictions to occur early (d), allowing to pick local maxima without breaking causality.

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers decouple computational depth from parameter count, and prior studies have demonstrated promising performance gains with increased computation. However, systematic design principles for configuring these models under strict iso-parameter and iso-FLOP constraints remain scarce. We contribute to this direction by improving information flow in looped models and systematically studying loop parameter configurations. Specifically, we refine this information flow via gated inner-loop state updates and a cross-stage residual connection. Building on this design, controlled studies identify a configuration combining a single-pass Core depth of 25%-35% of the total unrolled depth with reallocating saved parameters into extra routed experts per layer, improving performance at zero extra compute while preserving compatibility with existing training infrastructure. Evaluated after 1T pre-training tokens, our 69B MLA and 51B KDA Mixture-of-Experts models outperform budget-matched non-recurrent baselines by an average of 1.16 and 2.29 percentage points across four benchmarks, respectively. Further reproduction experiments on a common backbone with a 200B-token training budget show that our method achieves lower perplexity than other looped methods. Code for these reproduction experiments is available at https://github.com/lxi01766/Scaling-Looped-MoE-Language-Models-under-Matched-Budgets-Information-Flow-and-Parameter-Allocation.
authors: Shipeng Bai, Jiayu Qin, Hong Liu, Xili Wang, Jianchao Tan, Jiacheng Li, He Zhang, Yifan Lu, Jiaqi Zhang, Kefeng Zhang, Yuchen Xie, Xunliang Cai
bullets: Addresses the lack of design principles for looped models under strict iso-parameter and iso-FLOP constraints.
Uses gated inner-loop state updates and cross-stage residual connections to improve information flow.
Finds that a single-pass Core occupying 25–35% of unrolled depth, with saved parameters assigned to more routed experts, is an effective configuration.
After 1T tokens, 69B MLA and 51B KDA MoE models outperform matched non-recurrent baselines by average gains of 1.16 and 2.29 percentage points across four benchmarks.
Reproduction experiments with a shared backbone and 200B tokens yield lower perplexity than other looped methods.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models excel at image and video generation, but iterative denoising incurs substantial inference latency. Recent token-adaptive acceleration methods select Taylor prediction orders for the full-model residual using shallow-layer proxy scores. However, candidate orders are evaluated on these proxy features but used to predict the full-model residual, creating a proxy--target mismatch: the proxy-preferred order may not minimize residual prediction error. To address this mismatch, we propose \textbf{TORE} (\textbf{T}aylor \textbf{O}rder selection via \textbf{R}esidual \textbf{E}rror estimation), which selects token-wise Taylor orders based on estimated prediction errors for the full-model residual. Yet direct error evaluation requires future ground-truth residuals, which are unavailable during order selection. TORE therefore estimates prediction error by analyzing how errors arise in Taylor extrapolation. Specifically, it decomposes prediction error into truncation error and finite-difference derivative error, then estimates both contributions from cached residuals to preselect token-wise orders for upcoming skip steps. Extensive experiments show that TORE achieves $4.31\times$ speedup on FLUX.1-dev and $4.18\times$ on Wan2.1 while maintaining high generation quality and fidelity.
authors: Lei Tang, Baoquan Zhang, Yakun Zhang, Yunming Ye
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between shallow proxy scores and full-model residual prediction accuracy in token-adaptive acceleration.
Decomposes Taylor prediction error into truncation and finite-difference derivative errors.
Uses cached residuals to estimate these errors without unavailable future ground-truth residuals.
Preselects token-wise Taylor orders for upcoming denoising skip steps.
Reports 4.31× speedup on FLUX.1-dev and 4.18× on Wan2.1 while maintaining high generation quality and fidelity.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models benefit from large, diverse datasets for robotic manipulation, yet collecting robot demonstrations remains costly. Recent work has explored egocentric videos as a source of supervision, primarily drawing on demonstrations of human-object interaction. We show that in-the-wild videos can improve robotic manipulation even when they contain no demonstrations of object manipulation. Specifically, camera motion recovered from these videos provides an additional source of motion supervision that complements robot demonstrations. Building on this finding, we introduce CamAct, which incorporates this camera-motion supervision into VLA policies alongside robot demonstrations, extending the use of human videos for manipulation learning beyond object interactions. Experiments show that incorporating this video supervision during fine-tuning improves success rates from 96.40% to 98.10% on LIBERO and from 22.96% to 29.32% on RoboCasa 365. The resulting policy also demonstrates strong results in out-of-distribution generalization on LIBERO-Plus and real-world manipulation tasks.
authors: Haoming Gu, Yunpeng Qing, Zhi Hou, Weinan Zhang
bullets: Addresses the high cost and limited diversity of collecting robot demonstrations.
Recovers camera motion from egocentric human videos as complementary motion supervision.
Integrates this supervision with robot demonstrations during VLA policy fine-tuning.
Improves success rates from 96.40% to 98.10% on LIBERO and from 22.96% to 29.32% on RoboCasa 365.
Also shows strong out-of-distribution performance on LIBERO-Plus and real-world manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: A detector scores candidate detections, but the recall and false alarms at a given confidence threshold depend on the input distribution. We introduce Detector Operating Behavior Inference (DOBI), a second-level inference task: estimating a fixed detector's threshold-dependent, distribution-level operating response from the internal evidence of a single unlabeled image. DOBI treats the detector's threshold response, i.e. recall, false positives, and precision across thresholds, as a latent behavioral state under the current data condition. Controlled data-space sampling probes this state space offline, and a lightweight monitor learns the inverse map from one image to this state, whose single functional output supports multiple operating policies. In a controlled proof of concept with a fixed YOLOv10-Nano person detector and COCO-derived degradations, predicted PR behavior reduces mean absolute deviation from 0.128 for an image-independent mean-behavior prior to 0.054, and predicted functional distances track empirical regime distances (Spearman 0.96). From one unlabeled image, the inferred behavior selects operating points as well as a non-deployable lookup that knows the true regime (macro-regime $F_1$ 0.6604 for both, versus 0.6407 under pristine calibration; oracle 0.6620). On this discrete benchmark, regime-supervised curve lookups are strong controls. Pre-specified continuous and compositional probing shows where functional inference matters: on unseen combinations, the functional decoder has a lower mean curve error than a template lookup, increasingly with distance from the training conditions, whereas the lookup is more accurate for interpolation. These results establish the feasibility of single-image inference of distribution-level detector behavior over the probed conditions. Source code is available at https://github.com/beckerio/dobi
authors: Stefan Becker, Simon Weiss, Wolfgang H\"ubner
bullets: Motivation: detector performance at a confidence threshold varies with the input distribution, but the current distribution is often unlabeled.
Method: offline controlled data-space sampling probes detector behavior, while a lightweight monitor maps one image to the corresponding behavioral response curve.
Contribution: a single inferred functional output supports multiple threshold-selection and operating policies.

In a YOLOv10-Nano proof of concept with COCO-derived degradations, DOBI reduced mean curve deviation from 0.128 to 0.054 and achieved Spearman 0.96 agreement between predicted and empirical regime distances.
Scope: functional inference helped most on unseen combinations and extrapolation, while template lookups were more accurate for interpolation on the discrete benchmark.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a method (DOBI) to infer detector operating behavior (recall, precision) from a single unlabeled image. This is a form of test-time adaptation, fitting the Adaptation and Memory taxonomy.

papers.abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) with general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offers a flexible alternative to task-specific navigation policies, while reliable long-horizon execution remains challenging. Agents must track navigation progress, detect discrepancies between commanded and actual motion, and recognize when movement has passed relevant landmarks or entrances. We present Navigent, an agentic VLN framework built around a frozen MLLM and a Geometry-Grounded Execution Critic (GEC). GEC performs two complementary checks: action-to-motion consistency, which evaluates measured displacement against commanded movement, and motion-to-landmark consistency, which tracks agent-selected visual anchors and entrance candidates in world coordinates. Detected discrepancies interrupt the remaining action sequence and trigger reobservation, local adjustment, or node-based recovery. Historical visual memory supports progress tracking across extended routes. An offline self-improvement procedure further analyzes successful and failed training trajectories to refine navigation prompts and GEC logic while keeping model weights fixed. On the R2R-CE validation-unseen split (1,839 episodes) and RxR-CE validation-unseen split(3,669 episodes), Navigent achieves 84.0%/86.0% SR and 72.9%/69.1% SPL, respectively, demonstrating the value of geometry-grounded execution verification for reliable agentic navigation. authors: Xinyu Zhou, Weiren Cai, Yitong Chen, Shenghai Yuan, Zihang Mu, Boyu Ma, Jiahua Dong, Yanshuo Lu, Jiaqi Bai, Jianfei Yang
bullets: Addresses unreliable long-horizon navigation, including mismatches between commanded and actual motion and missed landmarks or entrances.
Uses a frozen multimodal large language model with a Geometry-Grounded Execution Critic (GEC).
GEC checks action-to-motion consistency and motion-to-landmark consistency using visual anchors and entrance candidates in world coordinates.
Detected discrepancies trigger reobservation, local adjustment, or node-based recovery; historical visual memory tracks progress.
Reports 84.0%/86.0% success rate and 72.9%/69.1% SPL on R2R-CE/RxR-CE validation-unseen splits, respectively.

papers.abstract: Satellite time series capture how land surfaces change over time. Pixel-wise temporal foundation models read a year of satellite observations per pixel, yet public benchmarks lack a temporal axis or subsample it to a few dates. We introduce Analemma, a temporal benchmark of six datasets that carry every 10 and 20 m Sentinel-2 band and a time series spanning a growing season, completed where their releases omit geometry, dates, or cloud masks. One frozen-encoder protocol evaluates all models across label ratios and three seeds, with two baselines without pretraining. The TESSERA model ranks first overall. A from-scratch model on monthly composites outranks every foundation model except OlmoEarth v1.3-Base, suggesting that temporal input explains most of the performance. Three evaluation choices left unstated by the source publications each shift TESSERA v1 by 7.6 to 18.6 mIoU, against top-two gaps of 0.6 to 2.8. Data, harness and leaderboard will be publicly released soon.
authors: Alex L\'opez-Cifuentes (Xoople), Laura Mart\'inez-Ferrer (Xoople), Juan Ignacio Bravo P\'erez-Villar (Xoople)
bullets: Addresses the lack of temporal benchmarks for pixel-wise geospatial foundation models.
Provides six datasets with 10 m and 20 m Sentinel-2 bands, growing-season time series, geometry, dates, and cloud masks.
Uses a frozen-encoder evaluation across label ratios and three seeds, including two non-pretrained baselines.
TESSERA ranks first overall, while a monthly-composite model trained from scratch surpasses all foundation models except OlmoEarth v1.3-Base.
Unspecified evaluation choices change TESSERA’s score by 7.6–18.6 mIoU, exceeding reported top-two gaps of 0.6–2.8.

papers.abstract: Code-driven video generation asks a coding agent to write and run rendering programs. This gives exact control over typography, data visualizations, synchronized audio, and multi-shot scenes, and it leaves an editable project behind. A program that exits cleanly can still render overlapping labels, a camera aimed away from its subject, broken object interactions, or narration that drifts out of sync, and none of these raise a runtime error. Feeding rendered frames and audio back into the coding session bloats its long-horizon context, while critiquing only the finished full-resolution render turns early design mistakes into costly rewrites. We introduce VibeVideoAgent, a training-free framework that lets coding agents inspect their drafts throughout production. Multimodal perception runs in short-lived contexts kept apart from the coder and returns compact, grounded Findings. Seven primitives operate on a unified multi-clock representation of assets and drafts: they explore media from coarse to fine, verify quoted requirements with evidence from every required modality, compare a draft with a reference or an earlier revision on separate clocks, and measure stream signals locally. A lightweight staged protocol has the agent test its riskiest decision on a minimal preview first. On all 239 VibeVideoBench tasks, with matched agent runtimes and a fixed perception model, VibeVideoAgent improves holistic audiovisual quality (L3) for Claude Opus 5.5 (4.03 -> 4.43, while L2 rubric compliance rises from 98.87% to 99.35%), GPT-6 Astra (4.03 -> 4.27), and Claude Sonnet 5.5 (3.97 -> 4.10), with the largest gains in audio-visual synchronization (up to +0.56). Controlled ablations show that each component contributes, and trajectory audits show that the granularity of code edits governs the trade-off between rubric adherence and perceptual quality.
authors: Xuanyu Zheng, Luoyuan Zhang, Yancheng Long, Haoyang Xu, Muxi Diao, Yuzhe Chen, Kaiyu Jiang, Bin Wen, Tingting Gao
bullets: Addresses perceptual failures that produce valid code but flawed videos, such as occlusion, poor camera framing, broken interactions, and audio drift.
Uses short-lived multimodal perception contexts that return compact, grounded findings without bloating the coding agent’s long-horizon context.
Introduces seven primitives over a unified multi-clock representation to inspect media, verify requirements, compare revisions or references, and measure local stream signals.
A staged protocol tests risky design choices on minimal previews before committing to costly full renders.
Across 239 VibeVideoBench tasks, it improves holistic audiovisual quality and especially audio-visual synchronization for three evaluated agents; ablations indicate all components contribute.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Architecture of VibeVideoAgent. (a) A three-clock Media specification 𝜎 addresses assets, stills, partial previews, and full renders, with crop-before-scale magnification and source-file hashing. (b) Seven stack-agnostic primitives explore media from coarse to fine, verify sourced requirements across modalities, compare two media on separate clocks, and probe signals without model calls, returning grounded Findings 𝑓𝑡 to an auditable ledger. (c) A staged protocol gates planning and then guides preview, assembly, repair, and delivery checks.

Figure 4. End-to-end authoring with VibeVideoAgent. (a) The recorded W0448 run with real frames. (1) plan_production decomposes the brief, and a single stage=preview lineup still verifies cross-age character identity before full rendering. (2) stage=assembly checks catch silent staging bugs in v1.mp4 even though the render exited cleanly: the backpack is held in hand, and in the Family beat no lid closes while the child already stands in the doorway. (3) compare_media(finding_id, media) confirms a targeted render.py patch across shifted clocks. (4) Deterministic probe_media checks finalize the seamless red-button loop. papers.selection_reason: Introduces a framework (VibeVideoAgent) for code-driven video generation that uses multimodal perception to close the perceptual loop. This fits the Multimodal Foundation Models category as it involves agents combining vision and language for generation tasks.
papers.title: VibeVideoAgent: Closing the Perceptual Loop for Code-Driven Video Generation
papers.tldr: VibeVideoAgent improves code-driven video generation by giving coding agents compact, staged, multimodal feedback throughout production instead of only after rendering.

papers.abstract: Relighting reconstructed 3D scenes remains challenging due to the complex nature of light transport: slow or approximate visual feedback restricts the editor's ability to fine-tune the results to satisfaction. We present a hybrid relighting approach that enables interactive, high-fidelity updates of direct and indirect indoor illumination without per-edit optimization. Our approach permits the editor to make a wide range of relighting edits at room-scale, with near-instant feedback. Our key insight is to precompute geometric light exchange rather than illumination responses, retaining an inexpensive transport solve that accommodates changes in emission and surface reflectance. We evaluate direct illumination on reconstructed 2D Gaussians using visibility-aware sampling of one-sided emitters, while propagating diffuse interreflection through sparse radiosity on a triangle proxy. A sparse projection fitted through Gaussian alpha compositing transfers the proxy solution to the reconstruction. Our formulation further supports fast fixture transformations and emitter insertion by recomputing light source injection. Across eight relighting conditions of our synthetic test suite, our sub-second edits improve relighting fidelity over prior path-traced editing by an average of 5\,dB PSNR, while reducing editing latency by up to three orders of magnitude. Qualitative results further demonstrate realistic, interactive relighting of real-world captures.
authors: Noah Rothenberger, Dor Verbin, Serge Belongie, Bernhard Kerbl
bullets: Supports room-scale edits to direct and indirect indoor illumination with near-instant feedback.
Precomputes geometric light exchange while retaining an inexpensive transport solve for changing emission and reflectance.
Combines visibility-aware direct lighting on 2D Gaussians with sparse radiosity on a triangle proxy, then projects results back to the reconstruction.
Handles fast fixture transformations and emitter insertion through recomputed light-source injection.

Across eight synthetic conditions, improves fidelity by 5 dB PSNR on average and reduces latency by up to three orders of magnitude versus prior path-traced editing; real-world captures show qualitative realism.

papers.abstract: Physical hand interaction depends on configuration, contact, and force, yet nearly identical appearances can conceal different contact states and exerted forces. We therefore formulate physical hand state estimation from egocentric video and wrist surface electromyography (sEMG), combining visual geometry with neuromuscular evidence to jointly recover these coupled components. To support this task, we introduce EgoMyo, a benchmark spanning 5.75M video frames, 50 participants, 34 contact configurations, and repeated donnings, synchronizing these inputs with 3D hand pose and with contact and normal force registered onto the hand surface from bare-hand pressure. Controlled analysis reveals that vision resolves spatial structure while sEMG better estimates force magnitude, that sEMG's gains concentrate in regions where vision is least reliable, and that contact localization limits force accuracy. Guided by these findings, we propose MyoBridge, which makes the hand region the unit of vision-sEMG fusion, lets each region gate its own share of sEMG, and distributes regional force magnitudes only over predicted contact vertices at inference. On held-out trials, MyoBridge reduces pose and force error by 39.8% and 18.5% over the strongest baseline and achieves the lowest pose error on unseen sessions and subjects.
authors: Guanglong Sun, Kanglei Zhou, Ziteng Wang, Nana Wang, Hengkai Tan, Xiaolong Liu, Hang Su, Yi Zhong, Jun Zhu
bullets: Physical hand state estimation is challenging because similar visual appearances can hide different contact states and exerted forces.
EgoMyo synchronizes egocentric video and wrist sEMG with 3D hand pose, surface contact, and normal force measurements across diverse participants, configurations, and repeated donnings.
Analysis finds that vision captures spatial structure best, while sEMG better estimates force magnitude, especially where vision is unreliable.
MyoBridge performs region-level vision-sEMG fusion, with learned regional sEMG gating and force allocation restricted to predicted contact vertices.
On held-out trials, it reduces pose error by 39.8% and force error by 18.5% versus the strongest baseline; contact localization remains a limitation for force accuracy.

papers.title: EgoMyo: Physical Hand State Estimation from Egocentric Video and Wrist Electromyography

papers.abstract: Real cameras are not pinholes, yet most dynamic Gaussian splatting assumes they are. Footage is therefore undistorted first, losing field of view or detail, especially with wide-angle and fisheye cameras. Static Gaussian splatting has largely solved this with ray-based rendering, which suits any camera. Native 4D Gaussians, which model motion in space-time, cannot use it directly: each Gaussian's orientation and size cannot be recovered reliably from its covariance. We present AnyCam4D, which trains native 4D Gaussians on original footage by ray-based rasterization, preserving field of view and resolution at about the per-step cost of standard projection. Our key contribution is a numerically stable way to obtain orientation and size: we condition a square root of the 4D covariance. Trained models render through other cameras, with rolling shutter, depth of field or chromatic aberration. With a synthetic 170-degree fisheye camera, training on original images improves peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) by 3.0-8.1 dB. On real footage, AnyCam4D has lower perceptual error than the standard projection adapted to each camera, at comparable PSNR and without camera-specific derivations. With the synthetic camera rotated 60-80 degrees away from the capture rig's view, it leads by 6.2 dB against ground truth.
authors: Sascha Kirch, Rafael Pag\'es, Jan Ond\v{r}ej, Clara P\'erez-Molina, Sergio Martin
bullets: Addresses distortion from undistorting wide-angle and fisheye footage, which can reduce field of view and detail.
Uses ray-based rasterization for native 4D Gaussians at roughly the per-step cost of standard projection.
Stabilizes Gaussian orientation and size estimation by conditioning a square root of the 4D covariance.
Supports rendering through cameras with rolling shutter, depth of field, and chromatic aberration.
Improves synthetic 170° fisheye PSNR by 3.0–8.1 dB and achieves lower perceptual error on real footage; gains reach 6.2 dB for substantially shifted viewpoints.

papers.abstract: Self-supervised video representation learning has achieved remarkable progress by leveraging large-scale unlabeled video data. Recent methods commonly extend Masked Image Modeling (MIM) to Masked Video Modeling (MVM), where video representations are learned by capturing semantic information from temporal contexts during masked content recovery. Unlike static images, videos exhibit inherent temporal variation, as visual objects continuously change their positions, appearances, and motion states across frames. Therefore, MVM needs to preserve semantic consistency while capturing temporal changes of corresponding regions, which raises two central challenges: 1) how to establish reliable temporal correspondence across frames, and 2) how to formulate an appropriate representation learning objective for modeling both semantic consistency and temporal variation. To address these challenges, we propose Variation-aware Temporal Correspondence for video Representation learning (VT-CoRe) framework. For challenge 1), VT-CoRe introduces a sandwich sampling strategy to construct two-sided temporal references and a Patch Registration Module (PRM) to establish reliable patch-level correspondence. For challenge 2), VT-CoRe imposes latent-space semantic alignment on registered representations through a self-distillation architecture and further proposes temporal variation modeling to constrain representation trajectories over time. Experiments on 8 downstream tasks across 16 benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and applicability of VT-CoRe across pixel-level, frame-level, video-level, and vision-based robotic learning scenarios. Complementary representation analysis shows that VT-CoRe learns a more structured latent space for variation-aware temporal correspondence learning.
authors: Yang Liu, Qianqian Xu, Peisong Wen, Siran Dai, Qingming Huang
bullets: Addresses unreliable temporal correspondence and the difficulty of jointly learning semantic consistency and temporal change in masked video modeling.
Uses sandwich sampling and a Patch Registration Module to establish two-sided, patch-level temporal correspondences.
Applies self-distillation for latent-space semantic alignment and constrains representation trajectories to model temporal variation.
Demonstrates effectiveness across 8 downstream tasks and 16 benchmarks, spanning pixel-, frame-, video-, and robotics-oriented learning.
Representation analysis indicates that the method learns a more structured latent space for variation-aware correspondence.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: The architecture of the proposed framework. Given a training video, we introduce a sandwich sampling strategy to select past, current, and future frames, with the past and future frames providing two-sided temporal references via the auxiliary branch. We propose the Patch Registration Module to align the past and future representations with the current one, thereby establishing reliable correspondence for latent-space reconstruction. We further project the registered representations into a separate space for variation-aware temporal modeling, where we use a second-order Taylor approximation to construct local representation trajectories with multiple parameter groups to adaptively fit different patterns.

Fig. 1: Motivation of this work. Extending masked image modeling (MIM) to masked video modeling (MVM) requires handling temporal variation beyond static semantic consistency, as video representations tend to evolve along the temporal sequence. This extension raises two key challenges: establishing reliable temporal correspondence across frames and designing an appropriate objective for video representation learning. VT-CoRe addresses these challenges by introducing sandwich sampling and patch registration to construct reliable temporal triplets, and further combines latent-space semantic alignment with variation-aware temporal modeling.

papers.abstract: Cross-modal self-supervised learning for paired side-scan sonar and underwater optical imagery is a promising direction for benthic habitat understanding, but it remains underexplored because existing methods do not fully exploit the one-to-many correspondences and geographic metadata available in real opti-acoustic surveys. This limits the ability to learn representations that are both semantically meaningful and geometrically consistent from abundant unlabeled marine data. To address this problem, we present GeoCAM, a geography-guided framework that learns a shared embedding space for sonar tiles and their associated optical views without semantic annotations. GeoCAM achieves its goal by combining three components: (i) a Set Attention Aggregator that adaptively summarizes multiple optical observations into a single tile-level representation; (ii) a geometry-weighted InfoNCE objective that converts GPS-derived footprint overlap into soft positive supervision; and (iii) an optional cross-modal masked reconstruction branch that encourages physically grounded cross-modal alignment. Experiments on the BenthiCat SSS-CAM dataset show that GeoCAM can be effectively exploited to learn which sonar and camera samples describe the same seabed patch, improving cross-modal retrieval and alignment over strong contrastive baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/FadiZidiDz/GeoCAM.
authors: Fadi Abdeladhim Zidi, Andrea De Salve, Giuseppe Celeste, Abdellah Zakaria Sellam, Paolo Spagnolo, Cosimo Distante
bullets: Addresses one-to-many sonar–optical correspondences and geographic metadata in unlabeled opti-acoustic surveys.
Aggregates multiple optical views with a Set Attention Aggregator.
Uses GPS footprint overlap as soft positive supervision in a geometry-weighted InfoNCE loss.
Optionally adds cross-modal masked reconstruction for physically grounded alignment.
On BenthiCat SSS-CAM, improves cross-modal retrieval and alignment over contrastive baselines.

papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) demonstrate impressive multimodal capabilities, yet suffer from hallucination - generating factually inaccurate content. Contrastive Decoding (CD) mitigates this by contrasting amateur and expert branches at the logit level. However, our investigation reveals that such logit-level interventions fundamentally compromise generation coherence, necessitating restrictive penalty constraints unrelated to hallucination suppression. We introduce Attention Contrastive Decoding (ACD), a training-free plug-in that complements logit-level CD by relocating part of the contrastive operations to the attention mechanism. Operating at an earlier stage of the forward pass, ACD performs smooth semantic-preserving interventions through an Adaptive Subtraction Strategy (ASS), which attenuates hallucination-associated attention patterns while amplifying critical visual information. Extensive experiments demonstrate that combining ACD with existing CD methods (e.g., VCD+ACD) produces substantially more coherent outputs with further reduced hallucinations, eliminating restrictive penalties while enabling trustworthy multimodal generation.
authors: Yujia Chen, Rui Sun, Huayu Mai, Wangkai Li, Zhangyu He, Bingzhou Wang, Aibing Li, Wenzhang Sun, Tianzhu Zhang
bullets: Logit-level Contrastive Decoding can harm coherence and requires restrictive penalty constraints.
ACD is a training-free plug-in that complements existing contrastive decoding methods.
Its Adaptive Subtraction Strategy adjusts attention patterns to suppress hallucination-related signals and emphasize important visual information.
Combining ACD with methods such as VCD reportedly yields more coherent outputs and further reduces hallucinations.
The approach targets trustworthy multimodal generation without restrictive penalties.

papers.abstract: Time-series foundation models (TSFMs) provide transferable numerical forecasting priors. However, forecast-relevant information may be conveyed in text without being reflected in the observed series. Many multimodal forecasting methods integrate such context through model inputs or intermediate representations. We investigate a complementary mechanism: text-conditioned parameter adaptation. We propose Context-to-LoRA for Time Series (C2LoRA-TS), which encodes text and generates temporary Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) updates for selected weight matrices of a frozen TSFM. Both the numerical backbone and text encoder remain frozen, and the method exactly recovers the frozen TSFM output when context is absent. Evaluated on Time-MMD across nine domains and three TSFM architectures, C2LoRA-TS achieves lower aggregate forecasting error than the frozen-TSFM and Static LoRA baselines for every architecture and seed. Replacing the instance-specific text with a single globally fixed context degrades performance for every architecture. These results support text-conditioned parameter generation as a viable strategy for multimodal forecasting with frozen TSFMs.
authors: Kunqi Li, Bin Liang, Zhidong Li
bullets: Addresses forecast-relevant information present in text but missing from observed time series.
Encodes text into temporary LoRA updates for selected weights while keeping the TSFM and text encoder frozen.

papers.abstract: Predicting the outcomes of robotic manipulation requires modeling both visual appearance and evolving 3D geometry. This poses two challenges: video compression can obscure fine-grained robot motion, while jointly predicting RGB and geometry demands sufficient generative capacity. We introduce Loop4D, a framework that addresses these challenges through motion-preserving 4D representations and recurrent generative refinement. Our 4D VAE encodes RGB and pointmap sequences into compact spatiotemporal latents while preserving motion details and geometric structure. Our RGB VAE combines geometry-guided supervision with predictive reconstruction to reduce compression-induced motion artifacts. Our geometry VAE uses lightweight adapters to adapt pretrained RGB representations while preserving their priors. Building on these representations, our Dual-Stream Looped Diffusion Transformer maintains separate appearance and geometry streams with shared Transformer weights and cross-modal connections. By reusing Transformer blocks across loops, we increase effective depth without replicating backbone parameters, enabling models with fewer parameters to improve joint RGB-geometry prediction through additional computation. Experiments demonstrate high-quality 4D generation and validate Loop4D in simulated robotic manipulation tasks.
authors: Gen Li, Fan Luo, Mengjun Lin, Shu Han, Bohan Li, Hao Zhao
bullets: Addresses motion detail loss during video compression and the difficulty of jointly predicting appearance and geometry.
Uses a 4D VAE to encode RGB and pointmap sequences into compact spatiotemporal latents while preserving motion and geometric structure.
Employs geometry-guided, predictive RGB reconstruction and lightweight-adapter geometry encoding built on pretrained RGB representations.
Uses a dual-stream diffusion Transformer with separate RGB and geometry streams, cross-modal connections, and looped block reuse for greater effective depth without duplicating parameters.
Demonstrates high-quality 4D generation and validation in simulated robotic manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Existing defenses against indirect prompt injection in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) are inherently reactive: prompt-engineering methods are often overridden by the injected instructions, while supervised detectors must be retrained for each new attack style. We propose a different paradigm: defend by maximizing relevance, not by detecting attacks. Our method, MINE, is training-free and attack-agnostic, and it also serves as a query-conditioned reranker. To evaluate defenses under realistic conditions, we introduce LC-Inj-SQuAD, a long-context benchmark with an average of 4,032 words per context. We evaluate on four datasets spanning short-context QA (Inj-SQuAD, Inj-TriviaQA), long-context QA (LC-Inj-SQuAD), and agent tool-call injection (InjecAgent). Across all four, MINE achieves the best accuracy--security trade-off among training-free defenses. It is also the only defense that stays usable against a fully adaptive attacker, generalizes to agent tool-call injection, and achieves the lowest inference latency on long contexts.
authors: Truong Phan, Ngoc-Quan Pham, Dat Quoc Nguyen
bullets: Addresses reactive defenses that can be overridden or require retraining for new attack styles.
Uses mutual information and embedding variance for query-conditioned reranking, without attack detection or training.
Introduces LC-Inj-SQuAD, a long-context benchmark averaging 4,032 words per context.
Evaluated across short- and long-context QA and agent tool-call injection settings.
Reports the best accuracy–security trade-off among training-free defenses, with robustness to adaptive attacks and low long-context latency.

papers.abstract: Multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) in real-world systems must handle unpredictable modality missingness caused by sensor failures, privacy masking, and unstable transmission. Existing methods either learn reliability-aware representations or reconstruct missing inputs, often using a single flattened encoder output. This overlooks deep encoders' semantic hierarchy and intra- and inter-modal interactions, causing semantic averaging and ill-posed mappings. We propose Hierarchical Semantic Learning (HSL), a framework that exploits semantic hierarchy for robust MSA with missing modalities. Hierarchical Semantic Decoupling exposes low-, mid-, and high-level feature streams from each modality encoder. Cross-Modal Cross-Level Semantic Reconstruction performs ladder-style recovery, using high-level semantics from observed modalities as global anchors to progressively reconstruct mid-level structures and low-level details of missing modalities. To stabilize cross-level reconstruction, Hierarchical Cascade Error Supervisor applies prototypical contrastive regularization to observed and reconstructed features, enforcing level-specific semantic consistency and limiting error propagation. Finally, Hierarchical Interactive Fusion captures dense interactions across modalities and semantic levels to produce robust predictions under diverse missingness patterns. Experiments on CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, IEMOCAP, and CH-SIMS show that HSL outperforms baselines in most missing-modality settings.
authors: Chunlei Meng, Rong Fu, Zhan Chen, Yi Liu, Zhuo Zou, LiDa Xu, Chun Ouyang, Zhongxue Gan
bullets: Addresses modality loss from sensor failures, privacy masking, and unstable transmission in real-world MSA.
Decouples each modality into low-, mid-, and high-level semantic feature streams.
Reconstructs missing modalities from high-level anchors through mid-level structures to low-level details.
Uses prototypical contrastive regularization to enforce level-specific consistency and reduce error propagation.
Outperforms baselines in most missing-modality settings across CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, IEMOCAP, and CH-SIMS.

papers.abstract: Transferring reasoning capabilities from large language models to smaller ones often requires extensive teacher supervision or costly student adaptation. We study projected cross-model Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Vector transfer, a two-stage approach that keeps both models frozen. First, we learn a task-level CoT Vector in the teacher using dataset-provided solution traces and final-answer supervision. We then train a lightweight linear projector to map the fixed vector into a smaller student's residual space. Student-side training uses only final-answer cross-entropy on a small subset of task training examples; it requires neither teacher outputs nor intermediate solution traces. We select the student injection layer and intervention scale on a labeled support set and report results on the disjoint remainder of each evaluation split. On GSM8K and MATH, the projected vector improves base students by 10.37-21.98 accuracy points across the evaluated teacher-student settings. On four code-generation benchmarks, the Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct student gains 3.23-4.67 pass@1 points, while the base Qwen2.5-7B student gains up to 9.65 points. These results show that a teacher-side reasoning vector can be reused across smaller students with different residual dimensions through projector-only adaptation.

papers.abstract: Vision-language agents act on native-resolution renders of multi-element pages, where one perturbed photo or a few altered text strokes can redirect the decision. Any content provider can craft such a perturbation on the open model behind the agent, so a plug-in purifier is the natural first line of defense. Yet diffusion purifiers were designed and evaluated at the fixed resolution of the diffusion model on classifier or natural-image benchmarks, and defense evaluations for agents test JPEG, blur and noise but no diffusion purifier. We present the first study of adversarial purification at the agentic level, for an agent built on Qwen3-VL-8B: purifiers run at native resolution on multi-element inputs, face grey-box attackers who know the agent's model but not the defense, and are compared at matched clean cost. We show that treating agentic inputs as classifier inputs misleads both evaluation and design. Resizing the input to the resolution of the diffusion model, as existing purifiers do, raises the TextVQA clean cost of the Divide-and-Conquer purifier (DC) from 4.0 to 35.7 points. On web-shop pages, DC keeps 85.0% grey-box robust accuracy against web-hardened perturbations, where cheap input transformations at matched clean cost keep at most 40.0%, and this robustness comes from the global noise level: input-estimated masks and noise levels add none. These findings hold on a disjoint held-out set and on a second VLM and yield three requirements for defenses, we release the protocol.
authors: Yan Lin, Zhongliang Guo, Jingyu Lin, Daizong Liu
bullets: Native-resolution, multi-element agent inputs can be redirected by perturbing a single photo or a few text strokes.
The study evaluates purifiers for Qwen3-VL-8B against grey-box attackers at matched clean cost.
Resizing inputs to the diffusion model’s resolution substantially increases the Divide-and-Conquer purifier’s TextVQA clean cost, from 4.0 to 35.7 points.
On web-shop pages, Divide-and-Conquer achieves 85.0% grey-box robust accuracy, versus at most 40.0% for cheap input transformations at matched clean cost.
Global noise level drives the robustness; input-estimated masks and noise levels add no benefit, with findings replicated on held-out data and a second VLM.

papers.title: Agentic-Level Adversarial Purification: Revisiting Diffusion Purifiers on Native-Resolution Agentic Inputs

papers.abstract: Infrared and visible images offer complementary cues for all-weather object detection, yet real-world sensor dropouts can leave one stream unavailable and degrade paired-input detectors. Meanwhile, existing modality-adaptive methods apply heavy cross-modal attention uniformly across scales, incurring prohibitive token overhead on high-resolution maps. We propose Admoab-DETR, a unified real-time detector supporting infrared-only, visible-only, and paired inputs with a single set of weights. Specifically, \emph{Resolution-Tiered Fusion} (RTF) allocates fusion capacity by spatial token density and feature granularity: a lightweight Spatial Modality Gate governs fine local fusion at the highest-resolution scale with zero-cost single-view pass-through, while channel-compressed deformable Admoab necks capture cross-modal correspondence at coarser semantic scales. Furthermore, \emph{Mode-Matched Feature Distillation} (MMFD) aligns multi-scale encoder features with an availability-synchronized full-fusion teacher, avoiding ill-posed cross-modal hallucination while cutting parameters by 18.1\% and paired latency by 39.6\% at zero inference overhead. We also construct Admoab, a strictly registered 20,000-pair infrared--visible benchmark across diverse scenes. Experiments show Admoab-DETR achieves state-of-the-art accuracy--efficiency trade-offs across missing-modality and paired benchmarks. Our code will be available at https://github.com/liwenchao0615/Admoab-DETR.
authors: Wenchao Li, Haoran Jia, Shuyuan Wen, Keyan Chen
bullets: Addresses performance degradation when one sensing modality is unavailable in real-world all-weather detection.
Uses Resolution-Tiered Fusion: lightweight fine-scale spatial gating and channel-compressed deformable fusion at coarser semantic scales.
Applies Mode-Matched Feature Distillation with an availability-synchronized full-fusion teacher to avoid ill-posed cross-modal hallucination.
Reduces parameters by 18.1% and paired-input latency by 39.6% without inference overhead.
Introduces the registered 20,000-pair Admoab infrared-visible benchmark and reports state-of-the-art accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across paired and missing-modality settings.

papers.abstract: Audio-visual large language models (AV-LLMs) are designed to represent the temporal structure of audio and video, yet it remains unclear how effectively they use this temporal information to relate sounds to visual events. To examine this, we probe an AV-LLM on an audio-visual synchronization task by shifting the audio so that the queried sound overlaps a different visual event. We observe that the model still favors the originally aligned event over the newly aligned one, indicating limited sensitivity to changes in audio-visual temporal alignment. To address this, we propose Modality-Shift Contrastive Decoding (MSCD), a training-free decoding method that emphasizes audio-visual temporal alignment in model predictions. MSCD contrasts logits under preserved and disrupted temporal alignment to favor predictions supported by aligned audio and video. We disrupt this alignment by temporally shifting either the audio or the video, while keeping the other modality fixed. Extensive evaluations with two AV-LLMs across three benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of MSCD for temporally grounded audio-visual understanding. In particular, MSCD improves accuracy over the base models on Daily-Omni by 2.2 and 2.8 percentage points for OmniVinci and video-SALMONN 2+, respectively, suggesting that emphasizing temporal alignment can also benefit broader audio-visual understanding.
authors: Minyeong Jeong, Yeonju Kim, Yong Man Ro
bullets: AV-LLMs may favor originally associated visual events even when audio is shifted to overlap a different event, revealing limited temporal-alignment sensitivity.
MSCD is a training-free decoding method that compares logits under preserved versus disrupted audio-visual alignment.
Alignment is disrupted by shifting either the audio or video while keeping the other modality fixed.
Evaluations on two AV-LLMs across three benchmarks show improved temporally grounded understanding.
On Daily-Omni, accuracy increases by 2.2 and 2.8 percentage points for OmniVinci and video-SALMONN 2+, respectively.

papers.title: Modality-Shift Contrastive Decoding for Temporally Grounded Audio-Visual Understanding

papers.abstract: Task allocation in contested-objective team games requires coordinated decisions under uncertainty, spatial constraints, and changing tactical conditions. In such settings, multiple agents must anticipate both teammate behavior and opponent actions. We study a hybrid predict-then-optimize approach for assigning controllable agents to objectives in real time. A masked multi-head model predicts tactical signals for each agent, including survival chance, local superiority, combat interaction, travel time, and objective contribution. These signals are combined with rule-based terms in a score matrix, and a minimum-cost flow solver computes coordinated global assignments constrained by capacity, occupancy, stability, and defensive strategies. Learning is limited to tactical scoring, while explicit rules and solver structure preserve controllability and interpretability. We evaluate the system using predictive metrics, offline assignment diagnostics, online A/B evaluation, and latency measurements. The system is an R\&D research prototype built on a commercial game and is not deployed in the shipped game. The results indicate that learned tactical estimates can support stable, feasible, and inspectable objective allocation under strict real-time constraints.
authors: Jonas Pech\'e, Dmitry Matveev, Vladimir Ciric, Lizaveta Sakalova, G\"unter Wallner
bullets: Addresses coordinated task allocation under adversarial actions, spatial constraints, and changing battlefield conditions.
A masked multi-head model predicts tactical signals such as survival, local superiority, interaction, travel time, and objective contribution.
Rule-based terms and a constrained minimum-cost-flow solver produce globally coordinated assignments.
Evaluated with predictive metrics, offline diagnostics, online A/B tests, and latency measurements.
Results suggest stable, feasible, and inspectable allocation under strict real-time constraints; the system remains an R&D prototype, not a shipped-game deployment.

papers.title: Strategic and Robust Task Allocation for Combat Objectives in Adversarial Multi-Agent Environments

papers.abstract: Recent advances in Gaussian splatting have enabled efficient underwater reconstruction, but sparse observations, light attenuation, and backscatter still leave scene regions underconstrained and cause novel-view artifacts. We present OceanFix, a reference-guided framework for sparse-view underwater 3D reconstruction that combines diffusion-based view repair with Gaussian scene refinement. Our repair model follows a two-stage training strategy that separates underwater appearance adaptation from geometric refinement. The first stage learns underwater appearance from reference observations and estimated medium features. The second uses camera poses and reference depth to align reference features, with relative-depth supervision guiding structural repair without requiring target-view depth at inference. We further propose medium-aware distillation that transfers repaired views into the 3D scene according to geometric repair demand and channel-specific optical observability. Through iterative rendering, repair, and distillation, OceanFix refines underconstrained regions while retaining supervision from the observed views. Experiments on underwater datasets demonstrate that OceanFix improves rendering quality in sparse-view 3D reconstruction, reducing visible artifacts and recovering finer scene details.
authors: Gen Li, Maoxin Chen, Yao Xiao, Xinyang Li, Yu Pan
bullets: Addresses underconstrained regions and artifacts caused by sparse observations, light attenuation, and backscatter.
Combines diffusion-based view repair with Gaussian scene refinement in an iterative render–repair–distill pipeline.
Uses two-stage training to adapt underwater appearance and then enforce geometric structure from camera poses and reference depth.
Applies medium-aware distillation based on geometric repair needs and channel-specific optical observability.
Experiments on underwater datasets show improved rendering quality, fewer visible artifacts, and finer recovered details.

papers.abstract: Cross-subject EEG-to-image retrieval suffers from substantial performance degradation on new subjects due to subject shift. Test-time adaptation (TTA) can mitigate this shift by adapting pretrained models with unlabeled target-subject EEG. However, most existing TTA methods struggle to match supervision granularity to each query's prediction confidence, leaving many queries without reliable pseudo-labels. To address this, we propose a novel framework named Hierarchical Selective Test-Time Adaptation (HSTTA). HSTTA builds a hierarchy over gallery image embeddings, uses hierarchical selective prediction to assign each EEG query a supervision granularity matching its current prediction confidence, and constructs adaptation objectives accordingly. We further propose Cross-Session Consistency Calibration (CSCC), an unsupervised method that calibrates the global confidence threshold to target a predefined accuracy level for hierarchical predictions. Moreover, we introduce Reciprocal Hierarchical Backoff (RHB), which moves queries lacking reverse-matching support to coarser nodes to mitigate error reinforcement. Experiments on two public benchmarks and ablation studies validate the effectiveness of HSTTA and its key components. On THINGS-EEG2, HSTTA outperforms the strongest EEG-specific TTA baseline by 17.9 (13.4) and 8.9 (3.7) percentage points in Top-1/Top-5 accuracy, respectively, under cosine (CSLS) ranking. Further analyses show that HSTTA yields more accurate pseudo-labels during adaptation, supporting more reliable model updates.
authors: Hongzhou Chen, Yuhao Wei, Lianghua He, Yihang Liu, Zengqiang Wang
bullets: Addresses performance degradation caused by subject shift in new-subject EEG retrieval.
Builds a hierarchy over gallery images and selects prediction granularity according to each query’s confidence.
Uses Cross-Session Consistency Calibration to set confidence thresholds without labels.
Uses Reciprocal Hierarchical Backoff to move unsupported queries to coarser categories and reduce error reinforcement.
Validated on two public benchmarks; on THINGS-EEG2, it improves over the strongest EEG-specific TTA baseline by up to 17.9 percentage points in Top-1 accuracy.

(b) HSTTA uses the gallery hierarchy to select an appropriate supervision granularity based on each query’s current confidence.
