papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) excel at static visual understanding and are increasingly applied to spatial planning, where a model interprets a visual layout and outputs an action sequence to reach a goal. Grid games are a common testbed for this ability because their rules are explicit and a solver can verify every move. Yet existing benchmarks mostly report end-to-end success rates, which hide whether a failure stems from visual perception, rule application, or multi-step planning. We introduce GridProbe, a diagnostic benchmark that 1) locates the failing stage between visual perception and planning and 2) verifies the diagnosis by targeted fine-tuning. On Sokoban, GridProbe pairs end-to-end solving with four probes (recognition, localization, single-step prediction, and state tracking) and gives every board both as an image and as an equivalent text grid. Evaluating seven MLLMs on Sokoban and a maze game reveals distinct bottlenecks behind similar success rates: proprietary models are limited by multi-step planning, whereas open-source models are limited by rule application or by visual grid indexing, i.e., counting rows and columns. Planning failures also hide perception failures: when planning is easier, the visual cost of the same model grows from 7.6 to 37.7 points. The diagnosis identifies what to train: fine-tuning only the vision module of the perception-limited model on board reading raises its interactive Sokoban success 3.5-fold (5.8% to 20.4%) and transfers zero-shot to the unseen maze game (single-turn success 13.8% to 67.1%), whereas the same data does not help a rule-limited model and training on solver solutions brings no gain. We will release the benchmark and code at https://github.com/suat-llm/GridProbe.
authors: Luoxi Zhang, Tianyi Tan, Jiawei Liu, Xingyu Zeng, Min Yang, Shiwen Ni
bullets: Introduces a diagnostic benchmark for separating perception, rule application, and planning failures in visual grid games.
Combines Sokoban solving with recognition, localization, single-step prediction, and state-tracking probes, using both image and equivalent text-grid inputs.
Across seven MLLMs, proprietary models mainly struggle with multi-step planning, while open-source models struggle with rule application or visual grid indexing.
Targeted vision-module fine-tuning improves a perception-limited model’s Sokoban success from 5.8% to 20.4% and transfers to an unseen maze game, while solver-solution training provides no gain.

papers.selection_reason: Develops a diagnostic benchmark to analyze failure modes in Multimodal LLMs during spatial planning tasks, providing insights into the gap between visual perception and planning in embodied agents.
papers.title: Lost in the Grid: Where Multimodal LLMs Fail Between Seeing and Planning

papers.abstract: Flow matching robot policies generate action chunks by integrating a learned velocity field at inference. However, under a fixed budget of neural function evaluations (NFEs), the integration result depends on the sampling schedule. This motivates optimizing the schedule to bring the generated action distribution closer to the demonstrations and improve task success. We propose Ground Your Steps (GYS), a training-free method that optimizes the sampling schedule by matching the generated and demonstrated chunk distributions at each observation. GYS applies truncated fractional differencing along each arm joint's action sequence and compares two types of pairwise differences between action chunks at each observation: differences of a generated chunk against a demonstration, and differences of two independent generated chunks against each other. After fractional differencing, these two pairwise-difference distributions coincide exactly when the distributions of generated and demonstrated action chunks match. GYS minimizes the energy distance between these distributions to obtain an improved schedule for each task and NFE budget. Compared with the uniform grid, GYS brings the generated chunk distribution closer to the demonstrated distribution and raises the success rate through the sampling schedule alone. On RoboTwin 2.0 benchmarks, GYS improves success rates at nearly every budget, with gains of 2.8 percentage points for both $\pi_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.7. The gains also transfer to three real-world manipulation tasks, reaching up to 3.3 percentage points. Code is available at https://github.com/D-Robotics-AI-Lab/GroundYourSteps.
authors: Licheng Yang, Yonghao He, Lingfeng Qian, Xin Shi, Wei Sui, Hu Su
bullets: Addresses the dependence of generated action chunks on the sampling schedule under a fixed neural-function-evaluation budget.
Uses truncated fractional differencing over joint action sequences and energy-distance matching between generated and demonstration-derived pairwise differences.
Optimizes a task- and budget-specific schedule using only the sampling process.
Improves success rates on RoboTwin 2.0 by 2.8 percentage points for both π₀.₅ and GR00T N1.7, with gains up to 3.3 points on three real-world manipulation tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Motivation and effects of GYS. (b) Across budgets, GYS places fewer interior sampling nodes near the action endpoint, where deviations may be amplified; green ticks mark uniform-grid nodes. (c) For two observation groups o1 and o2 pooled from the calibration set, GYS lowers the energy distance between the two transformed pairwise-difference distributions, the objective used to match transformed generated and demonstrated action laws. (d) Over 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, GYS improves mean closed-loop success at nearly every fixed budget.

The task prompts are, for PaP, “Pull the drawer open and place the yellow cube inside”; for SbC, “Place the green, blue, and yellow cubes into the regions of matching color”; and for SaC, “First stack the blue cube and the green cube in the designated region, then cover them with the upside-down cup”.

(b) An energy score compares both types of transformed pairwise differences paired with observation summaries, revealing location and dispersion mismatch. (c) Aligning these joint laws targets conditional agreement between transformed generated and demonstrated action distributions, illustrated for two observation groups. (d) The schematic shows how stepping across a late-time sensitive region can reduce endpoint mismatch relative to exact integration of the learned ODE.

papers.abstract: Agent harnesses today manage context on the model's behalf: when the window fills, the harness triggers a compaction that summarizes the history. We study the alternative, \emph{model-driven} context management, in which the model itself decides when and what to compact through a context API. We gave models control over their own context in \nooa, NVIDIA's open source agent harness, and compared the two strategies on document research and machine learning engineering across context budgets from 8K to 512K tokens. Models that use the context API effectively reach higher accuracy, often with fewer input tokens, especially at tight budgets: \textbf{GPT 6.1 nearly triples its score at a 32K budget} on OfficeQA Pro v2 (21\%~$\rightarrow$~56\%), and \textbf{Kimi gains with up to 41\% fewer input tokens}. Models differ widely, however, in how often they use the API, how aggressively they compact, and when they start compacting, and prompt changes shift that timing. Finally, we show that \textbf{inference engines can make model-driven edits cheaper}: by reusing the KV cache of the unchanged suffix after an edit, \textbf{we cut prefill compute by up to 15\% per request with no measurable change in accuracy}. Together, these results point to a new co-design frontier: models trained to manage their own context, served by inference engines that support KV cache editing.
authors: Alessio Devoto, Avinash Vem, Tara Safavi, Sanjay Kariyappa, Yu-Hsuan Tseng, Paul Furgale, Ricardo Silveira Cabral
bullets: Replaces harness-triggered summarization with a context API that lets models decide when and what to compact.
Evaluated on document research and machine learning engineering across 8K–512K-token budgets.
Effective API use improves performance at tight budgets: GPT 6.1’s OfficeQA Pro v2 score rose from 21% to 56% at 32K tokens, while Kimi used up to 41% fewer input tokens.
Models vary widely in compaction frequency, aggressiveness, and timing; prompt changes also affect when compaction begins.
KV-cache reuse after context edits reduced prefill compute by up to 15% per request without measurable accuracy changes.

papers.abstract: Two-frame video frame interpolation commonly resamples endpoint optical flow by the query time, which selects a constant-velocity straight-line path even though the same endpoint displacement is compatible with many intermediate trajectories. We present HermiteVFI, which replaces independent query-time motion prediction with one explicit continuous trajectory per pixel. The measured endpoint displacement fixes the two trajectory positions, while two latent endpoint derivatives learned from the frame pair control the interior path. A cubic Hermite curve is the minimum-degree polynomial that can independently satisfy these two position and two derivative boundary quantities. Its residual form contains linear motion exactly, structurally preserves the measured displacement endpoints for any network output, and has coefficients that are predicted once per frame pair and evaluated in closed form at arbitrary t. We further show that one interior query time gives a rank-deficient constraint on the two free trajectory coefficients, whereas any two distinct interior times are full rank at the representation level, motivating multi-time supervision. Appearance-derived directional cues help infer the latent derivatives that endpoint displacement alone cannot identify. On X4K1000FPS, SNU-FILM, and Vimeo90K-Septuplet, the largest gains occur for difficult non-uniform motion and high interpolation ratios. The amortization applies to trajectory-coefficient prediction; downstream reversal, refinement, and synthesis remain query dependent.
authors: Md Rifat Ur Rahman, Md Abtahi Majeed Chowdhury, Md Sakib Hossain Shovon, Jaesik Choi, Mohammad Ali Moni
bullets: Addresses the limitation of constant-velocity, straight-line motion assumed by common two-frame interpolation methods.
Predicts two latent endpoint derivatives from the frame pair and combines them with measured endpoint positions in a cubic Hermite curve.
The residual formulation exactly includes linear motion and preserves measured endpoints regardless of network outputs.
Multi-time supervision is motivated because two distinct interior times identify the trajectory coefficients, unlike a single time.
Evaluations on X4K1000FPS, SNU-FILM, and Vimeo90K-Septuplet show the largest gains for difficult non-uniform motion and high interpolation ratios.

The head does not take t as input and runs once per frame pair; only the last three stages repeat.

papers.abstract: Recent 3D generative models can produce high-quality meshes with complex structures and fine geometric details, with broad applications in games, film, and digital design. However, high-quality generation typically relies on long multi-step sampling processes that repeatedly evaluate large networks, leading to long inference times. At the same time, reference-driven tasks such as game-asset reconstruction and product digitization demand close correspondence to the input image: generated geometry must faithfully reconstruct the specific reference object. Acceleration must therefore reduce sampling computation while preserving the model's ability to reconstruct that object. To enable fast and faithful 3D generation, we introduce Spe3DUp, a coarse-to-fine framework based on Faithful Trajectory Distillation (FTD). FTD directly supervises few-step students with the teacher's input-conditioned denoising trajectories to preserve its generation behavior. We apply FTD separately to coarse geometry generation and geometric refinement, compressing both sampling processes while maintaining correspondence to the reference input. We further accelerate the complete mesh-generation pipeline with efficient geometry decoding and parallel remeshing. Experiments show that Spe3DUp maintains geometric quality and input correspondence close to those of the teacher, accelerates the coarse and refinement DiTs by 10.0x and 19.9x, respectively, and achieves a 7.7x end-to-end speedup over the original teacher pipeline.
authors: Liangchao Xu, Jiaye Fu, Youtian Lin, Feihu Zhang, Yao Yao
bullets: Targets the slow, multi-step sampling required by high-quality 3D generation.
Introduces Faithful Trajectory Distillation (FTD), which trains few-step students using input-conditioned teacher denoising trajectories.
Applies FTD separately to coarse geometry generation and geometric refinement in a coarse-to-fine framework.
Further accelerates mesh decoding and remeshing through efficient decoding and parallel processing.
Reports 10.0× and 19.9× speedups for coarse and refinement DiTs, and 7.7× end-to-end acceleration while maintaining quality and input correspondence.

papers.abstract: In 2D-3D localization, a camera estimates its pose by matching an image to a 3D map. A camera held in a hand or mounted on a robot can often choose its viewpoint before it takes the image. In this work, we ask whether an image detectability field is a useful viewpoint utility when the planner reads only the geometry of the map. The field can be queried at any 3D point near a surface. From the local geometry around the point, it predicts how likely a 2D image detector is to fire at the projection of the point. We use the trained field as it is, without fine-tuning it for view selection. A fixed SuperPoint and EPnP-RANSAC localizer then estimates the pose from the chosen view. We answer in two settings, each with a test registered before the runs. On synthetic ShapeNet objects with sparse point maps, summing the field over the visible landmarks beats counting them by +2.0 points of localization success rate (object-clustered 95% interval [+0.7, +3.2]). It also beats summing Harris-3D ranks by +2.2 [+0.8, +3.5]. On real indoor scenes from SceneFun3D, our adaptation of the learned view scorer LWL falls below counting on the test rooms. We therefore add the field to a learned per-landmark planner. On the test rooms with sparse maps whose landmarks the field also selects, the planner with the field beats the same planner without it by +1.8 points. It beats the planner with Harris-3D or curvature in its place by +1.0 and +0.8 points. All three room-clustered intervals lie above zero. In both settings, the field helps in sparse maps and is on par with Harris-3D in dense maps.
authors: Han Sun, Jun Li, Christy Jie Liang
bullets: The goal is to choose camera viewpoints using only map geometry before capturing an image.
A learned field predicts how likely local 3D geometry is to produce detectable 2D features, and is queried over visible landmarks.
With fixed SuperPoint and EPnP-RANSAC localization, field-based scoring improves localization success over landmark counting and Harris-3D on synthetic sparse maps.
In real indoor scenes, the field performs poorly as a standalone scorer but improves a learned per-landmark planner over versions without the field, Harris-3D, or curvature.
Benefits are observed in sparse maps; performance is on par with Harris-3D in dense maps.

The two images were captured at the picked poses, and only the fixed 2D–3D localizer sees them. Green dots are matches to landmarks that PnP-RANSAC keeps as inliers, and crosses are the other matches. The G+F pick localizes with 61 inliers (2.2◦, 5 cm). papers.abstract: In many applications, neural networks must learn input-output maps that respect prior knowledge such as physical laws, safety requirements, and operating limits. These requirements constrain which outputs are admissible for a given input and often admit second-order cone (SOC) representations, including norm bounds and robust linear inequalities. Examples in control include friction cones, thrust bounds, and input-robust control barrier function (CBF) conditions. However, existing approaches to enforcing general input-dependent SOC constraints require a conic solver, an iterative scheme whose feasibility depends on convergence, or an interior feasible point for each input. We propose SOC-Net, a neural network architecture that enforces input-dependent SOC constraints by construction for every input, even outside the training distribution. SOC-Net projects an affine lifting of the backbone output onto the reachable slice of a fixed product of Lorentz cones and maps the correction back to the output space. For separable constraints, this projection splits into one projection per cone, and each is available in closed form or reduces to a single scalar equation, regardless of the cone dimension. We prove that SOC-Net retains the expressive power of the backbone network under regularity conditions and accommodates end-to-end training by standard backpropagation with an explicit Jacobian. Experiments on contact force allocation with friction constraints and 3-D obstacle avoidance with an input-robust CBF demonstrate that SOC-Net satisfies the constraints at every evaluated input, with lower evaluation latency than the tested solver-based and iterative baselines.
authors: Seungseok Oh, Youngjae Min, Navid Azizan, Namhoon Cho
bullets: Targets constraints arising from physical laws, safety requirements, and operating limits, including norm bounds, friction cones, thrust limits, and robust control-barrier conditions.
Projects an affine transformation of the backbone output onto the feasible slice of a fixed product of Lorentz cones, then maps the correction back to the output space.
For separable constraints, projection decomposes into per-cone operations with closed-form solutions or a single scalar equation.
The architecture preserves backbone expressiveness under regularity conditions and provides an explicit Jacobian for end-to-end training.

Experiments in friction-constrained contact force allocation and 3-D obstacle avoidance show constraint satisfaction at every evaluated input and lower evaluation latency than tested solver-based and iterative baselines.

papers.abstract: World models are increasingly used in robotics to improve the performance of embodied models. Compared with general-purpose video generation, robotics places more stringent requirements on world models. Generated videos must satisfy fine-grained physical constraints on robot motion and object interactions. However, existing world model benchmarks can overlook robotics specific physical details and struggle to assess them accurately. To address this problem, we introduce WorldPhy, a world model benchmark for accurate, fine-grained evaluation of physical plausibility in robotics. Our benchmark contains 300 tasks, each consisting of an initial-frame image and a task instruction, covering diverse robotics scenes, task categories, viewpoints, and robot configurations. We further collect over 12K high-quality human annotations, and use them to train WorldPhyReward to accurately provide scores and reasons across six fine-grained physical dimensions and an instruction-following dimension. Comparisons with general VLMs and existing reward models show that WorldPhyReward better aligns with human ratings. We system- atically evaluate 13 frontier open and closed-source world models. The results reveal that current world models struggle to consistently maintain fine-grained physical plausibility across different robotics scenarios. Our code is available at https://github.com/chuziyuan139/ WorldPhy.
authors: Ziyuan Chu, Mingzhi Zheng, Kaiyue Zhang, Jinan Zhang, Linchao Zhu

WorldPhyReward aligns better with human ratings than general VLMs and existing reward models.

papers.abstract: Accurate 3D surface reconstruction from unposed images remains a fundamental challenge in computer vision. Recent feed-forward pointmap methods eliminate the need for camera poses but inherently produce discrete, sparse representations. In this paper, we present a generalizable pipeline that directly recovers continuous, high-fidelity 3D surfaces from unposed images by seamlessly integrating pointmap- and ray-based representations. Our approach first extracts explicit geometric priors using a pre-trained pointmap model. A query-view-centric selection module then identifies geometrically relevant reference views via a robust surfel voting mechanism. Next, a cross-attention regressor bridges target query rays with reference features to estimate a continuous coarse surface. Lastly, a raylet-based module aggregates local 3D features to carve out high-frequency details and analytical normals. Trained as a single foundation model on 9 diverse datasets, our method demonstrates exceptional zero-shot generalization on 6 unseen datasets, clearly surpassing state-of-the-art baselines in geometric accuracy and detail preservation.

Trained on 9 diverse datasets and reports strong zero-shot generalization across 6 unseen datasets, outperforming prior methods in geometric accuracy and detail preservation.

papers.abstract: In real-world applications like egocentric recording, visual accessibility, and surveillance review, visual evidence for Video Large Language Models (Video LLMs) is often only partially captured. A reliable model should match its response to the evidence: answering when sufficient, guessing from visible clues when partial, and abstaining when absent. Yet existing benchmarks enforce a binary answerable-or-unanswerable split, leaving partial evidence unmeasured and obscuring whether failures arise from missing evidence or misjudging sufficiency. We introduce ClueProbe, a diagnostic benchmark to (1) separate perceiving evidence from judging sufficiency, and (2) validate our diagnosis via targeted fine-tuning. ClueProbe comprises 1,721 human-annotated questions across 598 natural videos, labeled Answerable, Guessable, or Unanswerable, alongside controlled perturbations altering wording or visual input. Evaluating 10 open-source and proprietary Video LLMs reveals that failures stem from judgment rather than perception: models perceive the evidence yet lack graded sufficiency awareness, answering or refusing outright while rarely guessing from partial clues. Targeted fine-tuning shows that this reflects missing supervision rather than insufficient capacity: supervising the guess level lifts appropriate guessing from 1.6% to 40.4% without extra false refusals, whereas conventional refusal tuning rejects 92% of guessable questions. Data and code will be released at https://github.com/suat-llm/ClueProbe.
authors: Luoxi Zhang, Jiawei Liu, Yanlin Luo, Peiyang He, Junlin Zhu, Chun To Choi, Yang Xiong, Jiang Wu, Xingyu Zeng, Min Yang, Shiwen Ni
bullets: Introduces a three-way benchmark: Answerable, Guessable, and Unanswerable.

Evaluation of 10 Video LLMs attributes failures mainly to insufficient evidence-sufficiency judgment, not evidence perception.
Targeted guess-level supervision increases appropriate guessing from 1.6% to 40.4% without extra false refusals.
Conventional refusal tuning rejects 92% of guessable questions, highlighting the need for graded supervision.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) couple future imagination with action generation, but they execute every action chunk while ignoring the potential risk. To fill this gap, we present WAtcher, a safety-aware world-action framework in which the policy imagines the outcome of the candidate chunk before execution. For fast future preview, WAtcher builds on a compact WAM whose video expert imagines the visual outcome in only two denoising steps. In addition, we propose Safe-Guard, a lightweight module kept outside the WAM that scores each candidate chunk from its imagined outcome and triggers a bounded retreat when the risk is high. Safe-Guard is detachable and can be applied to other WAMs. To train Safe-Guard, we build an autonomous pipeline to collect hazard data from RoboTwin, LIBERO, and a real robot. Specifically, the pipeline perturbs expert demonstrations and labels each candidate chunk from the physical events recorded when it is executed, such as contacts and losses of support. Using the ~25,000 labeled windows from this pipeline, Safe-Guard reaches 92.1% balanced accuracy on a blind set, and cuts hazardous closed-loop trials on training tasks from 27.0% to 10.8% without lowering task success. On a held-out 300-question benchmark, it scores 94.2%, against 72.5% and 63.3% for zero-shot GPT-6-Astra and Claude Opus 5.5. WAtcher also reaches 90.4% and 82.4% average success on RoboTwin 2.0 and ManiSkill3, on par with or above leading WAMs, and 74.0% on five real-world tasks with Safe-Guard on, against 59.5% for $\pi_{0.5}$. Project page: https://zyshan0929.github.io/WAtcher
authors: Ziyu Shan, Xiao Ma, Kangrui Yu, Changjie Wang, Gaoyuan Wu, Zaijia Yang, Chuanrui Zhang, Qirui Li, Yanbo Zhang, Duomin Wang, Ziwei Wang

The system reports strong results across RoboTwin 2.0, ManiSkill3, and five real-world tasks, including 74.0% success with safety enabled.

papers.abstract: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) allows a wireless system to use the same waveform for communication and environment sensing. At mmWave frequency bands, ISAC enables diverse human sensing tasks, such as localization, gesture recognition, and pose estimation, with high precision. However, each task requires training a dedicated model, typically from scratch on a task-specific dataset, with no mechanism to flag unreliable predictions. This hurts the scalability, transferability, and reliability of mmWave ISAC models. In this work, we propose MUSE (Multi-task Uncertainty-aware Self-supervised Encoder), a unified framework for mmWave human sensing. MUSE leverages a self-supervised transformer model with per-dataset tokenization and is trained via masked autoencoding across five datasets. During fine-tuning, MUSE uses evidential classification heads that enable uncertainty quantification. MUSE replaces N separate encoders with a single shared transformer encoder, an N-times backbone parameter reduction, while achieving a 9.7 percentage points improvement in classification performance compared to the task-specific model, showing that learning jointly across tasks improves per-task generalization. Across four classification tasks, MUSE produces reliable uncertainty estimates that enable selective prediction, improving accuracy by abstaining on the least confident 20% of predictions. We further improve the reliability of the model's confidence estimates using temperature scaling and conformal prediction. Finally, MUSE's uncertainty signal remains reliable even under cross-user deployment, assigning higher uncertainty to wrong predictions than to correct ones 78% of the time, and recovering 9.2 percentage points of accuracy through selective prediction, with no additional retraining on the unseen user.

papers.abstract: Tool-using large language model (LLM) agents raise safety risks that are not captured by text-only refusal behavior, especially when tools can trigger high-impact actions. This concern is salient in military settings, where autonomous weapons raise the possibility of delegating force decisions to software agents. In this work, we study whether a drone agent's action boundary is stable under changes to the target descriptor. We evaluate recent and popular LLMs in a simulated perception-action pipeline over real-world drone imagery, where models can localize requested targets and invoke a simulated lethal tool. We find two concerning failure modes. First, some LLM agents invoke the lethal tool for ordinary generic descriptors such as \emph{people}, requiring no jailbreak at all. Second, an agent that initially appears conservative under protected descriptors can become unsafe under a simple semantic target shift.

papers.abstract: Legal due diligence in mergers and acquisitions requires lawyers to organize heterogeneous virtual data room documents, extract transaction-relevant information and consolidate reviewed findings into a due diligence report. We present LEXI (Legal Extraction and Intelligence), a work-in-progress system that demonstrates how large language models can support this process from document ingestion to report preparation. LEXI classifies documents under a configurable due diligence taxonomy, assigns relevant target entities, extracts predefined information with supporting passages and page-level provenance and prepares report content from reviewed findings. Structured outputs connect these stages and allow model-generated results to be passed through the workflow in a controlled form. Lawyers review and correct classifications and extractions and retain responsibility for legal assessments, recommendations, risk ratings and final report wording. Initial evaluations of the classification and extraction components provide preliminary evidence that the approach is feasible. LEXI illustrates how AI can be integrated across the legal due diligence workflow while preserving lawyer control over substantive legal judgment.

papers.abstract: We present CoTacWAM, a world-action model that learns shared contact semantics between wrist vision and touch, achieving the best observed performance in our nominal manipulation and missing-input evaluations. The two modalities observe the same local interaction through different signals: wrist images reveal nearby geometry, while touch records physical contact. Our approach connects their common contact meaning while preserving the evidence unique to each modality, giving the policy a joint description of interaction across available input combinations. This representation supports predictive action learning alongside head-view scene context and conditions corrections after an independent detector confirms a failed attempt. Experiments across four real-world tasks demonstrate improved manipulation performance over the evaluated baselines, robustness to missing local observations, and further gains from autonomous retries.

papers.abstract: Open-world aerial object search methods often rely on persistent spatial maps, learned world models, or task-specific policy training. To examine how far a minimal, training-free design can go, we introduce SimpleUAV, an agent built around a frozen, off-the-shelf vision-language model (VLM). SimpleUAV separates current-view target assessment from history-conditioned action selection, combining fresh candidate evidence with lightweight search context. Local geometry converts visual selections into bounded straight-line movements, depth-based checks halt blocked segments, and measured execution feedback guides subsequent decisions. This closed loop sustains search without persistent spatial maps or task-specific training. SimpleUAV achieves 41.61% Success Rate (SR) on UAV-ON and 11.98% on AerialDojo-200K, compared with 23.80% and 3.20% for the strongest prior baselines, respectively. With limited benchmark-specific adaptation, the same core agent transfers to aerial Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) on TravelUAV, improving Full SR by at least 19.66% across all three splits under L1 assistance. These results establish a strong baseline for evaluating when additional architectural complexity benefits aerial search.
authors: Jitai Hao, Liangxing Yang, Zhenyang Li, Fan Liu, Qiang Huang, Jun Yu
bullets: Addresses whether a minimal, training-free agent can handle open-world aerial search.
Separates current-view target assessment from history-conditioned action selection.
Uses local geometry, depth checks, and execution feedback to produce bounded movements and avoid blocked paths.
Achieves 41.61% SR on UAV-ON and 11.98% on AerialDojo-200K, outperforming reported prior baselines.
Transfers to aerial VLN on TravelUAV, improving Full SR by at least 19.66% across three splits with L1 assistance.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Architecture of SimpleUAV. Given a language goal and four RGB-D views (front, left, right, and downward), SimpleUAV executes three stages without persistent maps or task-specific training. (1) Select (Section 3.2): A frozen VLM detects candidate boxes (ℬ𝑡 ) from current RGB views. Depth and camera calibration provide 3D candidate locations to construct (𝒞𝑡 ), and a second VLM query selects an action (𝑎𝑡 ) using this catalog and lightweight interaction history. (2) Fly Straight (Section 3.3): The selected region or candidate determines a 3D waypoint (𝑤𝑡 ) for exploration (Exploreℎ , Explore𝑣) or Approach, and the UAV moves from 𝒙𝑡 along a bounded straightline segment. (3) Check & Halt (Section 3.4): Throughout motion, local depth checks test upcoming segments using a 3D safety capsule and halt the current segment when an obstacle is detected. Execution feedback guides the next observation and decision cycle.

papers.abstract: Executing monolithic neural weights, frontier foundation models, or entire multi-agent workflows uniformly on every input incurs substantial computational, latency, and monetary overhead. Conditional computation mitigates this cost by deciding dynamically which internal experts, model endpoints, or specialized agents to invoke per request. Yet token-level gating in sparse neural architectures, query-level model cascades, and task-level multi-agent coordination have largely progressed in disconnected research silos, obscuring recurring system failures and transferable fixes. In this systematic review, we synthesize 2,289 studies published between 2017 and September 2026 (selected from 13,884 unique records) across 20 methodological families under a unified two-step inspect-then-allocate framework. Discrete hard selection accounts for 70%, 83%, and 91% of token-, query-, and task-scale literature respectively, and computational overhead appears as a top operational bottleneck across every layer. Engineering safeguards remain sharply asymmetric: intra-layer gating prioritizes load balancing while rarely incorporating uncertainty estimation, whereas model selection and agent orchestration rely on confidence thresholds and budget rules while confronting miscalibration and cascading errors. At the same time, publication volume is accelerating fastest in agentic task delegation, where routing mechanisms are least often isolated experimentally and methodological bias risk is highest.
authors: Dat Tat Mai, Hung Tran Quy, Thai Viet Pham, James Jin Kang
bullets: Reviews 2,289 studies from 2017–September 2026 across 20 methodological families using an inspect-then-allocate framework.
Hard selection dominates token-, query-, and task-level research, while computational overhead is a bottleneck at every layer.
Intra-layer gating emphasizes load balancing but seldom uses uncertainty estimation.
Model cascades and agent workflows use confidence thresholds and budgets, but face miscalibration and cascading errors.
Agentic task delegation is growing fastest, yet routing is least often isolated experimentally and carries the highest methodological-bias risk.

papers.abstract: The 3D points kept in a map decide whether a camera can be localized against it, and this choice matters more as the map becomes sparser. Existing 3D keypoint detectors usually define saliency by semantics, repeatability, reconstruction or descriptor matchability. None of these definitions asks whether a point will actually be detected in an image, and as a result most of the points they select are not detected again in images. In this paper, we define 3D saliency as image detectability: the response of a 2D interest-point detector at a surface point, aggregated over all views in which the point is visible. We propose DetField, a continuous field over 3D space that takes a point cloud as input and predicts detectability at any location around it. The supervision is the response of a 2D detector, back-projected from images onto the point cloud. Multi-scale curvature invariants are passed to the decoder at every query point, bypassing the voxel pooling of the encoder. In a localization benchmark that isolates the choice of 3D points, DetField outperforms Harris-3D and five learned 3D keypoint methods on objects and on real indoor scenes. On unseen rooms, it improves localization success by 7.4 points over Harris-3D, the strongest baseline. On objects, it also leads under a 2D detector not used in training. On sparse maps, it stays ahead of Harris-3D on both objects and real scenes.
authors: Han Sun, Jun Li, Christy Jie Liang
bullets: Motivation: Existing 3D keypoint criteria do not directly measure whether points will be detected again in images, especially in sparse maps.
Method: Define 3D saliency as a surface point’s 2D interest-detector response aggregated across visible views, and supervise predictions by back-projecting these responses onto the point cloud.
Architecture: A continuous 3D field predicts detectability at arbitrary locations, using multi-scale curvature invariants at query points to avoid voxel-pooling information loss.
Results: DetField outperforms Harris-3D and five learned 3D keypoint methods on objects and real indoor scenes; on unseen rooms, it improves localization success by 7.4 points over Harris-3D.
Scope: The method also leads with an unseen 2D detector on objects and remains ahead of Harris-3D on sparse maps.

papers.abstract: Humans can recognize novel concepts from only a few observations by identifying defining visual attributes and eliminating alternative interpretations. However, a single observation is consistent with multiple possible concepts, and accurate visual perception alone is insufficient to determine the intended interpretation. Negative evidence can reduce this ambiguity by eliminating competing hypotheses. Inspired by Quine's gavagai problem, we introduce the Gavagai Benchmark to evaluate whether vision-language models can identify the attributes defining a novel concept from positive and negative examples. The benchmark consists of synthetic images depicting novel combinations of visual attributes and real images of newly described species. Using these datasets, we examine how models use negative examples to identify novel concepts and analyze the respective roles of visual perception and reasoning. Several models struggle even when correct attributes are provided, while others show large gaps when ground-truth attributes are replaced with model predictions. These diagnostic comparisons highlight challenges in both attribute perception and inference from limited evidence.
authors: Katsuya Ogata, Kazuya Nishimura, Yuta Nakashima
bullets: Evaluates concept learning under highly limited positive and negative evidence.
Uses synthetic images with novel attribute combinations and real images of newly described species.
Separates visual attribute perception from reasoning by comparing ground-truth and model-predicted attributes.
Finds that some models struggle even with correct attributes, while others degrade substantially when predicting attributes themselves.
Highlights the importance of negative evidence for eliminating competing interpretations.

papers.abstract: Precipitation nowcasting requires accurate short-term predictions under rapidly evolving spatiotemporal dynamics. Generative diffusion models can produce detailed and competitive radar forecasts by modeling conditional distributions. However, most existing approaches rely on separately trained components, such as deterministic branches or latent compression modules. More fundamentally, distribution matching alone fails to explicitly optimize operational forecast skill. We propose AlignPre, a streamlined pixel-space nowcasting framework that bridges this gap via skill-aligned post-training (SAPT). AlignPre employs an end-to-end flow-matching forecaster with a hierarchical spatiotemporal architecture for distribution matching and direct radar-field synthesis, without latent compression. During post-training, SAPT exploits the analytic structure of forecast verification scores to construct a differentiable objective. By backpropagating gradients of this objective from radar fields to the generator, SAPT turns forecast verification into direct training feedback. Across three real-world benchmarks spanning different forecast horizons, AlignPre consistently surpasses state-of-the-art deterministic and generative baselines in forecast skill, demonstrating that aligning generative modeling with domain-specific verification provides an effective paradigm for meteorological forecasting.
authors: Demin Yu, Kenghong Lin, Xutao Li
bullets: Addresses the gap between distribution matching and explicit optimization of forecast verification skill.
Uses an end-to-end hierarchical spatiotemporal flow-matching model that synthesizes radar fields without latent compression or separately trained components.
Introduces skill-aligned post-training (SAPT), a differentiable objective derived from the analytic structure of forecast verification scores.
Backpropagates verification-score gradients from predicted radar fields into the generator.
Outperforms deterministic and generative state-of-the-art baselines across three real-world benchmarks and multiple forecast horizons.

papers.abstract: Overall part-discrimination accuracy can conceal failures when image position favors the wrong bilateral part. We examine whether dense descriptors distinguish the correct part under this conflict and whether their discrimination scores help select matching coordinates. We evaluate position agreement and conflict within the same target images and annotated part pairs, using a bounding-box-side score to define the conditions. We compare the original descriptors with their even and odd components under horizontal reflection, examine feature upsampling with the backbone and adapters fixed, and test candidate-selection rules based on odd scores. On SPair-71k, odd discrimination accuracy falls from 86.66% under agreement to 19.63% under conflict for frozen DINOv2, compared with 95.27% to 86.16% for MARCO. With MARCO's input geometry fixed, odd accuracy in box-side conflict was 34.12% on the native grid and 88.84% after learned upsampling and pooling back to that grid. Odd-score rules improve on the original hard-peak matchers overall for DINOv2 and DINOv3 and on conflict queries for MARCO. With MARCO's soft decoder fixed, reranking the cosine peaks changes mean per-pair PCK by +0.47 pp. For supervised GeoAware-SC, using the odd score to select the localization window center yields only 15 net additional correct matches, with 330 corrections and 315 introduced errors. Evaluating discrimination under position conflict reveals failures hidden by aggregate accuracy. Reporting corrections and introduced errors separately also shows whether a discriminative score produces useful matching decisions.
authors: Pingan Wang
bullets: Aggregate part-discrimination accuracy can hide errors when image position favors the wrong bilateral part.
The study compares descriptor behavior under horizontal-reflection agreement versus conflict, including even/odd components, upsampling, and odd-score-based candidate selection.
On SPair-71k, frozen DINOv2 odd accuracy drops from 86.66% with position agreement to 19.63% under conflict; MARCO drops from 95.27% to 86.16%.
For MARCO, learned upsampling raises conflict accuracy from 34.12% on the native grid to 88.84% after pooling back to that grid.

Odd-score rules improve some hard-peak matching results, but localization gains are limited: MARCO reranking changes PCK by +0.47 percentage points, while GeoAware-SC yields 330 corrections and 315 introduced errors.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we introduce EiT by exploring the key design factors of pixel-space diffusion from three perspectives: model architecture, representation, and frequency domain. Inspired by Denoising Autoencoders (DAE) which perform denoising through a bottleneck, we construct a U-shaped pixel diffusion transformer that performs explicit compression along the channel dimension. In terms of representation, we find that both pixel and latent diffusion transformers exhibit a three-stage representation dynamics across layers and timesteps: denoising/local feature expansion, basis lift-up, and posterior projection. Moreover, earlier denoising and a longer basis lift-up stage are associated with better generation, which EiT naturally achieves through its channel bottleneck and increased network depth. From the frequency perspective, we establish the equivalence between pixel-space and frequency-space diffusion when keeping the network operating in pixel space. On ImageNet $256\times256$ and $512\times512$, EiT consistently outperforms JiT (Just image Transformers) in generation quality. Specifically, our EiT achieves better FID than JiT: 1.61 vs. 1.85 at $256\times256$, and 1.73 vs. 1.99 at $512\times512$. Remarkably, EiT can be seamlessly applied to video pixel diffusion by simply extending the patch size to temporal dimension and outperforms video latent diffusion in FVD evaluated on Kinetics-600 (resolution 256), under comparable total network parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/forever208/EiT
authors: Mang Ning, Le Zhang, Albert Ali Salah, Itir Onal Ertugrul, Jintao Zhang
bullets: Motivation: Pixel-space diffusion design involves interacting architectural, representation, and frequency-domain factors.
Method: EiT uses a U-shaped pixel diffusion transformer with explicit channel-wise compression inspired by denoising autoencoders.

Finding: Diffusion representations progress through denoising/local feature expansion, basis lift-up, and posterior projection; earlier denoising and longer basis lift-up correlate with better generation.
Result: EiT achieves lower FID than JiT on ImageNet at 256×256 and 512×512, and outperforms video latent diffusion in FVD on Kinetics-600 under comparable parameter counts.
Scope: The same approach extends to video by enlarging patch size along the temporal dimension.

papers.abstract: Multi-token prediction (MTP) modules and EAGLE-style drafters support efficient speculative decoding by reusing target-model hidden states. Their autoregressive use, however, introduces a training-inference mismatch: training supplies sequences of hidden states from the backbone or a single MTP step, whereas inference attends to a target-model prefix followed by a growing tail of recurrently generated MTP states. EAGLE-3's training-time test (TTT) explicitly simulates this behavior during training, at the cost of additional memory and specialized attention masks. We introduce two training-only methods for improving autoregressive drafting. Hidden State Mixing (HSM) samples among backbone and MTP hidden states aligned to the same prediction target, exposing the drafter to mixtures of states from different MTP steps without explicitly simulating inference. Hidden State Gradient Detach (HSGD) is a regularization method that stochastically blocks gradients through hidden state and embedding pathways while preserving the forward computation. Neither method adds inference cost. In joint pretraining followed by supervised fine-tuning, HSGD yields the highest acceptance rates at early draft positions, while HSM performs best later in the draft. These acceptance rate trends favor HSM for long-draft-length serving and HSGD for short-draft-length serving. Furthermore, across four Nemotron models and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, HSM-based MTP boosting with a frozen backbone improves mean acceptance length by up to 52.2% over the co-trained MTP. For EAGLE-3 drafters, HSM offers competitive acceptance with TTT, with 48% lower peak reserved training memory in a four-step Qwen3-8B comparison. HSM implementations are publicly available in Megatron-LM and NVIDIA Model Optimizer.
authors: Yaniv Galron, Rabeeh Karimi Mahabadi, Maor Ashkenazi, Roger Waleffe, Talor Abramovich, Tiyasa Mitra, Yoav Miron, Dor Tsur, Sanjeev Satheesh, Jimmy Zhang, Jiaji Huang, Yonatan Geifman, Mostofa Patwary, Mohammad Shoeybi, Bita Rouhani, Ran Zilberstein
bullets: Autoregressive drafters face a training–inference mismatch because inference uses growing recurrently generated hidden-state tails.
Hidden State Mixing (HSM) trains on mixtures of backbone and MTP hidden states aligned to the same target, avoiding explicit test-time simulation.
Hidden State Gradient Detach (HSGD) stochastically blocks gradients through hidden-state and embedding paths while preserving forward computation.
HSGD achieves the strongest early-position acceptance, while HSM performs best at later draft positions.
HSM improves mean acceptance length by up to 52.2% over co-trained MTP and uses 48% less peak reserved training memory than TTT in a Qwen3-8B comparison.

In the illustrated Bernoulli sample, 𝑧ℎ 3 = 0 allows the gradient from ℒ3 to propagate through ℎ2 𝑡 , whereas 𝑧ℎ 2 = 1 stops that downstream gradient at the preceding recurrent boundary, so ∇ℎ1 𝑡 ℒ3 = 0. The current MTP step and its local loss remain trainable; only the path into earlier steps is truncated. (b) Embedding-path detachment is analogous. When 𝑧𝑒 𝑑 = 0, the MTP gradient reaches the embedding table 𝐸; when 𝑧𝑒 𝑑 = 1, that branch is stopped. Other language-model and non-detached MTP paths continue to update 𝐸.

Figure 2 | Two training–inference mismatches in autoregressive MTP drafting. (a) Training with multiple position-specific MTP modules creates two inference choices. Option A uses each trained module once and therefore caps the draft length at the number of MTP modules. Option B recurrently reuses one module, removing that fixed limit but making the reused module consume its own generated states even though it was not trained on that recurrence. (b) Parameter sharing replaces the position-specific modules with one recurrent module, 𝜃MTP, which is explicitly reused across all MTP steps during training. This removes the architectural mismatch and permits recurrent inference beyond the number of MTP steps used during training. (c) A deeper hidden state exposure mismatch remains. During training, each MTP application consumes a complete sequence from one hidden state depth. During inference, the MTP cache retains a target-generated prefix and appends recursively generated states, producing an increasingly mixed-depth tail as drafting proceeds.

papers.abstract: Multimodal drafts learn from multimodal (MM) and text-only (TXT) supervision, yet their effects on alignment and how to combine them remain unclear. We diagnose draft-target alignment through paired predictions with and without visual input, decomposing distributional error into text-conditioned and visual-response components. Drafts with similar text-conditioned alignment can still differ markedly in visual-response risk and acceptance. Controlled continuation training shows that high-risk groups outperform random and low-risk groups, and visual-response risk guides MM training more effectively than aggregate risk. Building on these diagnostics, we propose MNRS-Joint, which configures joint supervision from a given draft's component-risk distributions, using modality-specific mean risks to determine the MM:TXT mixture. Across three warm-ups, its distinct mixtures fall in high-performing regions of the ratio sweeps. On LLaVA-1.5-7B, MNRS-Joint improves mean accepted length from 3.35 to 3.53 and mean speedup from $2.04\times$ to $2.16\times$ over composition-matched random training under greedy tree decoding. The gains also hold under stochastic chain decoding.
authors: Haozhe Du, Runze Liu, Jiaming Fan, Yitong Tao, Shuxia Lin, Chonghan Liu, Daming Cao, Xu Yang
bullets: Decomposes alignment error into text-conditioned and visual-response risks using predictions with and without visual input.
Finds that visual-response risk better identifies training groups and guides multimodal training than aggregate risk.
Introduces MNRS-Joint, which sets the MM:TXT supervision ratio from modality-specific mean risks.
Across three warm-ups, its selected mixtures perform well; on LLaVA-1.5-7B, accepted length rises from 3.35 to 3.53 and speedup from 2.04× to 2.16× versus composition-matched random training.
Improvements also hold under stochastic chain decoding.

papers.abstract: Generating coherent and explorable 3D worlds from scattered images with little or no visual overlap is a fundamental and long-standing challenge in computer vision, which existing geometry-aware methods fail to address. Meanwhile, existing image- and video-based methods may generate unseen regions but produce inconsistent geometry across views. To bridge this gap, we present WorldBridge, a framework for coherent and controllable 3D world generation under scattered images with little or no visual overlap. WorldBridge encodes scattered references into a global scene context to guide geometry and appearance generation across views. Our temporal and spatial reference attention mechanism further enhances the fidelity of temporal references along the target trajectory and supports flexible spatial references outside it. A plug-and-play latent-reference consistency strategy improves reference fidelity through reprojection-guided test-time optimization. We also introduce the WorldBridge benchmark suite to evaluate 3D world generation from scattered, low-overlap references, which is rarely explored by current benchmarks. Both qualitative and quantitative results demonstrate that our method enables controllable and coherent 3D world generation, surpassing the existing state-of-the-art solutions. Our project page is available at https://davidyan2001.github.io/WorldBridge/.
authors: Weilong Yan, Jingyu Hu, Hongli Xu, Yifan Zhan, Beibei Lin, Anbang Wang, Qinqian Lei, Jingwei Huang, Robby T. Tan
bullets: Addresses the inconsistency and limited coverage of existing geometry-, image-, and video-based methods for scattered-view 3D generation.
Encodes references into a global scene context to guide geometry and appearance across views.
Uses temporal and spatial reference attention to preserve trajectory fidelity while supporting references outside the target path.
Applies plug-and-play latent-reference consistency with reprojection-guided test-time optimization.
Introduces a benchmark suite for scattered, low-overlap 3D world generation and reports qualitative and quantitative gains over prior state-of-the-art methods.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance through instruction tuning, yet adapting them to sequential tasks requires Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning (MCIT). Existing replay-free methods expand prompts or routed LoRA experts across multi-layer decoders, incurring heavy parameter and routing overhead while shifting internal feature distributions. Instead, we identify the final linear layer of the vision-language projector as a high-capacity, coordinate-stationary bridge, where sequential updates easily induce interface drift by displacing historical visual tokens. While low-rank subspace adaptation offers a compact remedy, selecting directions solely from historical statistics or task gradients sacrifices plasticity or stability, and unconstrained multi-step updates still accumulate large drift. To resolve both issues, we propose Projector Refinement through Optimized Update Directions (PROUD), a continual subspace optimization framework for the terminal projector layer. At task onset, PROUD combines retained input statistics with initial gradients to analytically extract a metric-orthonormal subspace maximizing first-order task gain under a drift budget. During training, it regularizes updates within this fixed subspace via an exact Frobenius penalty before losslessly merging them with zero inference or routing overhead. Experiments on UCIT and CoIN across MLLM backbones show that PROUD outperforms recent replay-free baselines in continual accuracy while curbing forgetting with a fraction of trainable parameters.
authors: Hao Yu, Quan Cheng, Lijun Zhang
bullets: Targets interface drift in the projector’s final linear layer, where sequential updates can displace historical visual-token representations.
Analytically selects a metric-orthonormal subspace using retained input statistics and initial task gradients under a drift budget.
Constrains training updates to this fixed subspace with an exact Frobenius penalty, then merges them without inference or routing overhead.
Experiments on UCIT and CoIN across MLLM backbones report higher continual accuracy and less forgetting than replay-free baselines, using fewer trainable parameters.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of PROUD. Frozen upstream layers keep the final projector’s input features stationary. At each task, historical statistics and the initial task gradient select a metric-orthonormal input basis. papers.abstract: Given a continuous RGB-D stream and a language request, streaming 3D affordance grounding requires an agent to decide when to respond and where to locate the requested functional part using only observations available so far. Existing 3D affordance grounding methods typically assume complete scene observations, while streaming vision-language models lack fine-grained 3D functional grounding. Our goal is to jointly determine response timing and functional-part localization during continuous scene observation. We propose StreamAff, an evidence-guided response strategy that makes both decisions from the grounding model's own visual evidence. The model scores the visual patches of the frames it reads: their combined support, weighed against a wait option, decides when to respond, and the highest-scoring patch selects the frame to ground in. A conditional look-back policy lets the model answer from an earlier observation at the moment of the request or wait for new evidence, and zoom-and-refine grounding segments the part named in the answer on the 3D points of the selected frame. We further introduce StreamFun3D, a benchmark derived from real-world 3D scenes that evaluates response timing and grounding across four evidence settings: Current, History, Future, and Unobserved, together with StreamIoU, a metric that credits a mask only when the response is timely and grounded in a valid source frame. We adapt offline 3D affordance grounding methods and build external-decider baselines that pair vision-language models with our mask decoder. StreamAff achieves 30.14% StreamIoU on 15-second streams, a 40.6% relative improvement over the strongest of these baselines.
authors: Wenting Luan, Weilong Yan, Siqi Lu, Ming Li, Beibei Lin, Yongbin Zheng, Robby T. Tan
bullets: Addresses the gap between offline 3D affordance grounding and streaming vision-language interaction.
Uses visual-patch evidence to weigh responding now against waiting for more observations.
A conditional look-back policy can select an earlier frame or wait for new evidence.
Zoom-and-refine grounding segments the named functional part in the selected frame’s 3D points.
Introduces StreamFun3D and StreamIoU; StreamAff improves 40.6% relatively over the strongest external-decider baseline.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of StreamAff. RGB-D observations are stored as 3D-aware visual tokens. When to respond: at request step q = 11, the current frame yields WAIT (p∅ = 0.99); looking back over all 12 observed frames lowers p∅ to 0.06, triggering a response at the same step. Scores denote probability masses in this look-back read. Where to ground: the outlined top-scoring patch selects an earlier frame (i⋆ = 4). The model answers from the look-back read and uses its part phrase to segment that frame’s 3D points. Zoom re-encodes phraseselected windows at higher resolution and adds their features to the frame’s 3D features; Refine corrects the decoder mask voxel-wise.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison. Streaming (a,b): all methods see only arrived frames. StreamAff responds on time by retrieving past evidence (a) or waiting for visibility (b); Qwen3-VL deciders respond late or mask the wrong object. Offline (c,d): masks are shown on the 3D points of the same valid source frame. StreamAff better isolates target parts using only frames available at response, while Fun3DU and T-FunS3D use full streams. Yellow: annotated part; green: StreamAff; magenta/blue: baselines.

Figure 2. Construction and evidence settings of StreamFun3D. (a) Construction of a grounded streaming sample. (b) Examples of the four evidence settings. Green marks valid source frames and target parts.

papers.abstract: We present SPARC, a geometry-guided attention pruning framework that turns the native self-attention of pretrained video diffusion transformers into a unified mechanism for camera control and persistent scene memory. Our key insight is that attention connectivity can simultaneously serve as geometric conditioning for camera control and spatial addressing for historical memory retrieval. Motivated by the asymmetric contextual requirements of reconstructing observed content and synthesizing novel regions, SPARC restricts observed tokens to geometrically corresponding historical tokens and local spatiotemporal context, while preserving dense attention for unobserved regions. Correspondence-aware attention biasing and order-invariant historical positioning further enable stable retrieval across long temporal gaps. Without introducing additional learnable control or memory modules, SPARC achieves precise camera adherence and faithful scene revisitation while substantially reducing attention computation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of aggressive attention pruning in improving camera adherence, revisit consistency, and visual fidelity, with an inference speedup of over 50x when combined with four-step distillation. Project page is available at https://zju3dv.github.io/SPARC.
authors: Zesong Yang, Weikai Chen, Liyuan Cui, Yuan Li, Jiaxin Huang, Lutao Jiang, Runze Zhang, Yingda Yin, Xiaoyang Huang, Kai Yan, Keyang Luo, Xin Wang, Hujun Bao, Zhaopeng Cui
bullets: Addresses camera adherence and faithful scene revisitation in long-horizon camera-controlled video generation.
Uses geometric correspondences to guide attention and retrieve relevant historical scene content.
Restricts observed regions to matching historical tokens plus local context, while retaining dense attention for novel regions.
Adds correspondence-aware attention biases and order-invariant historical positioning for stable retrieval across long temporal gaps.
Reports improved camera adherence, revisit consistency, and visual fidelity while substantially reducing attention computation.

figures.caption: Figure 3. System Overview. For each target chunk, SPARC establishes token-level correspondences with historical observations through local geometric projection, and then prunes the backbone’s native self-attention to focus on geometrically corresponding historical tokens and local spatiotemporal context for previously observed regions, while newly revealed regions retain dense attention for flexible content synthesis. Historical RoPE re-indexing is employed to eliminate artificial temporal ordering biases among retrieved historical observations. The generated observations are subsequently appended to the history bank for continuous rollout.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison on DL3DV-Eval. Given the same input image and camera trajectory, we show frames generated with different methods along the roaming time. papers.abstract: Consistent and controllable 3D stylization is critical for visual computing applications such as immersive visualization, augmented and virtual reality content creation, and artistic scene rendering. While 2D image stylization has advanced significantly, extending these methods to 3D remains challenging due to the need for cross-view consistency, where stylized renderings must align across all viewpoints. Applying 2D stylization independently to each rendered view often results in inconsistencies across perspectives. Existing methods attempt to improve consistency by leveraging implicit radiance field representations, which model scene appearance as a function of spatial locations. However, these methods struggle with ambiguity in updating colors, as the indirect dependence between pixel appearance and learnable scene parameters makes it difficult to enforce consistent stylization during optimization. This work presents Surface-based Scene Stylization (Surf-Style), which reconstructs object surfaces in a 3D scene and uses these surfaces to achieve geometric consistency and localized stylization. Surf-Style defines a learnable appearance model over 3D space, which is modified to replicate the visual style of a reference image. Compared to state-of-the-art methods, our method achieves superior consistency and offers greater flexibility in controllable stylization, including the ability to target specific surface regions and combine different styles.
authors: Wanrong Hong, Ancheng Lin, Mukesh Prasad, Jun Li
bullets: Addresses cross-view inconsistencies caused by independently stylizing rendered 2D views.
Reconstructs scene surfaces to provide geometric consistency and localized style control.
Learns a 3D appearance model optimized to reproduce the style of a reference image.
Supports targeting specific surface regions and combining multiple styles.
The abstract reports better consistency and greater controllability than existing methods.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Difference between naive image-based stylization, NeRF-based methods, and our surface-based approach in 3D scene stylization. (a) Crossview Consistency: Naively stylizing rendered images without enforcing 3D geometry constraints lead to cross-view inconsistencies. NeRF-based methods [6], [8], [32], [41] offer limited consistency, as they use shared parameters (e.g., neural networks, voxel grids) to model appearance within a volume, causing appearance changes to spill over into unrelated regions. In contrast, our surface-based method recovers a surface model from the trained NeRF and stores appearance information independently at face vertices, reducing conflicts and inconsistencies. (a.1) and (a.2) Cross-view consistency illustration. (b) Controllable stylization: The naive method does not support geometryaware selection. NeRF-based approaches struggle to target specific regions, as they do not explicitly represent object structures. Our surface-based method enables selection over individual faces through explicit geometric modeling, allowing for localized stylization.

Fig. 3. Volume-based rendering vs. Surface-based shading. In volume rendering, pixel col rs are computed by interpolating features from surrounding grid points in 3D space, which often leads to imprecise and diffuse stylization. In contrast, our Surface-based approach stores appearance parameters directly on mesh vertices. A custom shader then interpolates these features along the mesh surface, enabling more spatially localized stylization effects.

papers.abstract: Planning with latent world models requires both accurate multi-step predictions and latent distances that reflect physical proximity to the goal. However, models are typically trained on ground-truth observations but must rely on their own imaginations during planning, while closer latent distances do not necessarily correspond to better task outcomes. Existing methods resort to auxiliary training objectives or additional task-cost readouts, which respectively incur extra training overhead or leave the latent geometry itself misaligned with task cost. We introduce CARE-WM, a drop-in training method that meets both requirements without additional supervision, a separate cost model, or any change to LeWM's architecture and Euclidean-cost planner. CARE-WM trains the predictor on its own predictions and adaptively calibrates the strength of latent regularization. With a single hyperparameter configuration, CARE-WM improves mean planning success over LeWM across all evaluated continuous-control tasks and matches or exceeds the best results of other LeWM-family methods on most tasks. Further analyses show lower open-loop latent prediction error and closer agreement between latent-cost rankings and physical task costs.
authors: Yuchen Lin, Kai Zhao
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between training on real observations and planning with model-generated imagined states.
Uses same-horizon self-conditioning plus constraint-adaptive latent regularization.
Requires no auxiliary supervision, separate task-cost model, or changes to LeWM’s architecture and Euclidean-cost planner.
Improves mean planning success over LeWM across all evaluated continuous-control tasks and matches or exceeds competing LeWM-family methods on most tasks.
Also reduces open-loop latent prediction error and better aligns latent-cost rankings with physical task costs.

papers.abstract: Linear attention offers an efficient solution for long-sequence modeling via linear complexity and fixed-size recurrent states. Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) introduces independent channel-wise control over erasure and writing, enhancing state-update expressiveness and in-context retrieval, yet it suffers from training failures during long-context training. We trace these failures to the asymmetry between reading and modification directions during erasure, which yields non-normal erase operators whose directional gains accumulate across tokens, triggering exponential state growth even without new writes. To resolve this, we propose \model{}, employing symmetric erasure to ensure non-expansive state propagation and decay-regulated residual writing to preserve writing flexibility. Theoretically, we establish an $O(\sqrt{T})$ upper bound on recurrent state growth while retaining chunkwise parallel computation. Experiments on ~1.6B parameter models show that \model{} achieves stable training alongside improved long-context retrieval. Compared to GDN-2, it boosts the 128K average RULER score by 6.80 points in the recurrent setting and average accuracy across nine downstream tasks by 0.62 points in the hybrid setting.
authors: Xichong Zhang, Xixuan Hao, Zhichen Liu, Le Zhou, Zeyu Zhang, Boyu Chen, Mingfei Lu, Zehao Lin, Bo Tang, Yonggang Zhang, Linyun Liu, Feiyu Xiong, Jianlin Su, Zhiyu Li
bullets: GDN-2 can fail during long-context training because asymmetric erasure creates non-normal state updates whose directional gains accumulate over time.
The proposed method uses symmetric erasure for non-expansive propagation and decay-regulated residual writing to retain flexible updates.
It preserves chunkwise parallel computation and theoretically limits recurrent-state growth to O(√T).
Experiments with approximately 1.6B-parameter models show stable training and improved long-context retrieval.
Relative to GDN-2, it improves the 128K average RULER score by 6.80 points in recurrent models and nine-task average accuracy by 0.62 points in hybrid models.

papers.abstract: Image-goal navigation asks a robot to reach the viewpoint of a target photograph without a map or goal pose. In three dimensions, this requires not only recognizing the goal but also estimating 3D displacement and generating continuous control actions to approach and settle at the target view. This is difficult because the same visual difference between current and goal image can require very different actions depending on the robot's velocity, yet monocular images alone reveal neither metric scale nor body motion. As a result, existing image-goal policies are limited to planar action spaces and rely on a state estimator for flight control. Policies that map directly from images to low-level control commands have been demonstrated for agile flight, but not toward goal images in unseen environments. We present the first image-goal navigation policy that directly commands thrust and angular rates for agile quadrotor flight in unseen 3D environments, without relying on state estimation (e.g., SLAM, VO, or SfM) or a separate velocity controller. We train a recurrent vision-based policy through a four-stage pipeline that combines geometric and motion supervision with privileged-teacher distillation and end-to-end reinforcement learning fine-tuning. On 1000 held-out flights in unseen environments, the policy achieves an 82.3% success rate with a mean terminal position error of 0.10m across successful flights. Deployed zero-shot on a real quadrotor, the policy reaches an 84% success rate over 25 trials in an unseen indoor environment.

Achieves 82.3% success over 1,000 simulated held-out flights, with 0.10 m mean terminal position error on successful flights.

papers.abstract: LLM-based user simulators are increasingly used to evaluate conversational assistants. Yet, these simulators can drift from their assigned goals or fail to exhaustively explore all specified options, causing evaluation errors incorrectly attributed to the assistant. Prior work has examined goal alignment in single-task settings, but many practical scenarios require simulators to execute multi-step workflows with sequential tasks, fallback logic, and cross-task dependencies, where simulator fidelity has not been measured. To close this gap, we introduce a benchmark of 500 workflows represented using the Hierarchical Task Network (HTN) abstraction. Our experiments reveal that the simulator's fidelity degrades sharply with workflow complexity, and that goal drift accounts for the majority of failures. Fidelity also depends on the assistant's response style, with the same simulator scoring substantially better or worse across styles. To address this, we propose ReUST (Reasoning + User State Tracking), a simple prompting strategy to maintain state information across dialogue turns. ReUST improves goal success rate by more than 12 points for mid-sized and large models, and reduces simulator sensitivity to the assistant's response style.
authors: Pusala Pavan Teja, Jayasimha Talur, Saab Mansour, Marcello Federico
bullets: Introduces a benchmark of 500 HTN-represented workflows covering sequential tasks, fallback logic, and cross-task dependencies.
Simulator fidelity declines sharply as workflow complexity increases, with goal drift causing most failures.
Fidelity varies substantially depending on the assistant’s response style.
ReUST, a reasoning and user-state-tracking prompting strategy, improves goal success by over 12 points for mid-sized and large models.
ReUST also reduces sensitivity to the assistant’s response style.

papers.abstract: A robot learning from one human demonstration may rarely succeed on its own, leaving reinforcement learning (RL) with little reward feedback. We introduce WISER-RL ({W}ake--sleep policy improvement loop, {I}mitation, and {S}elective {E}xperience {R}eplay), a composite reinforcement learning framework that turns assisted practice into autonomous control. During wake, GPTDAgger monitors disagreement among actions sampled by a diffusion policy. When disagreement crosses a threshold, a frozen GPT controller uses retrieved experience to continue the episode. During sleep, Conflict-Aware Experience Reweighting (CAER) compares visually matched successful trajectories and downweights conflicting action windows with more steps remaining to success. The policy imitates the reweighted successes and learns from both successes and failures through offline advantage-guided RL before collecting the next round. After final online PPO refinement, the autonomous policy succeeded in 100% evaluations on each of six LIBERO tasks and 100% trials on each of two real-robot tasks.
authors: Kwunhang Wong, Yang Bai, Qingyang Bao, Liudi Yang, Chenzhi Liu, Jiehong Lin, Wei Huang, Lin Li, Ziyuan Liu, Yujie Yang, Gitta Kutyniok, Zhongrui Wang, Xiaojuan Qi
bullets: Addresses sparse reward feedback when robots learn from only one demonstration.
Uses GPTDAgger during wake to detect diffusion-policy disagreement and invoke a frozen GPT controller with retrieved experience.
During sleep, CAER reweights conflicting action windows in visually matched successful trajectories for imitation and advantage-guided offline RL.
Applies final online PPO refinement before autonomous execution.
Reports 100% success on six LIBERO tasks and two real-robot tasks, with scope limited to the evaluated tasks and settings.

figures.caption: Figure 2. WISER-RL framework. one-shot bootstrapping initializes a diffusion policy, which improves through alternating wake– sleep rounds. During wake, diffusion-action disagreement triggers retrieval-guided GPT takeover, and rollouts are stored in episodic replay. Horizontal lines mark thresholds 0.6 and 0.8.

papers.abstract: LLM-based interactive learner simulators are increasingly used in educational applications, including teacher training and tutoring system development. A critical requirement for those simulations is cognitive fidelity: the simulated learner should maintain the assigned knowledge, misconceptions, and reasoning procedures throughout interaction. However, LLMs may express knowledge or problem-solving skills beyond the assigned learner's cognitive status, a phenomenon we refer to as competence leakage. In this exploratory study, we examine 3,339 simulated learner utterances from 130 teacher-learner simulator transcripts across three learning scenarios and identify over-competence as a prominent direction of cognitive-profile misalignment during interaction. We then investigate the recurrence of previously observed competence leakage cases under four matched-trigger evaluation protocols, ranging from isolated questioning to multi-turn interactions, across five model configurations. Overall, we observe higher violation recurrence under multi-turn protocols than under isolated question answering. More capable models generally show lower recurrence, whereas increased reasoning effort does not consistently improve cognitive fidelity and is even associated with slightly higher recurrence under multi-turn protocols in our matched-model comparison. These findings provide exploratory evidence of competence leakage phenomena in interactive learner simulation and suggest that single-turn question-answering type of evaluations alone may be insufficient, motivating the development of more systematic and reliable multi-turn protocols for evaluating cognitive fidelity in learner simulation.
authors: Zhen Xu, Beata Beigman Klebanov, Jamie N. Mikeska

More capable models generally reduce recurrence, while greater reasoning effort does not consistently improve fidelity.

papers.title: Too Smart for Its Own Good? Cognitive Fidelity and Competence Leakage in LLM Simulations of Young Learners
