papers.abstract: Few-shot adaptation transfers pretrained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to new domains using a small set of labeled images. Most methods fit prompts, representations, or classifiers within an adaptation procedure specified in advance. Yet the visual distinctions needed for recognition can differ substantially across domains, motivating the question: Can an LLM agent use few-shot examples and model observations to design the adaptation procedure itself? We propose Agentic Model Editing (AME), an agentic framework that jointly designs input transformations, encoder edits, feature computation, and classifier fitting as an executable, domain-customized adaptation program. The agent inspects images, class semantics, model parameters, intermediate representations, and activations to formulate hypotheses about the target task. It implements and tests candidate programs on the support set, with aggregate validation accuracy guiding refinement and selection. Each program fits a complete domain model that is fixed before testing. The agent and its tools are shared across domains, while each domain receives its own adaptation program. Across eleven datasets with CLIP ViT-B/16, AME achieves the highest average accuracies of 81.2% without back-propagation and 81.9% with back-propagation among the compared methods. Further experiments demonstrate applicability across VLM backbones and LLM agents.
authors: Yusheng Zhao, Xiao Luo, Zhiping Xiao, Ming Zhang
bullets: Addresses the limitation of fixed adaptation procedures when visual distinctions vary across domains.
The agent inspects images, class semantics, model internals, representations, and activations to form adaptation hypotheses.
It jointly designs input transformations, encoder edits, feature computation, and classifier fitting, then iteratively tests programs on support data.
Each selected program is fixed before testing, while the agent and tools are shared across domains.
Across 11 datasets with CLIP ViT-B/16, AME reports average accuracies of 81.2% without back-propagation and 81.9% with it, and also works across backbones and LLM agents.

papers.abstract: Rubric-based benchmarks such as HealthBench evaluate large language models (LLMs) on open-ended health consultations using case-specific physician criteria, many of which presuppose the healthcare institutions, medications, and care pathways of their source region. Under machine translation alone, these regional assumptions remain in the rubric, leaving responses appropriate in Japan uncredited or falsely penalized under foreign clinical rules. To adapt established clinical evaluation perspectives to Japan without authoring rubrics from scratch, we construct JHealthBench-L (79 patient-facing consultations, 1,022 criteria) through source-cited LLM drafting, single-specialist selection and revision, independent dual-physician review, and meta-review. Specialists rewrote only 4.4% of criteria from scratch, and independent reviewers approved 93.6% of Stage-2 criteria without issue. Comparing JHealthBench-L with a machine-translated baseline across 18 LLMs reveals that translation-only evaluation preserves coarse model rankings ($\tau = 0.817$, mean shift +0.027) yet flips verdicts on 17.7% of modified criteria (vs. 7.3% re-grading noise) and reduces false penalties on Japan-adapted negative criteria by 7.1 percentage points, masking item-level clinical mismeasurement behind stable leaderboards. Axis-level and paired analyses further show that context awareness and Japan-specific clinical criteria remain primary bottlenecks, whereas Japanese continual pretraining and reasoning post-training substantially improve locally grounded performance. Datasets, physician revision logs, and evaluation code are available at https://github.com/horshohei/JHealthBench-L.
authors: Shohei Hisada, Keisuke Orimo, Kenji Igarashi, Kota Sato, Masahiro Kazama, Mitsuhisa Ota, Shoko Wakamiya, Eiji Aramaki

papers.abstract: Foundation models (FMs) have advanced visual understanding and generation by providing semantically rich representations. However, this role of FMs remains underexplored in human motion. Large motion datasets offer diverse movements at scale, but often lack action labels for systematically evaluating learned representations on understanding tasks. Skeleton datasets enable such evaluation through established recognition protocols, yet are typically smaller and focus on predefined actions captured in controlled environments. To combine these strengths, we present MoSk, to the best of our knowledge, the first Motion-Skeleton foundation model to integrate motion and skeleton datasets. MoSk learns shared representations through self-supervised masked motion modeling. We incorporate joint-name embeddings to provide a common anatomical reference across various skeleton formats. A cross-attention decoder reconstructs masked motion from the encoder's features, with joint-name embeddings specifying the target joints. Experiments demonstrate strong action-recognition performance across diverse settings, including linear evaluation and fine-tuning. MoSk also substantially improves motion generation across multiple backbones through representation alignment, reducing FID on MotionMillion by up to 9.75 for unconditional generation and 3.83 for text-to-motion generation.
authors: Yun Chen, Munchurl Kim, Jeonghyeok Do
bullets: Addresses the gap between large, diverse motion datasets and smaller, labeled skeleton datasets.
Uses self-supervised masked motion modeling with joint-name embeddings to align different skeleton formats.
Employs a cross-attention decoder to reconstruct masked motion conditioned on target-joint identities.
Achieves strong action-recognition results under linear evaluation and fine-tuning.
Improves generation across multiple backbones, reducing FID by up to 9.75 for unconditional and 3.83 for text-to-motion generation.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of MoSk. (a) MoSk learns from a combined corpus of motion and skeleton sequences with different joint sets through masked modeling. Joint-name embeddings provide a shared anatomical reference across these formats, while masked modeling encourages the encoder to capture spatial and temporal motion structure. Decoder queries combine a shared learnable vector with joint-name embeddings to specify which joints to reconstruct from the encoded context. Each encoder/decoder block contains attention (MSA/MCA) and feed-forward (FFN) layers, each preceded by layer normalization (LN) and paired with a residual connection. (b) MoSk’s frozen encoder (except during semi-supervised and full fine-tuning) supports action recognition via a classification head and guides motion generators via training-time feature alignment. Snowflakes and flames denote frozen and trainable modules, respectively.

Figure 5. Unconditional generation on HumanML3D and MotionMillion. MotionJiT samples generated with and without MoSk representation alignment share the same sequence length and initial noise. Insets highlight foot contacts, with sliding marked in red (foot height below 5 cm and displacement above 1.67 cm per frame). Labels report foot-skating rate (%) and mean joint jerk (m/s3).

Figure 6. Additional unconditional generation on HumanML3D and MotionMillion. Paired samples show reduced foot sliding with MoSk. Foot-contact insets and metric labels follow the conventions in Fig. 5.

Figure 8. Inputs from motion datasets. Each row shows seven frames after conversion from motion features to MoSk’s unified input format, together with the corresponding text description. MoSk uses only joint positions during self-supervised training. Red and blue mark anatomical left and right, dotted lines trace pelvis trajectories, and grid spacing is 0.5 m.

Figure 3. Text-to-motion generation on MotionMillion and RoMo. We compare MotionJiT with and without MoSk representation alignment using identical captions, sequence lengths, and initial noise. Insets zoom in on foot contacts, with sliding marked in red (foot height below 5 cm and displacement above 1.67 cm per frame). Labels report foot-skating rate and mean joint jerk (m/s3).

Figure 1. Motivation. Motion datasets are large and diverse but often lack recognition protocols. Skeleton datasets provide such protocols but have limited scale and action coverage. MoSk integrates both sources into a unified corpus and is trained as a motion foundation model for both understanding and generation.

Figure 7. Additional text-to-motion generation on MotionMillion and RoMo. Each example shows the conditioning caption, its groundtruth reference motion, and MotionJiT generations with and without MoSk representation alignment. Insets and metric labels follow Fig. 5.

Figure 4. Construction of the NTU training corpus. (a) NTU-60 is a subset of NTU-120, and their X-Sub protocols assign common subjects to the same training and test splits. NTU-60 X-View separates training and test clips by camera, whereas NTU-120 X-Set separates them by recording setup. (b) MoSk therefore uses only NTU-120. To prevent data leakage, we retain clips in the intersection of the NTU120 X-Sub and X-Set training splits and exclude NTU-60 X-View test clips, yielding 18,757 training clips. papers.abstract: Unsupervised cross-modal homography estimation is challenging because appearance differences obscure shared geometric structures. Separating modality transfer from homography estimation helps reduce these differences, but accurate alignment still requires effective geometric representations and consistency constraints on the two subtasks. We propose GeoCo (Geometry-Aware and Consistency-Constrained Homography Estimation), a framework that addresses these two requirements without cross-modal transformation labels. Its homography estimator, RVHomo, adapts hierarchical features from a frozen vision foundation model (VFM) and fuses them with local CNN features to capture structural context and spatial detail. Two geometric consistency constraints encourage modality transfer to preserve geometry and homography predictions to remain consistent under synthetic geometric transformations. Through two-stage progressive distillation, we further obtain GeoCo-D, which uses the lightweight RVHomo-D estimator. An intermediate model first learns to perform cross-modal matching without modality transfer, then transfers prediction and feature knowledge to the student, eliminating online VFM extraction. Experiments on GoogleMap, OPT-SAR, FSD, and VIS-IR show that GeoCo reduces mean average corner error by 17.4-46.7% relative to the best-performing baseline on each dataset. GeoCo-D also outperforms all compared baselines while using 98.5% fewer parameters and 70.4% fewer FLOPs than the complete GeoCo teacher.
authors: Zhuoran Yang, Junchen Yu, Runmin Zhang, Linshan Li, Chenghao Zhang, Hui-liang Shen, Si-Yuan Cao
bullets: Addresses appearance gaps between modalities that obscure shared geometric structure during homography estimation.
RVHomo fuses hierarchical features from a frozen vision foundation model with local CNN features to capture both context and spatial detail.
Geometric consistency constraints enforce geometry preservation during modality transfer and prediction consistency under synthetic transformations.
Progressive distillation produces GeoCo-D, which avoids online foundation-model feature extraction through a lightweight estimator.

Across four datasets, GeoCo reduces mean average corner error by 17.4–46.7% versus the strongest baseline per dataset; GeoCo-D uses 98.5% fewer parameters and 70.4% fewer FLOPs than the teacher while outperforming compared baselines.

papers.abstract: Existing drone landing systems, whether model-based or learning-based, typically rely on predefined visual markers (e.g., ArUco tags) or are trained for specific platform categories, and often assume structured target motion. Recent open-vocabulary studies enable text-prompted target selection, but integrating this capability with learned closed-loop landing control remains underexplored. To this end, we present \textit{Ask to Land}, a mask-conditioned framework that enables a quadrotor to land on various platforms described by a user in natural language, including randomly moving platforms. The core of our approach is the integration of a frozen state-of-the-art open-vocabulary perception frontend (YOLO-World with MobileSAM) and a control policy learned by differentiable physics. By providing real-time, task-agnostic semantic segmentation masks as policy inputs, our framework enables the drone to land on prompt-selected targets without target-specific fine-tuning while continuously tracking dynamic target motion during descent. The frozen frontend processes the prompt, while the policy receives the mask without text embeddings or category labels. To efficiently optimize the control policy, we leverage differentiable physics learning via Backpropagation-Through-Time (BPTT), and employ a carefully designed reward that enforces visual alignment with the landing target and altitude-adaptive descent speed, together with stable control. Real-world deployments validate that our approach achieves landings on diverse user-specified objects, including static and moving platforms.
authors: Fangyu Sun, Guanyan Wu, Yang Deng, Jiahao Cui, Fanxing Li, Yuxiang Huang, Wenxian Yu, Danping Zou

Real-world deployments demonstrate landings on diverse user-specified static and moving objects.

papers.abstract: Understanding manga requires connecting who appears and who speaks with the events, character states, and relationships that unfold across panels. We study manga visual parsing through local story understanding: analyzing each double-page spread independently to capture and organize its story information in a reusable structured representation. We propose MangaParser, an agentic reading framework that jointly performs character clustering, speaker diarization, and speaker-to-character binding within a shared multimodal conversation, without additional training or fine-tuning. The agent uses structured story memory to guide character and speaker identification, inspecting relevant image regions when uncertain and refining its predictions and story records together as evidence accumulates. Quantitative evaluations show that our parser substantially outperforms manga-specific models across multiple backbones. Parsing examples illustrate how a unified representation links the character and speaker predictions with narrative content and supporting evidence. We further test reusability through story question answering using outputs generated before the questions are provided. The results confirm output reusability, offering a foundation for manga translation, content retrieval, and question answering.
authors: Yingxuan Li, Jiafeng Mao, Arata Furukawa, Mayu Otani
bullets: Addresses the challenge of connecting who appears and speaks with events, character states, and relationships across manga panels.
Uses an agentic multimodal conversation to jointly perform character clustering, speaker diarization, and speaker-to-character binding.
Maintains structured story memory, selectively inspects image regions, and refines predictions as evidence accumulates.
Outperforms manga-specific models across multiple backbones in quantitative evaluations, according to the abstract.
Its parsed outputs support downstream story question answering and applications such as translation and content retrieval.

papers.abstract: World-space human mesh recovery can lose spatial consistency even when camera-space body estimates are accurate. A single sequence-wide scale resolves global scale ambiguity but cannot correct local scale distortion along a reconstructed camera path. We present ScaleCurve, a framework that estimates time-varying metric corrections from human-ground geometry. We construct scale observations by comparing predicted foot geometry with locally fitted ground planes. Joint temporal optimization downweights inconsistent observations and couples neighboring scale estimates, allowing calibration to adapt along the camera path without freely following measurement noise. We scale camera translation increments and integrate them into a calibrated trajectory. With this camera fixed, we refine the lifted body motion using 2D image evidence and pretrained 3D dynamics, while restricting global trajectory rescaling. ScaleCurve achieves state-of-the-art performance on most evaluated metrics on both EMDB-2 and SLOPER4D. Consistent gains across three HMR backbones demonstrate its compatibility with diverse body estimates without retraining. Code will be made publicly available.
authors: Sanghyeon Lee, Jong Taek Lee
bullets: Addresses local scale distortion that remains after applying a single sequence-wide scale.
Derives scale observations from predicted foot geometry and locally fitted ground planes.
Jointly optimizes temporally consistent scale estimates while downweighting unreliable observations.
Calibrates camera translation increments, then refines lifted body motion with 2D evidence and pretrained 3D dynamics.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance on most metrics across EMDB-2 and SLOPER4D, with gains across three HMR backbones without retraining.

The estimated scales calibrate camera translation increments, which are integrated into a metric camera trajectory to lift the body into world coordinates. (B) Camera-Consistent Motion Refinement then improves the lifted motion using 2D image evidence and pretrained 3D dynamics while keeping the calibrated camera fixed.

papers.title: ScaleCurve: From Constant Scale to Consistent Motion for World-Space Human Mesh Recovery

papers.abstract: Dynamic object manipulation requires maintaining spatial and temporal alignment with targets that continue to move during inference and execution. Although future prediction can inform action correction, an accurate forecast does not establish whether modifying an existing action would be beneficial. We present Aegis-VLA, a world-model-guided vision-language-action (VLA) framework that generates predictive action corrections and separately determines whether and how strongly to apply them. A Trajectory World Model combines kinematic extrapolation with learned residual dynamics to predict object motion and estimate positional uncertainty. Discrepancy-Guided Action Refinement uses differences between history-only and base-action-conditioned end-effector forecasts to propose bounded arm corrections. A Reliability Gate learns when to admit corrections based on demonstration-relative improvements over base actions, and regulates their application during inference using predictive uncertainty and anticipated object--end-effector proximity. Rejected corrections preserve the corresponding base actions. Aegis-VLA introduces only approximately 2.45M trainable parameters. On the simulated Dynamic Object Manipulation (DOM) benchmark, Aegis-VLA achieves 56.72\% success over 1,800 evaluation trials, exceeding our reproduced DynamicVLA baseline of 45.44\% by 11.28 percentage points.
authors: Lennox Wei, Jiaqi Yao, Shixin Sun, Yuanzheng Zhang, Jianhua Han, Meng Tian, Shaohui Liu, Wangmeng Zuo
bullets: Addresses the challenge of keeping end-effectors aligned with moving targets during execution.
Uses a Trajectory World Model combining kinematic extrapolation and learned residual dynamics to forecast motion and uncertainty.
Proposes Discrepancy-Guided Action Refinement for bounded arm corrections and a Reliability Gate to decide whether and how strongly to apply them.
Rejected corrections preserve the original base actions, while accepted corrections are regulated using uncertainty and predicted object–end-effector proximity.
On the simulated DOM benchmark, it achieved 56.72% success over 1,800 trials, compared with 45.44% for the reproduced DynamicVLA baseline.

papers.title: Aegis-VLA: Reliability-Gated Action Refinement via a Trajectory World Model for Dynamic Object Manipulation
papers.tldr: Aegis-VLA improves dynamic object manipulation by predicting, reliability-checking, and selectively applying action corrections under uncertainty.

papers.abstract: Spatial intelligence concerns both scene structure and its temporal evolution. Yet a semantically correct description can conceal a quantitative error: recognizing that objects are approaching does not determine their closing speed or whether they will meet. Such errors are critical in collision avoidance, trajectory tracking, and reactive grasping, where actions depend on motion magnitude, timing, and relative geometry. We study quantitative kinematic understanding in multimodal large language models (MLLMs): resolving motion magnitude, rate, reference-frame dependence, and future spatial evolution from visual evidence. We introduce the Quantitative Kinematics Benchmark (QK-Bench), comprising 2,341 multiple-choice QA pairs from 379 videos and 17 tasks spanning Object-Centric Kinematics, Camera Ego-Motion Kinematics, and Multi-Object Kinematic Relations. Hidden geometric and temporal signals support trajectory construction and filtering, while fixed kinematic rules map physical quantities to verifiable answers, including categorical labels. Trajectory and question validation ensure target reliability and sufficient visual support in the sampled frames. All models receive a unified monocular RGB input. Evaluations of proprietary, open-source, and spatial MLLMs reveal substantial limitations: the strongest model achieves only 41.2\% overall accuracy, and spatial MLLMs show no consistent advantage. These findings indicate that current advances in spatial intelligence do not reliably transfer to quantitative kinematic understanding.
authors: Lennox Wei, Jiaqi Yao, Shixin Sun, Yuanzheng Zhang, Jianhua Han, Meng Tian, Shaohui Liu, Wangmeng Zuo
bullets: Introduces 2,341 multiple-choice questions from 379 videos across 17 quantitative kinematics tasks.
Covers object motion, camera ego-motion, and multi-object kinematic relations using monocular RGB input.
Uses validated trajectories, hidden geometric/temporal signals, and fixed kinematic rules to produce verifiable answers.
The best evaluated model reaches only 41.2% overall accuracy, while spatial MLLMs show no consistent advantage.
Shows that general spatial intelligence does not reliably transfer to quantitative understanding of dynamic scenes.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Overview of the QK-Bench construction pipeline. Stage I integrates geometric and temporal signals into a hidden kinematic cache, and Stage II derives deterministic quantitative targets and generates validated QA pairs through controlled option construction, reliability filtering, and balancing. Only monocular RGB frames, timestamps, and multiple-choice questions are exposed during evaluation.

Fig. 4. QK-Bench failure cases in Speed Change, Object Turning, Camera–Object Relative Distance Change, and Closest-Approach Prediction: plausible motion interpretations with incorrect quantitative judgments.

papers.abstract: Standard Transformers allocate independent dense weight matrices to every feed-forward network (FFN) layer, coupling parameters linearly with depth (O(L)) and discarding prior compute when scaling capacity. Conversely, weight-tied Looped Transformers decouple depth from parameters (O(1)) but enforce time-homogeneous updates. We formulate the L-layer FFN stack as a 3D Tensor Cuboid and introduce QuatTucker-ZigZagGPT, unifying: (1) 4D Quaternion Hamilton GEMMs in bfloat16 (4x FFN compression), (2) 64x64 Block-Diagonal Tucker SwiGLU Cores for depth-specific rotations over a shared basis, (3) Braided ZigZag Diamond Routing (L0 -> L2 -> L1 -> L3) for zero-FLOP top-down refinement, and (4) Exact 2D Zero-Loss Continual Scaling in both width and depth. We also introduce Annealed Gated Bounce-Back Scaffolding (GatedBounce), which self-distills to 0.0% inference overhead. Across algorithmic tasks (8-bit Parity, 56-seed routing ablations, Mod-53 Grokking) and language modeling (TinyStories, FineWeb-Edu), our model outperforms standard Transformers at 2x-7.6x compression. On A100, QuatTucker-ZigZagGPT-12 (39.0M backbone) beats StandardGPT-12 (85.0M backbone) at 5/5 controlled checkpoints. Continually scaling one lineage across 6.00B tokens via zero-loss width growth (rank 6144 -> 8192), two bit-exact depth expansions (L = 12 -> 16 -> 20, 70.9M backbone, max_diff = 0.000000), and WSD cooldown reaches 3.3582 FineWeb-Edu loss (28.74 PPL) and 44.75% full-split zero-shot accuracy across 16,955 questions (ARC-Easy, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, BoolQ), matching GPT-3 Small (125M, 300B tokens) at 50x fewer tokens.
authors: Shubham Barmase
bullets: Targets the linear parameter growth of independently parameterized Transformer layers and the time-homogeneity of weight-tied models.
Represents the FFN stack as a tensor and combines quaternion GEMMs, Tucker-factorized SwiGLU cores, ZigZag routing, and GatedBounce scaffolding.
Claims 2×–7.6× compression while outperforming standard Transformers across algorithmic tasks and language modeling benchmarks.
A 39.0M-parameter model outperformed an 85.0M-parameter StandardGPT-12 at all five reported controlled checkpoints.
Supports bit-exact continual scaling from 12 to 20 layers and width growth without loss changes, reaching 3.3582 FineWeb-Edu loss and 44.75% zero-shot accuracy.

papers.selection_reason: Transformer parameter compression and scaling, relevant to Efficient AI.
papers.title: Quaternion-Tucker ZigZag Networks: Halving Transformer Backbone Parameters and Enabling Exact 2D Zero-Loss Continual Scaling
papers.tldr: QuatTucker-ZigZagGPT compresses Transformer FFN backbones while enabling exact, zero-loss expansion in width and depth, achieving strong algorithmic and language-modeling results.

papers.abstract: Departing from the paradigm of diffusion and autoregressive models, Generative Refinement Networks (GRN) enables high-quality image generation through iterative refinements. However, this repeated processing over the entire visual representations results in substantial computation overhead. Furthermore, the binary representations and global refinement mechanism in GRN disable the direct application of acceleration strategies developed for other generative models. To accelerate GRN model, we first observe several key properties by analyzing the entire generative process. That includes the stage characteristic, dual branch similarity and more importantly, the $\textbf{refinement redundancy}$. Motivated by the observations, we present $\textbf{FasterGRN}$, a training-free acceleration method for the Generative Refinement Network. $\textbf{FasterGRN}$ first divides the GRN into the semantic establishment stage and detail refinement stage according to its semantic establishment. For alleviating the refinement redundancy mainly resulting from the detail refinement stage, we propose Adaptive Retention Expansion ($\textbf{ARE}$) and Selective Token Freezing ($\textbf{STF}$) to shrink refinement steps and reduce token computations, respectively. In the experiments on GenEval and DPG-Bench benchmarks, our method $\textbf{FasterGRN}$ achieves a $2.03\times$ sampling speedup while largely preserving image generation performance. Our evaluation on COCO datasets additionally demonstrates that $\textbf{FasterGRN}$ even outperforms the original GRN in image fidelity.
authors: Ziqian Zhang, Pengcheng Wang, Yulong Chen, Yaxing Wang, Senmao Li, Kai Wang
bullets: GRNs incur high computation because they repeatedly refine entire visual representations.
The method identifies semantic establishment and detail refinement stages, with redundancy concentrated in detail refinement.
Adaptive Retention Expansion reduces refinement steps, while Selective Token Freezing reduces token computations.
FasterGRN is training-free and achieves a 2.03× sampling speedup on GenEval and DPG-Bench while largely preserving performance.
On COCO, it also surpasses the original GRN in image fidelity.

papers.abstract: We present Auto-Features, a corpus for detecting a car's standard and optional features in advertisement text, given the feature catalogue of that exact vehicle. Sellers name the same feature in many ways. We therefore cast the task as feature-conditioned, or contextual, named entity recognition: extract the span that expresses one given catalogue feature. An entity-linking view follows from the same output. The corpus has a human-gold layer (430 adverts) from screened annotators and an LLM-silver layer (925 adverts) auto-annotated by a search-grounded LLM. We also contribute the way it was built. Every LLM output is validated, and each kind of failure has its own remedy. Malformed output is patched. Hallucinated content triggers a fresh attempt by a stronger model. Links to features outside the candidate list are dropped and counted (3 in 10,928 records). The LLM annotates alone only after its agreement with human annotators on link verification is comparable to human-human agreement. On advert-disjoint splits, a LoRA-tuned 4B LLM reaches 63.9% span F1 and 76.1% on the entity-linking view. A fine-tuned encoder reaches 59.0% and 74.1%. The margin is widest on catalogue features never seen in training (54.5% vs. 49.0%).
authors: Filippos Ventirozos, Ioanna Nteka, Tania Nandy, Peter A. Appleby, Matthew Shardlow
bullets: Frames feature extraction as contextual named entity recognition conditioned on the exact vehicle’s feature catalogue, with an entity-linking interpretation.
Contains 430 human-gold adverts and 925 LLM-silver adverts.
Uses validation and targeted remedies for malformed outputs, hallucinations, and out-of-catalogue links.
On advert-disjoint splits, a LoRA-tuned 4B LLM achieves 63.9% span F1 and 76.1% entity-linking performance.
Performance on unseen catalogue features is 54.5% span F1 for the LoRA-tuned LLM versus 49.0% for the encoder.

papers.abstract: Open-weight large language models (LLMs) for register-transfer level (RTL) design are usually improved by fine-tuning on curated Verilog corpora, which needs large sets of verified designs and GPU training. We present Kolpona, an agentic framework that improves such models without gradient training. Its first component is neuron programming, a new form of weight-space programming (WSP) that writes single neurons in closed form into the weights to remove failure habits found on practice tasks, and keeps each edit only when testbench results on fresh tasks favour it. At inference time, tool-using agents propose designs, and a label-free selection stage delivers one design per task from the specification, the candidates and their simulations alone. On Qwen3.5-4B, edits to 16 neurons raise the VerilogEval v2 pass@1 of the model alone from 31.7% to 55.4%, and the full framework reaches 77.6%. On Qwen3.8-27B, Kolpona lifts pass@1 from 73.1% to 94.9% on VerilogEval v2 and from 66.0% to 92.0% on RTLLM v2.1 on a single 32 GB GPU, above every published system in our comparison. The RTL edits also carry over to Python and raise the pass@1 of the 4B model alone from 84.8% to 91.5% on HumanEval+ and from 67.7% to 77.5% on MBPP+.
authors: Musa Tur Farazi, Md Nasir Uddin, Soumik Bhattacharjee, Tishna Sabrina, Chowdhury Mohammad Rakin Haider
bullets: Addresses the need for verified Verilog data and GPU-intensive fine-tuning.
Programs individual neurons in closed form to remove failure patterns, retaining edits validated on fresh testbench tasks.
Uses tool-using agents to generate candidates and a label-free selector to choose designs from specifications and simulations.
On reported benchmarks, the framework raises pass@1 to 77.6% for Qwen3.5-4B and 94.9%/92.0% for Qwen3.8-27B on VerilogEval v2/RTLLM v2.1.
Neuron edits also improve Python code-generation performance on HumanEval+ and MBPP+ for the 4B model.

papers.selection_reason: Gradient-free neuron programming improves LLMs without GPU training; transferable to efficient model adaptation.
papers.title: Kolpona: An Agentic Framework with Gradient-Free Neuron Programming for RTL Generation
papers.tldr: Kolpona improves open-weight LLMs for RTL generation without gradient training by programming neurons and using simulation-guided agents to select designs.

papers.abstract: Can a classifier computed in closed form on a frozen encoder match gradient fine-tuning? We present closed-form weight-space programming (WSP): a large language model (LLM), used as a design assistant, writes programs that read a frozen masked language model through cloze-style prompt templates at several layers, fit closed-form heads (shrinkage discriminant analysis, kernel ridge regression and the encoder's label-word prior) on labelled data, and select among a pool of candidate heads by cross-fitting. No gradient is computed and no encoder weight changes. We instantiate the framework on RoBERTa-large. On 11 development datasets with 512 to 8,192 training labels, WSP is ahead of full fine-tuning (FT) and LoRA at every label budget (by 0.3 to 0.6 points on average; the registered non-inferiority tests pass) and within 0.5 points of prompt-based fine-tuning (PFT); these datasets also shaped the recipe. With fewer labels its lead over FT and LoRA grows: 1.2 to 3.5 points with 64 and 128 labels, and 3.8 to 5.3 points in the few-shot setting of 16 labels per class, where WSP is again within half a point of PFT on the development datasets. On six held-out datasets, WSP stays ahead of LoRA and within half a point of FT on average, although with six datasets no registered test passes, and PFT is ahead, by 1.30 points with 8,192 labels. WSP never collapses and is deterministic, but it needs one encoder pass per template (17 here). We report all eight recipe versions, every decision that saw test results, and 27 ideas that did not help.
authors: Md Nasir Uddin, Musa Tur Farazi, Soumik Bhattacharjee, Tishna Sabrina, Chowdhury Mohammad Rakin Haider
bullets: WSP uses an LLM-written program to combine cloze-template representations from multiple encoder layers with closed-form classifier heads.
It selects among shrinkage discriminant analysis, kernel ridge regression, and label-word-prior heads using cross-fitting.
On development datasets, WSP outperformed full fine-tuning and LoRA across label budgets and remained within 0.5 points of prompt-based fine-tuning.
Its advantage over full fine-tuning and LoRA increased as labels became scarce, including the 16-labels-per-class setting.
On held-out datasets, WSP remained ahead of LoRA and near full fine-tuning, but prompt-based fine-tuning performed better; WSP requires one encoder pass per template.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Closed-form weight-space programming. At design time an LLM editor writes the program: the cloze templates a text is wrapped in, the views read from the frozen encoder, the closed-form heads (shrinkage LDA, kernel ridge, the MLM label-word prior) and the rule that selects among them. The plain input and Tv view templates are read as V = (1 + Tv) × 2 × L views (2 poolings at each of L layers); Tp ≥ Tv templates give label-word scores at <mask>, so one prediction reads the encoder 1 + Tp times. In our RoBERTa-large instantiation, Tv = 8, Tp = 16, L = 12, V = 216 and H = 113. The classifier’s weights are computed from labelled data, not trained, and no encoder weight changes.

LP-ml and LP-prompt-ml read many views, as WSP does: the top 12 layers of the plain input with both poolings (24 views), and the <mask> state of the 16 templates of WSP’s prior in the top 12 layers (192 views), each view reduced to principal components (6,144 features). WSP: mean over 3 data subsets (one run where the whole pool is used); FT, LoRA, PFT: mean over 3 seeds on the same subsets (collapsed seeds left out). WSP − PFT: the mean of the per-dataset differences, from unrounded accuracies. Development rows: these datasets shaped the recipe; held-out rows: programs fixed before any run on them. Table 16: The registered non-inferiority tests in full, with the complementary statistics added in the revision. k: datasets; Mean diff.: mean over datasets of WSP minus the baseline (points); SD: sample standard deviation of the per-dataset differences; 90% interval: two-sided t-interval. Non-inferior: one-sided paired t-test of H0: mean difference ≤ −0.5 with p < 0.05, and the lower bound above −0.5 (the registered test). Inferior: the complementary one-sided test of H0: mean difference ≥ −0.5. No correction for the 15 comparisons; with Bonferroni (α = 0.05/15) the development tests against PFT at 512 and 2,048 labels would not pass. With six held-out datasets, the registered test can pass for a truly level method only if the SD is below about 0.61.

papers.title: Fine-Tuning Without Gradients? Closed-Form, LLM-Written Classifiers on a Frozen Encoder

papers.abstract: Long sequence reconstruction must correct accumulated drift while preserving locally consistent geometry. In robotics and autonomous driving, embodied acquisition provides recurring platform- environment geometry and repeated observations of scene structure and platform motion. We present Embodied-VGGT, which exploits these cues to establish reliable local relationships and selectively preserve them during global refinement. Memory-Augmented Grounded Chunks (MAGC) builds on Scal3R's global context memory and uses relative scale references derived from predicted ground geometry to regularize test-time memory updates, encouraging cross-chunk consistency while limiting changes to reliable local geometry. Superpoint Alignment (SA) and Cross-Loop Optimization (CL) jointly address the robust establishment and preservation of geometric relationships. SA balances ground and non-ground evidence across spatial regions to estimate inter-chunk translation. CL uses geometric and motion consistency across interleaved windows to select coherent chunk groups, each receiving a shared Sim(3) correction that preserves its internal relative transformations during global optimization. Experiments on five public driving benchmarks demonstrate consistent and substantial improvements in long sequence reconstruction. On KITTI Odometry, Embodied-VGGT achieves a mean absolute trajectory error of 7.30 m and a Chamfer distance of 2.67 m, reducing these errors by 46.8% and 23.3% compared with the state-of-the-art baseline under same evaluation protocol. To facilitate reproducibility, we released our code: https://github.com/Ang-Sheep/Embodied-VGGT.
authors: Yiheng Han, Ziang Chen, Zhuyong Fu, Yiqing Yin, Nan Ma
bullets: Targets drift accumulation and local-geometry degradation in robotics and autonomous-driving reconstruction.
Uses Memory-Augmented Grounded Chunks (MAGC) to regularize test-time memory updates with predicted ground-geometry scale references.
Combines Superpoint Alignment for inter-chunk translation with Cross-Loop Optimization, which applies shared Sim(3) corrections to coherent chunk groups.
Improves reconstruction consistently across five public driving benchmarks; on KITTI Odometry, it reports 7.30 m trajectory error and 2.67 m Chamfer distance.
Code is publicly available for reproducibility.

(c) CL evaluates geometric and motion consistency across interleaved windows to select coherent chunk groups, each sharing a Sim(3) correction that preserves internal relative transformations during global pose-graph optimization. The refined poses and geometry yield the final 3D reconstruction and camera trajectory.

papers.selection_reason: Long-sequence 3D reconstruction for embodied driving and robotics; fits 3D vision perception.

papers.abstract: World-Action Models (WAMs) are a promising new paradigm of robot manipulation policies that jointly generate future video and actions. Successful manipulation requires both identifying where to interact and modeling how the robot and objects move. Yet standard adaptation methods, such as full fine-tuning and LoRA, do not explicitly select parameters aligned with these manipulation-specific capabilities. Motivated by this challenge, we discover two functionally specialized families of attention heads: Next-Interaction Heads, which localize upcoming grasp-and-release targets, and Motion Heads, which track movement across frames. Furthermore, we introduce HeadLight, a parameter-efficient refinement method that jointly adapts Next-Interaction Heads and Motion Heads. On RoboTwin tasks unseen during fine-tuning, HeadLight achieves 62.28% success, compared with 57.89% for full fine-tuning and 58.66% for LoRA, while updating only 1.1% of parameters. Inference-time ablations further validate the functional importance of these heads: ablating Motion Heads reduces manipulation success from 57.89% to 0.94%, while ablating Next-Interaction Heads lowers it to 40.61%, both substantially more than ablating equally many random heads. Finally, we show that our approach is effective across multiple WAM architectures and real-robot manipulation settings.
authors: Yuze Zhu, Jacky Li, Yusen Luo, Ken Jiankun Zheng, Chancharik Mitra, Trevor Darrell, Roei Herzig
bullets: World-action models must both identify where to interact and model how robots and objects move.
The authors identify Next-Interaction Heads for grasp-and-release target localization and Motion Heads for tracking movement across frames.
HeadLight jointly adapts these specialized heads instead of broadly fine-tuning the model.
On unseen RoboTwin tasks, it achieves 62.28% success versus 57.89% for full fine-tuning and 58.66% for LoRA.
Ablations show both head families are functionally important, with effectiveness demonstrated across architectures and real-robot settings.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of HeadLight. (1) We identify Next-Interaction Heads by their selective reliance on upcoming interaction targets over control tokens, and Motion Heads by the alignment of cross-frame attention with optical flow. (2) Ablating these heads causes distinct failures: missed grasps and disrupted object motion, respectively, whereas ablating equally many random heads largely preserves successful execution. (3) HeadLight selectively fine-tunes 24 Next-Interaction Heads in the video stream and 48 action heads paired with frozen video Motion Heads, while keeping all other heads frozen.

Figure 9. Layer–head distribution of selected heads in ZeroWAM and LingBot-VA. In both architectures, the identified NextInteraction Heads and Motion Heads concentrate primarily in the middle transformer layers.

papers.selection_reason: Adapts world-action models for manipulation via specialized attention heads, bridging robot learning and interactive world models.
papers.title: Targeted Adaptation of World-Action Models via Interaction and Motion Heads
papers.tldr: HeadLight efficiently adapts world-action models by targeting attention heads responsible for interaction localization and motion tracking, improving unseen-task manipulation performance while updating only 1.1% of parameters.

papers.abstract: Free-text 3D grounding, segmenting in a CT volume the region described by one sentence of the radiology report, could link reports to images at scale, but it is unclear where current models fail. We analyse the publicly released VoxTell model on all 381 findings of the 200-scan ReXGroundingCT validation set, where it grounds 53.5% of findings. Its failures are rarely about which lesion or side is meant. No miss lies on the side opposite to the one named, and findings are almost never confused with one another. Instead, predictions are too large, land on a neighbouring lesion on the correct side, or are missing for small findings, and diffuse findings are rarely grounded. Removing location words halves performance, to the level of label-only prompting, and anatomical rules derived from the sentence never improve the full-sentence output. The same pattern holds on the hidden 300-scan test set. Further progress therefore depends on extent estimation and small-lesion sensitivity rather than on anatomical post-processing.
authors: Abdullah Arif Sheikh, Kamalaker Dadi, Raju S. Bapi
bullets: VoxTell grounds 53.5% of 381 findings in the ReXGroundingCT validation set.
Errors rarely involve the wrong lesion or opposite side; predictions are often oversized or shift to a neighboring lesion on the correct side.
Small findings are frequently missed, while diffuse findings are rarely grounded.
Removing location words halves performance, and anatomy-based post-processing does not improve full-sentence predictions.
The same failure pattern appears on the hidden test set, emphasizing extent estimation and small-lesion sensitivity as priorities.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Free-text 3D grounding. Each sentence of a chest CT report is a separate prompt, and the model must return a 3D mask of exactly the region that sentence describes. The same scan is analysed in Fig. 2(a)–(d′).

The panels show the finding’s own prediction, i.e. several right-middle-lobe nodules missed (middle) and minimal bronchial wall thickening over-segmented along both hila (bottom).

Figure 3: Hit, partial and elsewhere. Top: a hit for bilateral upper-lobe ground-glass opacities (Dice 0.36), with the prediction confined to the right lung, where the opacities are most prominent. Middle: a partial miss for bilateral aeration differences in the lower lobes, where the prediction overlaps the lesion but is four times its volume (Dice 0.01). Bottom: an elsewhere miss for bronchiectasis in the right middle lobe, segmented at the right hilum instead.

Figure 2: How VoxTell fails (green = radiologist, red = VoxTell, rings mark small findings). Panels (a)–(d′) show the scan of Fig. 1 and (e) another patient. (a) Hit, consolidation (Dice 0.70). (b) Partial miss, with ground-glass opacities over-segmented 6.4× (Dice 0.07). (c) Elsewhere miss for “tree-in-bud appearance”, which names no location. (d, d′) A 287-voxel nodule prompted in full (Dice 0.85) and without location words (Dice 0.07). (e) Empty prediction for “linear opacities in the medial segment of the right middle lobe”. Further examples of each error type, including swapped misses, are given in Appendix A; wrong-side misses do not occur.

papers.selection_reason: Error analysis of free-text 3D grounding in CT volumes, directly relevant to spatial language grounding and 3D-aware multimodal reasoning.
papers.title: Where Does Free-Text 3D Grounding Fail? An Error Analysis of Report-Sentence Segmentation in Chest CT
papers.tldr: Free-text 3D grounding in chest CT usually fails on lesion extent and small or diffuse findings—not on identifying the correct lesion or side.

papers.abstract: We introduce Dual Mutual Information Regularization (DuoMI), a method for regulating expert routing across rounds in looped mixture-of-experts (MoE) Transformers. When two rounds of computation share an expert pool, their routers may favor different expert subsets, limiting the reuse of individual expert parameters across rounds. Even when aggregate expert usage is identical across rounds, we would still prefer each token to retain some experts while switching to others. DuoMI addresses both aspects of routing: it uses round-level marginal mutual information to limit the dependence of aggregate expert usage on the round, and token-level conditional mutual information to penalize average cross-round routing changes that fall outside a target interval. During training, DuoMI computes differentiable penalties from soft routing distributions over all experts. It adds no model parameters and leaves sparse Top-$k$ routing strategy unchanged at inference. On a looped OLMoE backbone in which paired adjacent layers share experts, DuoMI improves the average score across $15$ downstream tasks from $50.08\%$ to $51.82\%$, a gain of $1.74$ percentage points over the looped baseline.

bullets: Targets inconsistent expert selection across rounds, which can limit parameter reuse.
Combines round-level mutual information regularization for aligned aggregate expert usage with token-level conditional mutual information to control routing changes.
Uses differentiable penalties on soft routing distributions, while adding no parameters or changing sparse Top-k inference.
On a looped OLMoE backbone with shared experts, it raises the average score across 15 downstream tasks from 50.08% to 51.82%.

papers.abstract: Low-bit storage of optimizer states can substantially reduce the memory footprint of large-scale training. In practice, however, these states are not quantized once: at every training step, they are dequantized, updated, requantized, and written back. This iterative quantization pipeline can destabilize training. We identify a failure mode behind this instability: for states updated via exponential moving averages (EMAs), quantization errors are recursively fed into subsequent updates. As a result, biased errors accumulate over time while high-variance errors are amplified, particularly when the EMA decay factor is close to 1. To address this error accumulation, we propose BReD (Block Replay Dithering), a method that reduces rounding bias and controls rounding variance during quantization. BReD adapts classical subtractive dithering to optimizer-state quantization by combining deterministic seed replay with block-wise shared dither values, avoiding auxiliary random-tensor storage and per-element dither values generation. Across the default pretraining settings (five optimizers at 120M; AdamW and Muon at 1.1B and 3.4B model) and supervised fine-tuning (AdamW and Muon at 7B model), 4-bit BReD closely matches training with full-precision optimizer states, with PPL shifts $\leq0.5$ in pretraining and $\leq0.2$ in fine-tuning and average downstream performance changes within 0.7 points. Moreover, 3-bit BReD preserves stable convergence in the evaluated settings, offering a more aggressive alternative. Our implementation of BReD is available at: https://github.com/ZhanHeshen/BReD
authors: Heshen Zhan, Youhan Huang, Yunke Peng, Yao Wang, Linghui Kong, Ziwei Zhu, Qingyu Han, Yaoyuan Wang, Congliang Chen, Ruoyu Sun
bullets: Problem: Repeated quantization errors in EMA optimizer states accumulate recursively, destabilizing training, especially with decay factors near 1.
Method: Combines deterministic seed replay with block-wise shared subtractive dithering to control rounding bias and variance without storing auxiliary random tensors.
Contribution: Adapts subtractive dithering to optimizer-state quantization under an efficient, storage-conscious design.
Results: Across the evaluated pretraining and fine-tuning settings, 4-bit BReD closely tracks full-precision optimizer-state training; 3-bit BReD also maintains stable convergence.
Scope: Reported results cover the tested optimizers, model sizes, and training settings; broader generalization is not established by the abstract.

papers.abstract: Looped multi-view reconstruction refines scene features by repeatedly applying a shared transformer block. Making these updates cheaper requires knowing how an approximation at one step affects the rest of the refinement. We study this with paired interventions in D\'ej\`a View and stacked reconstruction transformers, separating the error an approximation injects, how that error propagates, and how it affects the output. In D\'ej\`a View, approximation errors are attenuated more strongly than matched random perturbations under a scale-adjusted state-error measure, and a local Jacobian decomposition separates the contribution of channel gating from the response to spatial error structure. Spatial approximations made early benefit from subsequent refinement, whereas cross-step reuse depends on which quantity is cached and how reuse steps are spaced. At equal final norm, approximation errors change the predicted rotations 1.55 times as much as random errors. These findings guide our proposed method, which reduces spatial resolution and pools keys and values early in refinement, then interleaves attention-output reuse with full attention, and is adapted through lightweight self-distillation. Across five reconstruction benchmarks, the balanced configuration runs $1.63\times$ faster than the official 16-step D\'ej\`a View model with a 1.86-point reduction in average pose AUC@$3^\circ$. At matched latency, it exceeds the interpolated curve of a trained baseline using full refinement blocks by 4.73 points in AUC@$3^\circ$ and improves the corresponding geometry metrics.
authors: Siyuan Zhang, Yuhan Chen, Yangyang Ning, Nan Wang, Jun Yan
bullets: Studies how approximation errors are injected, propagated, and translated into reconstruction outputs in Déjà View and stacked reconstruction transformers.
Finds that early spatial approximations are mitigated by later refinement, while cross-step reuse depends on the cached quantity and reuse spacing.
Shows approximation errors affect predicted rotations 1.55× more than matched random errors at equal final norm.
Proposes early spatial reduction and key/value pooling, interleaved attention-output reuse, and lightweight self-distillation.

Across five benchmarks, the balanced model is 1.63× faster with a 1.86-point average pose AUC@3° reduction; at matched latency, it improves AUC@3° by 4.73 points over an interpolated full-refinement baseline.

papers.abstract: Conventional embodied UAV tracking couples target observability with heading control because targets may leave the field of view of forward-facing cameras. We investigate a complementary paradigm that uses full-spherical perception to follow designated targets without active heading adjustment. To support this setting, we introduce 360UAV-ETrack, a simulation benchmark comprising 2,652 sequences, over 1.73 million synchronized observations, eight tracking tasks, and 150 held-out closed-loop scenarios. We propose 360UAV-TVLA, a panoramic vision--language--action (VLA) framework integrating persistent visual referring (PVR), compressed temporal memory (CTM), and geometry-aligned trajectory supervision (GTS) for instance identification, motion reasoning, and three-dimensional control. Experiments across two VLA backbones show consistent gains over standard fine-tuning, with normalized average tracking frames increasing from 22.56\% to 35.28\% for $\pi_0$ and from 25.68\% to 33.64\% for $\pi_{0.5}$. Our benchmark further reveals a substantial gap between offline imitation accuracy and closed-loop tracking reliability, establishing a challenging testbed for future research https://libingyu01.github.io/360UAV-ETrack_360UAV-TVLA/
authors: Bingyu Li, Wu Du, Zhiyuan Zhao, Junyu Gao, Xuelong Li
bullets: Introduces 360UAV-ETrack, a simulation benchmark with 2,652 sequences, eight tracking tasks, and 150 held-out closed-loop scenarios.
Proposes 360UAV-TVLA, combining persistent visual referring, compressed temporal memory, and geometry-aligned trajectory supervision.
Improves normalized average tracking frames for two VLA backbones: 22.56%→35.28% for π₀ and 25.68%→33.64% for π₀.₅.
Finds a substantial mismatch between offline imitation accuracy and reliable closed-loop tracking.
Targets full-spherical perception for tracking without active heading adjustment.

papers.abstract: Robot world models are increasingly used to evaluate and plan policies, yet robot training data are dominated by successful demonstrations. Off the happy path, when a grasp is misaligned or mistimed and the object is pushed, tilted, or slips, their predictions break down. Across five pretrained action-conditioned models, object-motion error is at most 10.4% lower than that of a static baseline that copies the first frame, and two models are worse than this baseline. We present WorldReforge, which teaches world models what happens when manipulation goes wrong. We construct the Reforge dataset of 62k simulated trajectories by perturbing reference grasps in position, orientation, and closure timing, recording each resulting push, slip, or failed pickup with ground-truth object pose, contact, and surface points. WorldReforge turns this ground truth into two training signals without additional inference cost. Interaction Alignment focuses reconstruction on the small object and contact regions that a global loss underweights, and Surface Correspondence trains backbone features to follow the same physical surface points across frames. On Cosmos3 Nano, WorldReforge reduces object trajectory error by 28.2% overall and by 35.0% on unseen objects, and it lowers the error in predicting how two actions' outcomes diverge by 43.3%. Although trained only in simulation, it also improves reconstruction on DROID and on real failure videos. Controlled data studies show that failed contact and successful holding teach complementary physics: failed contact teaches how objects respond, and holding teaches how a grasped state persists. Our code, data, and models are available at aim-uofa.github.io/WorldReforge/.
authors: Zhiyue Zhao, Mingyu Liu, Bolin Zhang, Liyang Li, Guangyu Huang, Canyu Zhao, Jinchuan Shi, Haokai Zhang, Hao Chen, Chunhua Shen
bullets: Existing action-conditioned world models struggle off the happy path, with some performing no better than—or worse than—a static first-frame baseline.
The Reforge dataset contains 62k simulated failure trajectories covering pushes, slips, and failed pickups with ground-truth object motion and contact geometry.
Interaction Alignment emphasizes object and contact regions, while Surface Correspondence tracks physical surface points across frames without extra inference cost.
On Cosmos3 Nano, WorldReforge reduces object trajectory error by 28.2% overall and 35.0% on unseen objects, and reduces action-outcome divergence error by 43.3%.
Simulation-trained models also improve reconstruction on DROID and real failure videos; failed contact and successful holding provide complementary learning signals.

papers.abstract: Flow-based generative policies offer expressive action modeling for embodied control, yet achieving efficient one-step generation under reward-driven policy optimization remains challenging. In particular, evolving action distributions during online reinforcement learning may introduce inconsistencies between instantaneous-velocity learning and interval-averaged action generation. To address this challenge, we propose iMFPO, a one-step generative policy optimization framework with decoupled velocity learning and drift-aware velocity alignment. A shared interval-conditioned actor supports instantaneous-velocity supervision and interval-averaged action generation. JVP-corrected velocity regression is jointly optimized with reward-driven policy objectives, with action-level guidance from a frozen PPO teacher during training. At inference, iMFPO directly generates actions through interval-averaged velocity prediction, achieving one-step control without iterative flow integration. Across Go2, G1, H1, and Spot, zero-latent evaluation yields mean returns of 35.69, 34.44, 416.23, and 29.86. On Go2, action-generation latency drops from 15.57 ms to 0.41 ms relative to 64-step RFPO. Code: https://github.com/AIGeeksGroup/iMFPO. Website: https://aigeeksgroup.github.io/iMFPO.
authors: Lisiyu Pan, Ting Huang, Zeyu Zhang, Hao Tang
bullets: Addresses inconsistencies between instantaneous-velocity learning and interval-averaged action generation as policies evolve during online reinforcement learning.
Uses a shared interval-conditioned actor with JVP-corrected velocity regression, reward-driven objectives, and guidance from a frozen PPO teacher.
Directly predicts interval-averaged velocities at inference, avoiding iterative flow integration.
Evaluated on Go2, G1, H1, and Spot, with reported mean returns of 35.69, 34.44, 416.23, and 29.86, respectively.
On Go2, reduces action-generation latency from 15.57 ms with 64-step RFPO to 0.41 ms.

papers.abstract: Accurate novel-view synthesis of B-mode ultrasound images requires modeling acoustic propagation through tissue and the resulting appearance variations across probe poses. We propose Ultrasound Propagation Physics-informed Gaussian Splatting (UPP-Gauss), which integrates these acoustic interactions into an explicit Gaussian representation. UPP-Gauss constructs acoustic maps by sampling three 3D Gaussian fields using the probe pose and acoustic beam propagation direction, then combines these maps according to ultrasound propagation to synthesize B-mode images. Across three acoustically diverse datasets, UPP-Gauss achieves the best reconstruction quality with efficient rendering, improving PSNR over the best baseline on each dataset by 1.43 dB on average. These results demonstrate accurate and efficient B-mode novel-view synthesis through explicit Gaussian modeling of ultrasound propagation.
authors: Guil Jung, Seok-Hwan Oh, Myeong-Gee Kim, Young-Min Kim, Hyeon-Jik Lee, Sang-Yun Kim, Hyeok-Jun Kwon, Hyuk-Sool Kwon, Hyeon-Min Bae
bullets: Models appearance changes caused by tissue acoustics and varying probe poses.
Samples three 3D Gaussian fields using probe pose and beam-propagation direction.
Combines the resulting acoustic maps according to ultrasound propagation to synthesize B-mode images.
Achieves the best reconstruction quality across three acoustically diverse datasets, improving PSNR over the strongest baseline by 1.43 dB on average.

papers.abstract: Existing methods for adapting autoregressive (AR) language models to diffusion generation focus mainly on full-attention architectures. More efficient hybrid architectures remain underexplored. We introduce DiCALM, a recipe for converting the hybrid convolution-attention models of the LFM2 family (LFM2 and LFM2.5) from AR to masked-diffusion generation. DiCALM progressively extends LFM2's causal gated convolution so that it captures local context in both directions. It combines this extension with a masking warm-up and joint AR--diffusion training. In controlled experiments, DiCALM performs comparably to the corresponding fine-tuned LFM2.5-based AR models and delivers consistent speedups over them at both the 350M and 1.2B scales: over 1.4x on average and up to 1.79x.
authors: Phong Le, Ngoc-Quan Pham, Dat Quoc Nguyen
bullets: Addresses the limited study of diffusion adaptation for efficient hybrid architectures.
Progressively makes LFM2’s causal gated convolution bidirectional to capture local context.
Uses masking warm-up together with joint autoregressive–diffusion training.
In controlled experiments, performs comparably to fine-tuned LFM2.5 AR models.
Provides consistent speedups at 350M and 1.2B scales: over 1.4× on average and up to 1.79×.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) leverage future visual modeling for robotic action learning, with recent studies exploring alternative or complementary objectives beyond conventional RGB prediction. We introduce Event-WAM, which incorporates event-derived visual changes as auxiliary future supervision alongside RGB. Event-WAM constructs temporally structured event representations from RGB demonstrations and encodes them using a frozen pretrained RGB video VAE, without training an event-specific VAE. Joint RGB--Event latent flow matching provides appearance- and change-oriented supervision without requiring event observations or explicit future generation at inference. Across simulated benchmarks, Event-WAM maintains comparable performance under standard conditions, while robustness gains under perturbations are benchmark-dependent, including improvements on LIBERO-Plus. Real-world evaluations further demonstrate improved manipulation success under both standard and unseen perturbation conditions. Further analyses show that policy improvements are not consistently accompanied by higher future prediction fidelity, suggesting the potential of change-oriented supervision for action learning.

bullets: Builds temporally structured event representations from RGB demonstrations and encodes them with a frozen pretrained RGB video VAE.
Uses joint RGB–event latent flow matching to supervise both visual appearance and changes without event inputs or explicit future generation at inference.
Maintains comparable performance in standard simulated conditions, with benchmark-dependent robustness gains, including on LIBERO-Plus.
Improves real-world manipulation success under standard and unseen perturbations.
Finds that better policy performance does not consistently require higher future-prediction fidelity.

papers.abstract: General-purpose multimodal foundation models enable robots to adapt during deployment from observations and execution feedback, without task-specific demonstrations or training. However, the robot retains what it learns only in the model's working context. Once the task ends, it loses this execution knowledge, such as how to carry a bowl between two grippers. On the next attempt at the task, the robot may take just as long and repeat the same mistakes. To avoid this repetition, robots must retain execution knowledge across attempts. Yet replaying past actions is insufficient, because their effects depend on the current conditions. Procedures that determine actions from the current scene address this, but when they meet conditions that earlier attempts did not cover, revising them requires the measured effects of earlier actions. We therefore propose SEEK, an agentic framework that retains both, enabling robots to improve across attempts while keeping the underlying model fixed. To adapt retained knowledge to the current scene, SEEK adopts a Self-Evolving Programmatic Policy (SEPP) that encodes manipulation as executable procedures and determines each action from current observations. As the robot executes these procedures, SEEK records the measured effects of its actions, including those from failed attempts, in a Persistent Action-Effect Bank (PAEB). Where a retained procedure applies, it acts without a model request; where it meets a condition it does not cover, this evidence guides its revision. On RoboDojo, knowledge retained over ten attempts raises SEEK's average task score from 27.0 to 54.4 and its success rate from 19.7% to 48.0% across all 42 tasks. On 34 of these tasks with GPT-6.2 Astra, SEEK reaches 80.1 after five attempts, against 49.6 for the same model acting directly, and uses 77.6% fewer model requests. https://zeyangguan.github.io/SEEK-Agentic-Robot-Manipulation/
authors: Zeyang Guan, Qihao Zhao, Rui Gong, Zhang Haitian, Yalun Dai, Yangyu Huang, Lingao Xiao, Haozhe Du, Xuehui Yu, Ye Lu, Jianjun Gao, Ruoyu Wang, Haowen Bai, Hao Li, Scarlett Li, Kim-Hui Yap
bullets: Addresses the problem of robots repeating mistakes because execution knowledge is lost when a task ends.
Uses a Self-Evolving Programmatic Policy to choose actions from current scene observations.
Stores measured effects—including failures—in a Persistent Action-Effect Bank to revise procedures when needed.
Across 42 RoboDojo tasks, ten retained attempts increased average score from 27.0 to 54.4 and success rate from 19.7% to 48.0%.
With GPT-6.2 Astra on 34 tasks, SEEK reached 80.1 after five attempts versus 49.6 for direct acting, while using 77.6% fewer model requests.

papers.abstract: Language-instructed manipulation requires robust closedloop policies, yet action-labeled robot trajectories are costly and limited in coverage. Human and robot videos provide complementary spatiotemporal priors for crossembodiment control. We propose X-World, which adapts pretrained video diffusion to variable views. A Q-Former compresses hidden states into tokens for a shared flowmatching expert that predicts action chunks. Datasetspecific projections map native states and actions. We adapt the backbone on large-scale robot and human videos, freeze it for action-only pretraining of the Q-Former and action expert, then post-train on the target platform. At inference, X-World responds at 20 Hz and overlaps updates with execution via asynchronous real-time chunking. X-World performs strongly on LIBERO and under zero-shot shifts on LIBERO-Plus. On hardware, it averages 81.7% success across six bimanual tasks on the side-mounted dual-arm UR5e, one of three real-robot configurations presented.
authors: Chun Gu, Xiaofei Wei, Yiming Chen, Juntong Zhang, Li Zhang
bullets: Addresses the cost and limited coverage of action-labeled robot trajectories.
Adapts pretrained video diffusion to variable views using a Q-Former and shared flow-matching action expert.
Uses dataset-specific projections to handle different states and actions, followed by target-platform post-training.
Reports strong performance on LIBERO and zero-shot shifts on LIBERO-Plus.
Achieves 81.7% average success across six bimanual tasks on a side-mounted dual-arm UR5e configuration.

Action pretraining learns this interface with the video backbone frozen; target-domain post-training updates all modules using video and action supervision.

papers.abstract: Some environments cannot be traversed by a single quadruped robot, for example a ledge that one robot can climb only from its partner's back or a gap that must be bridged with boxes. Solving them requires cooperative task and motion planning (TAMP). Previous works are limited to the motions of a single robot or only select actions from a predefined set of skills. We propose a framework with two parts: task planning that invents motions not defined in advance, and motion generation that realizes the invented motions. Both parts consist of large language model (LLM)-based modules and code-based modules. Task planning divides the trajectory of the whole task into steps and fixes the robot poses at the step boundaries. Motion generation produces keyframes that describe the motion of each step and turns them into a continuous trajectory through kinematic synthesis. The code-based modules check every plan and motion and return failures to the LLM-based modules for correction. The whole trajectory is then refined by trajectory optimization to satisfy the dynamics. On three simulated courses with two RAIBO2 robot models, our framework produced kinematically valid references in all 30 trials, all of which converged in trajectory optimization. Compared with several baselines, our framework showed advantages in success rate, dynamic feasibility, execution time, and generation time and cost. Project page: https://woojin8098.github.io/CoTAMP/
authors: Woojin Kim, Jemin Hwangbo
bullets: Targets environments that a single quadruped cannot traverse, such as ledges and gaps requiring object bridging.
Task planning decomposes the task and specifies robot poses at step boundaries, while motion generation creates keyframes and continuous trajectories.
Code-based modules validate plans and motions, providing failures to LLM modules for iterative correction.
Trajectory optimization refines the full motion to satisfy dynamic constraints.
In simulation, all 30 trials produced kinematically valid references that converged during optimization, with reported advantages over baselines in success rate, feasibility, and efficiency.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has demonstrated remarkable performance in aerial scene reconstruction, motivating its recent extension to true digital orthophoto maps (TDOMs) generation. We propose Tortho-Gaussian++, a novel 3DGS training framework that suppresses geometric drift and floaters and automatically prunes unreliable peripheral regions, coupled with a robust gravity-aligned TDOM rendering solution. First, we explore geometric support via viewing-ray-based geometric observability analysis, quantitatively characterizing the reliability for each Gaussian and subsequently pruning peripheral regions with particularly weak geometric support. Second, the optimizer state initialization is refined for newly created Gaussians during densification, intrinsically suppressing drift and floaters without external priors. Lastly, a robust gravity direction estimation solution is designed, combining image-derived gravity cues, camera-distribution priors and nadir views, to achieve a gravity-aligned orthogonal projection reference for TDOM rendering. Extensive experiments on multiple large-scale UAV (Unmanned Aerial Vehicle) datasets demonstrate that our Tortho-Gaussian++ outperforms vanilla 3DGS by 0.5-3.5 dB in average PSNR and yields comparable or superior performance to prior-guided 3DGS methods. Notably, it reduces the training time, VRAM and Gaussian number by 45.5%, 47.2%, and 58.6%, respectively. Qualitative evaluations confirm that our method effectively suppresses drift and floaters, while robust gravity direction estimation reduces tilt-induced facade artifacts in TDOMs.
authors: Xiang Wang, Xin Wang, Zongqian Zhan
bullets: Addresses unreliable geometry and gravity misalignment in 3DGS-based aerial TDOM reconstruction.
Uses viewing-ray geometric observability to assess Gaussian reliability and prune weakly supported peripheral regions.
Refines optimizer-state initialization for densified Gaussians to suppress drift and floaters without external priors.
Estimates gravity robustly from image cues, camera-distribution priors, and nadir views for aligned orthogonal rendering.
On multiple large-scale UAV datasets, it improves average PSNR over vanilla 3DGS by 0.5–3.5 dB and reduces training time, VRAM, and Gaussian count.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed Tortho-Gaussian++. (A) Viewing-ray-based geometric observability analysis quantifies the geometric support of each Gaussian during training, enabling automatic pruning of weakly supported Gaussians after training. (B) Optimizer-state inheritance transfers the parent’s accumulated moment estimates to newly created Gaussians while retaining the shared optimizer step count, suppressing geometric drift and floaters caused by amplified parameter updates. (C) Robust gravity direction estimation combines imagederived gravity cues, camera-distribution priors, and nadir views through confidence-based selection and fusion. The resulting down-vector establishes a gravity-aligned orthogonal projection reference for rendering the pruned Gaussian scene into a TDOM.

papers.abstract: Visual process reward models (PRMs) can detect calculation errors yet assign high scores to steps that misread visual relations. Supervision based on subsequent answer success does not directly establish whether a step's relational claim holds. To strengthen visual-relation verification, we first build an automated pipeline that programmatically verifies each claim and identifies the required objects, relations, and image regions. It produces RelProcessTrain and RelProcessBench (RPB), which tests whether scores respond appropriately to relational evidence through controlled image edits and step rephrasings. Building on this pipeline, we further introduce RelPRM, a visual-relation-oriented method for process reward modeling with two training mechanisms. Relation-evidence self-distillation constructs views preserving necessary objects, relations, and dependencies, reducing the burden of finding decisive evidence in complex scenes and transferring reliable evidence-assisted judgments to full images. Relation-evidence-driven consistency training encourages appropriate score changes when relation edits reverse a step's truth, stability under irrelevant edits, and similar score changes across paraphrases. At inference, RelPRM directly scores the current step using only the original image and reasoning context. RelPRM achieves 66.2% on VisualProcessBench (VPB) and 68.4% on RPB, gains of 4.2 and 9.9 percentage points over VisualPRM-8B. These results show that training for visual relations improves both relational verification and step assessment across broader multimodal reasoning tasks.
authors: Zhaoxing Zhang, Ziqiu Gui, Cheng Chen
bullets: Addresses PRMs that reward steps making incorrect claims about visual relationships despite correct final answers.
Builds an automated verification pipeline and releases RelProcessTrain and the relation-focused RelProcessBench (RPB).
Uses relation-evidence self-distillation and consistency training to promote sensitivity to relevant relation changes, robustness to irrelevant edits, and paraphrase stability.
Scores each reasoning step at inference using only the original image and reasoning context.
Reaches 66.2% on VPB and 68.4% on RPB, improving over VisualPRM-8B by 4.2 and 9.9 percentage points, respectively.

papers.abstract: Medical reasoning agents combine large language model (LLM) reasoning with clinical workflows and specialized neural tools. However, general-purpose LLMs receive limited training exposure to domain-specific medical tools, and the uncertainty and distributional shifts of neural tool outputs make selecting tools from simple descriptions significantly more challenging than in deterministic settings such as calculators or dictionary lookups. In this paper, we propose EATS, an experience-augmented tool selection strategy that leverages accumulated tool-use trajectories to improve tool selection in medical reasoning agents. EATS constructs a memory of past interactions, including queries, tool choices, arguments, and self-evaluated feedback, and retrieves relevant experiences to guide tool selection for new queries. As memory construction does not require ground-truth supervision, EATS scales naturally with test-time experience. We evaluate EATS on tool-augmented medical reasoning tasks, including closed-ended visual question answering and free-form report generation. Experiments on four public datasets, ChestAgentBench, CheXbench, MIMIC-CXR, and SLAKE-VQA, across three multimodal LLMs, Qwen3-VL 2B, Qwen3-VL 32B, and GPT-5.5, show consistent gains in tool selection behavior and downstream medical reasoning performance. Code is available at https://github.com/Limingyuan001/EATS.
authors: Mingyuan Li, Tong Jia, Haoran Wang, Wenbo Qi, Ziyuan Yang, Bowen Ma, Jie Gui, Baosheng Yu
bullets: Medical LLM agents struggle to select specialized tools because tool outputs are uncertain and distribution-shifted.
EATS stores queries, tool choices, arguments, and self-evaluated feedback from prior interactions.
Relevant experiences are retrieved to guide tool selection for new medical queries.
Evaluated on visual question answering and report generation across four public datasets and three multimodal LLMs.
The abstract reports consistent improvements in tool selection and downstream medical reasoning performance.
