papers.abstract: Looped language models can adapt computation for predicting a token without a proportional rescaling in unique model parameters by adjusting the number of loops. This property has been used for self-speculative decoding, taking shallow loops as fast drafters and deep loops as verifiers, which is effective since drafting still uses full parameters. In this paper, we show that shallow loops can be also predictive of several future tokens and leverage this to drastically accelerate the inference of looped language models. To that end, we present Floodgates, a simple self-speculative decoding method that appends a block of mask tokens as a suffix and learns via low-rank adaptation to draft these tokens in parallel. Across seven models, five benchmarks, a range of batch sizes, and both greedy and sampled decoding, Floodgates is the fastest lossless decoding method in most cases, attaining up to 7.5x acceleration. Through analysis, we show that this speedup is enabled by all-depth training of looped models, with the shallow drafter's ability to leverage full-depth computation by conditioning on deep prefix cache evaluated during verification.
authors: Ayhan Suleymanzade, Sean McLeish, Sehoon Kim, Jinwoo Kim, Antoine Bosselut
bullets: Looped models vary computation through the number of recurrent loops without proportionally increasing unique parameters.
The method appends mask-token suffixes and uses low-rank adaptation to draft several tokens simultaneously.
It exploits deep prefix-cache information during verification, allowing shallow drafts to benefit from full-depth computation.
Across seven models and five benchmarks, Floodgates is usually the fastest lossless method across batch sizes and decoding modes.
The approach is specific to looped models trained at all depths.

papers.abstract: Latent video generators are trained on clips of a few seconds, and much of this limit lies in their tokenizers, which spend as many tokens on a static frame as on a moving one and need future frames that do not exist during generation. We introduce DeltaRAE, a causal representation autoencoder for video. Its derivative tokenization encodes periodic anchor frames in full and all remaining frames with a few tokens each, and its causal encoder and decoder read a frozen pretrained image encoder. On UCF-101 and Kinetics-600, a standard diffusion transformer trained on DeltaRAE latents is competitive with state-of-the-art video tokenizers. DeltaRAE halves the tokenizer GFLOPs on 16-frame clips relative to keeping the same number of patch tokens for every frame, and it represents a minute of video with 18.8x fewer tokens. The tokenizer trains end to end on one-minute videos, and in video prediction a generator on its latents produces a full minute of video. The same generator collapses within 15 seconds in most videos when the tokenizer has the same token budget but no pretrained encoder.
authors: Mingzhuo Yu, Shengcao Cao, Chengzhi Mao, Yong Cheng, Di Jiang, Lijun Yu
bullets: Targets video tokenizers that waste equal tokens on static and moving frames and require unavailable future frames.
Uses derivative tokenization with full anchor-frame representations and a few tokens for remaining frames.
A causal encoder–decoder leverages a frozen pretrained image encoder.
Matches competitive video-tokenizer performance on UCF-101 and Kinetics-600 while halving tokenizer GFLOPs on 16-frame clips.
Represents one minute of video with 18.8× fewer tokens and supports minute-long video prediction; removing the pretrained encoder causes collapse within 15 seconds in most videos.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Architecture of DeltaRAE. (a) Causal representation autoencoder. A causal encoder updates learnable registers from frozen semantic features augmented by a pixel-residual stem. The updated registers are projected and normalized into latent tokens for causal decoding. (b) Derivative tokenization. To exploit shared content over time, periodic anchor groups receive a full set of primitive tokens, while the remaining groups use fewer derivative tokens with earlier groups as context. (c) Streaming generation. A DiT generates successive chunks, reusing each chunk’s tail latents as the next input prefix. The assembled latent sequence is decoded into a 60-second video.

papers.abstract: Forklifts play a critical role in warehousing and distribution, but existing automation systems remain limited in handling complex tasks that require sequential decision-making. Recently, vision--language--action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising approach for multi-step decision-making by directly generating control actions from visual observations and language prompts. Although VLA-based control has been extensively researched for manipulators, to the best of our knowledge, its application to forklifts remains unexplored. Therefore, this study demonstrates the integration of VLA control for an autonomous forklift unloading task with limited real-world data. Moreover, training VLA models typically requires large-scale datasets. As there is currently no public dataset for forklift operations, we use a VLA model pretrained primarily on robotic manipulator data and construct a training dataset via simulation, which can be scaled up at low cost. We then adapt the pretrained VLA model to forklift control using 9.38 h of simulation data and 0.8 h of real-world demonstrations, with the latter accounting for approximately 8% of the collected forklift data by duration. The integrated system was validated through 72 real-world trials across four model variants. The results show that the proposed system can accomplish an unloading task even with limited real-world data.
authors: Koshi Oishi, Seigo Ito
bullets: Addresses sequential decision-making for forklift unloading, an application of VLA control not previously explored in the abstract.
Constructs a scalable forklift-control dataset through simulation because no public forklift dataset is available.
Adapts a manipulator-focused pretrained VLA model using 9.38 hours of simulation data and 0.8 hours of real-world demonstrations.
Validates four model variants in 72 real-world trials, showing task completion despite limited real-world data.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Integrated system. A VLA policy is first constructed using readily available web data and manipulation data, and it is then adapted to the target forklift using simulator-generated data and a small amount of real-world data. papers.abstract: End-to-end driving policies increasingly operate without explicit HD maps at inference, raising the question of what road knowledge they actually internalize. To probe this knowledge through model outputs, we introduce Road-KSU, a framework that automatically converts HD maps and actor annotations into a road-centric scene graph. From this, we derive road-focused question answering and reasoning targets, complemented by map-based trajectory compliance metrics. Pairing Road-KSU with geographically disjoint splits yields a $2 \times 2$ evaluation crossing output modality (language vs. action) with place familiarity (seen vs. unseen roads). On NAVSIM, 95% of test samples lie within 10m of a training sample, and scores of 13 published planners on turns rise steeply with the number of training drives through the test location, pointing to memorized road geometry. Retraining on geographically disjoint splits and probing with Road-KSU confirm that action-space performance degrades most on unfamiliar turns, with failures dominated by geometric compliance. Language accuracy, however, drops on road-centric VQA on straight and curved roads alike, and remains stable on dynamic scene content. Scaling the training data further reveals a double dissociation: more drives through the same places improve driving on unseen roads but leave road question answering unchanged, whereas spreading a fixed data budget over more places increases road question answering with little change in driving performance. These findings show that improved driving scores need not imply broader road understanding on unseen roads, and identify geographic diversity as key to transferable road knowledge.
authors: Lena Wild, Christian Helten, Katie Z Luo, Jakob Thumm, Rafael Valencia, Patric Jensfelt, Marco Pavone
bullets: Introduces Road-KSU, which converts HD maps and actor annotations into road-centric scene graphs, questions, reasoning targets, and trajectory-compliance metrics.

papers.abstract: A world model lets an agent anticipate the consequences of its actions and use imagined futures to make decisions. We introduce Normalizing-Flow World Model (NFWM), which pairs an invertible observation encoder with an action-conditioned probabilistic predictor. Because the encoder is invertible, the predicted distribution over latent states defines a distribution over future observations. Maximizing the exact conditional likelihood of those observations therefore trains the representation and dynamics jointly. An agent can plan directly in the learned latent space and decode sampled trajectories to inspect possible futures. On Teleport, these samples capture the two possible outcomes of the same action. In Flappy Bird, a world model trained by likelihood alone supports reward-based planning that reaches 100 pipes in all ten evaluated games. For goal-conditioned control, an auxiliary inverse-dynamics objective shapes the coordinates used to compare predicted states with a goal. On LIBERO, NFWM uses this distance to select successful action sequences more often than LeWM and SMWM. In Atari Boxing, training on imagined trajectories improves a policy beyond its behavior-cloned initialization. Together, these results establish normalizing flows as capable world models.
authors: Zijia Li, Yong-Hyun Park, Shusheng Yang, Jiatao Gu

papers.abstract: When the lead robot cannot continue, what should it send the teammate that must finish the route? We replay a frozen receiver at each contact under alternative messages. Across 3,920 autonomous departures in 106 environments, adding the view before the lead's last action block to its executed actions raised success by 7.51 percentage points (pp) per RxR handoff and 8.54 pp per SAGE handoff. Per departure the gains were 2.23 and 1.44 pp, respectively. The lead continuing in simulation defines the empirical full-history ceiling (Solo). At contact, the lead had accumulated a median of 41 frames. Sending one frame when available recovered 24% of the full-history advantage over actions alone in SAGE and 30% in RxR. Over an estimated progress cue in SAGE, the image rescued 100 routes and reversed 54 successes. Near-goal receivers finished outside less often (63.1% to 51.7%, post hoc). In secondary comparisons the earlier view outperformed the contact view by 6-7 pp per handoff. Exact-route specificity and image gains at controlled starts with mostly unknown progress or outside the goal region remained unresolved. Gains were detectable from about 7 kB per handoff. Random transmission matched within size bins nearly equaled the learned sender's team success. At a required handoff, a view of the approach to the last maneuver helps the receiver finish.

papers.abstract: Audio-visual understanding requires perceptual grounding, temporal understanding, and semantic inference. Multi-teacher distillation can consolidate these capabilities, but direct probability matching does not explicitly capture teacher prediction changes across audio-visual conditions. We introduce OmniMeld, a multi-teacher on-policy distillation method that integrates domain expertise through modality-response-guided distribution matching. We train four teachers covering grounding and correspondence, temporal dynamics and event structure, causal and inferential reasoning, and contextual and holistic understanding. Each sample is routed to its corresponding teacher for supervision conditioned on student-generated answer prefixes. We derive transport costs from teacher prediction changes over shared candidate tokens across audio-visual conditions, using optimal transport to match student predictions to those of the teacher under complete audio-visual input. We also construct OmniMeld-20K for domain-specialized teacher training. The dataset spans four capability domains, with responses structured into evidence, reasoning, and answer sections and verified through consistency checks and media-based review. Experiments on audio-visual and general video understanding benchmarks demonstrate competitive teacher performance among similarly sized open-source models. The student improves over its base model across all evaluated benchmarks and surpasses the teachers' base model on several benchmarks.

Introduces OmniMeld-20K, covering four domains with evidence-, reasoning-, and answer-structured responses verified for consistency and media grounding.
The distilled student improves over its base model across evaluated benchmarks and exceeds the teachers’ base model on several benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Random Network Distillation (RND) is a scalable novelty signal for RL based on a fixed random target network and a trained predictor. However, it can overgeneralize: the predictor extrapolates the random target off the data manifold, causing novelty scores to collapse on unfamiliar inputs. This paper analyzes this failure through a kernel-theoretic lens. Under a GP target model and an NTK-regime predictor, we show that the RND novelty score is a cross-kernel residual variance: it is governed jointly by the target covariance kernel and the predictor NTK, rather than by either one alone. This identifies overgeneralization as spectral under-excitation. Motivated by this view, we formulate spectral target design as a principle for shaping RND novelty geometry. As a concrete instance, we replace the implicit random-network target with a bandwidth-controlled Random Fourier Feature (RFF) target, redistributing residual signal toward modes less attenuated by the predictor. Experiments on offline D4RL, online Atari, and Fetch manipulation benchmarks show improved novelty discrimination and downstream RL performance. The code for the RL implementation is available at https://github.com/tuuktuc86/RFF-RND.
authors: Minseok Jeong, Yechan Lee, Hyewon Choi, Jeongyong Yang, SooJean Han
bullets: RND can assign low novelty to unfamiliar inputs because its predictor extrapolates the random target off the data manifold.
A kernel analysis shows novelty is a cross-kernel residual variance determined jointly by the target covariance and predictor NTK.
The paper interprets overgeneralization as spectral under-excitation and proposes spectral target design to reshape novelty geometry.
Replacing the standard target with a bandwidth-controlled RFF target improves novelty discrimination and downstream RL performance across offline, online, and manipulation benchmarks.

Figure 10: Energy decomposition of DRND on synthetic manifolds. The first row shows the base RND-like component β∥fθ(x)− µ(x)∥2, which provides a coarse separation between data and offmanifold regions but remains overly smooth. The second row shows the distributional correction term (1− β)b2(x), which partially sharpens the energy landscape by reweighting prediction errors. The third row shows the combined novelty signal b(x) = β∥fθ(x)− µ(x)∥2 + (1− β)b2(x). While the correction term improves contrast in simple settings such as Multi-Blob, DRND remains insufficiently sensitive to local manifold geometry in more structured datasets, including Ring, Spiral, and TwoMoons.

Figure 11: Comparison of input-dependent conditioning mechanisms in RND on two-dimensional synthetic manifolds. Rows correspond to Gating-, Bilinear-, and FiLM-conditioned RND, respectively, while columns show Multi-Blob, Ring Gap, Spiral, and Two-Moons datasets. Background contours visualize the RND energy over the input space, and cyan points denote training samples. Gating induces locally smooth but axis-aligned modulation, Bilinear conditioning yields sharp, directiondependent distortions, and FiLM produces smoother, globally consistent energy landscapes that better respect curved manifold geometry.

Figure 8: Energy landscapes of RFF-RND on the Two Moons dataset over varying α and m. (Top Row) Varying the RBF length-scale α with m = 64 fixed. (Bottom Row) Varying the RFF feature dimension m with α = 1.0 fixed. Overall, smaller α yields more localized (but noisier) energy bands around the manifold, whereas larger α over-smooths the landscape and blurs manifold boundaries. Increasing m improves the kernel approximation and stabilizes the energy, producing smoother and more consistent manifold separation.

Right: the residual spectrum is the product of these two terms. Empirical residuals obtained by sampling target functions and applying the NTK residual operator follow the predicted frequency-wise structure.

Across widths, RFF-RND produces a localized energy landscape that separates the data manifold from off-manifold regions. Wider predictors sharpen the low-energy region around the sampled manifold, but the overall manifoldaware structure remains consistent.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance in chemical knowledge and reasoning, yet it remains unclear whether they can solve problems whose answers must be discovered through experimentation. We investigate this question through Unknown Chemical Identification, where a model must actively design experiments, interpret observations, update hypotheses, and ultimately identify a hidden substance. We introduce ChemDeduce, an interactive evaluation framework for assessing LLMs through simulated experiments. ChemDeduce formulates chemical identification as a sequential decision process and provides a stateful simulated laboratory with explicit instrument and operational constraints, enabling scalable and reproducible evaluation of iterative experimental reasoning. We benchmark eight frontier LLMs on 200 chemicals, yielding 1600 model--target pairs and 4800 episodes over three independent repetitions, and evaluate identification accuracy, operational compliance, interaction efficiency, and trajectory-level reasoning quality. Despite generating seemingly plausible experimental plans, current models achieve an average identification accuracy ranging from 23.83% to 67.33%, revealing substantial limitations in experiment selection, evidence interpretation, and sequential hypothesis refinement.
authors: Hengyi Cai, Yuqi Tang, Zichang Li, Huajun chen, Qiang Zhang, Keyan Ding
bullets: Frames unknown chemical identification as sequential decision-making under instrument and operational constraints.
Introduces a stateful, reproducible simulated laboratory for evaluating iterative experimental reasoning.
Benchmarks eight frontier LLMs across 200 chemicals, 1,600 model–target pairs, and 4,800 episodes.
Measures identification accuracy, operational compliance, interaction efficiency, and trajectory-level reasoning quality.
Observed average identification accuracy ranges from 23.83% to 67.33%, highlighting weaknesses in experiment selection, evidence interpretation, and hypothesis refinement.

(d) Evaluation Metrics cover identification accuracy, laboratory-operation validity, successful observation acquisition, interaction efficiency, budget exhaustion, and trajectory-level experimental reasoning quality.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are widely used for image segmentation. However, existing methods either use a decoder or use patch-based approach which trades boundary precision against the number of decisions as coarse grid cells mix foreground and background pixels, while finer grids require many more predictions, and autoregressive mask generation adds sequential decoding overhead. We propose SPiXSeg, which shifts the output from per-patch to per-superpixel label assignment, using superpixel tokens formed by aggregating patch-level visual features. An off-the-shelf model partitions each image into task-agnostic superpixels, so the partition is computed once and reused across tasks. A Spix-to-Mask (S2M) module scores each superpixel token in a single MLLM forward pass by directly comparing the MLLM's hidden representations, without autoregressive generation or a separate scoring network, and the selected superpixels are mapped directly to pixels without refinement. Without any trainable decoder head or post-hoc refinement, SPiXSeg achieves an average cIoU of 80.5 with LLaVA-1.5-7B and 81.9 with InternVL2.5-8B on RefCOCO, RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg and, when trained only on COCO-Stuff, extends to open-vocabulary semantic segmentation with mIoU of 29.0, 59.5 and 95.4 on ADE20K, PASCAL Context and PASCAL VOC, outperforming several SoTA MLLM baselines. Our results suggest that a fixed, query-agnostic superpixel partition is enough for accurate language-guided segmentation.
authors: Piyush Tiwary, Sohini Dutta, Prathosh A. P
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between coarse patch boundaries, costly fine-grained predictions, and sequential mask decoding.
Aggregates patch features into task-agnostic superpixel tokens using a fixed partition computed once per image.
Scores superpixels in one MLLM forward pass by directly comparing hidden representations, then maps selected regions to pixels.
Achieves 80.5/81.9 average cIoU with LLaVA-1.5-7B/InternVL2.5-8B on RefCOCO variants and supports open-vocabulary semantic segmentation when trained only on COCO-Stuff.
The approach omits a trainable decoder head and post-hoc refinement; its scope depends on the quality of the fixed superpixel partition.

papers.abstract: This paper proposes a new paradigm and method for giving large language models spatial understanding. Standard language models operate exclusively over discrete words (secondary representations of things rather than continuous space itself), forcing them to guess geometry verbally. Whereas most multimodal approaches equate spatial grounding with camera images or video frames, spatial structure itself is not a picture: it consists of coordinate frames, solid boundaries, and how objects move and relate to each other in continuous space. Motivated by this distinction, we place continuous object tokens combining pose (position, orientation, and scale) and signed-distance shape embeddings alongside word tokens inside a single uninterrupted transformer sequence, allowing language and geometry to attend to each other as object scenes are built and updated step by step. Control tokens switch output automatically between natural-language words and continuous object state updates to a persistent object workspace, while an attention mask blocks earlier prose when generating the answer, so responses must be read directly from settled geometry. To prove this method works, we attach a narrow parallel spatial stream (+4.4% weights) alongside unfrozen Qwen3-1.7B layers. In our two-dimensional tests, the model spawns and transforms multi-object scenes from English descriptions, transfers shapes to held-out nouns, and relies causally on the workspace to answer spatial questions.
authors: Lo\"ic Magnan, Tomasz Kozlowski
bullets: Motivates continuous geometric representations—poses, boundaries, and relations—as distinct from image-based spatial grounding.
Interleaves word tokens with continuous object tokens encoding pose and signed-distance shapes in one transformer sequence.
Uses control tokens and a persistent object workspace to alternate between language generation and geometric scene updates.
An attention mask forces answers to be derived from the settled workspace rather than earlier prose.
In 2D tests, the model constructs and transforms multi-object scenes, transfers shapes to unseen nouns, and causally uses the workspace for spatial questions.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of the spatial workspace paradigm. Words and continuous objects share a single sequence through the language model (treated as a black box). Each object combines a 5-element pose (𝑥, 𝑦, cos 𝜃, sin 𝜃, 𝑠) with a 32-element signed-distance shape embedding ®𝑧32 compressed from its 128-point outline [13], projected by𝑊in into object embeddings ®𝑒obj alongside word embeddings ®𝑒𝑤 projected by𝑊emb. Control tokens switch between natural language (Word Head) and object representation (Object Head). Emitting the <LOOK> token masks the entire prior sequence so the model can only read the current geometry from the object workspace.

Figure 6. Coordinate-free scene layout. The user prompt contains only relative natural-language statements with no coordinates or sizes; the model constructs a 2 × 2 workspace layout across four held-out nouns and answers from <LOOK>.

Figure 2. Parallel spatial stream and attention mask on Qwen3-1.7B [12]. (a) Across each of the 28 pretrained layers, a 256-dimensional parallel spatial block runs alongside the 2048-dimensional language stream (+4.4% added parameters). Language features are down-projected from 2048 to 256 dimensions so language and geometry enter each spatial block at equal width, and spatial updates are projected back into upper language layers (ℓ ≥ 6) through zero-initialized cross-projections (𝐵 = 0). (b) Attention visibility across the sequence: text tokens attend causally, object tokens within the same <STEP> or <LOOK> block attend to each other bidirectionally, and <LOOK> blocks all earlier text and intermediate steps.
Figure 4. Assembling scattered held-out nouns across translations and rotation. Dotted outlines and arrows mark the previous step; dark dashed outlines on <LOOK> show exact target polygons.

Figure 3. Judging whether one object sits inside another after step updates. Colored contours decode 32-element shape embeddings and 5-element poses; dark dashed outlines on <LOOK> show exact target polygons.

papers.tldr: The paper introduces a language–geometry transformer that builds and updates continuous 2D object scenes directly alongside text, enabling spatial reasoning without images.

papers.abstract: Understanding large-scale 3D urban scenes requires representations that capture both multi-scale geometric structures and complex spatial relationships. However, existing 3D vision-language methods primarily emphasize global semantic alignment or object-level representations, leaving structured relational modeling underexplored within unified contrastive and generative frameworks. In this paper, we present 3D CoCa v3, a scene-graph-enhanced contrastive and generative framework for urban 3D scene understanding. Our framework features a Pyramid Vision Encoder for multi-scale geometric representation learning and a language-model-based decoder with question-guided caption retrieval and visual cross-attention. We further introduce MSG-based relational descriptions to enrich contrastive 3D-language alignment with structured spatial relationships. To support semantic and relational supervision, we construct City3D-9.6K, a multi-view urban vision-language dataset with aligned visual-geometric observations, scene captions, and scene graphs. Extensive experiments on City-3DQA demonstrate that 3D CoCa v3 achieves 88.35% and 64.79% overall top-1 accuracy on the sentence-wise and city-wise splits, surpassing 3D CoCa v2 by 20.88 and 3.57 percentage points, respectively. Furthermore, 3D CoCa v3 achieves the best performance on GeoEval3D, demonstrating its effectiveness in urban spatial reasoning and geometric understanding. Code is available at https://github.com/AIGeeksGroup/3DCoCav3.
authors: Nannan Zhang, Ting Huang, Zeyu Zhang, Haoyu Chen, Yanjie Zhu, Hao Tang
bullets: Addresses limited structured relational modeling in existing 3D vision-language methods.
Uses a Pyramid Vision Encoder, a language-model decoder with question-guided caption retrieval and visual cross-attention, and MSG-based relational descriptions.
Introduces City3D-9.6K, a multi-view urban vision-language dataset containing geometric observations, captions, and scene graphs.
On City-3DQA, reaches 88.35% sentence-wise and 64.79% city-wise top-1 accuracy, improving over 3D CoCa v2 by 20.88 and 3.57 percentage points.
Achieves the best performance on GeoEval3D, indicating strong urban spatial reasoning and geometric understanding.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of 3D CoCa v3. A multimodal decoder subsequently integrates question-relevant scene captions and projected visual features into a LoRA-adapted Qwen backbone for urban 3D question answering.

Figure 1. Comparison of 3D CoCa, 3D CoCa v2, and our 3D CoCa v3. Previous methods focus on indoor 3D scene understanding through contrastive learning, generative captioning, and testtime search. Our framework extends this paradigm to urban scenes with geometry-aware multi-view representations, MSG-based relational descriptions, and question-guided multimodal decoding.

(b) Multi-view scene graphs (MSG) associate shared entities and spatial relationships across viewpoints, providing structured context for scene-level caption generation.

papers.abstract: Massively multilingual translation models usually have one tag per language and no control over regional varieties, and they cover a region's smaller languages poorly or not at all. We report three fine-tunes of MADLAD-400-3B-MT, each adding target tags with low-rank adaptation (LoRA), back-translation of monolingual text and replay of the base model's own translations: for Spanish as written in Spain, for Latin American Spanish, and one model for three Romance languages of the Iberian Peninsula, Asturian ( ), Aragonese ( ) and Aranese ( ). For the Spanish varieties we annotate the 250.9M documents of MADLAD-400's Spanish split with a domain-supervised Spain vs. Latin America classifier and select variety text with a rule that admitted no Latin American document in a 340-document reference set. The Castilian model chooses Spain's everyday vocabulary in 97% of a targeted test (base model 62%) and vosotros for informal plural address in 70% (10%), while improving chrF++ on human references. A first finding is tag collapse: with a new tag initialised from , the parent tag drifts to the new variety (84-87% identical outputs). In the Iberian model, contrastive pairs and a separate learning rate for the tag embeddings keep each tag in its own language. Trained only on publicly available data, mostly the TAN-IBE Wikipedia corpora, the Iberian model matches or beats the TAN-IBE Marian systems in four of six Spanish directions on FLORES+, is 1.9 BLEU behind in Spanish->Aranese, and is second only to SalamandraTA-7B in most directions. The exception, Spanish->Aragonese, reflects a difference of written variety between Aragonese Wikipedia and the FLORES+ reference, not model quality. papers.abstract: In-Hand Object Scanning (IHOS) from monocular video captured by a commodity smartphone holds immense potential to democratize 3D digitization for non-expert users, facilitating applications in digital archiving, augmented reality, and custom fabrication. Yet, IHOS remains largely understudied due to a lack of realistic datasets and systematic benchmarks. To bridge this gap, we introduce ToysRUs, a high-quality dataset featuring diverse figurines captured by 4K Ultra High-Definition (UHD) monocular videos. Studying IHOS from first principles, we examine structure-from-motion (SfM) for camera pose estimation, which is key to IHOS. We identify two key challenges: small baselines between consecutive frames, and sparse feature matches across large-view, long-range frames, further exacerbated by dynamic hand occlusions. Guided by these insights, we propose performing SfM on video sub-sequences sampled at sufficient angular intervals, and iteratively stitches the corresponding sub-trajectories into a unified global trajectory. Furthermore, for high-fidelity surface reconstruction, we introduce occlusion-aware 2D Gaussian Splatting, which incorporates opacity rendering and omits the opacity loss on hand regions. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations demonstrate that our framework significantly outperforms existing approaches, including neural implicit representations and 3D foundation models, in both geometric accuracy and photometric fidelity.
authors: Di Wu, Jeeeun Kim, Shu Kong
bullets: Introduces ToysRUs, a high-quality 4K UHD monocular-video dataset of diverse figurines for in-hand object scanning.
Identifies small inter-frame baselines, sparse long-range matches, and dynamic hand occlusions as key challenges for structure-from-motion.
Estimates camera poses by running SfM on angularly spaced video subsequences and iteratively stitching their trajectories.
Uses occlusion-aware 2D Gaussian Splatting that models opacity while excluding hand regions from the opacity loss.
Reports better geometric accuracy and photometric fidelity than existing neural implicit and 3D foundation-model approaches.

figures.caption: Figure 9: Qualitative comparisons. We visualize the reconstruction results using splat mode, Gaussian centers, RGB rendering, and the final reconstructed surface mesh. Our full OA-2DGS pipeline (w/ A, W) effectively integrates opacity supervision with the hand occlusion mask, proving essential for extracting clean, high-fidelity object geometry under severe hand occlusions.

Nevertheless, this demonstrates that the reconstructed colored surfaces by our method serve as a base model for custom fabrication and 3D printing.

Figure 4: Flowchart of the proposed method. Given an RGB video, it segments and tracks the foreground object, background, and hand. Then, it performs SfM over subsequences of frames on the foreground object, resulting in multiple sub-trajectories of camera poses and point clouds (§4.2). Next, it stitches them into a global camera trajectory and a dense point cloud (§4.3, Fig. 5). Lastly, it applies occlusion-aware 2DGS to reconstruct a colored surface (§4.4).

Too small intervals such as 1 risk CamStitch with the notorious small baseline issue (Fig. 3); too large intervals (>8) yield too few feature matches to reliably run SfM, degrading the final performance. Nevertheless, CamStitch is resilient to a large range of sampling intervals.

Figure 8: Visual results with progressive modifications on SfM (Table 3). Naive SfM, operating on raw video frames, fails to recover camera poses. When focusing only on target objects, SfM improves but produces incomplete camera trajectories. CamStitch (a crucial component in Castoags) recovers the full camera trajectory and helps reconstruct high-quality mesh.

Figure 5: Stitching sub-trajectories and point clouds. Although a pair of inter-subsequence frames may have too few 2D feature matches, 2D feature matches from more inter-subsequence frames and intra-subsequence 2D-to-3D correspondences (derived from SfM) collectively produce sufficient amounts of 3D correspondences. With such, we compute a Sim3 transformation matrix between the two point sets, allowing to stitch sub-trajectories and point sets into a global trajectory and a dense cloud, respectively.

Figure 13: Qualitative results on OmniObject3D. We evaluate camera pose estimation (left) and surface reconstruction (right). We also provide quantitative results on camera pose estimation (see Table 7) and surface reconstruction (see Table 8).
Figure 14: Failure cases. Castoags reconstructs incomplete mesh surfaces under specific conditions: single-color textures, transparent materials, and smooth surfaces.

While Color-NeuS [72] achieves comparable visual quality, it requires ∼12 hours per object, which severely hinders its practical application in IHOS. In contrast, our approach delivers highly competitive visual fidelity in merely ∼20 minutes, demonstrating a massive leap in efficiency.

Figure 3: A dilemma in pose estimation on an IHOS video. (A): Leveraging dense frames suffers from the notorious small baseline issue [40, 58, 8, 5], yielding erroneous depth estimates and camera trajectory drift. (B): Sampling sparse frames ensures wide baseline but produces insufficient feature matches, causing unreliable pose estimation, early termination, and incomplete reconstruction.

papers.abstract: Reusing past experience in long-horizon tasks requires more than storing successful procedures: Language agents must distinguish which procedures apply and what work remains as execution progresses. We introduce MetaDecomp, an in-context meta-learning framework for adaptive task decomposition that jointly learns a task-relative state space and reusable procedures. Its outer loop builds procedural memory from successful training executions, representing task progress as abstract states and procedures between states as directed acyclic graphs of operations and dependencies. As new progress distinctions are learned, MetaDecomp revisits historical execution evidence to reassess state assignments and reorganize the procedures they support. With memory fixed at test time, the inner loop refines an initial decomposition and revises it from environmental feedback, combining applicable procedure fragments with task-specific steps missing from memory. Evaluated on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld over three seeds, MetaDecomp achieves the highest mean performance among the compared methods in four of five settings, for example, an 86.3% success rate on ALFWorld with Qwen3-4B. Fixing the initial schema or omitting historical reprojection reduces performance in component ablations. MetaDecomp also uses fewer inference tokens than ReAct and AutoRefine in all five settings. Cross-benchmark analysis identifies a low-performance area where partial coverage degrades success relative to hidden memory; high coverage improves success, while low coverage changes little. Code will be released upon acceptance.
authors: Ziyi Wang, Yixiao He, Yichen Wu, Ruite Lu, Jiayu Wang, Ying Wei

Evaluated on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, it achieves the highest mean performance in four of five settings and uses fewer inference tokens than ReAct and AutoRefine.
Partial procedural coverage can hurt performance relative to hidden memory; high coverage helps, while low coverage has little effect.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) have widely adopted diffusion-based action generation for continuous robot motions, enabling fine-grained control across diverse tasks. However, recent studies have shown that their performance is highly sensitive to initial noise, with resulting action errors that make recovery difficult during execution. Existing approaches search for favorable noise initializations to improve performance, yet the action expert itself remains sensitive to noise. In this work, we reveal that initial noise induces a consistent directional bias in action space that closely aligns with the noise's temporal mean. We thus introduce a simple yet effective framework that improves robustness to initial noise through interventions during both training and inference. During training, we enforce consistent action predictions from antithetic noise pairs $(\epsilon, -\epsilon)$ and, at inference, remove the noise's temporal mean. Our method substantially reduces action deviation and improves task performance across simulation benchmarks. In real-robot experiments, our method increases the average task success rate of $\pi_{0.5}$ from 40% to 68%, with more stable and consistent execution.
authors: Junmyeong Lee, Dongmin Shin, Wooseok Jeon, JunGyu Lee, Seunghyun Shin, Hae-Gon Jeon

papers.abstract: Barrier certificates provide formal safety guarantees for neural network controlled systems by ensuring that system trajectories avoid unsafe regions over time. However, after deployment, previously unseen obstacles or constraint changes may introduce new unsafe regions, invalidating the original certificate and potentially leading to unsafe behavior. We address this setting with adaptive piecewise barrier certificates, which preserve the original certificate and policy in unchanged regions while introducing localized updates around newly emerged unsafe regions. The central question is how to perform such updates efficiently during system execution without retraining from scratch. Our key idea is to cast deployment-time adaptation as a localized certificate repair problem and reduce it to an optimization task that leverages the learned structure of previous barrier certificates, enabling fast updates without global retraining. We further design a staged repair framework that progressively transitions from localized repair to joint policy-certificate updates and, when necessary, localized retraining. Empirical results on four benchmarks with five new obstacles show that our method succeeds in all cases and completes within tens of seconds on average, whereas retraining from scratch fails in most cases. On instances where retraining succeeds, our method is 17.3$\times$ faster on average. It incurs only 16.2% performance degradation relative to the original policy.
authors: Xiaoyang Lv, Peixin Wang, Jianhao Bai, Bai Xue, Min Zhang, Luke Ong
bullets: Addresses deployment-time safety failures caused by previously unseen obstacles or changed constraints.

Formulates local repair as an optimization problem informed by the existing certificate, with staged escalation to joint updates or localized retraining.
Across four benchmarks and five new obstacles, repair succeeded in all cases within tens of seconds on average, while retraining from scratch usually failed.
When retraining succeeded, the proposed method was 17.3× faster on average, with 16.2% performance degradation relative to the original policy.

papers.abstract: Video anomaly understanding (VAU) requires reasoning about event progression, interactions, and the contextual conditions that distinguish abnormal behavior from common activity across diverse scenes. Although video agents enable multi-round analysis, the predefined analytical operations may not adequately satisfy these diverse reasoning demands. In this paper, we present EvoVAU, a framework that evolves a reusable tool library for a frozen video solver. Guided by task outcomes and execution trajectories, an external proposer identifies potential limitations in the library and refines it, retaining task experience as analytical operations that can be reused across questions. Specifically, Cross-Version Contrastive Feedback guides tool refinement by combining current errors with paired execution trajectories from historical corrections and regressions. Adoption-Aware Selection accepts a candidate library only when overall development-set accuracy improves and corrections outnumber regressions among questions on which the solver invokes new or modified tools. Using a small development set, EvoVAU alternates tool refinement with candidate evaluation and selection. At test time, the evolved library remains fixed, with no further involvement from the proposer. Experiments on several VAU benchmarks demonstrate strong performance and the flexibility of the evolved library across anomaly domains.
authors: Benfeng Wang, Chao Huang, Yudong Cheng, Chengliang Liu, Wei Wang, Wenqi Ren
bullets: Targets VAU’s need to reason about event progression, interactions, and contextual abnormality across diverse scenes.
An external proposer identifies tool limitations and refines the library based on task outcomes and execution trajectories.
Cross-Version Contrastive Feedback uses current errors alongside historical correction and regression trajectories.
Adoption-Aware Selection keeps candidate libraries only when development accuracy improves and corrections exceed regressions for affected questions.
Experiments across several VAU benchmarks show strong performance and flexibility across anomaly domains; the abstract provides no quantitative results.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of EvoVAU. (a) Frozen Execution. The video solver answers VAU questions using the current tool library Tt, with its model parameters frozen. (b) Cross-Version Contrastive Feedback. Paired execution records from the preceding round provide historical corrections and regressions, complemented by current errors. (c) Tool Refinement. The external proposer refines the tool library to form Ct, retaining unchanged tools. (d) Adoption-Aware Selection. The candidate is evaluated on the full development set. A candidate is accepted only if overall accuracy improves and corrections outnumber regressions on questions where the solver attempts to use a new or modified tool (wrench). Blue–yellow pairs compare current and candidate answers to the same question; filled and hollow nodes indicate correct and incorrect answers. Node counts are illustrative.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) support robot control through visual prediction, but dense future modeling repeatedly encodes static context already available in the current observation, while action-relevant changes are often spatially sparse. We study sparse dynamic representation learning, retaining the current observation as a contextual anchor and using a small set of compact dynamic tokens to represent anticipated changes. We develop CompactWAM, a sparse-dense joint predictive framework that enables sparse representation learning within a video-supervised shared backbone, without requiring a reconstruction objective for the sparse pathway. Since a limited token budget alone does not specify which information to retain, we introduce Dynamic Forcing, which pairs direct action supervision with privileged dense future guidance to promote action relevance and dynamic fidelity. While action prediction gradients directly drive compact tokens to capture control-relevant cues, dense future guidance further shapes them via action functional guidance that matches sparse and dense contributions to the action expert, and dynamics-aware distribution matching, which aligns temporal relational changes relative to a static reference. At inference, a single visual forward pass encodes current observations and compact dynamic tokens for action generation, eliminating dense future modeling. CompactWAM achieves 98.4\% success on LIBERO and 77.9\% on LIBERO-Plus, retaining respective success rates of 98.3\% and 76.6\% with only 9.2\% of the dense future token budget. Evaluations on RoboTwin~2.0 and real-world manipulation further demonstrate the effectiveness of the learned sparse predictive representations.
authors: Ziqiang Li, Shisheng Chen, Yunnan Wang, Wenyao Zhang, Zili Lin, Yuyang Zhang, Xudong Yang, Fangzhuo Jin, Chenyu Zhou, Wenjun Zeng, Xin Jin
bullets: Addresses redundant encoding of static context and the spatial sparsity of action-relevant changes in world action models.
Retains the current observation as context while representing anticipated changes with a small set of dynamic tokens.
Introduces Dynamic Forcing: action supervision plus action-functional and dynamics-aware guidance from dense future representations.
Achieves 98.4% success on LIBERO and 77.9% on LIBERO-Plus, while using only 9.2% of the dense future token budget with minimal reported performance loss.
Additional evaluations on RoboTwin 2.0 and real-world manipulation support the effectiveness of the sparse representations.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) unify future video prediction and action generation for robotic control, but their reliance on iterative denoising incurs substantial inference costs. Distilling these models into few-step generators offers a promising route to efficient deployment, yet maintaining task performance under aggressive step reduction remains challenging. Existing methods rely on point-wise trajectory consistency distillation, which pursues high visual fidelity while leaving downstream action information unexploited in optimizing video generation, and also lacks explicit distribution-level alignment. To address this, we propose DriftWAM, a few-step WAM distillation framework that incorporates the actions induced by predicted videos into video learning. Specifically, DriftWAM integrates action-aware video drifting, which performs video distribution matching through a joint visual--action similarity kernel to steer sample evolution under the guidance of these induced actions, with action-guided video regularization, which leverages the compatible teacher--student matches identified by the joint kernel to backpropagate action-level gradients directly into the video generator. Evaluations on the RoboTwin 2.0 and LIBERO benchmarks, as well as in real-world robotic manipulation tasks, show that DriftWAM consistently outperforms prior consistency distillation methods across few-step settings at the same inference speed.
authors: Minyang Li, Siyu Xu, Yunke Wang, Ying-Cong Chen, Chang Xu, Daochang Liu
bullets: WAMs are costly at inference because they require iterative denoising, while aggressive step reduction can hurt task performance.

Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and real robotic manipulation tasks show consistent gains over prior consistency-distillation methods at matched inference speed.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Training Overview of the video branch in DriftWAM. On the left, the teacher generates reference video–action pairs offline, while the student produces video candidates under the same context c. Sharing the same frozen parameters, the teacher in the middle extracts visual features and computes action responses for both student and teacher videos. The resulting visual and action-response distances feed the joint kernel, whose attraction and repulsion weights determine the targets for LV drift in the upper branch. In parallel, the lower branch uses the same kernel to select student–teacher pairs for LV reg, which aligns the paired videos’ action responses and directly backpropagates action-level gradients to the video generator.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) renders photorealistic novel views in real time, but its per-scene training (optimization) remains slow. Recent fast training methods such as FastGS shorten training to a few minutes by reducing the number of Gaussians. Profiling FastGS, we find two costs that remain even in its compact model. First, rasterization is still the largest cost, and redundant work remains in it. Second, the loss computation does not shrink with the number of Gaussians, so its share of the training time grows as the model becomes compact. We present SprintGS, a training framework built on FastGS that keeps the model compact and reduces both costs. For rasterization, scheduled tile culling limits each Gaussian to the tiles where it matters, using a coarse footprint that is annealed to the exact one before training ends; convergence-aware pruning removes converged, nearly transparent Gaussians; and a shuffle-efficient backward pass reduces the data exchanged between GPU threads. For the loss, a fused loss computes the loss and its image gradient in the forward pass without a loss map, removing most of its cost. SprintGS trains 2.15x faster than FastGS at comparable quality, and 1.81x faster in its high-quality setting. It also accelerates other fast training methods and dynamic, sparse-view, and surface reconstruction.
authors: Ryosuke Watanabe, Tomoaki Konno
bullets: Targets remaining bottlenecks in fast 3DGS training: rasterization and loss computation.
Uses scheduled tile culling, convergence-aware pruning, and a shuffle-efficient backward pass to reduce rasterization overhead.
Introduces a fused loss that computes the loss and image gradient during the forward pass without constructing a loss map.
Trains 2.15× faster than FastGS at comparable quality and 1.81× faster in its high-quality setting.
Also accelerates dynamic, sparse-view, surface-reconstruction, and other fast-training settings.

papers.abstract: Self-improvement is now a practical recipe for embodied policies: a policy collects experience, is retrained, and is kept when a judge rates it higher. However, the judge is usually trained or chosen inside the same loop, so its evidence is not independent of the policy. We introduce SealedLoop, an evaluation framework that adds a sealed judge: an evaluator outside the loop that the improver cannot see or optimize against. A new policy is kept only when a sequential test on the sealed judge confirms the gain, with a bounded probability of keeping a worse one. Running the same loop under each judge, we separate two sources of a false gain, which we call judge error (the loop's judge is wrong on its own data) and transfer gap (a real gain there does not carry over to unseen conditions). We evaluate on LIBERO manipulation, NAVSIM driving, and a full-scale real vehicle. In manipulation, a success classifier accepted 65 of 196 failures in one generation. In driving, policies that gain on the loop's own frames lose in an unseen city, so even an exact in-loop judge would keep 8/15 of them. When the sealed test decides, a driving loop built to improve ends with a better policy than under its own critic (0.674 against 0.649 PDMS, from 0.638), and on driving pairs with known sealed gain the test accepted 11 of 12 real gains and none of 59 losses. In a real-world field experiment on a published improvement step, the reinforced version drove further into a curve than the version it started from in all 6 blind pairs, though neither completed it. These results show that evidence from inside the loop, however accurate, is not enough to decide whether a policy has improved. SealedLoop offers a foundation for trustworthy self-improvement of embodied policies, in which progress is judged by evidence the improving system cannot influence.
authors: Zilin Huang, Zhengyang Wan, Kangan Qian, Zihao Sheng, Sikai Chen
bullets: Self-improving embodied-policy loops can mistakenly keep worse policies because their judges are trained or evaluated within the same loop.

A real-world field test showed the improved policy drove farther into a curve in all 6 blind pairs, although neither policy completed the curve.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed in Japanese-language settings, yet multimodal safety evaluation has been largely English-centric. We extend the Multimodal Safety Test Suite (MSTS) of R\"ottger et al. (2025) to Japanese as the 12th language, contributing 320 machine-translated and post-edited cases with reference answers plus 82 culturally localized Japanese images. We introduce an evaluation framework that (i) extends MSTS's 3-class safety grouping with a 5-point scale that also rewards useful (not just safe) responses, and (ii) separates image recognition from safety judgment to isolate recognition errors. Using this framework, we evaluate five modern Japanese VLMs (Gemini-3-Flash, GPT-5, InternVL3, LLM-JP-4-VL, Qwen3-VL) against human evaluation, and find substantial variance in the safety readiness across the models. Finally, we evaluate two LLM-as-a-Judge models and find that providing a reference answer improves agreement with human safety judgments, though recall for detecting unsafe responses remains limited, underscoring the difficulty of automating multimodal safety evaluation. The dataset created for our study will be released upon publication.
authors: Su Myat Noe, Hisami Suzuki, Kouta Nakayama, Naoaki Okazaki
bullets: Addresses the English-centric nature of existing multimodal safety evaluations for Japanese-language VLM deployment.
Adds 320 translated and post-edited cases with reference answers and 82 culturally localized Japanese images to MSTS.
Uses a 5-point scale rewarding both safety and helpfulness, while separating image recognition from safety judgment.
Evaluates five Japanese VLMs against human judgments and finds substantial differences in safety readiness.
Reference answers improve LLM-as-a-Judge agreement with humans, but unsafe-response recall remains limited.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned video world models generate future observations from an initial frame and a camera trajectory, but often fail to align camera commands with visual dynamics or represent full 6-DoF scene transformations. We present DuoWM, a first-person drone video world model with two complementary visual conditions. Action flow projects future camera positions and orientations into each target frame, while Object flow forward-warps the initial observation and overlays local 6-DoF transformations to ground the induced scene motion. We further introduce transform-aware pretraining, which pairs object appearance with explicit transformation axes before standard RGB video training. On Sekai-drone dataset, DuoWM achieves the best results across video quality, 3D consistency, and trajectory following. Compared with Captain Safari, the state-of-the-art method, our approach reduces real-domain FVD and LPIPS by 17.2\% and 21.6\%, respectively, while improving game-domain AUC@30 from 0.5003 to 0.5719 and AUC@15 from 0.3088 to 0.3747.
authors: Zixuan Li, Kangyao Huang, Meng Xu, Wan Tian, Xiaoyu Tang, Jinge Sun, Yingliang Yao, He Chen, Lingzhong Meng, Yunzhi Xue, Jingyu Chen
bullets: Targets poor alignment between camera commands, visual dynamics, and full 6-DoF scene transformations.
Uses Action flow to project future camera poses into target frames and Object flow to warp the initial view with local 6-DoF motion.
Introduces transform-aware pretraining that associates object appearance with explicit transformation axes before RGB video training.
On the Sekai-drone dataset, achieves the best reported video quality, 3D consistency, and trajectory-following results.
Relative to Captain Safari, reduces real-domain FVD and LPIPS by 17.2% and 21.6%, and improves game-domain AUC@30 and AUC@15.

papers.abstract: Diagnosis of congenital heart disease (CHD) requires understanding the spatial relationships between cardiac structures, which clinicians assess by scrolling through CT or cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) slices and rotating 3D reconstructions. Although automated methods have advanced cardiac segmentation, identifying congenital heart defects from volumetric scans remains an open challenge. The two existing approaches rely on handcrafted diagnostic rules limited to static anatomical abnormalities. We introduce CHD-Bench, the first benchmark for interactive CHD diagnosis, defining a multi-label task and evaluation protocol over 247 CT and MRI scans from three cohorts covering 38 CHD types. We also present CHD-Harness, open-source software that runs a VLM in a 3D Slicer environment through 22 tools, manages each examination, and records the resulting diagnosis and supporting views. We evaluate off-the-shelf medical, open weight, and closed weight VLMs and compare them with a 3D CNN classifier and published rule-based results. Gemini 4 Argon with CHD-Harness achieves the highest macro F1 across all three cohorts (0.63, 0.63, and 0.43). Allowing for interactive examination raises its macro F1 by up to 20 points over static views. These results establish CHD-Bench and CHD-Harness as a foundation for developing and evaluating VLMs for interactive CHD diagnosis.
authors: Gautham Krishnan P, Shrisharanyan Vasu, Aniketh Vijesh, Rajagopalan Rameshbabu, Harikrishnan Anil Maya, Sarin Xavier, Mahesh Kappanayil, Gilad Gressel
bullets: Introduces a multi-label interactive CHD diagnosis benchmark spanning 247 CT/MRI scans, three cohorts, and 38 CHD types.
Provides CHD-Harness, open-source software connecting VLMs to 3D Slicer through 22 examination tools and recording diagnostic evidence.
Compares medical, open-weight, and closed-weight VLMs with a 3D CNN and rule-based methods.
Gemini 4 Argon with CHD-Harness achieves the highest reported macro F1 across cohorts: 0.63, 0.63, and 0.43.
Interactive examination improves macro F1 by up to 20 points over static views; broader clinical generalization remains outside the reported scope.

papers.abstract: Human takeovers offer corrective supervision for vision-language-action (VLA) policies, but their contribution to offline post-training must be separated from that of continued optimization. We introduce FailPoint-X, a benchmark for offline VLA post-training with human takeovers. To represent uncertainty in failure onset, an annotator marks an interval for each failure, and training takeovers start at seeded frames sampled within it. From one fixed $\pi_{0.5}$ checkpoint, which also initializes post-training, we assemble 629 natural failures across 10 LIBERO-X task families at up to five difficulty levels. All 2,823 takeover attempts are logged; 2,400 are accepted recoveries, of which 2,320 are used for post-training. Evaluation restarts every method from the fixed midpoints of 384 held-out failure intervals. Under matched actor-update counts, we compare behavior cloning of recoveries, value-based offline learning on recoveries and failed rollouts, and continued training on existing demonstrations. Within 1,200 steps on the 240 L1-L3 held-out failures, cloning improves recovery by 29.4 percentage points (pp) over the demonstration-only control; the value-based learner does not establish a further gain (1.5 pp). In exploratory evaluation from L1-L5 nominal starts at the same horizon, cloning loses 30.0 pp of success relative to the base policy; mixing in demonstrations reduces the loss to 16.5 pp, a reduction that shrinks under a stricter, pre-specified horizon. Restorable failure states and a shared evaluator let all methods be compared from identical starts.
authors: Zirui Li, Yujie Yan, Jingxuan Qian, Yangang Ren, Haizhou Yin, Haoran Xu, Chen Lv

Annotates failure-onset intervals and samples takeover starts within them to capture onset uncertainty.
Builds a benchmark from one fixed mid-training checkpoint with 629 natural failures, 2,823 takeover attempts, and 2,320 training recoveries across 10 task families.
With matched update counts, recovery behavior cloning improves held-out L1-L3 failure recovery by 29.4 percentage points within 1,200 steps; value-based learning adds no further established gain.
On nominal L1-L5 starts, cloning reduces success by 30.0 percentage points, while mixing demonstrations limits the loss to 16.5 points; effects shrink under a stricter horizon.

papers.abstract: Optimizing indoor climate systems plays a critical role in achieving the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals 11 and 13. However, indoor delayed thermodynamic responses and partial observability severely hinder existing reinforcement learning (RL) methods, which are primarily limited by implicit thermal inertia, occupancy dynamic prediction, and cumulative prediction errors during long-horizon rollouts. Thus, we propose a novel occupant-centric indoor climate control framework. It develops indoor environmental world models to predict future physical thermal baselines and dynamic occupancy, explicitly capturing latent thermal inertia. By formulating adaptive regulation as counterfactual advantage learning against future environments via a Branching Dueling Q-Network, and integrating a Held-Action TD-{\lambda} target, it effectively mitigates delayed credit assignment. Additionally, a proposed physics-aligned smoothness regularization suppresses high-frequency actuator fluctuations, potentially extending equipment service life. Experiments on SemiBuildingSim and Sinergym demonstrate that our method achieves a superior multi-objective trade-off. Compared to the best-performing methods, it further reduces energy consumption by 11.2%, occupant discomfort by 44.2%, and action fluctuation by 47.3%, achieving better sample efficiency and cross-region effectiveness. This interdisciplinary study offers an energy-efficient, occupant-centric AI solution for control science, building science, and energy sustainability.
authors: Xu Yang, Kailai Sun, Dianyu Zhong, Irfan Qaisar, Yu Yang, Qianchuan Zhao, Jian Kang
bullets: Addresses delayed thermal responses, partial observability, occupancy dynamics, and long-horizon prediction errors in indoor climate control.
Builds world models for future thermal baselines and dynamic occupancy while explicitly modeling latent thermal inertia.
Uses counterfactual advantage learning with a Branching Dueling Q-Network and Held-Action TD-λ targets to improve delayed credit assignment.
Adds physics-aligned smoothness regularization to suppress high-frequency actuator changes.

In SemiBuildingSim and Sinergym, reports reductions of 11.2% in energy consumption, 44.2% in discomfort, and 47.3% in action fluctuation, with improved sample efficiency and cross-region effectiveness.

papers.abstract: Wearable assistants must localize interface elements from camera observations when direct screenshot access is unavailable, yet existing GUI grounding benchmarks primarily evaluate native screenshots. We introduce GlassGround, a new benchmark that pairs native screenshots with wearable camera observations while holding GUI states, instructions, and targets fixed. GlassGround contains 3,250 tasks across Android and iOS, captured using four wearable devices under four viewing conditions. Across ten open-source models, mean grounding accuracy drops from 94.8% on screenshots to 48.5% on camera images. Further analysis reveals that changes in target scale, screen geometry, and background cannot fully explain this performance degradation. We then study two ways to narrow this gap. At inference time, local zooming and screen rectification help but leave most of the gap. For training-time adaptation, we build on GlassGround's paired-view design and introduce PairDistill, a baseline that aligns target representations across views alongside coordinate supervision. Trained on independently collected data and using no screenshots at inference, it improves camera-image accuracy by 9.4 and 12.2 points on two backbones and transfers to unseen devices and operating systems. Combined with local zooming, it reaches 69.6% and 64.4%, but does not close the gap. The GlassGround dataset and code are available at https://github.com/yunnw/GlassGround.
authors: Yun Wang, Siyue Sun, Jiaying Du, Xinyi Wei, Xiaoming Zhai, Zhenlin An, Ninghao Liu
bullets: Introduces a benchmark pairing identical GUI states, instructions, and targets across screenshots and wearable-camera observations.
Covers 3,250 Android and iOS tasks captured with four wearable devices under four viewing conditions.
Across ten open-source models, mean accuracy falls from 94.8% on screenshots to 48.5% on camera images.
Presents PairDistill, which aligns target representations across views during training without requiring screenshots at inference.
PairDistill improves camera-image accuracy by 9.4 and 12.2 points on two backbones; combined with local zooming, it reaches 69.6% and 64.4%, but the gap remains substantial.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the GlassGround benchmark construction. (a) Each benchmark unit pairs a native screenshot (Clean) with an egocentric observation (Physical) of the same GUI state, instruction, and target. (b) Physical displays are captured with four headworn devices under four viewing conditions. (c) Tasks are constructed on clean screenshots using candidate discovery, VLM-based task proposals, and full human verification. papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made substantial progress in visual reasoning, but extended generation over large visual contexts remains computationally expensive. During autoregressive decoding, visual attention is recomputed for every generated token, even when consecutive tokens rely on similar visual evidence. We introduce VAPOR (Visual Attention Persistence with On-demand Refresh), a training-free framework that reduces this redundancy by reusing visual attention outputs across decoding steps and refreshing them when needed. VAPOR caches the visual attention output while continuing to update textual attention at every step, helping reduce visual grounding drift during extended reasoning. To decide when to reuse cached outputs, VAPOR estimates visual attention mass using a low-rank approximation. It also uses prefill-based attention consistency and cache age to make independent Persist and Refresh decisions for each attention head. VAPOR retains the full visual key-value (KV) cache, so all visual tokens remain available when new evidence is needed. Experiments on eight image and four video reasoning benchmarks across two MLLM families show that VAPOR improves accuracy over dense attention on nearly all benchmarks while achieving 1.11-1.21x decoding speedups. Compared with the strongest state-of-the-art acceleration baseline in each setting, VAPOR further improves accuracy by 0.35-2.15 percentage points while achieving comparable or lower decoding latency. Our code is available at https://github.com/Su-my/VAPOR.
authors: Mingyu Su, Wei Wu, Erle Zhu, Chengxing Xie, Deyao Hong, Hongning Wang
bullets: Targets the high cost of recomputing visual attention for every generated token in long visual-context reasoning.

Retains the full visual KV cache so all visual tokens remain accessible when new evidence is needed.
Across image and video benchmarks, improves accuracy over dense attention while delivering 1.11–1.21× decoding speedups.

papers.abstract: World models predict what happens under an action, but choosing between actions requires comparing their outcomes in the same physical situation. Factual transitions alone determine action-wise marginal futures and average effects, but not individual effects or the probability that switching actions causes harm. We introduce WhatIf, a counterfactual world model for manipulation that couples candidate futures through shared latent physics and transition noise inferred from factual history. Each candidate action induces a sparse object-factor causal graph describing the physical pathways it activates. Rolling out these graphs under the shared situation anchors predictions to observed outcomes and confines action contrasts to the objects each action reaches. Shared type-conditioned functions support varying numbers of objects, while a round-trip loss enforces action-invariant abduction without counterfactual labels. We show that replacing an individual effect with its conditional mean incurs mean-squared error equal to its conditional variance, motivating comparisons between coupled futures. Building on these comparisons, Counterfactual Advantage Planning (CAP) ranks plans by their advantage over an incumbent within shared situations and constrains the probability of harm. Paired advantages reduce estimator variance by a factor of $1-\rho$, where $\rho$ is the correlation between branch outcomes, and cancel model errors shared by both branches. Each executed transition provides hindsight advantages to update the physics posterior, the next plan, and an amortized policy without a learned critic. We further establish when observational transitions identify interventional dynamics. Paired simulator interventions evaluate counterfactual accuracy, graph recovery, compositional generalization, and decision quality.
authors: Xu Yang, Kailai Sun, Qianchuan Zhao
bullets: Factual transitions alone cannot estimate individual action effects or the risk that switching actions causes harm.

Counterfactual Advantage Planning ranks plans against an incumbent, controls harm probability, reduces variance through paired advantages, and updates from executed transitions without a learned critic.
Paired simulator interventions assess counterfactual accuracy, graph recovery, compositional generalization, decision quality, and conditions for identifying interventional dynamics.

papers.abstract: Code-as-Policy agents generate, execute, and revise robot programs, but often lack explicit mechanisms to govern what persists across executions: which actions are retained within a trial and which code modifications carry over to subsequent runs. This leaves two critical aspects of agent behavior insufficiently controlled: step-level execution and cross-run adaptation. We present RegHarness, a two-level harness that governs both forms of persistence for the RATs agent team, without relying on a vision-language-action (VLA) policy or demonstrations. Within each trial, run-time governance evaluates each proposed step from a reset scene, replaying the committed steps, while a fixed-rule controller commits the step only when both RATs' verifier and a task-long LLM auditor approve it. Between runs, a coding agent uses logged failures to develop and test revisions to skills, primitives, and rules, which remain disabled by default until explicitly enabled by the authors. Using a single low-cost model across all run-time roles, RegHarness achieves an 87.8% success rate (158/180) on paired LIBERO-PRO trials, compared with 39.4% for RATs, and a 72.0% success rate on MolmoSpaces trials. A $2\times2$ ablation study of RegHarness's two levels shows that its skill refinement alone increases RATs' successful trials from 71 to 135, whereas run-time governance alone achieves 105 and RATs' native stepwise reset-and-replay mode achieves only 46. These findings suggest that, for Code-as-Policy agents operating with low-cost models, task success depends not only on how generated programs are executed, but also on the quality of the reusable skills they invoke and how those skills evolve across runs.
authors: Shengming Liu, Yunyi Gao, Xinyi Wang, Jianyong Sun, Shuai Wang, Yi Deng, Li Chenye, Mingcai Zhou, Sim Kuan Goh

papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and LLM based agents have expanded the capabilities of AI glasses, enabling egocentric visual question answering, memory retrieval, and proactive assistance. These applications involve diverse inputs, including speech, images, and video, and range from simple device control to complex visual reasoning, posing challenges for efficient computation and communication. While video centric capabilities have received considerable attention, simple text based and device executable tasks remain underexplored despite their prevalence in daily interactions. Efficiently supporting diverse workloads within a unified assistant remains an open challenge. We propose JOVE ICE, an intent guided cloud, edge, and device collaborative framework that routes requests among AI glasses, a paired smartphone, and cloud servers according to user intent. JOVE ICE integrates hierarchical intent classification with dynamic subagent orchestration to select efficient execution paths and flexibly incorporate new applications through specialized subagents. Analysis of real world AI glasses requests reveals that simple device control tasks account for over 30% of interactions, which JOVE ICE handles directly on device to avoid unnecessary cloud computation and costs. Evaluations on three public benchmarks demonstrate that JOVE ICE reduces time to first token by approximately 13% and token usage by over 11% compared with conventional device and cloud architectures, while maintaining task quality. These results demonstrate the potential of intent guided collaboration to improve the efficiency and scalability of AI glasses.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in world models for game interaction and control have increased the demand for large-scale gameplay videos paired with camera trajectories. However, capturing synchronized camera trajectories often requires game-specific pipelines, limiting scalability. We therefore propose GameWeaver, a unified diffusion framework that automatically produces paired video--camera data through three complementary tasks: camera pose estimation from observed video, video generation along a prescribed camera trajectory, and joint video--camera generation from a reference image and text. First, each tipxel stores the normalized 3D coordinates of a pixel ray's endpoint in a reference coordinate frame. The resulting three-channel tipxel fields and RGB frames share the pretrained video model's VAE. Next, a fully trainable dual-stream Transformer exchanges appearance and geometry features through bidirectional gated attention and conditions both streams on shared text features. Finally, deterministic fitting recovers camera intrinsics and normalized trajectories from generated tipxel fields. In our evaluation tasks, GameWeaver achieves a normalized translation MSE of 0.0029 for camera control; for joint generation, it scores 85.48 out of 100 on instruction adherence versus 64.71 for the best cascade on that metric, validating the feasibility of the proposed approach.
authors: Lifan Jiang, Yifan Huang, Jixuan Zhang, Peifeng Wang, Yuying Ma, Dehai Zhao, Deng Cai, Boxi Wu

Reports 0.0029 normalized translation MSE for camera control and 85.48/100 instruction adherence for joint generation, compared with 64.71 for the best cascade.

papers.abstract: Judging open-world robot manipulation is hard because layouts, articulated fixtures, and valid goal configurations vary widely. On RoboCasa365, simulator predicates agree with human judgments on only 69.09\% of rollouts, and a frontier VLM judge on 86.12\%. We present \textbf{PROVE} (Predict-to-Specify, Observe-to-Verify), which first specifies what success should look like and then checks the outcome. PROVE refines success conditions from the instruction, the initial scene, a target-object reference image, and a generated goal image. The goal image only sharpens the conditions and never serves as evidence. On 6,500 human-annotated rollouts over 65 atomic actions, PROVE reaches \textbf{96.83\%} agreement. Applied to open-source policies, it reports far lower success than native checks and changes their ranking. To reduce evaluation overhead in policy learning, we distill PROVE into \textbf{PROVE-Lite}, a 4B evaluator that needs no reference images. In one forward pass, PROVE-Lite predicts the outcome and the terminal state of each task condition. It reaches \textbf{91.20\%} agreement while running about 38$\times$ faster than PROVE. Mapped to a severity-aware reward, its diagnoses improve PPO post-training over both simulator and binary rewards.
authors: Bowen Lyu, Yunan Liu, Liaoyuan Fan, Qinchuan Cheng, Jiafei Duan, Cheston Tan, Shijie Li

PROVE uses the instruction, initial scene, target-object image, and generated goal image to refine success conditions; the goal image is not used as evidence.
On 6,500 human-annotated rollouts spanning 65 atomic actions, PROVE achieves 96.83% agreement with humans.
PROVE-Lite distills the approach into a reference-image-free 4B evaluator, reaching 91.20% agreement and running about 38× faster.
Severity-aware diagnoses from PROVE-Lite improve PPO post-training over simulator and binary rewards.
