papers.abstract: Scaling robot demonstration datasets requires collection systems that accommodate more participants and diverse tasks, yet teleoperation barriers and task-adaptation effort limit this expansion. We present RoboJackVR, a standalone virtual reality (VR) game in which players manipulate simulated robots to execute combat skills and contribute demonstrations. MuJoCo simulation and demonstration recording run locally on the headset, removing the need for an external PC or simulation server during collection. Tutorials, skill selection, combat consequences, and character progression organize repeated task attempts within a continuing game. Task contracts declare assets, controls, resets, success criteria, and recording semantics; separate game configurations specify guidance, attempt groups, skill effects, and course placement. Shared bindings connect these declarations to task execution, outcome handling, and recording, allowing tasks to reuse the game flow while retaining their control and success semantics. Batch tools package supported resources and generate configurations, with manual adaptation and review for new interfaces and unsupported predicates. We instantiate the approach with SO101-Nexus-derived and LIBERO tasks. On the 66 LIBERO-90 tasks covered by the collected data, ACT policies trained solely on VR demonstrations retain approximately 91% of the full-standard simulation-demonstration baseline's success rate on held-out initial states, averaged over four training seeds. These results support the utility of play-collected VR demonstrations for policy learning in this setting.

bullets: Addresses teleoperation barriers and the effort required to adapt data collection across diverse robot tasks.
Runs MuJoCo simulation and demonstration recording locally on a VR headset, without an external PC or server.

Introduces reusable task contracts and game configurations, with batch tooling for packaging resources and generating configurations.

On 66 covered LIBERO-90 tasks, ACT policies trained only on VR demonstrations achieved approximately 91% of the full-standard simulation-demonstration baseline’s success rate on held-out initial states, averaged over four seeds.

papers.abstract: A cart can follow its reference trajectory while its cargo floats above the deck. Asset4D-Bench tests whether coding agents recover objects, motion and interactions from visual references as editable Blender scenes. Its 114 conditions span image editing, video reconstruction with matched full or partial starter assets, and independently selected from-scratch tasks. We independently reopen projects and measure them against native reference states. The 228 archived scores include original delivery outcomes and versioned measures of scene quality. On 24 from-scratch tasks, each model earns full dynamics credit on 14. Of these, three GPT-6.1-Sol and eight GPT-6-Astra reconstructions earn zero relation points. Under the fixed scoring weights, relations contribute 5.15 points to the 6.50-point Sol-minus-Astra difference in mean recovered fidelity. Differences in execution and recovery policy across archived runs preclude a causal estimate of starter-asset effects.

Relation errors accounted for most of the reported mean-fidelity gap between GPT-6.1-Sol and GPT-6-Astra under the fixed scoring weights.

papers.abstract: Cultural alignment requires large language models (LLMs) to infer often-implicit social norms from a scenario and its cultural context. Existing approaches typically adapt individual models or supply external cultural knowledge, while learning norm inference independently of downstream response generation remains underexplored. We introduce NORMCRAFT, a modular framework that decouples norm inference from response generation. Through norm-centric multi-view supervision, we train an LLM as a norm generator to recover shared norms from prospective, adherence, and violation scenarios without downstream response labels. The generated norms guide a separate, frozen LLM (the responder). With Qwen3.5-4B as the responder, NORMCRAFT outperforms prompting and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) baselines on four of five downstream metrics. On SafeWorld, its responses reflect the reference norms more often (Coverage) and more precisely (Faithfulness), exceeding Responder SFT by 18.0 and 14.1 percentage points, respectively. Direct norm evaluation also shows higher norm quality than the base and few-shot generators. The same trained generator improves cultural alignment on SafeWorld across fourteen frozen LLMs spanning five families and 0.8B to 27B parameters, with the largest gains for the smallest models.
authors: Tangyuan Zhang, Zhuang Li, Fatemeh Shiri, Xiangyu Zhao, Junyu Yan, Xiuzhen Zhang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of inferring culturally appropriate norms without relying on downstream response labels.
Trains a norm generator with multi-view supervision from prospective, adherence, and violation scenarios.
Uses generated norms to guide a separate, frozen responder LLM.
With Qwen3.5-4B, outperforms prompting and SFT baselines on four of five downstream metrics, including higher norm coverage and faithfulness on SafeWorld.
The generator transfers across 14 frozen LLMs from five families and 0.8B–27B parameters, with largest gains for smaller models.

papers.abstract: Visual language models (VLMs) have demonstrated exceptional capabilities across various multimodal tasks, but they remain susceptible to hallucinations, undermining their reliability. Existing hallucination benchmarks primarily focus on identifying hallucinations and describing their manifestations, often neglecting their underlying causes. Specifically, multimodal hallucinations can stem from two distinct failure modes: text modality bias (TMB), reflecting an over-reliance on misleading text input; and language prior (LP), reflecting a reliance on previously learned knowledge. To differentiate these failure modes, we propose VTK-Bench, a benchmark that explicitly separates three information sources: visual information (V), textual information (T), and prior knowledge (K). By establishing mutually exclusive answers corresponding to V, T, and K, VTK-Bench enables fine-grained attribution analysis of model responses. Furthermore, we introduce discrete attribution and soft attribution metrics to characterize information source preferences. Extensive experiments on 11 representative open-source VLMs show that LP is more prevalent than TMB in most evaluated models. Notably, TMB decreases substantially with model scaling, whereas LP exhibits relatively limited improvement and remains the dominant failure mode. These findings highlight the importance of different information source preferences for a deeper understanding of multimodal hallucinations.
authors: Yao Lu, Yuhang Zheng, Yaxin Gao, Zhe Tang, Zhaowei Zhu, Jiaheng Wei, Yunhao Wang, Shanqing Yu, Qi Xuan
bullets: Separates three information sources: visual input (V), textual input (T), and prior knowledge (K).
Uses mutually exclusive answers to attribute model responses to V, T, or K.
Introduces discrete and soft attribution metrics for measuring information-source preferences.
Evaluates 11 open-source VLMs and finds language-prior errors more prevalent than text-modality bias.
Model scaling substantially reduces text bias but yields limited improvement against language-prior failures.

papers.abstract: Nowadays, robots need to be retrained whenever their operating environment changes, and this prohibitive training cost keeps them far from daily use. The community is calling for innovations that bestow on a robot the ability to safely grasp different objects under different conditions without excessive training data and computing power. In response to this call, we present a general-purpose manipulator mission-planning framework, allowing a robot to safely perform manipulation tasks, such as grasping objects that fit in its gripper, across different operating environments without retraining its controllers. The framework rests on two innovations: a finite-state abstracted model, bisimilar to the original system dynamics, that describes accessibility of the space in front of the robot under its given arm and gripper, and a block-conservative specification generation method that turns each manipulation task under any specific operational environment into specifications about state accessibility of the abstracted model. A task proven feasible and safe on the abstracted model is guaranteed to be safe and achievable by the robot. Real-world case studies conducted on a Unitree G1 U1 humanoid show that manipulation tasks commonly encountered in daily life, such as grasping an object, pressing an elevator button or picking up a berry, can be handled within this framework, where an abstracted model of the G1 U1 robot is built only once to avoid costly model reconstructions, and different tasks are simply captured by specific block-conservative specifications, achievable by a generic mission planner with vision-based feedback control.
authors: Mingkang Long, Rong Su, Luhang Hong, Qingqing Wang, Ruochen Tai

Builds a finite-state abstraction of the robot’s accessible workspace that is bisimilar to its original dynamics.
Generates task- and environment-specific, block-conservative accessibility specifications for the abstracted model.
Provides safety and feasibility guarantees: successful abstract-model plans are safe and achievable by the robot.
Real-world demonstrations on a Unitree G1 U1 humanoid include grasping objects, pressing elevator buttons, and picking berries using vision-based feedback.

papers.abstract: Hybrid simulators embed learnable components such as neural networks in physical solvers and train them on reference trajectories. Many scientific solvers feature hard switches, such as a tripping power line, an igniting grid cell, or depolarizing brain tissue, where the loss exhibits discrete jumps across switch flips, leaving standard automatic differentiation to capture only its smooth part. Existing training paradigms face a fundamentally challenging trade-off, as gradient-based relaxations smooth the switches and introduce bias across jumps, whereas derivative-free methods treat the solver as a black box and discard path gradients of the continuous dynamics. Here we introduce EventFlip, which flips a near-threshold switch from a stored state, replays the original solver, and measures the loss difference between the two runs, in effect a finite difference across the switch. By perturbing every threshold with small Gaussian noise, we cast each switch as a stochastic binary decision and derive an unbiased gradient estimator that combines the continuous path gradient with a jump term constructed from these counterfactual rollouts. EventFlip-Rand optimizes this noise-averaged objective, whereas EventFlip-Hard operates on the deterministic hard-switch simulator used at deployment and provably targets the complete discontinuous loss. Under an identical forward evaluation budget, we benchmark EventFlip against twelve baselines across a power-grid cascade, a detonation wave, and cortical spreading depolarization, achieving the lowest error on every task and reducing the strongest baseline's error by factors of 1.5, 1.4, and 1.4, respectively.
authors: Tianrun Gao, Ruiqi Feng, Haomin Wen, Tailin Wu, Liangqiong Qu, Xiaomeng Huang, Ruiqi Shu
bullets: Hard switches create discontinuous losses that standard automatic differentiation misses.
EventFlip flips near-threshold events, replays the solver, and measures counterfactual loss differences.
Gaussian threshold noise enables an unbiased gradient estimator combining continuous and jump terms.
EventFlip-Rand optimizes a noise-averaged objective; EventFlip-Hard targets the deployed deterministic simulator.
Across three scientific tasks and matched forward budgets, EventFlip achieved the lowest reported error against twelve baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of EventFlip. (a) The hard loss exhibits discrete jumps across switch flips, whereas standard automatic differentiation captures only the smooth part. (b) The base trajectory (blue) and the flip branch (orange) share an identical rollout prefix before diverging at a sampled near-threshold switch. (c) Both branches re-evaluate all subsequent switches and arrive at distinct final grid states. The resulting downstream loss difference weights the jump term, which combines with path gradient to form a complete update.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robotic manipulation requires historical context, yet retaining extensive visual histories incurs growing storage and retrieval costs, while aggressive compression risks losing fine-grained information needed for subsequent decisions. Moreover, executed action histories capture intermediate behaviors that sparse visual observations may miss. Preserving this complementary context efficiently calls for modality-specific memory mechanisms that balance recent detail with long-term retention. To this end, we introduce $\mathrm{M}^{2}$-WAM, a world-action model equipped with hierarchical visual and interaction memories. $\mathrm{M}^{2}$-WAM preserves recent visual observations in dense short-term memory while consolidating entries evicted from this window into fixed-size associative long-term memory through gated delta updates. Within the same short- and long-term hierarchy, interaction memory encodes executed action prefixes into compact temporal representations, complementing visual observations with behavioral context. These complementary memories are integrated into world-action modeling through layer-wise retrieval, enabling memory-augmented action generation with a bounded online memory footprint independent of episode length. On the memory-dependent simulation benchmarks MIKASA-Robo and RMBench, $\mathrm{M}^{2}$-WAM achieves +53.2% and +61.2% absolute improvements in average success rates over Fast-WAM, respectively. These gains extend to real-world manipulation, where $\mathrm{M}^{2}$-WAM achieves a +29.3% absolute improvement over LingBot-VA in average success across three tasks. These results suggest that $\mathrm{M}^{2}$-WAM offers a promising approach to efficient memory-augmented world-action modeling.
authors: Xiaopeng Zhang, Weiqi Yuan, Xin Zhu, Jiaxi Huang, Yueqi Hu, Yin Zhang, Jian Yao, Yanjie Li

Integrates visual and interaction memories through layer-wise retrieval for memory-augmented action generation with episode-length-independent online memory.
Reports absolute average-success improvements of 53.2% and 61.2% over Fast-WAM on MIKASA-Robo and RMBench, and 29.3% over LingBot-VA across three real-world tasks.

papers.abstract: Hallucinations in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often arise from visual assumptions that go unchecked. Self-reflection, multi-agent debate, and counterfactual verification can reinforce erroneous conclusions when they rely on the same unverified visual assumptions. External visual tools can provide verifiable evidence, but models may select the wrong tools, supply incorrect parameters, or ignore or contradict the evidence they obtain. In this work, we propose EVA, an Evidence-seeking Visual Agent that reframes multimodal reasoning as an explicit process of evidence acquisition and verification. At the core of EVA is a unified evidence-grounded execution pipeline designed to address the above challenges through two tightly coupled mechanisms. First, we introduce Iterative Tool Replanning, which dynamically refines tool selection and parameters based on intermediate observations, improving the reliability of tool usage. Second, we develop Evidence Consistency Verification, an answer validation mechanism that improves alignment between the final prediction and the collected evidence, mitigating evidence--reasoning inconsistencies. In addition, to balance robustness and efficiency, EVA incorporates Selective Evidence Routing, an adaptive fast--slow reasoning strategy that determines when external evidence is necessary. Visually straightforward queries are handled via direct reasoning, while complex or high-risk cases trigger tool-based evidence acquisition. By jointly addressing how to reliably acquire evidence and how to use it consistently, EVA transforms multimodal reasoning from passive answer validation into explicit evidence-backed decision making. Experimental results demonstrate that EVA achieves significantly improved reasoning reliability over direct VLM inference and multi-agent methods, while maintaining efficiency through selective tool invocation.
authors: Ting Lei, Yu Chen, Yang Liu

papers.abstract: Generating laboratory assets that faithfully reproduce the appearance, structure, and joint motions of real equipment remains challenging. Existing asset generation methods struggle to directly generate simulation assets for all equipment observed in operation videos and to faithfully reproduce the appearance, joint motions, and internal cavities of the real equipment. To address the challenge, we present Lab2Sim, an agentic framework that generates editable, simulation-ready laboratory equipment assets from egocentric or multi-view operation videos. Lab2Sim comprises four specialized agents. The Evidence Agent combines video observations with laboratory knowledge to specify equipment parts, materials, and functional requirements, which guide the Asset Agent in constructing editable Blender assets. The independent Verifier checks the generated geometry and appearance against the evidence and requirements, providing targeted feedback for revision. The Simulation Integration Agent converts verified Blender assets into simulation instances with physical properties and articulated mechanisms, using execution feedback to refine their behavior. Experiments on human and robot laboratory scenes show that Lab2Sim achieves higher visual fidelity and stronger interaction capability than coding-agent and real-to-sim baselines, including a Codex baseline using the same underlying model. We further demonstrate valve-controlled drainage and use the generated asset library to reproduce laboratory scenes and operations in RoboTwin, supporting reusable simulation environments for robotic laboratory tasks.

papers.abstract: Conversational sports analytics requires accurate, evidence-based responses with low latency. Changes in query distributions, data resources, and model behavior can degrade static agent configurations, motivating controlled evolution guided by runtime evidence. We present Sports Agent, a self-evolving framework integrating an Agentic SQL Model for structured-data reasoning, a harness for planning and tool orchestration, and a unified Feedback Engine connecting online execution with offline evolution. The engine assesses responses and execution trajectories, verifies factual claims, diagnoses failures, and generates evolution signals. Model evolution combines SQL-to-Question Scaling for coverage expansion with Graph-Guided Scaling for error-targeted synthesis. Generated questions undergo trajectory distillation and quality filtering for iterative supervised fine-tuning, followed by a separate Post-RL stage. Harness evolution translates recurrent failures into bounded prompt and skill updates, validated through independent audits, execution replay, and regression testing. Performance-tolerance checks guard against unacceptable degradation during simplification. The resulting Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-based model outperforms Qwen3.8-Max on sports question answering and analysis while achieving approximately three times the inference efficiency. Across 30 harness-evolution rounds, the aggregate performance score improves by 10.8 points. In a live sports analytics product, the evolved system improves factual correctness by 10.5 points and average response length, a proxy for answer richness, by 158.1%, while reducing average latency by 41.3% relative to the baseline.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) optimization updates the Gaussian parameters one training view at a time, tens of thousands of times. Unlike such single-view updates, multi-view batches reduce dependence on individual training views, and second-order optimization reduces the number of updates with larger, structured parameter changes. Because fewer updates leave fewer chances to correct a change that fits only the views used in one update, scene coverage becomes more important for each second-order update. Multi-view second-order updates, however, are expensive. Pixel sampling reduces this cost, but two issues remain. First, selecting views without considering overlap leaves some views redundant. To address this, we propose a view selection strategy that reduces this redundancy. Second, existing work processes the sampled pixels of each view in a separate pass and recomputes alpha compositing for these pixels from scratch. We introduce two implementation strategies that reduce both overheads by processing the sampled pixels of multiple views in joint passes and reusing the transmittance and accumulated color cached during rendering. On three datasets, our method reaches higher PSNR than the sampled second-order baseline in less than half its optimization time, with competitive SSIM and LPIPS.
authors: Hyunseung Son, Young Sun Choi, Youngsik Yun, Kibeom Hong, Youngjung Uh
bullets: Motivation: Multi-view second-order updates can improve optimization but are costly and sensitive to scene coverage.
Method: Select less-redundant views to increase coverage within each update.
Implementation: Jointly process sampled pixels across views and reuse cached transmittance and accumulated color.
Results: Across three datasets, achieves higher PSNR in less than half the optimization time, with competitive SSIM and LPIPS.
Scope: Evaluated on three datasets against a sampled second-order baseline.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of one update of our method. From Gaussians initialized by a sparse SfM point cloud or a dense pretrained 3DGS model, Scene-Distributional View Sampling selects training views with low redundancy, forming the multi-view batch Bt. The views are rendered, and pixels are sampled per tile so that their rays provide residuals. papers.abstract: 4D occupancy forecasting models 3D scene evolution to support future prediction and scenario generation in autonomous-driving world models. Semantic occupancy abstracts image color and texture into discrete labels, leaving 3D voxel arrangements as the primary cues for distinguishing local shapes within each class. Existing methods borrow image-encoding frameworks to obtain compact latent representations through height channelization or plane factorization, but do not sufficiently model within-column height patterns and cross-column relations jointly before compression, weakening these geometric cues. Forecasting also underutilizes complementary history and struggles to retain reliable observation evidence. We therefore propose GeoTex, an occupancy world model combining geometry-as-texture encoding with history-grounded forecasting. GeoTex Representation jointly encodes within-column height patterns and cross-column relations into compact continuous latent representations and restores 3D structure through content-dependent height unfolding and geometric interaction. GeoTex Prediction retains initial evidence throughout rollout in fixed cross-observation relational memory and incorporates complementary recent history through target-referenced residual updates. After prediction training, decoder-only adaptation improves semantic decoding of predicted states. GeoTex improves average forecasting mIoU and IoU by 9.79% and 11.91% relative to GenieDrive while reducing parameters from 3.47M to 2.33M, with gains increasing at longer horizons. Code is included in the supplementary material.
authors: Shijun Guo, Yaming Yang, Haoran Xu, Wei Zhao, Ziyu Guan, Cai Xu, Peixi Peng

Decoder-only adaptation improves semantic decoding of predicted occupancy states.
Reports 9.79% higher forecasting mIoU and 11.91% higher IoU than GenieDrive, while reducing parameters from 3.47M to 2.33M; gains grow at longer horizons.

papers.abstract: The Locate-Then-Edit framework enables efficient knowledge updates in large language models without requiring full retraining. Recent research has increasingly focused on sequential editing, where knowledge arrives continuously and the model is updated incrementally. However, existing sequential methods commonly suffer from catastrophic forgetting and model collapse after only a few hundred edits. In contrast, batch editing - which jointly optimizes all edits and yields the optimal solution under a specified editing objective - can support tens of thousands of edits with high edit efficacy while preserving the model's general capabilities, resulting in a substantial performance gap between the two editing paradigms. In this paper, we demonstrate that this gap can be closed via a batch-equivalent sequential editing approach. Moreover, we investigate the underlying mechanism of model degradation in existing sequential methods by analyzing the convergence behavior of weight perturbations as edits accumulate. Our analysis reveals that current methods typically exhibit linear or logarithmic growth in perturbation, whereas the proposed batch-equivalent method achieves time-invariant growth, thereby theoretically guaranteeing long-term stability and preserving the integrity of pretrained knowledge throughout massive-scale sequential editing.
authors: Bingqing Liu, Wei Liu, Zhiying Deng, Jun Wang, Yuhua Li, Ruixuan Li
bullets: Sequential model editing often causes catastrophic forgetting and model collapse after only hundreds of edits.
Batch editing remains effective across tens of thousands of edits while preserving general capabilities.
The paper analyzes accumulated weight perturbations to explain degradation in existing sequential methods.
Existing methods show linear or logarithmic perturbation growth, while the proposed approach maintains time-invariant growth.
This behavior provides a theoretical guarantee of long-term stability and preservation of pretrained knowledge during large-scale editing.

papers.abstract: Multimodal memory enables long-horizon vision-language agents to preserve and retrieve past experiences. While prior research has focused on memory construction and retrieval, effectively using the provided memory remains a challenge for vision-language models (VLMs). We find that VLMs often fail to answer downstream questions even when sufficient multimodal evidence is provided. To investigate why VLMs struggle, we replace memory images with reference captions and observe substantial performance gains, suggesting difficulties in reading visual evidence directly. However, model-generated captions may omit critical information, limiting this approach in practice. These limitations motivate a closer examination of memory utilization, revealing failures in both evidence reading and downstream question answering. Building on this distinction, we propose \textbf{MemRU}, a two-stage training framework that improves evidence reading through supervised fine-tuning (Read SFT) and downstream evidence utilization through Group Relative Policy Optimization (Use GRPO). Experimental results demonstrate that our 8B model generalizes across three unseen multimodal memory systems, outperforming Qwen3-VL-32B and approaching GPT-5-mini.
authors: Junseok Kim, Kyungmin Min, Kyomin Jung
bullets: VLMs often fail to answer questions despite having sufficient multimodal evidence in memory.
Replacing memory images with reference captions substantially improves performance, exposing difficulty in directly reading visual evidence.
MemRU separates evidence reading from evidence utilization, training them with Read SFT and Use GRPO, respectively.
An 8B MemRU model generalizes across three unseen multimodal memory systems, outperforming Qwen3-VL-32B and approaching GPT-5-mini.
Generated captions can omit critical information, so caption-based memory use is not always reliable.

papers.abstract: UAV detection and tracking remain constrained by the scarcity of high-quality training data. Existing game-engine-based synthetic UAV data suffer from a substantial synthetic-to-real gap, while the high cost of manually collected real-world UAV data limits dataset scale. Therefore, we introduce WorldUAV, a high-quality UAV dataset constructed through an efficient framework powered by world models. Specifically, WorldUAV directly integrates UAVs into readily available real-world videos, naturally preserving realistic backgrounds, illumination, and scene dynamics. Leveraging the spatiotemporal priors of world models, it generates UAV videos with plausible motion, pose variations, and cross-frame consistency, effectively narrowing the gap between synthetic and real data. We further develop an agentic pipeline orchestrated by a multimodal large language model that acquires sources, plans UAV trajectories, invokes synthesis, and verifies generated videos, enabling fully automated dataset construction. WorldUAV comprises 6,878 UAV videos and 205,778 UAV images. Experiments show that WorldUAV significantly improves the performance of UAV detectors. Moreover, it substantially reduces dataset construction costs, requiring only 15 seconds and USD 0.0005 API cost per high-quality UAV image. Our work offers both a high-quality dataset and a scalable data generation paradigm for UAV detection and tracking.

An MLLM-orchestrated pipeline automates source acquisition, trajectory planning, synthesis, and verification.
Contains 6,878 videos and 205,778 images; improves UAV detector performance while reducing generation cost to 15 seconds and USD 0.0005 per image.

papers.abstract: When a large language model (LLM) evicts prompt keys and values at the end of prefill, it must decide what to keep before it sees the queries from subsequent decoding steps. Generating a draft continuation can approximate those queries at the cost of extra autoregressive steps. Can we use the embedding of the first output token, already available from the final prefill logits, to construct low-cost pseudo queries that approximate future decoding queries? We start with FTQ-8, which places eight copies of the first token ID at consecutive future positions and reads their attention to the prompt in one causal forward pass. Each copy sees a different prefix, but a generic opening such as the offers a poor literal guess for seven successive tokens. Faster and Better Query (FBQ) preserves the first embedding and learns an additive offset at each of the seven remaining positions. We train these offsets to predict the average prompt attention of a full-cache continuation. On LongBench, FBQ performs comparably to eight-step Lookahead Q-Cache at the same cache budget, using a single forward pass to compute all probe queries.
authors: Jiankun Zou, Daixing Chen, Tongtong Yuan
bullets: Addresses cache-eviction decisions made before future decoding queries are available.
Extends FTQ-8 by adjusting seven repeated first-token embeddings with learned additive offsets.

papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation has recently proven highly effective for improving autoregressive models, but its applicability to DLMs remains poorly understood. We present the first systematic study of KD for DLMs and uncover two non-intuitive failures of classical forward-KL (FKL) distillation: (i) student perplexity does not improve monotonically with more teacher-generated data, and (ii) on the same teacher-generated corpus, FKL distillation underperforms simply training the student with the original DLM denoising objective. To address them, we propose a unified, data-free distillation framework for masked DLMs. First, the framework runs an off-policy distillation phase that absorbs general knowledge from a static set of teacher-generated data. Then, the framework employs on-policy distillation which consists of three techniques: a trajectory loss along the student's own reverse process, confidence reweighting that down-weights tokens where the teacher is unsure, and a trust-region anchor that stabilizes the moving target. On MDLM, the resulting student attains a GPT-2 perplexity of $24.75$, surpassing the teacher's $27.04$; on Dream-7B distillation to a 93M student model, the framework reduces Qwen-2.5 perplexity from the FKL-distilled baseline of $25.23$ to $19.83$ while preserving performance on zero-shot general capability benchmarks.
authors: Yuxuan Sun, Yuanjian Xu, Jianing Hao, Yu Li, Sowmen Das, Zhong Li, Sangwoong Yoon, Miguel R. D. Rodrigues
bullets: Classical forward-KL distillation does not reliably benefit DLMs: more teacher-generated data may not improve perplexity, and it can underperform the original denoising objective.
The framework first uses off-policy distillation on static teacher-generated data to transfer general knowledge.
It then applies on-policy distillation with reverse-process trajectory loss, confidence reweighting, and a trust-region anchor.
On MDLM, the student reaches 24.75 GPT-2 perplexity versus the teacher’s 27.04; on Dream-7B, perplexity improves from 25.23 to 19.83 for a 93M student.
Zero-shot general capability benchmark performance is preserved in the reported Dream-7B distillation setting.

papers.selection_reason: Systematic study of knowledge distillation for diffusion language models, a training/architecture contribution to language foundation models.
papers.title: Rethinking Knowledge Distillation for Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: A systematic study finds that standard forward-KL distillation can fail for diffusion language models, and introduces an on-policy, data-free framework that substantially improves student perplexity while preserving general capabilities.

papers.abstract: The Smart Buildings Challenge asks for one HVAC control policy that runs office buildings and weather it has never seen, from the building's metadata and sensor streams alone. Our controller sees no data from the target building before it runs and is not tuned per building; its few global constants were set on development scenarios. Each zone has a first-order grey-box model that starts from coefficients computed from the floor plan and is updated online by recursive least squares, and a planner and a closed-form mapping turn the models into plant commands. On two sets of buildings and weather that we generated, a validation set and a stress set with real-year weather, it scores 0.145 and 0.159 times the starter kit's PID baseline, and 0.095 times on a holdout built after all versions were fixed and scored once. It improves on every building, also against our two implementations of ASHRAE Guideline 36: per set it scores 0.60 to 0.71 times a basic version and 0.83 to 0.96 times one partly tuned on the public leaderboard, which wins one of 54 scenarios; with a 5 {\deg}C frost target for empty zones on both, the margin over the tuned version shrinks to 1.4% on the stress set, where one of six buildings is 0.2% worse. In an ablation on a reduced-order model, removing both the floor-plan prior and online identification costs 28%, 20% and 42% on the validation, stress and holdout sets, far more than the two effects combined: either source of building-specific information recovers most of what is lost without both. On one office floor in a second simulator, BOPTEST, this does not carry over: with identification on, the two priors give similar results, but the floor-plan prior alone, with constants fitted on the competition's simulator, is the least stable arm. These simulation results motivate testing floor-plan-initialised adaptive control in buildings that have drawings but no operating data.
authors: Elias T. -H. Shieh, Chun Fu
bullets: Targets one untuned HVAC policy that operates unseen office buildings using metadata and sensor streams only.
Initializes first-order grey-box zone models from floor-plan coefficients and updates them online with recursive least squares.
On generated validation, stress, and holdout sets, achieves 0.145, 0.159, and 0.095 times the starter PID baseline, respectively.
Ablations show that either floor-plan information or online identification recovers most of the benefit of using both.
Results do not fully transfer to BOPTEST: online identification makes the priors comparable, while the floor-plan-only controller is least stable.

papers.selection_reason: Online identification and adaptive control for unseen environments; fits deployment-time online learning and adaptation interests.
papers.title: Online Identification Can Replace a Floor-Plan Prior on Unseen Buildings
papers.tldr: Online system identification largely replaces the need for an accurate floor-plan prior for HVAC control in unseen buildings, though transfer to another simulator is mixed.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 4D trackers recover camera motion, depth, and point trajectories from short video clips, but chaining windows over long videos degrades their accuracy. We find that replacing inter-window alignment with ground-truth transforms leaves tracking error essentially unchanged. Static-point error instead grows with time since last observation: repeatedly predicting a static point from windows that no longer observe it corrupts previously recovered geometry. We call this failure forgetting. Merely retaining the last observed positions of unseen points reduces error by 26% on PointOdyssey without modifying the tracker. We introduce Recall4D, a training-free framework that augments a frozen tracker with a persistent world state and sparse motion anchors. Static points retain their world-space positions outside the camera view and are refined by averaging observations decoded at sparse keyframes while in view. For dynamic objects, the tracker decodes sparse representative anchors, while geometric skinning propagates their displacements to dense queries. Across two long-horizon benchmarks, Recall4D improves the accuracy of its backbone while running 7.6-9.0$\times$ faster, and its accuracy gains carry over to five further backbones and three other long-sequence tasks, demonstrating its generality.
authors: Tianle Lyu
bullets: Inter-window misalignment is not the main cause of long-video tracking degradation; static-point error increases after points leave view.
Retaining last observed positions reduces PointOdyssey error by 26% without changing the tracker.
The training-free method augments frozen trackers with persistent world state, sparse keyframes, and geometric skinning for dynamic objects.
It improves backbone accuracy across two long-horizon benchmarks while running 7.6–9.0× faster.
Gains transfer across five additional backbones and three other long-sequence tasks, indicating broad applicability.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free persistent world state to mitigate forgetting in long-horizon 4D reconstruction.
papers.title: Recall4D: Forgetting, Not Misalignment, Limits Long-Horizon Feed-Forward 4D Reconstruction
papers.tldr: Recall4D shows that long-horizon 4D reconstruction fails mainly because trackers forget previously observed geometry, and fixes this with persistent state and sparse motion anchors.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained ego-vehicle action recognition turns large-scale driving video into structured, searchable driving scenarios, providing a foundation for discovering critical maneuvers and systematically developing and evaluating autonomous driving models. However, large-scale driving videos often lack explicit ego-action labels, and existing datasets vary in action definitions, annotation granularity, and available supervision. We introduce EgoManeuver, a unified benchmark of 16 lateral and 6 longitudinal actions constructed from seven public driving datasets. Our multi-source labeling system leverages existing annotations and complementary evidence available in each source dataset, including vehicle signals, ego poses, HD-map topology, and captions, to assign labels under a unified fine-grained action taxonomy. We further standardize temporal action boundaries across datasets and validate the resulting labels through kinematic consistency checks and targeted human review. The resulting benchmark contains 86.6K segments spanning 190.8 h across 26 countries and provides a long-tail-aware evaluation protocol. We also introduce DenseEgo, a video-based baseline that combines spatially aware representations with dense per-step action supervision. On the EgoManeuver, DenseEgo achieves 82.7 lateral and 83.5 longitudinal mAP, outperforming the strongest existing video model by 1.5 and 5.0 points, respectively. Finally, we demonstrate one way to integrate DenseEgo with a language-model agent for retrieving driving videos that match user-specified actions and scenarios. All code, datasets, and model weights will be publicly released.
authors: Zhipeng Bao, Wenjie Zhao, Qianwen Li
bullets: Introduces a taxonomy of 16 lateral and 6 longitudinal ego-vehicle actions.
Constructs 86.6K segments covering 190.8 hours across 26 countries using multi-source evidence and standardized temporal boundaries.
Validates labels with kinematic consistency checks and targeted human review, and provides a long-tail-aware evaluation protocol.
Presents DenseEgo, a spatially aware video model with dense per-step supervision, achieving 82.7 lateral and 83.5 longitudinal mAP.
Demonstrates language-model-assisted retrieval of driving videos by user-specified actions and scenarios; code, data, and weights are planned for release.

papers.title: Fine-Grained Ego-Vehicle Action Recognition from Driving Video
papers.tldr: EgoManeuver unifies fine-grained ego-driving action labels across seven datasets, enabling improved video-based maneuver recognition and scenario retrieval.

papers.abstract: Transformer-based 3D reconstruction models such as VGGT and $\pi^3$ predict cameras, depth and point maps directly from many input views. Causal attention models such as StreamVGGT extend them to online video but cache all past tokens, so their total compute grows quadratically with the stream length. Recurrent models such as CUT3R and TTT3R keep a fixed-size state at constant cost, but they progressively forget early geometry. We present LinearVGGT, a hybrid model distilled from StreamVGGT, which uses Mamba2 layers for efficient sequence modeling in three of every four global layers. The remaining layers use register-guided sparse attention to retrieve a few relevant past frames, compensating for the limited exact long-range recall of Mamba2. Our distillation needs only 9\% of the GPU hours and 31\% of the training frames that StreamVGGT uses to learn from VGGT. LinearVGGT keeps an almost constant latency of 27 ms per frame over 1,024 frames and is on average $12 \times$ faster than StreamVGGT. It outperforms its teacher and is competitive with the state-of-the-art streaming model LingBot-Map, while running $2.5\times$ faster and using $2.7\times$ less memory.
authors: Haoyu Kang, Pingzhi Li, Ruichen Zhang, Tianlong Chen
bullets: Addresses the quadratic compute of token-caching streaming transformers and the long-term forgetting of fixed-state recurrent models.
Uses Mamba2 in three of every four global layers, with register-guided sparse attention to retrieve relevant past frames.
Distillation from StreamVGGT requires 9% of its GPU hours and 31% of its training frames.
Maintains approximately 27 ms per frame over 1,024 frames and is 12× faster than StreamVGGT.
Outperforms its teacher and matches state-of-the-art streaming performance while running 2.5× faster and using 2.7× less memory than LingBot-Map.

papers.abstract: Purpose: Figure retrieval from reference atlases in expert domains like forensic pathology, dentistry and geology must work without labels or training pairs, on content that often cannot leave local hardware, and on images outside the training data of image-text encoders. This work proposes a structure-aware pipeline that satisfies all three, retrieving figures through the page structure recovered by layout geometry and a local open-weight 8B VLM. Methods: A geometry-based pairing method is introduced, in which the model receives a schematic of the detected boxes and selects each picture's caption without access to pixels or text. Caption retrieval is evaluated on three private corpora (29 books, 10,421 figures, 218 queries) with blind human grading, against a lexical baseline, generated descriptions and five image-text encoders. Results: Geometric pairing was correct for 96%, 92% and 77% of pictures in the three domains, against 76%, 45% and 53% for the better of two document parsers. A hosted model given the schematic was equally accurate, while coordinates as text lost 22 points. Caption retrieval obtained an nDCG@5 of 0.85, 0.87 and 0.76, against 0.54, 0.51 and 0.27 for the best cross-modal encoder and 0.41, 0.28 and 0.30 for generated descriptions. Pairing errors carried over to retrieval. Conclusion: The proposed pipeline achieves accurate figure retrieval with small local models and no in-domain training, where general and biomedical image-text encoders fall far behind. Its geometry-only pairing is the most accurate of five methods and exposes no content, even to a hosted model. Code and prompts are released.

papers.abstract: Tool use learned during supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is not always retained during reinforcement learning (RL). We study how properties of SFT data may affect this retention by constructing Low, Medium, and High SFT datasets with approximately matched token budgets but different tool-call depths. Under the same RL recipe, the three initializations reach similar RL training accuracy yet exhibit markedly different tool-use dynamics: tool initiation increases in Low, declines in Medium, and collapses in High. We observe that these datasets also differ substantially in the amount of reasoning preceding each tool call. In particular, High trajectories contain considerably less pre-call reasoning, motivating the hypothesis that pre-call reasoning may affect how well tool use is calibrated and, consequently, whether the corresponding behaviors are retained during RL. An idealized theoretical analysis provides a selective-retention view of this process: advantages in overall and tool-conditioned accuracy can be preserved under outcome-only optimization, while tool initiation increases only when tool-using trajectories are more successful than the tool-free alternative. Guided by this analysis, we rank the original High trajectories by average pre-call reasoning length and retain the highest-ranked examples while approximately matching cumulative SFT token exposure. This simple filtering strategy improves post-RL accuracy and tool-conditioned final-answer success without consistently increasing tool initiation across multiple benchmarks. These results suggest that pre-call reasoning is a useful dimension of SFT supervision for understanding and improving tool-use retention under downstream RL.
authors: Kaiwen Hu, Hyunin Lee, Joseph Suh, Serina Chang, Shuai Shao, Yong Zhang, Namyong Park, Xiaoqiang Luo, Luke Simon, Somayeh Sojoudi
bullets: Matched-token SFT datasets with different tool-call depths show divergent RL dynamics: tool initiation rises, falls, or collapses depending on the initialization.
High-tool-call trajectories contain substantially less reasoning before tool calls, motivating pre-call reasoning as a calibration and retention factor.
Theory suggests tool initiation grows only when tool-using trajectories outperform the tool-free alternative under outcome-only RL.
Selecting High-dataset examples with the longest average pre-call reasoning improves post-RL accuracy and tool-conditioned success across multiple benchmarks.
The filtering strategy does not consistently increase tool initiation, so its benefit appears focused on retention and answer quality rather than usage frequency.

papers.abstract: Computing per-player feedback strategies in $N$-player adversarial differential games is challenging as the associated coupled Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman system is high-dimensional and generally lacks classical solutions. We address this by approximating viscosity solutions using physics-informed neural networks within a policy iteration scheme with a vanishing-viscosity annealing schedule. Theoretically, we establish an explicit $\varepsilon$-Nash guarantee by bounding per-player regret via computable residuals and prove our method reaches this stopping criterion in finite time. For two-player zero-sum games, we further establish a computable bound on the approximation error of the value function. Numerical experiments on pursuit-evasion scenarios illustrate the tightness of these computed bounds and the framework's scalability to high-dimensional environments.
authors: Takuma Adams, Andrew C. Cullen, Tansu Alpcan
bullets: Targets coupled, high-dimensional Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman systems that may lack classical solutions.
Uses physics-informed neural networks with policy iteration and vanishing-viscosity annealing to approximate viscosity solutions.
Provides an explicit ε-Nash guarantee by bounding each player’s regret through computable residuals.
Proves finite-time attainment of the stopping criterion and derives a computable value-function error bound for two-player zero-sum games.
Pursuit–evasion experiments demonstrate tight computed bounds and scalability to high-dimensional environments.

papers.abstract: Multi-scale architectures are widely adopted in all-in-one image restoration (AIO-IR) to capture larger-scale context at low-resolution stages and refine details at high-resolution (HR) stages. However, processing spatially large feature maps at HR stages incurs substantial computational costs and memory traffic, making efficient HR processing challenging. To address this challenge, we propose High-resolution Global-Local Restoration (HiGLR), an efficient multi-scale AIO-IR network grounded in an analysis of spatial redundancy in self-attention and convolutional feed-forward networks (ConvFFNs). Specifically, this analysis identifies three key redundancies: per-query readout at the finest-scale stage, key routing across neighboring queries at intermediate stages, and spatial mixing in the expanded feature spaces of ConvFFNs. Accordingly, HiGLR replaces costly self-attention at the finest-scale stage with a learned input-independent kernel. At intermediate stages, we propose a Block-Routed Hybrid Attention, which combines coarse-scale dense attention with fine-scale block-sparse attention over value residuals relative to coarse summaries, and shares routing indices across neighboring queries. We further introduce a Dual-Space FFN that performs spatial mixing in a compact space and pointwise nonlinear transformation in an expanded space, enabling efficient kernel fusion. Combining these designs, HiGLR achieves state-of-the-art performance while delivering up to a $4.24\times$ inference speedup over existing methods.
authors: Dongheon Lee, DongJae Lee, Sewhan Chun, Chanseul Cho, Youngwook Kim, Youngmin Ro, Yonghyun Jeong
bullets: High-resolution stages are costly because large feature maps create substantial computation and memory traffic.
The analysis identifies redundancy in finest-scale attention, intermediate-stage key routing, and ConvFFN spatial mixing.
HiGLR replaces finest-scale self-attention with a learned input-independent kernel.
Block-Routed Hybrid Attention combines coarse dense attention with fine block-sparse attention and shared routing.
A Dual-Space FFN separates compact-space spatial mixing from expanded-space nonlinear transformation for efficient kernel fusion.

papers.abstract: Learning reusable latent actions from action-free videos offers an effective route to improving Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies. However, reconstruction-oriented latent actions do not necessarily benefit policy learning: as they may encode task-irrelevant static appearance with scene identity, or entangle slowly varying task progress with fine-grained execution dynamics in limited discrete code. We propose FreshVLA, a VLA framework built on a frequency-guided, dynamics-sensitive learning paradigm for acquiring temporally hierarchical continuous latent actions. FreshVLA uses a high-pass prior to guide visual transition encoding toward dynamical regions, thereby reducing reliance on static appearance cues. It further organizes latent actions into coarse-grained task progress and fine-grained execution dynamics through cross-timescale sampling and frequency-domain regularization, enhancing their capacity to represent long-horizon behaviors. During policy training, we freeze the pretrained latent action encoder and transfer its representations to robot control through joint flow-matching of latent and robot actions. FreshVLA achieves 98.2% average success on LIBERO and 98.0% on LIBERO-Long, exceeding GR00T-N1.6 on the latter by 3.6%. It also reaches an average sequence length of 4.52 on CALVIN and strong overall success rate of 80.4% in the zero-shot LIBERO-PLUS evaluation. Furthermore, FreshVLA exhibits greater robustness to visual perturbations and a more distinct division of roles between two branches in modeling low- and high-frequency motion, respectively. In 35-step action regression, it achieves a 51.3-percentage-point higher relative error reduction than its hierarchical discrete counterpart. Real-world experiments demonstrate that FreshVLA improves the average success rate over $\pi_{0.5}$ by 7.5%. The FreshVLA project page is available at https://freshvla.github.io/.
authors: Jiaming Liang, Yifeng Zhan, Rongyi He, Mu Li, Jiaqi Fan, Zhiyuan Zhang, Qiwei Liang, Zhengjie Zhang, Boyang Cai, Ningyuan Zhang, Xingjian Jing, Qiang Nie
bullets: Uses a high-pass prior to focus visual transition encoding on dynamical regions rather than static scene appearance.

Reports strong results across LIBERO, LIBERO-Long, CALVIN, LIBERO-PLUS, and real-world experiments, including 98.2% success on LIBERO and a 7.5% improvement over π0.5.
Shows greater robustness to visual perturbations and clearer low-/high-frequency motion specialization than its hierarchical discrete counterpart.

papers.abstract: Standard attention's key-value cache grows linearly with context length. Bounding it raises the question of what a sequence model should retain for long-context reasoning. We argue this choice should be learned, and introduce State Space Attention (SSA), which learns to keep a bounded set of past representations and reads them with standard attention. A learned scorer rescores every chunk against newly arriving context and the rest of memory. A fixed-context Transformer is then the special case that always keeps the most recent tokens. We train the scorer and reader jointly, either moving gradually from a differentiable soft weighting of memories to hard retention, or with hard retention from the start. To produce signal for the scorer, we generate supervised samples during training, a technique we call recovery. We compare SSA with recurrent models, bounded-memory attention methods, and full-attention Transformers across retrieval, variable tracking, multi-hop reasoning, and language modeling. On our retrieval and reasoning benchmarks, SSA matches or comes within a few points of full attention on most tasks, far outperforms a Transformer with the same readable budget on every long-context retrieval task we evaluate, and matches or outperforms one with about 4 times that budget, while using constant inference memory. The largest remaining gap to full attention at small language model scale is on RULER. SSA makes a fixed number of tokens useful over a longer context, and since it reads memory with standard attention, we propose that it can be stacked with KV cache eviction methods. We also pretrain and post-train 400M-parameter models and measure how SSA's training and inference costs scale with context length and model size. Together, these experiments examine the capabilities and limitations of learned memory retention for long-context sequence modeling.
authors: Ege \c{C}akar, Cengiz Pehlevan
bullets: Addresses the linear growth of standard attention’s key-value cache by learning context-dependent memory retention.

Across retrieval, variable tracking, reasoning, and language modeling, SSA substantially outperforms equal-budget bounded attention and can match or exceed attention with roughly four times its readable budget on retrieval tasks.
Its main remaining gap to full attention at small model scale is on RULER; the approach is evaluated across different training and inference context/model scales.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents can self-improve over time by utilizing procedural memory derived from prior task trajectories, yet the distinct utilities of memories derived from local successes and failures remain underexplored. This work studies this question in a realistic setting with heterogeneous streams of multi-domain tool-use tasks and various environment constraints common in real-world scenarios. We develop \emph{Dual-Polarity Memory with Periodic Maintenance} (DualPM), a simple, retrieval-free memory workflow characterized by (1) customizable reflection and procedural memory generation from both local successes and failures within each trajectory, and (2) periodic memory consolidation over long task streams under a given memory capacity, preventing memory explosion. Online prequential evaluation with fine-grained metrics reveals that failure memory more strongly broadens coverage, success memory better streamlines execution, while combining both polarities effectively integrates both benefits. Further studies demonstrate that DualPM enables cross-domain memory generalization and continual memory adaptation, while external evaluation on EvoMemBench reveals the portability and effectiveness of DualPM as a general long-term procedural memory method.
authors: Tianmai M. Zhang, Hoda Shajari, Amr Hendy, Xiaohu Liu, Piyush Behre, Omar Zia Khan, Ankur Gupta
bullets: Studies how success- and failure-derived procedural memories support continual adaptation across heterogeneous, multi-domain tool-use tasks.
Introduces a retrieval-free workflow with customizable reflection, memory generation from both outcome types, and periodic consolidation under fixed capacity.
Online evaluation finds failure memory broadens coverage, success memory improves execution efficiency, and combining both captures both benefits.
Shows cross-domain memory generalization and continual adaptation over long task streams.
External evaluation on EvoMemBench supports DualPM’s portability as a general long-term procedural memory method.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we study distributionally robust reinforcement learning with Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence-defined uncertainty sets. The goal is to find a policy that maximizes the robust value function, defined as the worst-case value over all transition kernels in the uncertainty set. Assuming access to a generative model, we aim to understand the sample complexity of finding an $\epsilon$-optimal robust policy. The best-known sample complexity results in the literature show a non-trivial gap of $\mathcal{O}\{\max\{p_\wedge^{-1}(1-\gamma)^{-1},(1-\gamma)^{-2}\}\}$ between the upper and lower bounds, where $p_\wedge$ denotes the minimum positive transition probability of the nominal transition kernel, and $\gamma$ is the discount factor. More importantly, existing results on the lower bound only cover a limited range of the uncertainty level. In this paper, we develop tighter and complete upper and lower bounds for robust RL with KL-defined uncertainty sets. Our upper bound is the tightest among all existing studies, and it improves upon the best-known bound by at least the order of $\mathcal{O}(\min\{p_\wedge^{-1},(1-\gamma)^{-1}\})$ for uncertainty level $\delta\in(0,1)$. Furthermore, our lower bound holds for any uncertainty level. Our upper and lower bounds (nearly) match in various regimes, providing improved results for this problem.
authors: Yudan Wang, Zilong Deng, Nathaniel D. Bastian, Shaofeng Zou
bullets: Studies finding an ε-optimal policy that maximizes worst-case value over uncertain transition kernels, assuming access to a generative model.
Derives tighter upper and lower sample-complexity bounds than prior work.
The upper bound improves the best-known result by at least an order of min{p₍∧₎⁻¹, (1−γ)⁻¹} for uncertainty level δ∈(0,1).
Provides a lower bound valid for every uncertainty level, extending prior lower-bound results.
Upper and lower bounds nearly match across multiple regimes, substantially clarifying the complexity of robust RL with KL uncertainty sets.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon video generation is key to interactive world modeling, physical intelligence, and spatial reasoning, yet maintaining geometric consistency and accurate camera control remains challenging without 3D grounding. We introduce \textbf{VivaWorld}, a framework for generating geometry- and view-consistent long videos from an image. We first construct a compositional hybrid 3D representation that combines reconstructed point clouds, which preserve observed scene geometry and appearance, with generated textured meshes, which provide complete object geometry across $360^\circ$ novel views. We also introduce a connected-region filter removing inconsistent floating components for robust cross-view reconstruction and propose a hybrid camera embedding that combines global and object-anchored Pl\"{u}cker rays to capture both scene-level camera motion and camera-object relationships, and inject it together with the visual guidance into a video generation model via a control adapter. Extensive experiments show VivaWorld achieves state-of-the-art visual quality and camera control, while supporting controllable novel-view synthesis, long-horizon scene exploration, and physical AI. Project page is available at: https://research.nvidia.com/labs/sil/projects/vivaworld/
authors: Ying Jiang, Donglai Xiang, Anita Hu, Masha Shugrina
bullets: Targets geometric inconsistency and inaccurate camera control in long-horizon video generation.
Combines reconstructed point clouds with textured meshes to preserve observed details and complete unseen object geometry.
Uses connected-region filtering to remove inconsistent floating components during reconstruction.
Introduces hybrid global and object-anchored Plücker-ray camera embeddings injected through a control adapter.
Reports state-of-the-art visual quality and camera control, with controllable novel-view synthesis and long-horizon scene exploration.

papers.abstract: Orthogonal finetuning (OFT) adapts a pretrained weight by an orthogonal transform and preserves its singular values and row angles, but existing methods construct an exact or approximate orthogonal transform at every optimization step. We measure how far a transform $A$ is from orthogonal by its orthogonality defect $\|A^\top A-I\|_2$. For OFTv2, which truncates a Cayley-Neumann series, we show that the truncation order does not determine the defect. At its default order, block defects in checkpoints from the reference implementation span five orders of magnitude. We propose Restarted Tangent Orthogonal Finetuning (RTOFT), which uses the first-order update $W(I+S)$ of a weight $W$ with a skew-symmetric $S$ and restores exact orthogonality by a polar decomposition only when the drift $\|S\|_2$ reaches a tolerance $\tau$. The defect of $I+S$ is exactly $\|S\|_2^2$. Therefore, reading the drift after every update and restoring before the next forward pass guarantees a defect of at most $\tau^2$ in every forward pass, independently of the loss, data, model, and optimizer. A final restoration makes the returned transform exactly orthogonal. On GLUE, RTOFT reduces the training time of block-diagonal, subspace, and butterfly parameterizations from $1.10$-$1.58\times$ to $0.97$-$1.13\times$ that of LoRA, and its block-diagonal version exceeds LoRA by $1.98\pm0.39$ points on the six-task average over five seeds. At $\tau=0.10$, the largest drift read during training stays between $0.10$ and $0.12$ across DeBERTaV3, Qwen, and diffusion models, whereas it ranges from $0.17$ to $1.65$ when restoring once per epoch. In all seven settings of our ablation, the tangent update is worse without restoration than with it, and restoring after every step yields no measurable accuracy gain over restoring at the tolerance and costs $4.5$-$27.5\%$ more per step.
authors: Lanxin Zhao (The University of Sydney), Xiaoyu Li (University of New South Wales), Dai Shi (University of Cambridge), Junbin Gao (The University of Sydney), Andi Han (The University of Sydney)
bullets: Existing OFT methods construct an exact or approximate orthogonal transform at every optimization step, incurring unnecessary overhead and potentially unpredictable defects.
RTOFT applies the first-order update W(I+S), with skew-symmetric S, and uses polar decomposition only when ||S||₂ reaches tolerance τ.
Because the orthogonality defect of I+S is exactly ||S||₂², checking drift before each forward pass guarantees defect ≤ τ²; a final restoration gives an exactly orthogonal result.
On GLUE, RTOFT reduces training time relative to LoRA across several parameterizations and its block-diagonal variant improves the six-task average by 1.98±0.39 points over five seeds.
Restoring only at the tolerance matches per-step restoration accuracy in the reported ablation while costing less; scope includes language and diffusion-model experiments.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon diffusion-based planning for kinodynamically constrained systems requires both scalability and feasibility, yet existing diffusion planners typically sacrifice one for the other. We present DFLAT, a diffusion-based planning algorithm that operates directly on a differentially flat trajectory representation. Instead of diffusing over time-discretized controls, DFLAT denoises a compact set of Hermite curve parameters in the flat-output space, consisting of intermediate waypoints together with the endpoint tangents of each segment. Every denoised sample maps to a dynamically consistent trajectory, so feasibility holds by construction rather than being restored afterward. Experiments on challenging tractor-trailer planning benchmarks show that DFLAT matches or exceeds the success rates of existing baselines at consistently lower planning times, particularly on long-horizon problems requiring multiple forward-reverse maneuvers. In cases where kinodynamic RRT requires over 100 seconds, DFLAT plans in subsecond time, enabling practical deployment.
authors: Ege Yuceel, Taekyung Kim, Keyvan Majd, Hideki Okamoto, Bardh Hoxha, Sayan Mitra, Georgios Fainekos
bullets: Targets the scalability–feasibility tradeoff in diffusion planning for kinodynamically constrained systems.
Diffuses over Hermite curve parameters—intermediate waypoints and segment endpoint tangents—instead of discretized controls.
Maps every denoised sample to a dynamically consistent trajectory, making feasibility hold by construction.
Matches or exceeds baseline success rates with consistently lower planning times on tractor-trailer benchmarks.
Achieves subsecond planning in cases where kinodynamic RRT takes over 100 seconds, especially for multi-maneuver horizons.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of DFLAT. Given a long-horizon planning task requiring multiple forward and reverse motions (bottom), Coarse Waypoint Planning (CWP) produces a coarse waypoint prior in flat-output space. At each reverse diffusion step i = N, . . . , 1, candidates are drawn by perturbing the waypoint poses and the segment-local Hermite parameters, lifted through the inverse flatness map into dynamically consistent trajectories, and scored under the planning cost. The score-weighted mean seeds the next step, refining the coarse prior into a low-cost trajectory for the downstream tracking controller.

Fig. 4. Sample trajectories from DFLAT. Green slots mark the start pose, orange slots mark the goal. Red segments are forward maneuvers, blue segments are reverse maneuvers, and purple markers are the waypoints. Left: nine benchmark environments of increasing planning horizon. Top: short (T, Court, Island). Middle: medium, requiring a reversal or a tight passage (U-Turn, Compound Gate, Pinch Point). Bottom: long (Shopping Mall, Parking Lot, Zig-Zag). DFLAT produces a collision-free trajectory respecting the dynamic limits in every case, at low latency. Right: DFLAT Playground, an interactive web-based demo in which all maps can be tried with different start and goal poses and custom obstacle placement, with DFLAT replanning in the browser.3

Fig. 2. Trajectory refinement during DFLAT denoising on a parking-lot scenario from the Long benchmark, shown at three stages from the coarse initialization (i = N ) to the final solution (i = 1). Red segments are forward maneuvers, blue reverse, and purple markers the waypoints. Refining the waypoints and Hermite parameters yields a smoother, lower-cost maneuver while remaining dynamically consistent.
Fig. 3. Acceleration-controlled tractor–trailer model (Accel-TT) used in the experiments, with acceleration a and steering rate ω as control inputs.

Fig. 5. CWP-only trajectory (red) and full DFLAT trajectory (blue). CWP cheaply recovers a collision-free but dynamically infeasible reference. DFLAT jointly optimizes waypoints and segment derivatives, yielding a smooth, feasible trajectory.

papers.abstract: A growing body of recent work addresses the retargeting of human hand-object demonstrations to robotic hands. To train whole-robot policies, however, the retargeted motions must be kinematically feasible and physically executable, and be produced efficiently at scale. We present DexEngine, a simulation pipeline that turns human manipulation data into train-ready, physically executable arm-hand trajectories. DexEngine first places each clip's hand-object motion where the arms can reach it, finds an arm motion that follows the human hands, and then corrects the motion in physics simulation with residual reinforcement learning. From nine human hand-object datasets, we generate about 5,200 clips for each of four dexterous hands, augmented into 65,000 trajectories (116 h) and 325,000 episodes (578 h) in total. Even with arms attached, DexEngine tracks objects more accurately than prior floating-hand methods and runs over 10x faster than RL-based ones. Policies trained on our data far outperform those trained on the same clips without physics correction or with the arms attached after a floating-hand correction, showing that fine-tuning data need physics correction. Mid-training on our data further improves them at equal fine-tuning budget, in simulation and on a real robot.
authors: Wongyun Yu, Honggeun Kim, Donguk Lee, Minchan Kim, Kyoung Whan Choe, Minsu Cho
bullets: Addresses the need for kinematically feasible, physics-corrected arm-hand motions when retargeting human demonstrations.
Uses reachable scene placement, arm-motion tracking, and residual reinforcement learning in simulation to correct trajectories.
Processes nine datasets into roughly 5,200 clips per hand, expanded to 65,000 trajectories and 325,000 episodes.
Tracks objects more accurately than floating-hand methods while running over 10× faster than RL-based alternatives.
Physics-corrected data improves policy performance in simulation and on a real robot, including when used during mid-training.

papers.abstract: Backdoor attacks pose a severe threat to modern NLP models by embedding hidden triggers that induce malicious behavior at inference time. Recent unlearning methods such as gradient ascent (GA) attempt to remove backdoors by maximizing the loss on poisoned samples; however, these methods can suffer from a critical limitation: they may shift the trigger's influence to other classes rather than eliminating it. In this work, we propose Trigger-Invariant Contrastive Unlearning (TICU), a framework for mitigating textual backdoor behavior by enforcing prediction and representation invariance to trigger insertion. TICU constructs clean and trigger-inserted counterfactual pairs, then fine-tunes the model so that both inputs produce consistent output distributions and aligned hidden representations. To preserve clean-task performance, TICU also retains the supervised classification loss on clean data and constrains parameter drift from the original model. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets, model architectures, and attack settings show that TICU improves triggered accuracy and reduces trigger-induced prediction shifts compared with existing baselines, while maintaining competitive label-flipping performance and limiting clean-task degradation.
authors: Santosh Chapagain, Shah Muhammad Hamdi, Soukaina Filali Boubrahimi
bullets: Addresses a limitation of gradient-ascent unlearning, which can shift trigger effects to other classes instead of removing them.
Creates clean/triggered counterfactual pairs and enforces consistency in both predictions and hidden representations.
Retains clean-data classification loss and constrains parameter drift to limit degradation of the original model.
Experiments across datasets, architectures, and attack settings report improved triggered accuracy and reduced trigger-induced shifts versus baselines.
Maintains competitive label-flipping performance while limiting clean-task degradation.

papers.abstract: Egocentric video records what a person looks at, but often misses what their body does: the hands leave the frame, and arm motion goes unseen. An exocentric camera recovers this context, but it must be installed wherever the activity happens. Active acoustic sensing can recover it from the wearables themselves: a device's speaker emits inaudible chirps, and its microphone senses the motion of the hands, arms, and nearby objects from their echoes. Yet no public dataset pairs it with egocentric video. We present EgoCARBS, with two deliverables. The first is a multimodal dataset and benchmark: 15 participants cook unscripted meals in their own kitchens wearing camera glasses and an off-the-shelf smartwatch that both sense with active acoustics, synchronized with egocentric and exocentric video and the watch's audio and IMU, with 4,019 verb-noun action annotations in 11.4 hours. The second is a study of what the wearables add to egocentric video. On verb recognition, they add at least as much as an exocentric camera for participants seen in training, and even more for new participants, for whom the exocentric camera does not help. Active acoustics alone provides most of this gain, and helps most where the camera does not see the hands. Trimmed action recognition, detection, and anticipation remain open. We will release the data, our data collection and annotation tools, and pre-trained models.
authors: Saif Mahmud, Vineet Parikh, Bharath Hariharan, Cheng Zhang
bullets: Addresses the limitation that egocentric cameras often miss hand and arm movements during activities such as cooking.
Provides synchronized egocentric/exocentric video, smartwatch active acoustics, audio, and IMU data from 15 participants cooking in their own kitchens.
Includes 11.4 hours of recordings and 4,019 verb–noun action annotations, with benchmarks for action understanding.
Wearable sensing matches or exceeds the benefit of an exocentric camera for verb recognition, especially for unseen participants.
Active acoustics supplies most of the improvement and is most useful when the camera cannot see the hands; trimmed recognition, detection, and anticipation remain open.

papers.abstract: Robot agents discover reusable skills by revising programs from execution feedback and retaining experience for later tasks. This process can fail when an agent treats an unsuccessful program as evidence that the task is physically impossible, ending exploration with revision budget remaining. We study this failure in Qwen3.8-27B and examine two decisions that shape skill discovery: I) how execution failures are diagnosed, and II) which lessons enter the shared skill library. Failure diagnosis requires the agent to reconstruct physical action effects from multimodal traces, while independent reproduction of a proposed repair does not require adequate task performance from its source program. We introduce Skeptic, a training-free protocol that uses measured action outcomes to guide repair and measured task success to govern skill admission. A grounded event log reports action effects and object end states from depth images and proprioception, separating sensor observations from inferred diagnoses. Verified promotion adds a development-success requirement on the source program to the existing independent reproduction check. Across 60 audited tasks, the mean number of tasks with false impossibility judgments decreases from 19.5 to 8.5 per campaign. On 80 LIBERO-Pro tasks and seven Robosuite tasks, Skeptic improves held-out success by 14.9 and 11.7 percentage points, with frozen model weights and the same program-revision budget.
authors: Wenfang Sun, Jianghao Deng, Wenzhe Yin, Yingjun Du, Cees G. M. Snoek
bullets: Targets two failure points: diagnosing execution failures and admitting lessons into the skill library.

Across 60 audited tasks, false impossibility judgments fell from 19.5 to 8.5 per campaign.
Improved held-out success by 14.9 percentage points on 80 LIBERO-Pro tasks and 11.7 points on seven Robosuite tasks, with frozen weights and the same revision budget.
