papers.abstract: Modern large language model (LLM) inference increasingly adopts disaggregated architectures that separate Prefill (P) and Decode (D) phases. Meanwhile, Expert Parallelism (EP) has been widely adopted in large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model serving. However, load imbalance still slows down MoE inference because each layer must wait for the busiest EP rank. The main source of latency differs between prefill and decode. Prefill is compute-bound, and its MoE layers' latency is determined by the maximum token count of the busiest rank. At the same time, under moderate batch sizes, Decode is memory-bound, so the latency is dominated by the maximum active-expert count across ranks. To solve both problems under a unified framework, we present RankCast, a system that reduces rank-level maximum token counts during prefill and active-expert counts during decode. For every token, RankCast preserves the predicted Top-p experts and chooses the remaining k-p from its Top-L candidates (L > k). In prefill, RankCast yields a price per rank that steers flexible assignments to less loaded ranks. In decode, RankCast closes experts on the busiest ranks while preserving the constraints for each token. Both paths are implemented and tested in the state-of-the-art inference frameworks SGLang and DeepEP. We overlap RankCast's kernels with model execution and reuse the existing DeepEP communication channel for metadata transmission. On Qwen3-235B-A22B with EP=8 and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B with EP=16, RankCast removes over 75% of the busiest rank's excess prefill load, improves prefill input throughput by up to 19%, and reduces decode time per output token by up to 10%. The quality cost is below one percentage point.
authors: Kaidi Fu, Xu-Hao Lu, Pingwei Sun, Jianchao Tan, Yuchen Xie, Xunliang Cai
bullets: Addresses EP load imbalance, where each MoE layer waits for the busiest rank.
Uses Top-p expert assignments unchanged and selects the remaining experts from Top-L candidates to steer load.
In prefill, it reduces maximum token counts per rank; in decode, it limits maximum active-expert counts.
Integrated with SGLang and DeepEP, with overlapped kernels and reused communication channels.

On two large Qwen models, it removes over 75% of excess prefill load, improves prefill throughput by up to 19%, reduces decode time per token by up to 10%, and incurs under one percentage point of quality loss.

papers.abstract: A common indication that a fine-tuned model has forgotten a deleted record is a membership-inference score near chance (ROC-AUC $\approx 0.5$). This reading is sound only if the comparison population represents how the record should behave after a valid deletion---a counterfactual that is rarely validated. We test this premise in a controlled $2\times2$ study pairing two membership-inference benchmarks, ArxivMIA and BookMIA, with two language models, Llama-3.2-1B and Qwen2.5-1.5B. Exact retraining validates the membership reference: it lies within the prespecified chance band on ArxivMIA but reaches $0.122$ on BookMIA, causing the same metric to reject an empirical deletion reference. A post-hoc BookMIA/Qwen diagnostic replaces benchmark label-0 records with same-pool, never-fine-tuned records and moves the reference from $0.257$ to $0.523$, supporting population mismatch in that cell. Each approximate-unlearning checkpoint is judged jointly on membership removal, deletion-targeted shift beyond non-deletion variation, and utility. On the admitted ArxivMIA/Llama axis, no tested configuration of gradient ascent with retain descent (GA+GD), negative-preference optimization with retain training (NPO-RT), or teacher--student unlearning (SCRUB) passes. A score near chance is not evidence of forgetting until a reference establishes what chance means.
authors: Mayank Gulati, Gerhard Wunder
bullets: Exact retraining showed that the expected membership-inference reference can vary across benchmarks and models.
On BookMIA/Qwen, replacing benchmark negatives with never-fine-tuned records shifted the reference from 0.257 to 0.523, indicating population mismatch.
The study evaluates unlearning using membership removal, deletion-specific change beyond natural variation, and utility.
No tested GA+GD, NPO-RT, or SCRUB configuration passed all criteria on the admitted ArxivMIA/Llama setting.
Scope: results cover two benchmarks, two models, and selected approximate-unlearning methods.

papers.abstract: AI coding agents increasingly write and submit code with limited human review, and much of it passes functional tests while remaining insecure. We show that these failures persist. Across 14 task sequences, Codex, Claude Code, and Qwen Code fixed a vulnerability 85.7% of the time when shown the failing security test, then reintroduced the same vulnerability class in a new session 26.7% of the time, about as often as agents that had never seen it (27.5%). The capability is present; the retention is not. Neither recording the repair in the agent's persistent context nor supplying published secure coding principles closed the gap: the recorded fix stayed tied to the family of the task it came from, and the principles, written for human developers, remained too general to apply to the code at hand. The knowledge exists; it is not activated. We call the missing ability security self-improvement: an agent learns from its own security failures so that each lesson persists across sessions, applies to new code, and does not break what works. We present PRECEPT, which equips coding agents with this ability through an evolving library that starts from authoritative secure coding principles and revises them against the agent's own failures, so that each principle comes to fire on the code where that agent actually goes wrong. A revision is kept only if fresh executions show it makes code more secure while keeping functional success within a small tolerance of the agent without the library. Improvement continues across evolution steps rather than saturating after the first. On task families never seen during evolution, PRECEPT's weakest agent reaches 97.1% secure working code, above the strongest unaided agent at 81.9% and the strongest baseline at 87.7%.
authors: Keyan Guo, Rupam Patir, Haipeng Cai, Hongxin Hu
bullets: Coding agents often fix vulnerabilities when shown a failing security test but frequently reintroduce the same flaw in later sessions.
Persistent repair records and generic secure-coding principles do not reliably transfer lessons to new code.
PRECEPT evolves an agent-specific library of security principles by revising them against the agent’s own failures.
Revisions are retained only when fresh executions improve security while keeping functional success within a small tolerance.
On unseen task families, the weakest PRECEPT agent achieved 97.1% secure working code, versus 81.9% for the strongest unaided agent and 87.7% for the strongest baseline.

papers.abstract: Open-source LLMs that are optimized for reasoning, such as VibeThinker, aim to democratize AI by bringing high-capability models to users with limited resources. They are broadly available but lack regulation and external guardrails; therefore, in order to integrate them safely into human society, it is critical that they perform in a safe manner. There are popular and intuitive arguments for why improved reasoning should improve safety, but recent evidence suggests that, in fact, the opposite may be true. This paper aims to characterize and mitigate this issue. First, it develops a metric for evaluating LLMs optimized for reasoning, and shows that increasing reasoning across multiple model families increases the unsafe rate in all cases. Second, it proposes a method for restoring safety by combining evolution strategies with a post-training guardrail (ESPG). Compared to alternative methods for safety post-training such as GRPO, ESPG is simple to implement, requires no GPU memory beyond that of inference, and works with remarkably few training samples (e.g.\ 30), yet makes the model significantly safer. The study thus establishes a path towards safe post-training of open-source AI models.
authors: Ehsan Latif, Roberto Dailey, Risto Miikkulainen, Elliot Meyerson
bullets: Introduces a metric for evaluating safety in reasoning-tuned LLMs.
Finds that increasing reasoning raises unsafe rates across multiple model families.
Proposes ESPG, combining evolution strategies with a post-training guardrail.
ESPG requires inference-level GPU memory and few training samples, while substantially improving safety.
Motivated by the need for safer deployment of broadly accessible, unregulated open-source models.

papers.abstract: This study investigates model predictive control (MPC) of a multirotor drone (unmanned aerial vehicle, UAV) carrying a cable-suspended payload, comparing conventional shifted initialization with Transformer-based warm starting of a sequential convex programming (SCP) optimizer. The controller uses a coupled mechanical model with an elastic cable and a double-pendulum representation of the suspended load. Its formulation includes move-blocked control inputs, finite-difference sensitivities, constrained quadratic subproblems, and input-feasibility projection. A Transformer trained on expert SCP solutions predicts an initial control sequence, which is subsequently refined by the same optimizer used for the conventional methods. Numerical experiments compare zero, shifted, and Transformer initialization under identical controller settings. For independently solved MPC problems, Transformer initialization reduces computation time relative to zero initialization. In sequential closed-loop simulations, however, shifting the preceding optimized control sequence provides the lowest computation time, while all three methods produce similar tracking behavior. These findings emphasize the importance of comparing learned warm starts with conventional initialization methods that reuse previous MPC solutions. The measured optimization times exceed the control sampling period; consequently, real-time implementation is not demonstrated. Keywords: Model predictive control; sequential convex programming; Transformer; warm start; cable-suspended payload; multirotor drone.
authors: Athanasios Zeris
bullets: Studies MPC for a multirotor UAV carrying a cable-suspended payload modeled as an elastic cable with a double pendulum.
Compares zero, shifted, and Transformer-based initial control sequences for a sequential convex programming optimizer.
The Transformer is trained on expert SCP solutions, while all predicted sequences are refined by the same optimizer.
Transformer initialization reduces computation time versus zero initialization for independent MPC problems.
In closed-loop simulations, shifting the previous solution is fastest; measured times exceed the sampling period, so real-time operation is not demonstrated.

papers.abstract: Language that describes an articulated object is often about its state: the drawer pulled out the furthest, the door opened halfway, push the drawer all the way in. Existing 3D language fields attach one feature to each point and cannot tell these descriptions apart, and 4D language fields condition on video time, which has no kinematic meaning and cannot be set by a user. We present ArtLang-4D, which reconstructs an articulated object from a single monocular RGB-D video and equips it with a dynamic language field indexed by articulation time t, the normalized state of its joints, instead of video time. The geometry is a canonical triangle field whose triangles follow typed screw joints, discovered from the video without any joint initialization. The language field is supervised by a t-tagged caption bank that describes each part with comparative state phrases in a whitened open-vocabulary text space. A free-form query is answered by maximizing part relevance jointly over parts and states, which returns both the part and the articulation state it describes; a command is then executed by moving only that part along its recovered joint. On the 100 objects of Articulate-100, ArtLang-4D recovers more accurate joints and part geometry than reconstruction and articulation baselines, retrieves the queried state far more reliably than a state-agnostic language field, and executes language commands with lower motion error.
authors: Sylvia Yuan, Dan Wang, Ravi Ramamoorthi, Xinrui Cui
bullets: Addresses the inability of static or video-time language fields to distinguish different articulation states.
Reconstructs canonical geometry with typed screw joints discovered without joint initialization.
Learns a dynamic language field from captions tagged by normalized articulation state.
Jointly identifies the relevant part and state for queries, then executes commands by moving that part.
On Articulate-100, improves joint and geometry recovery, state retrieval, and command motion accuracy over baselines.

papers.abstract: Detailed knowledge of a user's persona is valuable for personalizing generative AI models and agents, yet such details are difficult to obtain and change over time. We address the task of inferring persona attributes from a single day of mobile activity logs. No suitable publicly available benchmark exists for this task, so we introduce a synthetic benchmark of 1,600 persona-log pairs. We target on-device inference so that raw logs never leave the phone, which makes memory rather than speed the limiting constraint: a day of activity yields roughly 30K tokens, whose key-value cache alone exceeds the INT4 weights of a 4B-parameter model. We therefore propose a log filtering method that retains only behaviorally distinct entries. Filtering reduces the memory footprint by up to 39% across nine models from four families and more than halves prefill time, while maintaining or improving prediction quality. For Qwen3-4B it removes 2.5GB, bringing the model from well beyond a realistic per-process budget to a manageable one. Within our benchmark, these results indicate that preserving diverse behavioral events matters more for persona prediction than retaining every semantically similar log entry.
authors: Ahmed Alajrami, Ondrej Bohdal, Seokwoo Song, Taegeon Um, Peyman Hosseini, Savas Ozkan, Mete Ozay, Taha Ceritli

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are often asked which of two actions in a video happened first, given only a few sampled frames. Such frames can show that both actions occurred without showing which came first, so a reliable model should state an order only when the frames establish it. Forced-choice temporal benchmarks treat every input as answerable and reward lucky guesses, while answerability benchmarks do not separate frames that miss an action from frames that show both actions but not their order. We introduce EvOrderBench, a real-video benchmark of 579 event families. Each family fixes an episode and a question and varies only the frames: of two four-frame inputs, only one establishes the order, and two six-frame inputs extend the other one with either the frames that resolve the order or frames that do not. Every input is labeled for whether its frames establish each action and their order. Across sixteen open-weight configurations and three closed-source references, the best open models order nearly as accurately as the references when the frames establish the order, but withhold correctly on at most 83% of the inputs where they do not, against at least 90% for every reference; forced-choice accuracy cannot reveal this gap. Open models withhold mainly when the frames show neither action; once the frames show one or both, most of them commit to an order. Thinking narrows the gap, even when it is switched on within a single checkpoint, mainly by separating sufficient from insufficient evidence rather than by making models more cautious overall. Accurate ordering thus does not imply knowing when the frames fall short, and benchmarks should reward withholding alongside ordering.
authors: Xiaoqin Feng, Yuqi Li, Xinyuan Li, Neil Rodrigues, Xianglong Wang, Kuiye Ding, Yingli Tian
bullets: Introduces a real-video benchmark spanning 579 event families with frame sets that vary in whether they establish event order.
Labels whether each sampled input shows each action and whether it establishes which happened first.
Open models approach reference-model accuracy when order is visually established, but withhold less reliably on insufficient evidence.
Models most often withhold when neither action is shown; seeing one or both actions commonly triggers unjustified ordering.
Reasoning improves evidence sufficiency judgments, highlighting the need to reward correct withholding alongside temporal ordering.

papers.abstract: Freezing older adapters does not ensure that a continual learner will select and use them properly at inference time. When multiple adapters exist, routing among them and identifying the adapter whose representation space matches the query's answer can be difficult. We propose CONTLORA, which replaces stored examples with compact class statistics for adapter selection and classification. Gaussian class models in a frozen representation select LoRA adapters, while accumulated feature moments exactly recover a class-balanced ridge classifier for fixed training features. Trained without retaining images or feature vectors, CONTLORA reaches 88.55% accuracy on 20-task CIFAR-100 and 86.99% on CUB-200. Across three benchmarks in the matched component study, its mean final accuracy differs from an independently trained stored-feature counterpart by at most 0.07 percentage points. Ablations show that improved task coverage need not improve classification and adapter composition also matters. On held-out classes, competitor-centered likelihood scores improve novelty AUROC over raw likelihood without altering routing ranks. These results support statistical memory as an alternative to example-retention approaches in the evaluated settings, while identifying task ambiguity as an ongoing limitation.
authors: Alireza Heidari, Thomas Veasey, Mariano Tepper
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of selecting the appropriate adapter when multiple frozen adapters are available.
Models classes with Gaussian statistics in a frozen representation for adapter routing.
Accumulated feature moments exactly recover a class-balanced ridge classifier for fixed training features.
Achieves 88.55% on 20-task CIFAR-100 and 86.99% on CUB-200; it closely matches stored-feature performance across three benchmarks.
Improves novelty detection with competitor-centered likelihood scores, while task ambiguity remains a limitation.

papers.title: The Geometry Is the Memory: Task-Density Routing for Continual LoRA

papers.abstract: Most vision-language models (VLMs) specialize in offline video understanding; in contrast, their post-trained versions, streaming VLMs, can perform live interactions. We investigate whether streaming VLMs can replace their offline parent models on offline tasks. Such replacement could reduce deployment costs and improve efficiency. We propose Streaming Tax to systematically evaluate streaming VLMs on offline tasks. Our exploration spans three core dimensions: understanding, trustworthiness, and generalization across 15 benchmarks. Our findings reveal a critical gap between offline capability preservation and practical replaceability. This gap emerges at two stages: streaming adaptation can alter trustworthy behavior even when offline understanding is largely preserved, while the native streaming protocol can introduce further performance losses. Our analyses show that some of these losses arise from restricted access to historical visual evidence and failures to deliver usable responses. Importantly, regarding safety, streaming models often leave both harmful and legitimate requests unanswered rather than genuinely refusing unsafe ones. We then propose Stream++, a training-free plugin to improve streaming VLMs on offline tasks.
authors: Zhi Yang, Junzhou Chen, Jindong Wang
bullets: Evaluates streaming VLMs on offline tasks across understanding, trustworthiness, and generalization using 15 benchmarks.
Finds two sources of performance loss: streaming adaptation can change trustworthy behavior, and the native streaming protocol can limit visual history and response usability.
Shows that safety behavior often manifests as unanswered requests—including legitimate ones—rather than appropriate refusal of harmful requests.
Introduces Stream++, a training-free plugin designed to improve streaming VLM performance on offline tasks.

papers.abstract: A looped language model repeatedly applies the same block to its hidden state before predicting each token. The number of passes is its recurrent depth. Increasing this depth gives the model more computation per token with the same parameters. Can the shared block learn from the predictions it makes at greater depth? Following prior work, we retrofit pretrained OLMo-2-1B with a shared recurrent block and continue mid-training over varying recurrent depths. In the four-pass model, additional passes mainly redistribute probability among tokens that already rank highly after one pass. We use the continuations generated at greater depth to train only the shared block through a single pass, without reference answers or correctness filtering. We call this transfer preference write-back. Write-back further improves one-pass and multi-pass accuracy on most tasks. At their target depths, the updated models outperform a non-recurrent control matched for mid-training data and token budget on all six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, with a mean relative gain in accuracy of up to 46.2% across tasks. At four-pass inference, one-pass training outperforms full-depth training on the same targets in the model with input injection. This advantage disappears in the matched model without injection. On GSM8K, using the updated block only on passes two through four recovers nearly the entire four-pass gain, showing that an update learned in one pass can improve later applications of the same block.
authors: Hui Chen, Joshua Elsdon, Can Goksen
bullets: Increasing recurrent depth adds per-token computation while keeping parameters shared.
Deeper passes mostly reweight tokens already favored after the first pass.
Preference write-back trains the shared block from deeper continuations using no reference answers or correctness filtering.
Updated models outperform matched non-recurrent controls across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, with reported mean relative gains up to 46.2%.
A one-pass-learned update can improve later passes; the benefit depends on whether input injection is used.

papers.abstract: World models typically predict future observations in pixel or latent space, limiting their ability to directly represent true 3D scene evolution. We present SplatWAM (Splatting World Action Model), a generative world model that learns action-conditioned dynamics directly over compact 3D Gaussian primitives. A tokenizer SplatWAM-T first encodes a variable number of unposed views into a fixed budget of Gaussian tokens. A dynamics model SplatWAM-D then predicts future Gaussian states in a single forward pass per action, using log-Euclidean covariance coordinates and differentiable rendering supervision to facilitate learning in an explicit 3D space. Each predicted state can be rasterized from arbitrary viewpoints, enforcing a shared 3D representation across views by construction. On OGBench Scene, SplatWAM renders novel views 12x faster than video world models (~80 FPS on an RTX 5090) with up to 2.0 dB higher PSNR. We further introduce SplatWAM-P, a lightweight flow-matching policy head jointly trained with the dynamics model. Across 8 task suites, model-free Gaussian-token policies outperform pixel-based counterparts by up to 24.8 percentage points. SplatWAM-P improves over Latent Particle World Model (LPWM) by 12 percentage points and matches HIQL without a learned value function. On LIBERO, our ~1B model outperforms WorldVLA (~7B) and the robot-pretrained OpenVLA (~7B), while matching OpenVLA-OFT when both are trained without large-scale robot pretraining. Code and checkpoints will be released.
authors: Frank Tsu-Fang Lu, Karthik Sundar Senthilkumar, Christopher Thirgood, Oscar Mendez, Simon Hadfield
bullets: Encodes variable numbers of unposed views into a fixed set of Gaussian tokens, then predicts future Gaussian states per action.
Uses explicit 3D dynamics, log-Euclidean covariance coordinates, and differentiable rendering to maintain consistent representations across viewpoints.
Renders novel views about 12× faster than video world models at roughly 80 FPS, with up to 2.0 dB higher PSNR on OGBench Scene.
Its jointly trained flow-matching policy improves over LPWM by 12 percentage points and reaches performance comparable to HIQL across task suites.
On LIBERO, the roughly 1B-parameter model outperforms larger WorldVLA and robot-pretrained OpenVLA models under the reported settings.

papers.abstract: Scenes inside a scattering medium contain solid surfaces, such as the seabed or rocks, and a semi-transparent medium, such as water, fog, or smoke. Recent Gaussian-based methods produce realistic images of scenes in scattering media, but traces of the medium can remain visible in surface-only renders. Neural fields separate surfaces and medium more accurately, but they are slow to train and difficult to edit. Both approaches evaluate the medium only along camera rays, so its effects along reflected and refracted rays are not modeled. These limitations prevent reliable surface recovery, independent editing of surfaces and the medium, and consistent rendering of inserted objects. We present FoamSurf, a hybrid representation that models surfaces with planar Gaussian surfels and the medium with space-filling Voronoi cells. A single differentiable ray tracer composites both along arbitrary rays, while training priors keep them separate without segmentation masks. Across real underwater scenes, synthetic scenes, and dense fog, FoamSurf achieves image quality on par with the state of the art and the most accurate surface-medium separation among the compared methods. The recovered components can be removed, edited, or stylized independently, and the same reconstruction supports inserted mesh objects with attenuation and scattering along both direct and reflected or refracted rays. Together, these capabilities enable scene restoration, editing, and composition within a single reconstructed model. Project page: https://grzegorzwilczynski.com/foamsurf/
authors: Grzegorz Wilczy\'nski, Julia Farganus, Krzysztof Byrski, Rafa{\l} Tobiasz, Miko{\l}aj Zieli\'nski, Dominik Belter, Przemys{\l}aw Spurek
bullets: Addresses residual medium artifacts, slow training, difficult editing, and ray-limited medium modeling in existing methods.
Represents surfaces as planar Gaussian surfels and the medium as space-filling Voronoi cells.
Uses one differentiable ray tracer to composite both components along arbitrary rays, with training priors instead of segmentation masks.
Across underwater, synthetic, and foggy scenes, matches state-of-the-art image quality and provides the most accurate surface–medium separation among compared methods.
Supports independent removal, editing, and stylization, plus inserted objects with attenuation and scattering along direct and indirect rays.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of FoamSurf. Surfels (left, bottom) hold the surfaces and Voronoi cells (left, top) hold the water. One differentiable ray tracer visits surfel hits and cell boundaries in their order along the ray. It tracks one transmittance for the direct signal and one for the backscatter (bottom plot). Each medium segment lowers them at its own rates, and each surfel hit lowers both. The tracer also renders the surface alone, the medium alone, and the surfel opacity. The loss compares the rendered view with the photo. Its gradients update both representations, and densification and pruning adapt the surfels.

Figure 7. Lego with three surrounding clouds. Rows show the full scene, object, and medium, with PSNR against separate ground truth. All methods share initial surface points. papers.tldr: FoamSurf jointly reconstructs surfaces and scattering media with editable, differentiable rendering that models effects along direct, reflected, and refracted rays.

papers.abstract: Tracking motion capture with a whole-body musculoskeletal model means coordinating hundreds of muscles through contact, and current controllers take hours to days of GPU time to train, so every tuning decision is expensive. SuperMimic trains a tracking policy by backpropagating through the rollouts of a learned world model. We extend it to MS-Human-700 (700 muscles) and MyoFullBody (354 muscles), with MuJoCo's activation dynamics inside the world model. To make its training fast, our recipe takes the speedups developed for the Unitree G1, replaces three of their settings that fail on muscles, and adds four changes of our own: observations without muscle geometry, data collection concurrent with the updates, Beta exploration noise that keeps every excitation in $[0,1]$, and 50 Hz control. On one RTX 5090 it trains MS-Human-700 in 6.3 minutes to the held-out return that SuperMimic's published hyperparameters reach in 3.9 hours, 37$\times$ sooner, and in 20 minutes to lower tracking errors than theirs after 10 hours. It trains MyoFullBody 34$\times$ sooner without retuning. Ablations show what is specific to muscles: a higher policy learning rate stalls half of the runs, and clipped Gaussian noise adds a tonic co-contraction that Beta noise avoids. Finally, refining the policy's actions through the world model at test time lowers the position error by a further 26% with no held-out clip failing, and reaches the same return after 5.1 instead of 6.3 minutes of training. Code, the training recipe and videos are on the project page https://muscle-supermimic.beanpow.top.
authors: Kaibo He, Maciej Bakowicz, Shihe Zhou, Yusen Feng, Yanan Sui, Dhanush Radhakrishnan
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost of coordinating hundreds of muscles under contact for motion-capture tracking.
Extends SuperMimic with MuJoCo activation dynamics to MS-Human-700 and MyoFullBody, plus muscle-specific training changes including Beta exploration noise and 50 Hz control.
Trains MS-Human-700 37× faster than the published SuperMimic setup and MyoFullBody 34× faster, without retuning.
Test-time action refinement reduces position error by a further 26% and reaches the same return with less training.
Ablations identify muscle-specific failure modes: overly high policy learning rates can stall training, while clipped Gaussian noise causes tonic co-contraction.

The world model fϕ predicts velocity increments and contacts and integrates the positions semi-implicitly and the activations by MuJoCo’s own rule. In the policy and critic update, the tracking return Ĵ (Eq. (6)) of an H-step rollout of πθ through fϕ from start states of B is backpropagated into πθ . The collection runs on a second CUDA stream concurrently with the two updates. At test time, the policy’s action is refined by gradient ascent on J through fϕ (Sec. 3.4). papers.abstract: Reliable deployment of Vision Language Models (VLMs) requires that a model's expressed confidence remain grounded in what it can actually see, and that it recognize when the visual evidence is too ambiguous to commit to a confident response. Standard post-training uses outcome reward models (ORMs) that supervise only the final decision, rewarding a confident answer regardless of whether the image supports one, while existing methods either tend to detect uncertainty post-hoc or assume an objective verdict always exists. We instead split multimodal reasoning into two stages: perception, where the model must factually describe the scene, and calibration, where it must judge whether that evidence is sufficient to commit to a conclusion. We introduce HumblePRM, a lightweight process reward model (PRM) that scores each stage independently, rewarding agreement between evidence and expressed confidence rather than outcome correctness alone. Training with HumblePRM increases abstention due to uncertainty on ambiguous inputs considerably while leaving accuracy on clear images roughly unchanged. We also find that the improvement transfers to Gemma 4 E4B, a larger, popular edge model. Our findings show that process reward supervision is a promising route to VLMs with better calibrated abstention, ensuring more reliability rather than unpredictable behavior.
authors: Saket Reddy, Ke Yang, ChengXiang Zhai
bullets: Targets a weakness of outcome-only reward models, which may favor confident answers even without sufficient visual evidence.
Splits reasoning into perception—describing the scene—and calibration—deciding whether the evidence supports a conclusion.
Uses a lightweight process reward model to score these stages independently and align confidence with observed evidence.
Increases uncertainty-driven abstention on ambiguous inputs while keeping accuracy on clear images roughly unchanged.
The improvement transfers to the larger Gemma 4 E4B edge model.

figures.caption: Figure 1: HumblePRM vs. ORM supervision on an ambiguous input. The perception step correctly describes how the capsules lack any labeling or context, but the calibration step declares the scene clearly safe and attempts to help without verifying that the capsules are really vitamins, potentially providing dangerous medical advice. The ORM scores only the outcome and cannot separate a misread image from a correctly read one that is miscalibrated, while HumblePRM scores each step independently and attributes the failure to calibration.

Table 3: Gemma 4 E4B study, testing whether the effect transfers across model family and scale. The training pipeline, reward models, and evaluation are identical to Table 2; only the policy backbone changes.

Table 7: Reward model training example for a clearly safe image paired with safe context, illustrating an incorrect perception step. The perception step wrongly identifies the image as blurry, and the calibration step then reasons validly from that false premise; because each step is scored conditional on the steps preceding it, the calibration step is labeled correct even though the trace as a whole is wrong. The PRM receives a label at every step separator, allowing the failure to be localized to perception, while the ORM receives one only at the final step.

Table 6: Reward model training example for an ambiguous image, with a correct perception step, calibration step, and response. The PRM receives a label at every step separator, while the ORM receives one only at the final step.

Table 8: Reward model training example for a clearly unsafe image, illustrating an incorrect calibration step. The perception step describes the scene faithfully, correctly identifying the shattered storefront and the explicit forced-entry indicator, but the calibration step overrides that evidence by inventing a benign professional intent and declaring the request permissible. The response then acts on that verdict. The ORM sees only that the trace ended badly, while the PRM sees a label at every step separator and attributes the failure to calibration rather than to perception.

Table 1: Composition of the two training datasets: 3,000 step-labeled traces for the reward models and 2,500 image–prompt pairs without CoT for the policy, spanning the same four input categories. Clearly safe, safe context pairs a benign image with a benign request, Clearly safe, unsafe context pairs a benign image with a harmful request, Clearly unsafe covers images that are explicitly harmful in and of themselves, and Ambiguous covers images whose visual evidence is insufficient to support either a safe or an unsafe verdict. Reward model traces are split by which stage is corrupted; CP/IP denote correct/incorrect perception, CC/IC correct/incorrect calibration.

Table 4: Help vs. abstain rates for Qwen and Gemma (positive class = abstain). TPR = ambiguous images where model abstains, TNR = clear safe images where model helps, FPR = clear safe images where model abstains (the over-abstention rate), & FNR = ambiguous images where model helps. In both families, the PRM model achieves much better TPR on ambiguous images with only a mild increase in over-abstention (FPR).

Table 5: Examples of intrinsically ambiguous images. Each image supports at least two plausible readings that call for different responses, one of which is unsafe, and nothing visible in the image settles which reading is correct.

Table 2: Qwen 3.5 2B policy model results. MSSBench measures accuracy on clear images; filtered MMSafetyBench measures the rate of abstention attributed specifically to visual ambiguity on ambiguous images. Both reward models are Qwen 3.5 0.8B trained on identical data, differing only in whether supervision is applied at every reasoning step or at the outcome alone.
Table 9: Comparison of ORM and PRM reasoning traces across three multimodal prompts, showing differences in perception and calibration steps and the resulting refusal or compliance behavior.

papers.title: HumblePRM: Improving VLM Abstention in Ambiguous Situations through Process Reward Modeling
papers.tldr: HumblePRM improves VLM reliability by rewarding evidence-grounded confidence and appropriate abstention when images are ambiguous.

papers.abstract: Visual reasoning requires models to identify relevant visual evidence and use it to derive correct answers. Outcomebased reinforcement learning (RL) faces two key challenges in this regime: it yields no learning signal when perceptual errors cause all sampled responses to fail, and it broadcasts a uniform advantage across every token within a response. Conversely, while visual self-distillation offers dense guidance from evidence-centered image crops, student learning from token distributions alone often fails to elicit correct final answers. Motivated by an audit of training rollouts that exposes these complementary failure modes, we introduce ViCARD (Visual Credit Assignment with RewardGated Distillation), which integrates per-token visual supervision with verified correctness rewards. For each rollout group, we leverage a teacher with its input image cropped to the relevant visual area, and use this to provide per-token supervision to the student while also valuing correctness. If all sampled rollouts fail, ViCARD samples an additional crop-teacher answer and activates on-policy distillation only if that answer is correct. Together, these mechanisms provide fine-grained visual credit within informative reward groups and a learning signal for otherwise uninformative all-fail groups. Extensive comparisons across model scales demonstrate that ViCARD improves fine-grained visual reasoning performance over RL and distillation baselines, while retaining broad visual reasoning capabilities.
authors: Zijian Huang, Jiasi Chen
bullets: Addresses two RL limitations: all-fail rollouts yield no signal, and uniform response-level advantages obscure token-level credit.
Uses a teacher model on a relevant image crop to provide fine-grained visual supervision alongside correctness rewards.
For all-fail rollout groups, activates on-policy distillation only when an additional crop-teacher answer is verified correct.
Experiments across model scales show improved fine-grained visual reasoning over RL and distillation baselines while preserving broad visual reasoning.
Scope: relies on identifying relevant visual crops and verified teacher answers for corrective supervision.

papers.abstract: Concept drift detection is a fundamental component of data stream learning, yet its empirical evaluation remains based on loosely defined protocols, ambiguous alarm semantics, and inconsistent metrics. We propose a principled benchmark grounded in an explicit formulation of drift observability and alarm semantics. Our framework introduces finite detection windows and repeated alarms, enabling a clear separation between detection accuracy, timeliness, and stability, and employs a reproducible observer to provide a controlled and interpretable performance signal. Building on this formulation, we define normalized evaluation metrics and a composite score addressing limitations of existing measures. We validate the framework through a large-scale stress-testing evaluation of 10 detectors across 9 learner configurations and 16 datasets.
authors: Lorenzo Iovine, Giacomo Ziffer, Emanuele Della Valle
bullets: Addresses ambiguous alarm semantics, loosely defined protocols, and inconsistent metrics in drift-detector evaluation.
Defines drift observability and alarm semantics using finite detection windows and repeated alarms.
Separates detection accuracy, timeliness, and stability, with a reproducible observer for controlled evaluation.
Introduces normalized metrics and a composite score to address limitations of existing measures.
Stress-tests 10 detectors across 9 learner configurations and 16 datasets.

papers.abstract: We propose the Audio-Visual Query Transformer (AVQFormer), a highly efficient architecture built upon a 2.7B parameter LLM featuring a fixed-length $K=16$ semantic alignment module, stabilized via Adaptive Self-Critical Sequence Training (ASCST) with Entropy Regularization. Multimodal Large Language Models (LLMs) often rely on global audio representations to compensate for inefficient, frame-based visual encoders. While our Phase 1 prompted evaluations demonstrate that the Multimodal Base Model achieves strong deep semantic alignment (scoring 0.889 on BERTScore F1), optimizing this architecture for legacy metrics reveals a performance gap. We explore this gap as a hypothesis we term temporal alignment friction: a conflict where global audio representations disrupt the chronological sequence of visual frames, leading to penalties under visually-focused evaluation metrics. Consequently, by stripping away the audio, our Video-Only ablation conforms more closely to this rigid syntax, achieving 63.0 CIDEr. While trailing larger models such as Qwen2.5-VL (67.4 CIDEr), this establishes a strong baseline for sub-3B parameter LLM-based models. This indicates that CIDEr, as applied to datasets such as MSR-VTT, may exhibit a bias toward visually grounded syntax, limiting its ability to fully capture multimodal semantic richness.
authors: Albert Chiwara, Erhan Guven
bullets: The work proposes a fixed-length (K=16) Audio-Visual Query Transformer built on a 2.7B-parameter LLM.
Adaptive Self-Critical Sequence Training with entropy regularization stabilizes reinforcement-learning optimization.
The authors hypothesize “temporal alignment friction”: global audio features can disrupt visual chronology and hurt visually focused metrics.
Removing audio yields 63.0 CIDEr, below Qwen2.5-VL’s 67.4 but providing a strong sub-3B baseline.
The results suggest CIDEr on datasets such as MSR-VTT may undervalue multimodal semantic richness.

papers.title: A Semantics-First Approach to Multimodal Video Captioning with Frozen Encoders and Stabilized Reinforcement Learning

papers.abstract: Agile humanoid locomotion requires controllers that can adapt to rapidly changing motion demands while remaining stable and robust. Recent locomotion controllers are typically designed with either a dense reward that is carefully shaped to encourage steps and penalize falling, or by using a reference tracking reward which teaches the controller to follow predetermined motions. Once a behavior that maximizes the reward is discovered, the controller ceases to learn. While generally stable, reference tracking methods focus on motor control separately from motion generation. Self-play has been proven as an effective technique for superhuman performance on several multiagent games like Go, Starcraft, hide-and-seek, and capture-the-flag. We train neural networks to play the game of multiagent tag in a physics simulator to study if new motion generation and control strategies can emerge through sparse feedback and competitive self-play. We present MJTag, a task suite for role-conditioned locomotion during competitive pursuit-evasion. Our model is a role-conditioned policy for a low-level locomotion controller and optional planar velocity commands. MJTag's league-based play with sparse feedback enables a locomotion controller to adopt new strategies, including dodging, sprinting, and tackling.
authors: Nathan A. C. Hogg, Matt Hyatt, Neil Klingensmith, George K. Thiruvathukal
bullets: Addresses the limited adaptability of dense-reward and reference-tracking locomotion controllers.
Introduces MJTag, a role-conditioned pursuit-evasion task suite for locomotion learning.
Trains a low-level locomotion policy with optional planar velocity commands in a physics simulator.
Uses competitive, league-based self-play with sparse feedback rather than fixed motion references.
The learned controller exhibits strategies such as dodging, sprinting, and tackling.

papers.tldr: MJTag uses sparse-reward, league-based self-play in a simulated multiagent tag game to pretrain humanoid locomotion controllers that develop agile pursuit and evasion behaviors.

papers.abstract: An RGB-D camera that films an object being moved, often from one viewpoint, sees one side of it and how its parts move. We present ArtKit, which takes such a video as input to create an articulated model with complete parts, a kinematic tree, and typed joints. Our central idea is generating the hidden geometry and verifying it against what the camera sees. A generative part prior proposes complete, part-decomposed geometry based on the first frame. Point tracks, grouped into rigid trajectories, split and merge the generated parts into links. We then fit revolute and prismatic joints, with a visibility-aware energy ensuring that the articulated model explains the depth observed across the video. A rule checks against the video to choose between synchronous group fits and per-frame chain fits, so that one pipeline serves a diverse range of articulated objects, such as household items and robotic hands. Finally, we regenerate each link of the chosen fit as one part and keep it wherever it agrees better with the observations. We evaluate on Articulate-100 and on HArt, a new benchmark of 60 PartNet-Mobility objects and 8 robotic hands and grippers rendered as RGB-D videos with ground-truth parts and joints. ArtKit reduces the axis and part motion errors of the strongest baseline by more than half on the objects, as well as the axis error on the hands. ArtKit also runs on real recordings and generated videos.
authors: Sylvia Yuan, Dan Wang, Vivian Yu, Ravi Ramamoorthi, Xinrui Cui
bullets: Addresses incomplete visibility when objects are moved and filmed from one viewpoint.
Uses a generative part prior, rigid point trajectories, and motion-based splitting/merging to form links.
Fits revolute and prismatic joints with visibility-aware depth consistency.
Chooses between synchronous-group and per-frame chain fitting, then regenerates links to better match observations.

Evaluated on Articulate-100, the HArt benchmark, and real recordings; it substantially reduces reported axis and part-motion errors versus the strongest baseline on benchmark objects, and reduces axis error on hands.

Point tracks are grouped into robust rigid trajectories, with tracks that no rigid body explains left out, the generated parts are split and merged into links, and the links give the articulation graph. [O] Observation-driven articulation (Sec. 3.3). Typed joints are fitted to the depth of every frame with track and smoothness terms by a pool of synchronous group fits and per-frame chain fits, each giving per-frame joint amounts qk,f . The video alone is used to select one fit. Each selected link then re-prompts X-Part with its own box, and the regenerated part is kept where it fits the link’s points better.

papers.abstract: AI models vary enormously in capability and price. Model routing exploits this by sending easier tasks to cheaper models. However, a single agentic task often combines easy and difficult subtasks, making one model choice for the entire task inefficient. We introduce partial routing, which guides a frontier lead model to delegate suitable subtasks to a cheaper worker model. From both models' past runs, we identify recurring subtasks and measure each model's quality and cost on them. These measurements produce delegation guidance, with a parameter, $\delta$, controlling how much is delegated. The lead decides when and what to delegate during execution, without training either model. On held-out tasks from ViBench and Terminal-Bench 4.0, partial routing achieves higher mean task performance than the lead alone and task-level routing. With $\delta = 0.75$, it raises the lead's ViBench score from 70.2 to 78.5 at 19% lower cost, and its Terminal-Bench pass rate from 54% to 61% at similar cost. Giving the lead only the subtask breakdown, without a worker, also reduces cost on both benchmarks and raises the Terminal-Bench pass rate. These results show that analysis of past runs can support more efficient planning and more effective delegation, with little cost and implementation overhead.
authors: Siddharth Arya, Kshitij Jain
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of choosing one model for tasks containing both easy and difficult subtasks.
Uses past runs to estimate recurring subtask quality and cost for each model, producing delegation guidance controlled by δ.
The lead model decides during execution which subtasks to delegate; neither model requires training.
On ViBench, performance increased from 70.2 to 78.5 with 19% lower cost; on Terminal-Bench, pass rate rose from 54% to 61% at similar cost.
Scope: evaluated on held-out ViBench and Terminal-Bench 4.0 tasks, with little implementation overhead.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces partial routing for agentic workflows, delegating subtasks based on past performance, a form of test-time optimization and online adaptation.
papers.title: Partial Routing: Trace-Tuned Delegation for Resource-Efficient Agentic Workflows
papers.tldr: Partial routing lets a capable lead agent delegate selected subtasks to a cheaper model, improving performance while reducing cost without additional training.

papers.abstract: The goal of continual learning (CL) is to adapt to new data (plasticity) while retaining the knowledge acquired from old data (stability). Existing methods are explicitly designed to focus on balancing stability and plasticity to mitigate the challenge of catastrophic forgetting while promoting learning. However, the impact of order and nature of samples from the new data that the network is trained on remains an under explored factor. We argue that a CL algorithm should have the ability to rank incoming samples in terms of their relationship with prior data and their effect on the learning process. In this work, we investigate if scoring and prioritizing incoming data based on their semantic relationships with the model's current knowledge can benefit CL. We propose SACK, short for Sequentially Acquiring Concept Knowledge, a plug and play technique for continual learning methods. SACK dissects categorical knowledge of the model into fine-grained concepts, computes the relationships between previously learned concepts and new concepts in each experience, and uses this relationship knowledge for prioritizing new samples. Experiments across several types of CL methods (regularization, replay, and prompt based) in class incremental and task incremental settings demonstrate that integration of SACK not only improves accuracy and reduces forgetting but also handles long tail distribution, helps focus on semantically interpretable regions, and yields better calibrated and robust models compared to prior approaches.
authors: Shivanand Kundargi, Kowshik Thopalli, Tejas Gokhale
bullets: Addresses the underexplored impact of new-sample order and content on stability and plasticity.
Decomposes categorical knowledge into fine-grained concepts and relates old concepts to concepts in each new experience.
Uses these relationships to rank and prioritize samples as a plug-and-play addition to existing CL methods.
Across regularization-, replay-, and prompt-based methods, SACK improves accuracy, reduces forgetting, and supports long-tail data.
It also promotes semantically interpretable focus and produces better-calibrated, more robust models, according to the abstract.

Each method is evaluated with three independent class-order permutations, with shaded regions indicating variability across permutations. In all cases, SACK consistently improves both mean accuracy and stability across experiences, demonstrating that the order-robustness observed with iCaRL in the main paper generalizes across diverse CL frameworks.

Figure 1: Overview of SACK: Sequentially Acquiring Concept Knowledge. Given a model after experience t, we extract human-interpretable visual concepts from its internal representations and compare them with the concepts describing the incoming classes. SACK computes class-wise semantic relevance scores that prioritize examples whose concepts align closely with previously learned knowledge. These concept-aligned sampling weights guide the training of experience t+1, forming a lightweight curriculum that improves accuracy, stability, and interpretability across continual learning streams.

Figure 10: Effect of varying the concept-selection threshold τ on SACK with different continual learning baselines (LwF (Li & Hoiem, 2017), CODA-Prompt (Smith et al., 2023), DER and DER++ (Buzzega et al., 2020)). papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown promise for general-purpose robotic manipulation, but adapting to changing environmental conditions still remains challenging. Recent test-time steering methods have shown promise in enabling adaptive VLA policies by utilizing additional computation during deployment. In this paper, we consider best-of-$N$ test-time steering for VLA models, where multiple action candidates are sampled from a fixed policy and a verifier is used to select the best one during deployment. We show that increasing $N$ does not always improve performance when the verifier is inaccurate, and can favor candidates whose scores exploit prediction errors, a form of reward hacking. We study this effect on 60 LIBERO-Safety task-level cases using a $\pi_{0.5}$ policy, with ten repetitions per case. We introduce controlled errors in a MuJoCo trajectory verifier and show that as $N$ increases, selected candidate rewards diverge from the accurate verifier rewards, leading to reward hacking. We also show that verifier calibration and softmax-based candidate selection can mitigate reward hacking in some settings.
authors: Vanshaj Khattar, Jing Liu, Toshiaki Koike-Akino, Ming Jin, Ye Wang
bullets: Studies best-of-N steering, which samples multiple actions and selects one using a trajectory verifier.
Shows that larger N can increase reward hacking: selected candidates exploit verifier prediction errors.
Evaluates the effect across 60 LIBERO-Safety task-level cases with ten repetitions each using a π₀.₅ policy.
Controlled MuJoCo verifier errors reveal divergence between selected candidates’ predicted and accurate verifier rewards.
Verifier calibration and softmax-based selection can mitigate reward hacking in some settings.

papers.abstract: AI agents built on large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong capabilities in automated decision-making. However, LLMs may produce incorrect answers with high confidence, limiting their applicability in decisions that affect individuals and organizations. Reliable confidence scores are necessary to gate such decisions, and existing estimates are frequently unavailable or too coarse to support effective gating. This work uses supervised learning to train models to predict the correctness of LLM-generated answers, enabling automated confident responses and routing uncertain ones for human review. A linear confidence score head is fitted to the final-layer hidden state of the frozen LLM backbone, and text-only metamodels are trained as an alternative for closed models. All results come from a single 2B-parameter backbone, on graded answers that are about 98% SQuAD and the remainder TruthfulQA. Against multiple baselines, the confidence score head outperforms all baselines and metamodels, automating the largest fraction of the workload at high accuracy targets. Prompted confidence scores can appear well calibrated yet lack the resolution needed for thresholding. Although transferability to unseen datasets is modest, the confidence score head remains the most robust approach. The proposed confidence scoring framework enhances the safety of automating LLM-based agents and can be adapted to gate other properties, including safety or compliance.
authors: Luiz G. A. Alves, Aaron Vermeersch
bullets: LLMs can give incorrect answers with high confidence, making reliable confidence estimates important for high-stakes automation.
The approach trains a linear confidence head on the frozen backbone’s final-layer hidden state; text-only metamodels support closed models.
On graded answers drawn mostly from SQuAD and partly from TruthfulQA, the confidence head outperforms evaluated baselines and metamodels for high-accuracy gating.
Prompted confidence scores may appear calibrated but lack sufficient resolution for thresholding.
Transfer to unseen datasets is modest, though the confidence head is the most robust approach in the study.

figures.caption: Figure 2: LLM architecture and new confidence score head. The confidence score head reads the final-layer hidden state h ∈ R2304 at the last token of the concatenated prompt and generated answer and maps it to a probability by standardizing it coordinate-wise to z, then applying a linear layer and a sigmoid. The LLM backbone (gemma-2-2b-it, 26 layers, 4-bit) is frozen during training, and only the parameters of the confidence score head are updated. The answer is generated autoregressively under the output schema and appended to the sequence before the confidence score head reads it. The last position attends over the whole sequence so that a single vector can depend on the answer, the question, and the context together.

Figure 4: Automation performance of the confidence score estimation approaches. a) Accuracy of the automated answers as a function of the acceptance threshold. b) Coverage, i.e., the fraction of answers that are automated, as a function of the acceptance threshold. The star in both panels marks a shared operating point. At threshold 0.53, the confidence score head’s automated answers are 95% accurate and cover 62% of the workload.

Figure 3: ROC curves comparing the classification performance of the confidence score estimation approaches. Values in parentheses indicate each model’s ROC-AUC. The confidence score head is shown in red, the three metamodels in blue, the typed-decision model in green, and the remaining baselines in different shades of gray.

Figure 1: AI agent decision-making. The same agent in both panels retrieves, reasons, and produces an answer. a) All answers are acted on, and every wrong answer reaches the action unchecked. Alternatively, every answer can be routed to a reviewer in a human-in-the-loop approach. In this case, throughput is capped by the reviewers, and no answer is acted on without review. b) A confidence score for each answer gates the action. Answers above a threshold are acted on without review, while those below are routed for human review. The threshold value shown is illustrative.

Table 1: Calibration performance of the confidence score estimation approaches. ECE = expected calibration error. ECE, Brier score, and Reliability are better when lower, whereas Resolution, which measures discrimination, is better when higher. Brackets are 95% bootstrap intervals. papers.abstract: A developer who reproduces a video model's error on a short clip can replay that clip after an update. How often does a correct clip answer mean the original test now passes? On 960 prespecified CG-Bench questions, we updated from Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct to Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct. Accuracy on a 64-frame sample spanning the full video rose from 27.9% to 33.3%. Before scoring the newer model, we froze 388 clips on which the older model reproduced its exact reference error. The updated model passed the reference on 51 of 116 clip passes (44.0%, 95% Wilson interval 35.3-53.0%) and on 16 of 272 clip failures (5.9%). Closing cases on a clip pass would have declared 65 unresolved reference failures fixed. Requiring a clip pass would have missed 16 of the 67 reference fixes (23.9%). In a separate 1,028-video study with different checkpoints and direct option scoring, only 15 clips passed, and the 16-frame reference confirmed one. For the generated-answer update, the short replay identified cases worth checking, while the original input remained necessary to verify individual fixes.
authors: Raj Shan
bullets: On 960 CG-Bench questions, accuracy rose from 27.9% to 33.3% after updating from Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct to Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct.
Among 388 clips reproducing the older model’s exact error, a clip pass matched a reference pass 44.0% of the time, while a clip failure still contained a reference fix 5.9% of the time.
Using clip passes to close cases would have falsely marked 65 unresolved failures as fixed; requiring a clip pass would have missed 16 of 67 actual fixes.
A separate study found only one confirmed fix among 15 clip passes, reinforcing that the original input is needed for individual verification.

papers.abstract: Four-dimensional cone-beam computed tomography (4D-CBCT) images the anatomy of a breathing patient, but sees each breathing phase from only a few angles. Breathing, however, is a smooth motion that repeats; it has a phase. Existing methods exploit this either by reconstructing the anatomy as a function of the breathing phase, often through bins, or by estimating smooth dynamic motions in time. Yet none of these grounds one smooth motion in the phase. We thus propose to share projections across breathing phases with splines. Specifically, we represent the 4D volume with dynamic Gaussians whose motion uses B-splines in space and time. We ground the motion state in the respiratory phase, which we read from well-studied conventional surrogates. Projections at the same phase in different breathing cycles then constrain the same anatomy and motion. On simulated lung scans, our method, BreathSplat, outperforms recent dynamic methods in reconstruction and motion accuracy, including those given the ground-truth phase. We further show qualitatively, on two real patient scans, that our method provides clearer reconstructions than the state of the art.
authors: Sujong Shin, Sang-Il Choi, Kwang Moo Yi
bullets: Addresses sparse-angle imaging of anatomy undergoing repeated breathing motion.
Represents the 4D volume with dynamic Gaussians whose spatial and temporal motion follows B-splines.
Uses conventional respiratory surrogates to ground motion states in breathing phase.
On simulated lung scans, it improves reconstruction and motion accuracy over recent dynamic methods, even those given ground-truth phase.
Qualitative results on two real patient scans show clearer reconstructions than the state of the art.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview. Before optimization we use a conventional surrogate to retrieve the respiratory phase of every projection. We deform one set of canonical Gaussians with the low-rank B-spline motion of DIGS [18], whose temporal B-splines we define on this phase, making the motion periodic and aligned to breathing cycles by construction. We then fit both the motion and the Gaussians with the projections, with a TV prior considering the edges.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison on a real patient scan. We show the reconstruction outcome for SPARE (Varian patient 1, phase bin 06). The first and third rows show axial and coronal slices, and the others are the zoom-ins. All columns use the same slice locations and display windows. Fu et al. and STNF4D are provided with the SPARE phase bins. Our method clearly reconstructs the pulmonary vessels and the bone edges, while other methods show lower quality.

Figure 3. Qualitative comparison. The first and third rows show axial and coronal slices of DIR Case 3 with irregular breathing, and the second and fourth rows show the zoom-ins. All methods use the same time point, slice locations, and display windows. Our method provides the best reconstruction with fine pulmonary structures.

Figure 5. Qualitative comparison on 4D-Lung and SPARE. The first and third rows of each panel show axial and coronal slices of (a) 4D-Lung Case 4 and (b) SPARE Case 3, both simulated with irregular breathing, and the second and fourth rows show the zoom-ins. All methods within each case use the same time point, slice locations, and display windows. Our method provides the best reconstruction with fine pulmonary structures.

Figure 1. Teaser. Our method reconstructs a real patient scan more sharply than the state of the art. Pulmonary vessels and bone edges that the dynamic baselines blur stay sharp in our reconstruction. Each panel shows the same axial slice of SPARE [43] (Varian patient 3, phase bin 01) with the same display window, and the inset enlarges the marked region.
Figure 6. Evaluation-only body masks. We show the masks for DIR Case 1, 4D-Lung Case 1, and SPARE Case 3. These masks are separate from the body region that we take from V0.

Figure 7. Edges of V0 and of the reference volumes. Comparison of the edge map from the static FDK reconstruction V0 with those from the reference volumes (Sec. 4.1) at three time points in one breathing cycle of simulated SPARE Case 3. Most edges of V0 lie on edges of the reference volumes at all three time points.

Table 1. Comparison with the state of the art. We average the values over the 10 DIR and 4D-Lung cases and all evaluated time points. We mark methods that use ground-truth phase bins with ∗. We also provide the baseline motion error assuming static reconstruction. We mark the best values of each column in bold, excluding our method with the ground-truth phase, which we provide as reference. Our method provides the best performance on every metric.

Table 3. Ablation study. We compare with various modifications of our method on the synthetic data. Accurate grounding is critical to the best performance. Using one value per phase bin to represent motion provides slight degradation, but results in abrupt motion as bins are discontinuous. Implementation choices also provide minor gains. Edge PSNR is the PSNR of voxels within two voxels of edges.

Table 4. Hyperparameter sensitivity. We report the changes in body metrics on the 10 DIR and 4D-Lung cases relative to the selected values. We select the values on the three SPARE cases. All values of K use the same number of projection renderings. On DIR and 4D-Lung, the selected values are within 0.05 dB in body PSNR of the best value in each sweep.

Table 2. Landmark and volume accuracy on real anatomy. We also report the tracking performance (TRE) of expert-annotated landmarks of the five DIR cases, simulated from their real phase volumes. We also report the body PSNR averaged over the 10 phases of the first cycle. We mark methods that use ground-truth phase bins with ∗. We also report the error which a static model would make as reference. Our method tracks the landmarks the best, which also leads to better body PSNR.

papers.title: BreathSplat: Grounding One Smooth Motion in the Breathing Phase for 4D Cone-Beam CT
papers.tldr: BreathSplat reconstructs smooth, phase-grounded 4D-CBCT motion by sharing projections from the same breathing phase across cycles.

papers.abstract: Many hard manipulation tasks come down to a spatial constraint that only a few motions satisfy, such as passing a part through a gap barely wider than itself or separating two interlocked parts. These motions depend on the exact geometry of each scene, so demonstrations and skills recorded elsewhere rarely transfer. We therefore ask: when manipulation hinges on spatial constraints, can robots reason out the right motions? We introduce RoboARC, a benchmark of 90 tasks in six constraint types over rigid and soft materials, on three robots in MuJoCo. Every task is a frozen scene with a physics-based grader and a verified reference solution that replays bit-identically. Each task comes in a Privileged regime, with the full simulator state and resets, and a Standard regime with real-sensor inputs (camera images and proprioception) and a single attempt without resets. We evaluate seven coding agents and four VLA policies, none trained on these tasks. The strongest agent, GPT-6 Astra in Codex, solves 86% of the tasks in the Privileged regime and 43% in the Standard regime, and the four VLA policies, run zero-shot, solve none of their 18 one-arm puzzles. On 15 puzzles that GPT-6 Astra solved in the Privileged regime and failed in the Standard regime, object poses add 4 points and part geometry 13, but both together add 36, from 24% to 60%. Only 7% of the coding agents' failed runs pass more than half of a task, and 53% of the failed runs in the Standard regime are stuck on a single step. Frontier coding agents already reason out the right motions for many of these tasks once they know where the parts are and what shape they have. From their own sensors, in a single attempt, the strongest solves fewer than half of the tasks. The website can be found at https://roboarc.embodied-first-exam.ai
authors: Qineng Wang, Jianwen Lyu, Pingyue Zhang, Reuben Tan, Xiaoyu Huang, Tonghe Zhang, Kangrui Wang, Yelong Shen, Jianfeng Gao, Guanya Shi, Ruohan Zhang, Manling Li
bullets: Introduces 90 physics-graded tasks spanning six spatial-constraint types, rigid and soft materials, and three MuJoCo robots.
Compares seven coding agents and four zero-shot VLA policies under privileged-state and single-attempt sensor-based regimes.
The strongest coding agent solves 86% with privileged state but 43% from camera and proprioceptive inputs; VLA policies solve none of 18 one-arm puzzles.
Combining object poses and part geometry substantially improves performance, while many standard-regime failures get stuck on a single step.
Scope: benchmark results use frozen simulated scenes, physics-based grading, and verified reference solutions.

figures.caption: Figure 2 | Overview of RoboARC. Top: the two regimes share the scene, physics and grader. In the Standard regime a coding agent sends action chunks and receives RGB-D images, joint readings and the instruction, without resets. In the Privileged regime it also reads the full simulator state and may reset. VLA policies run under the Standard rules with RGB images. One grader replays the physics of every run. Bottom: one task per constraint type, from the initial to the solved state.

Figure 3 | Task curation pipeline, shown for interlocked claws 05. Each task is designed at a difficulty rating, frozen as one scene, solved by a verified reference, replayed bit-identically, stress-tested and packaged in both regimes.

Figure 8 | Methods and rollouts of the solved Privileged trials. (a) Share of each agent’s solved trials whose code contains a sampling-based planner, a graph-search planner, a search with simulator rollouts, or scripted waypoints only. (b) Rollouts per solved trial, with the median on the right.

Figure 10 | Four failed runs in the Standard regime: three forms of failed attempts and one way a run ends. Each panel gives the label, the task and the agent, three frames of the run, a quote from the agent’s log and what went wrong. Red rings mark the error, and a magnifier marks a zoomed frame. In the Perception panel the post and the ring are coloured. The Planning and Execution panels are two runs of GPT-6 Astra on the same step, so one constraint can fail in either form.

Figure 10 shows four failed runs of the Standard regime. In the Perception case (GLM, slotted post ring), the agent takes the post for the ring in the wrist camera, so the gripper closes on air. In the Planning case (Astra, fiber bundling), the agent pushes the sheath straight on as planned. The grip holds, but the fibers bend around the ring’s rim. In the Execution case (Astra, the same step in another run), the plan is sound, but the grip slips as the wrist turns and the sheath swings upright. In the Gave up case (Opus, lock picking), the agent stops on its own with about 28 minutes of its time left, citing time. Closing these gaps calls for estimating poses and part geometry from the cameras, planning the key step before acting, and correcting each motion from feedback as it runs.

papers.abstract: Degraded images make vision-language models answer wrongly. Using synthetic paired blur, noise, and low light, we trace which clean image states can still repair those answers from the vision encoder through the language model. In four encoder models, 12 to 23 ranked tokens recover half of the full-patch effect, whereas random orders require four to fifteen times as many; encoder-free Gemma needs 22.2 versus 53.1. Full-block repair expires at a model-specific language-model crossing. The matched reverse-direction intervention is algebraically identical to text-token restoration, so its gap from image restoration measures a redundancy band rather than an independent predictor. A clean-image gray-ablation crossing independently predicts held-out repair with 1.53-layer error, against 3.65 for shared depth. Gemma MMBench has the only large attention-to-repair point gap; Gemma GQA does not. Restormer provides a non-oracle consistency check on two models.
authors: Vishal Bhutani, Prasang Gupta, Sumanth Chundru, Kevin Paul
bullets: Synthetic blur, noise, and low-light degradations are used to trace repair from the vision encoder through the language model.
In four encoder models, 12–23 ranked tokens recover half the full-patch repair effect, while random ordering needs 4–15× more tokens.
Full-block repair ends at a model-specific language-model crossing; encoder-free Gemma requires 22.2 versus 53.1 tokens in the reported comparison.
A clean-image gray-ablation crossing predicts held-out repair with 1.53-layer error, outperforming shared-depth prediction at 3.65 layers.
The attention-to-repair gap is large for Gemma MMBench but not Gemma GQA; Restormer provides a non-oracle check on two models.
