papers.abstract: We present ArtTet, a method that reconstructs an articulated object from multi-view observations of two articulation states and outputs one watertight mesh per rigid part together with the joints that move them. Mesh splatting gives explicit triangles, but it treats the object as one scene. It extracts a single global surface and cannot keep the triangles of different parts apart; the mesh it exports is layered, self-intersecting, and full of holes. ArtTet follows a divide-and-conquer strategy instead. We first divide the object into rigid parts with dynamic- and geometric-constrained articulation and ownership inference. A multibody registration of the two states recovers the parts and their screw joints. Rigid-body rules on attachment, contact, and swept motion then correct joint types and part labels without any part annotation. We then divide space into part cells with an articulated tetrahedral partition, and conquer each cell with its own differentiable signed distance field on a shared tetrahedral grid. In these partitioned marching tetrahedra the fields are mutually exclusive by construction, so the extracted part meshes are closed and never overlap. All part meshes are optimized jointly from the images of both states through the recovered joints. On Articulate-100, ArtTet gives the most accurate axis directions, part motions, and part geometry over all objects among methods that use no part masks, and its part meshes have virtually no open boundary edges. We also show reconstructions of real captures from the SplArt dataset.
authors: Sylvia Yuan, Dan Wang, Ravi Ramamoorthi, Xinrui Cui
bullets: Addresses layered, self-intersecting, and hole-filled meshes produced when articulated objects are reconstructed as a single scene.
Uses two articulation states to infer rigid parts, screw joints, motion, and part ownership without part annotations.
Applies rigid-body rules for attachment, contact, and swept motion to refine joint types and labels.
Uses an articulated tetrahedral partition and mutually exclusive signed distance fields to extract non-overlapping closed part meshes.
On Articulate-100, achieves the best reported axis, motion, and geometry accuracy among methods without part masks, with virtually no open boundary edges; also works on real SplArt captures.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of ArtTet. (A) Dynamic- and geometric-constrained articulation and ownership inference. A multibody initialization splits the fused depth of both states into a static body and K rigid parts with joints Tk. A refinement alternates a symmetric energy on the motions with ownership repair on the labels, under dynamic and geometric joint constraints. A triangle model is then fitted to the images through the fixed joints. (B) Divide. A Delaunay tetrahedralization of the observed points is labeled as empty or as one of the parts by a visibility minimum cut over both states and a swept-motion exclusion, giving one cell per part. (C) Conquer. Each part owns a signed distance field ϕk on a shared tetrahedral grid. The exclusive fields ψk cannot overlap, differentiable marching tetrahedra extracts one closed mesh per part, and all meshes are optimized from the images of both states through the joints.

Figure 7. Qualitative comparison on Articulate-100. Part meshes in state 1, colored by part; both states are in Fig. S4. Gaussian methods are shown after TSDF fusion, which merges neighboring parts and leaves holes and blobs on thin panels. ArtTet keeps doors and drawers as separate closed meshes that move about the recovered joints.

Figure 8. Ablations. Top, part labels and joint axes (red) in state 1, with the ground-truth axes in transparent blue for each row of Table 2 and the ground truth, colored by part. Bottom, a second object in state 0 meshed by TSDF fusion, restricted Delaunay, the partition alone, and partitioned marching tetrahedra, each with a close-up of the boxed region to its right.

Figure 5. Optimizing the part fields. (a) Raw fields of the frame and the door overlap (left). The exclusive fields give each point to the part that is most inside, so the parts meet at a seam (right). (b) The target is outside in free space, follows the observed depth at the surface, is inside only within a shell ∆ behind it, and is outside where nothing was seen. (c) Every sign change on a grid edge costs, so a lone flip without image support is removed. (d) A door swept along a wrong joint enters the static divider, which the swept loss penalizes.

Figure 4. Articulated tetrahedral partition. (a) The segment from a camera to its observed depth crosses only empty space, so every tetrahedron on it gains a free-space vote. (b) A ray of state 1 that sees the door is moved into the canonical frame by T −1 k of the door. (c) Posed at η, the door sweeps the shaded region and passes through two tetrahedra labeled static (red outline). The one that touches the door goes to the door (blue), and the other goes to the outside (white).

Figure 3. Joint typing. (a) rk adds the coverage of the target (red) to the forward fit (green). (b) A drawer fit picks up a small rotation about a nearly orthogonal axis, but a pure translation explains it almost as well. (c) A real hinge lies on its part, a spurious axis does not.

papers.title: ArtTet: Watertight Part Meshes of Articulated Objects from Rigid-Body Rules and Partitioned Marching Tetrahedra
papers.tldr: ArtTet reconstructs articulated objects as separate, watertight meshes for each rigid part by combining motion reasoning with partitioned differentiable surface extraction.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has recently gained popularity as a faster alternative to Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) in 3D reconstruction and view synthesis methods. Leveraging the spatial information encoded in 3DGS, this work proposes FOCI (Field Overlap Collision Integral), an algorithm that is able to optimize trajectories directly on the Gaussians themselves. FOCI leverages a novel and interpretable collision formulation for 3DGS using the notion of the overlap integral between Gaussians. The formulation presented applies to different robot morphologies (e.g., fixed and mobile base manipulators, legged robots, UAVs) and handles both static and dynamic Gaussian-Splat environments. Contrary to other approaches, which represent the robot with conservative bounding boxes that underestimate the traversability of the environment, we propose to represent the environment and the robot as Gaussian Splats. This not only has desirable computational properties, but also allows for orientation-aware planning, allowing the robot to pass through very tight and narrow spaces. We extensively test our algorithm in both synthetic and real Gaussian Splats, showcasing that collision-free trajectories for legged, aerial and manipulator robots can be computed in seconds, even with hundreds of thousands of Gaussians making up the environment. The code is available at https://github.com/leggedrobotics/foci

papers.abstract: Video diffusion and world models generate plausible videos but do not reliably match the requested camera direction and travel distance. We present DreamTour, a training-free framework that generates camera tours from a single image with more accurate control over camera motion. DreamTour first uses a frozen image inpainting prior to extend the photograph beyond its original field of view while preserving the input pixels. Depth-based rendering of this extended scene along the requested camera path produces approximate target views that serve as spatial guidance. We introduce Layout Steering, which aligns early video latents with these views through decaying low-frequency corrections, leaving later denoising to refine appearance and dynamics. For longer tours, we autoregressively generate the video segments, repeating guidance construction from each segment's final frame to maintain camera control across the full trajectory. DreamTour improves directional accuracy and travel calibration on VBench while maintaining competitive video quality. On WorldScore, it strengthens camera control and scene consistency across chained movements. Together, these results demonstrate that training-free spatial guidance enables more accurate and consistent camera control in pretrained video diffusion and world models.
authors: Srikumar Sastry, Meher Gitika Karumuri, Chenqi Li, Sarosij Bose, Mellon Zhang, Allen Tu, Ziyang Long, Yen-Liang Lin, Alexander Schwing, Nathan Jacobs
bullets: Extends the input image beyond its field of view using a frozen inpainting prior while preserving original pixels.
Renders depth-based views along the desired camera path to provide spatial guidance.
Uses Layout Steering to apply decaying low-frequency corrections early in denoising, then lets later steps refine video appearance and dynamics.
Autoregressively chains segments for longer tours, rebuilding guidance from each segment’s final frame.
Improves directional accuracy, travel calibration, camera control, and scene consistency on VBench and WorldScore while maintaining competitive video quality.

papers.abstract: Recent dynamic Gaussian splatting methods encode temporal change, either as smooth functions of time or as constrained updates between frames. We observe that their reconstruction quality degrades significantly under fast motion. In challenging dance sequences, their PSNR drops by 1.1-4.0 dB on high-motion frames compared to low-motion frames. To overcome this limitation, we propose VersionGS, a method that directly encodes per-frame Gaussian states and uses motion estimation only to guide reconstruction. Within each group of frames, unchanged Gaussians keep their current versions in a shared dictionary, while modified Gaussians are appended as new versions. To maximize version reuse, we introduce selective sequential construction, which refines the Gaussians selected by optical flow, photograph differences or rendering errors and leaves the others unchanged. The dictionary is then pruned, fine-tuned with simulated quantization and encoded as images. Adjusting the pruning ratio trades off storage and quality without rebuilding the dictionary. On the fast dance sequences of DanceNet3D, VersionGS improves foreground PSNR by 2.7 dB over the best baseline, and its PSNR decreases by less than 0.3 dB on the highest-motion frames. On N3DV and Technicolor, it requires 6.0x and 5.7x less storage than TAD-GS, the strongest baseline overall, while achieving even higher PSNR. Finally, playback is fast and requires no motion model or neural network, only a 3DGS rasterizer.
authors: Shihang Wei, Yichi Zhang, Fengqing Zhu
bullets: Addresses quality degradation of existing dynamic Gaussian splatting methods on high-motion sequences.

On DanceNet3D, improves foreground PSNR by 2.7 dB over the best baseline and loses less than 0.3 dB on the highest-motion frames.
Uses 6.0× less storage on N3DV and 5.7× less on Technicolor than TAD-GS while achieving higher PSNR; playback needs only a 3DGS rasterizer.

papers.abstract: Understanding ultra-long videos requires retrieving sparse, query-relevant evidence from extensive video histories. Existing similarity-based retrieval methods are efficient, but they encode the question and the video content independently and thus often miss evidence whose relevance requires reasoning over both. Generative large language models (LLMs) can perform such reasoning, but they typically generate text over multiple rounds of search, which makes each query slow and costly. In this work, we introduce DeLoVi (Decision Models for Long Video), a framework that leverages pretrained decision models to retrieve evidence from ultra-long videos. Like an LLM, a decision model reads the question together with the candidate evidence, so it can reason over both. Unlike an LLM, it directly outputs a relevance score without generating text, which makes it fast and inexpensive. We first present DeLoVi-S, a simple method that generates captions for short video clips and uses a decision model to rank those captions by their relevance to a question. A generative LLM then answers the question using the top-ranked captions. Despite its simplicity, DeLoVi-S achieves state-of-the-art performance on three ultra-long video understanding benchmarks, EgoLifeQA, EgoMemReason, and MM-Lifelong, and generalizes effectively to long-video understanding benchmarks, VideoMME-L and LVBench. However, DeLoVi-S scores every caption for every question, so its cost grows linearly with video length. To reduce this cost, we propose an automated policy evolution framework that iteratively refines the memory construction and retrieval policies around a fixed pretrained decision model. The resulting method, DeLoVi-E, maintains comparable performance while reducing input tokens by 34x on average compared with DeLoVi-S. It also runs over 3x faster than the best prior method on EgoLifeQA while achieving higher accuracy.
authors: Ce Zhang, Baiqi Li, Seongsu Ha, Gedas Bertasius
bullets: Addresses the failure of independent similarity retrieval to find evidence requiring joint reasoning over queries and video content.
DeLoVi-S ranks captions of short clips with a decision model, then uses a generative LLM to answer from the top-ranked evidence.
DeLoVi-S achieves state-of-the-art results on three ultra-long video benchmarks and generalizes to additional long-video benchmarks.
DeLoVi-E evolves memory and retrieval policies to reduce input tokens by 34× on average while maintaining comparable performance.
On EgoLifeQA, DeLoVi-E runs over 3× faster than the best prior method while achieving higher accuracy.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of DeLoVi. (a) DeLoVi-S divides the video into short clips of 10 to 30 seconds and captions every clip. A decision model scores the relevance of every clip caption to the question, and an LLM answers the question from the top-K clip captions. (b) DeLoVi-E answers the question in three steps. In Step 1, the decision model searches over a memory tree and selects the most relevant 3-minute window. The clip captions of this window are the first input of Step 3. In Step 2, keyword matching (BM25 [39]) shortlists the clip captions that share words with the question, and the decision model ranks the shortlisted captions by their relevance. Each top-ranked clip is passed to Step 3 together with its neighboring clips. In Step 3, the LLM answers the question from the clips of Step 1 and reports its confidence. If the LLM is not confident, the ranked clips of Step 2 are added in order and the LLM answers again, until it is confident.

Figure 8. Qualitative example of DeLoVi-S. The question asks for the color of the power bank that the camera wearer used last time and is asked on Day 6 of EgoLife, after 41 hours of video. The decision model assigns a relevance score to the memory entry of every clip, and the 100 clips with the highest scores are given to the LLM. We show the three top-ranked clips with their frames and memory entries. All three clips show the camera wearer handling a power bank on Day 6. The top-ranked clip is from the morning of Day 6 and does not show the power bank used last time, and the annotated evidence is ranked second. The LLM reads the retrieved memory entries in temporal order with their timestamps and answers correctly.

Figure 7. Requests to the decision model. (a) In a score request, the decision model receives the question and one memory entry and outputs a probability for each of the four levels. The relevance score is the expected level, normalized to [0, 1]. We show the instruction for EgoLifeQA, and its description of the video is adapted to each benchmark. (b) In a ranking request, the decision model receives the input fields, the instruction, and the candidates, and outputs a selection probability for each candidate.

Figure 1. Accuracy and runtime on EgoLifeQA. All methods use GPT-6 Luna as the LLM, and runtime is measured per question. DeLoVi-S achieves the highest accuracy, and DeLoVi-E is the fastest method while achieving the second-highest accuracy. Compared with MERIT [9], the strongest prior method, DeLoViE is 3.8× faster with 1.0% higher accuracy.

Figure 3. Accuracy gain of DeLoVi-S over MERIT at different time scales on MM-Lifelong. To answer a question, each method has to search an entire video, and the average video duration is 23.6, 51.9, and 105.6 hours on the day, week, and month splits, respectively. Both methods use the same LLM (GPT-6 Luna). MERIT is more accurate on the shortest video, whereas DeLoVi-S outperforms it on the longer videos.

Figure 9. Qualitative example of DeLoVi-E: answering from the first evidence window. The question asks what should be arranged in Alice’s room and is asked on Day 6, after 37 hours of video. In Step 1, the decision model selects Day 2, then the hour from 22:00 to 22:58, and lastly the 3-minute window from 22:48 to 22:51 (green), based on the summaries of these nodes. The clips of this window form the first evidence window, in which Alice describes the plans for the room. Each numbered box shows the frames and the memory entries of one evidence window. The LLM answers from this evidence window with a confidence of 0.97, so the search stops after a single LLM call.

Figure 6. Prompts for memory construction. (a) Prompt of the captioner. (b) Prompt of the free-text summaries of the initial policy and of DeLoVi-E. (c) One line of the timeline of an hour in DeLoVi-E, written from the summary of one 3-minute window. (d) One line of the index of a day in DeLoVi-E, written from the summary of one hour.

Figure 10. Qualitative example of DeLoVi-E: clip re-ranking after an answer that is not confident. The question asks which drinks the camera wearer usually does not buy at the supermarket. In Step 1, the decision model selects the hour of the supermarket visit and one of its 3-minute windows, and the LLM is not confident in its answer from this evidence window (confidence 0.62). In Step 2, BM25 shortlists 50 of the 763 clips, and the decision model re-ranks them. We show the ten top-ranked clips. Each of the first three forms a further evidence window together with its neighboring clips (boxes 2 to 4). The third and fourth evidence windows contain two statements of the camera wearer about not drinking coffee. The LLM answers after the 1st, 2nd, and 4th evidence windows, and its confidence reaches 0.91 after the 4th, so the search stops after three LLM calls.

Figure 5. Evolution dynamics on the validation set. Each point is the policy of one iteration, and darker points are later iterations. The input tokens per question (log scale) decrease throughout the evolution, while the accuracy stays close to that of the initial policy. DeLoVi-E (star) uses 6.5× fewer tokens than the initial policy with 1.9% higher accuracy. It also achieves similar accuracy to DeLoVi-S (square) with 34× fewer tokens.

papers.tldr: DeLoVi uses fast decision models to reason over questions and video evidence, enabling accurate and substantially cheaper search in ultra-long videos.

papers.abstract: Learned manipulation policies, from task-specific imitation policies to vision-language-action (VLA) models, rely primarily on RGB images. While some studies report gains from sensor depth, others avoid depth cameras because of measurement noise. Depth cameras introduce both noise and missing depth values (holes), whose relative effects remain unclear. In this study, we calibrate a sensor model using a real wrist-mounted stereo camera and separately evaluate noise and holes on RGB-D imitation policies with three visual encoders in simulation. We found that complete depth improves success by approximately ten percentage points, and most of this gain persists even at twenty times the camera's noise level. In contrast, holes covering about one-sixth of the wrist image eliminate the detectable benefit of depth. The validity mask strongly influences depth reliance: marking a small fraction of pixels as invalid reduces reliance, while filling holes and marking them valid restores most of the benefit. Policies trained on clean depth also lose performance when holes appear only at deployment, sometimes falling below RGB-only performance. These findings suggest that depth cameras for learned policies should therefore be judged by depth coverage more than measurement precision.
authors: Inayat Rasool, Chulwoo Pack, Shabbir Ahmed
bullets: The study separates depth noise from missing-value holes using a calibrated wrist-mounted stereo-camera model and simulated RGB-D imitation policies.
Complete depth improves task success by about ten percentage points, with most of the benefit surviving noise at 20× the camera level.
Holes covering roughly one-sixth of the wrist image remove the detectable advantage of depth.
Validity masks shape depth reliance: marking pixels invalid reduces reliance, while filling holes and marking them valid restores much of the benefit.
Deployment-only holes can make policies trained on clean depth perform worse than RGB-only policies.

(e) Benefit compares a depth policy with an RGB-only policy. Reliance compares the same policy with its depth intact and with its depth blanked or taken from another scene.

Fig. 3. Effects of depth noise and missing values on PICKCUBE performance. (a) Noise scaled by factors of 5–100 without holes. (b) Hole rates scaled up to four times the calibrated level at fixed noise. The top panels show the benefit relative to RGB-only policies, while the bottom panels show reliance on depth removal (solid lines) and, in (b), scene reliance (dashed lines). Triangles indicate the halving points of blank-depth reliance, and the dotted line marks the calibrated camera level. Noise largely preserves the benefit and reliance on depth, whereas holes substantially reduce both. Error bars represent one standard error across 8 training seeds.

Fig. 1. Effect of depth input quality on manipulation performance on PICKCUBE. Top: Representative wrist-camera inputs, with missing depth values highlighted in red and validity masks shown in the insets (black indicates invalid pixels). Bottom: Change in task success rate relative to the RGB-only policy using the same encoder. Complete depth improves performance, whereas sensor-induced holes eliminate this benefit. Filling missing depth values and marking them as valid largely restores the improvement. Error bars represent one standard error across 8 random seeds.

Fig. 4. Effect of the validity mask, and of holes that appear only at deployment on PICKCUBE. (a) Benefit over RGB-only policies; (b) Reliance with blank depth. Holes are left empty or filled from the nearest valid pixel, and the mask either marks them (shaded) or marks every pixel as valid. Hole-free sensor depth is the reference. (c) Success of policies trained without holes and deployed with them. Dotted lines show the RGB-only policy. Marking every pixel as valid raises reliance, but only filling the holes as well restores the benefit. Error bars show one standard error over 8 seeds.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates the specific failure modes of depth sensors in learned manipulation policies, providing actionable insights on depth coverage vs. precision.
papers.title: Why Does Sensor Depth Fail Learned Manipulation Policies? Finding the Failure Mode with ACT
papers.tldr: Depth helps learned manipulation policies mainly when it has broad coverage; missing values hurt far more than substantial measurement noise.

papers.abstract: A surgeon first finds what is wrong, then fixes only that part. We use this idea for video grounding, where video-language models often find the right moment in a long video but write its time wrong. In Temporal Weight Surgery (TWS), a general-purpose LLM reads the model's weights and activations, finds where the error arises and repairs it there, without gradients. Separate sessions find the same cause, and this diagnosis of where and why the model fails is our main contribution. Three GPT-6 Astra sessions trace a dropped digit in TimeLens-8B to one MLP layer, and the largest edit gains 7.9 mIoU on 1,215 unseen questions and 18.3 on videos of 30 minutes or more. Two Claude Opus 5.5 sessions trace minutes written as seconds in Qwen3-VL-8B to the separator and gain 2.9 and 1.3. Before any edit, its answers often have the right minute and the wrong separator, and fixing only the separator lifts their mIoU from 13.1 to 19.2. Every improving edit beats a random edit of its size, and the edited models run as fast as before.
authors: Ali Asgarov, Chris Thomas
bullets: Targets cases where models identify the correct video moment but express its timestamp incorrectly.
LLM sessions inspect weights and activations to localize the source of errors, such as an MLP layer or separator token.
Edits improve grounding across TimeLens-8B and Qwen3-VL-8B, including larger gains on long videos.
Improving edits outperform same-sized random edits, and edited models run at the original speed.
Scope is limited to the reported timestamp-error cases and evaluated model/session settings.

figures.caption: Figure 2. The TWS editor diagnoses failures and writes weight updates through two tools. In the shaded editing loop, the editor calls the GPU forward-pass tool, which runs practice batches by generation or teacher forcing, reads the scores and activations, writes code in the CPU Python kernel and saves complete edited tensors W ′, which the next call loads. The shown architecture is shared by Qwen3-VL-8B and TimeLens-8B. Orange and purple mark the independent Qwen query and value/output edits. Teal marks the three TimeLens MLP edits. The bottom note marks Qwen3.5-0.8B’s repetition edit. The 1,215 test questions stay hidden from the editor. Supplementary Fig. S1 gives diagnostic details.

Figure 7. Timestamp repair moves the answer to the event. Each example shows the query, frames at the centres of the base and edited answers, and the intervals (blue true, grey base, teal TWS query edit). Answers keep the model’s formatting; the parser reads 8:45 as minutes and seconds whatever unit follows. These are the four largest IoU gains among held-out practice answers that changed from seconds to m:ss.

Figure 4. TWS gains most over all TimeLens-8B test videos, and repairs long ones without harming short ones. Test mIoU overall and by video length, from the answers of Fig. 3. The arrow marks the gain of TWS (run 17) on videos of 30 minutes or more, +18.51 [+15.06,+22.24]; under 10 minutes it is level with the base model (+0.30, NS). The times-ten rule gains more on the longest videos but loses on shorter ones, where it also stretches correct early answers.

Figure 3. TWS beats a random edit of its size on every model, and steering on two of three. Test gains over the base model on the 1,215 test questions with 95% bootstrap intervals over videos, all on one machine against the same base answers (run 17 gains +7.82 here, +7.89 in Tab. 1). Brackets give TWS minus steering. On Qwen3-VL-2B the output rule is level with TWS (+0.88, NS).

Figure 5. Before any edit, Qwen3-VL-8B often writes the right minute with the wrong separator. (a) The first number the base model writes against the true start minute (square-root axes), for the 294 test answers whose “:” logit lies within 15 of the top token at the separator. It is the true minute in 131 (45%, against 16% by chance), 95 in the first minute and 36 later. (b) Their mIoU as written and with “:” forced and the rest written by the model, no weight changed; for an event at 15:34 to 15:40, “15.0 - 18.0 seconds” (IoU 0) becomes “15:35 - 15:40 seconds” (IoU 83).

Figure 6. How the TWS query edit changes answers and accuracy. (a, b) Predicted against true event centres, as shares of the video, on 246 held-out practice questions; the diagonal marks correct centres, shading the first 2%, where predictions fall from 86 to 54, and open markers zero IoU. (c) Practice mIoU by edit strength; κ = −4 reverses the edit. (d) Paired gains at κ = 4 by video duration (questions in parentheses, one standard error).

Calls count batched requests to the forward-pass tool (10 for attention weights, 30 or 50 for all weights). Parentheses give MLP Frobenius norms relative to the base tensors. Practice ∆mIoU uses the session’s subset and one standard error; † marks reuse for strength selection, ‡ thinking mode. GPU hours of a session’s forward-pass calls (L40S for Claude, B200 or A40 for Astra, A40 for steering; wall-clock hours in parentheses; the editor’s own LLM calls excluded) or of LoRA’s training on one L40S. Gains are paired with the base model on each machine.

Table 2. TWS gives the highest test mIoU on all three models. Test mIoU on VUE-TR (TR), VUE-TR-V2 (V2) and both pooled (All, 1,215 questions), from the answers of Fig. 3, all on one machine. TWS is each model’s best edit (runs 17, 4 and 12), and the random edit has its size. ∗The times-ten rule for TimeLens-8B. Best in bold.

papers.selection_reason: Repairs video grounding models via LLM-based weight editing, relevant to video understanding and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: Temporal Weight Surgery: Repairing Video Grounding with LLM Editors
papers.tldr: Temporal Weight Surgery uses LLMs to diagnose and selectively edit video-grounding model weights, correcting timestamp errors without gradients while preserving inference speed.

papers.abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) generates massive data streams, making edge computing essential for low-latency applications and 5G networks. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) enable adaptation through in-context examples rather than parameter updates, but evolving streams challenge context relevance and computational efficiency. This work introduces SAIL, a framework for sparse adaptation of TFMs that reuses the model's key--value cache between adaptation events. SAIL reconstructs its support set only when drifts in stream structure indicate potential context inadequacy, while the structural representation itself is updated by changes in predictive performance. SAIL combines prequential error monitoring with online, class-specific micro-clustering to detect changes in cluster mass, class separability, and feature-space coverage. Upon adaptation, a context budget is allocated proportionally to class mass, and the most recently updated micro-clusters provide representative observations for refitting. This limits context redundancy and computational cost while preserving recent structural information.
authors: Jo\~ao Neves, Afonso Louren\c{c}o, Lizy K. John, Eric P. Xing, Jo\~ao Gama
bullets: Targets context staleness and computational overhead in streaming IoT and edge-computing settings.
Reuses the model’s key–value cache between adaptation events instead of continuously rebuilding context.
Combines prequential error monitoring with class-specific online micro-clustering to detect structural changes.
Allocates context by class mass and selects recent micro-clusters as representative support examples.
Designed to reduce redundant context and computation while retaining recent stream structure.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of SAIL. During routine prediction, the TFM reuses its key–value (KV) cache across successive batches. SAIL combines (i) identifies potential context inadequacy by monitoring changes in class-specific micro-cluster mass and feature-space coverage; (ii) reconstructs contexts, allocating the support-set budget proportionally to class mass and selects the most recently updated micro-clusters; (iii) monitors prequential prediction error and uses backtracking to identify reliable instances for updating the micro-clustering representation. Either drift signal triggers TFM adaptation, with a KV cache rebuilt.
Figure 6: Structural changes and predictive outcomes under mass-discrepancy-triggered versus periodic refitting.
Figure 5: Effect of SAIL’s class-specific micro-cluster compression on inference cost, context size, and accuracy loss.
Figure 7: Performance-based and mass discrepancy adaptation against alternative adaptive and fixed periodic policies.
Figure 2: Streams selected across 80 benchmarks.
Figure 4: Effect of periodic sliding-window contexts on Δ feature-mean, Δ class-distribution, and coverage gap.
Figure 9: Micro-clustering hyperparameters.
Figure 8: Sparse adaptation hyperparameters.
Table 4: List of 68 benchmarks considered, but not selected.

papers.selection_reason: Sparse adaptation of tabular foundation models on evolving data streams with drift detection and context reconstruction.
papers.title: Sparse Adaptation for In-Context Learning on Data Streams
papers.tldr: SAIL enables efficient in-context adaptation of tabular foundation models on evolving data streams by updating context only when structural drift signals that it is needed.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing seen images from fMRI has advanced through diffusion models, but the current state-of-the-art Brain-IT pipeline still has a lossy bottleneck: its low-level branch outlines the figure well, yet the diffusion model that follows frequently mispaints colour, object identity and layout. We move one step backward and condition the refiner directly on the fMRI-derived low-level image, using six one-hidden-layer MLP heads (scene, main-subject category, count, colour, object, layout) to predict the content prompt that guides a frozen Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 model. On the 930 shared NSD concepts, scored with Brain-IT's own metric code on the same ground truth, NeuroRefine reaches a CLIP image cosine of 0.755 against 0.735 for Brain-IT enhanced and produces markedly sharper images, while the saturated 2-way identification is unchanged. The low-level image supplies an explicit spatial prior rather than a lossless layout: refinement trades some layout agreement (0.541 against 0.638) for semantic fidelity and texture. We then show that the standard panel is multi-factor: a high PixCorr can coexist with completely different content, so we read the low-level and semantic factors separately and quantify where they disagree. Finally, we trace the cortical sources of the prompt heads across subjects and report their causal lesion profile and the fMRI noise ceiling. Direction errors are left to future work.
authors: Runqi Xu, Vince D. Calhoun
bullets: Addresses Brain-IT’s tendency to misrepresent colour, object identity, and layout after low-level image reconstruction.
Uses six one-hidden-layer MLP heads to predict scene, subject category, count, colour, object, and layout prompts from fMRI-derived images.
Guides a frozen Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 model with these prompts on 930 shared NSD concepts.
Achieves a CLIP image cosine of 0.755 versus 0.735 for Brain-IT enhanced, with sharper reconstructions; 2-way identification remains unchanged.
Separately analyzes low-level and semantic factors, cortical sources, lesion profiles, and the fMRI noise ceiling.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of NeuroRefine. fMRI betas (39,548 fsaverage surface vertices) feed two pathways. (A) Low-level / spatial pathway: a per-subject VGG feature readout trained with InfoNCE predicts multi-layer VGG features, which a Deep Image Prior inverts into a low-level image that supplies the coarse spatial layout. (B) Content pathway: six independent MLP heads (scene, subject, count, colour, object, layout; 1024 units, GELU, dropout 0.3) predict structured content that is assembled into a content prompt. The frozen Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 editor takes the low-level image as an image condition and the content prompt as text, and returns a 1024× 1024 reconstruction (20 steps, cfg 4.0). Unlike Brain-IT (Beliy et al., 2026), which conditions its SDXL refiner on a caption, NeuroRefine conditions the refiner on the low-level image itself. Lower panels: head attribution on the surface and the evaluation protocol.

Figure 3: Stages of the pipeline. Rows are concepts where NeuroRefine wins; columns are the seen image, the low-level image, Brain-IT semantic, Brain-IT enhanced, caption+Qwen, retrieval+Qwen and NeuroRefine.

Figure 5: Retrieval as conditioning. The retrieved photograph carries the right content in a different arrangement; conditioning on the low-level image instead retains far more of the input arrangement.

Figure 1: Reconstruction of seen image by NeuroRefine. Each pair shows the seen image (left) and our reconstruction (right), using the full NSD dataset (40 hours) for subject 1. The low-level branch supplies a spatial prior, six one-hidden-layer MLP heads predict the content prompt, and the frozen Qwen-Image-Edit2511 refiner restores texture, colour and sharpness.
Figure 9: Head attribution on the inflated fsaverage surface (saliency, row-normalised per head; top row left hemisphere, bottom row right hemisphere). All six heads load on visual cortex.

Figure 6: Subject-1 reconstructions on four of the shared concepts: seen image, low-level input, Brain-IT enhanced and NeuroRefine. The cross-subject comparison is quantitative (table 3); persubject head-prompt renders exist for subject 1 only, so this figure shows subject 1.

Figure 11: Failure modes, one row per type. Object substitution: a bird on a wire becomes an airplane (c226). Instance/species substitution: a giraffe becomes a zebra (c832). Scene substitution: a fruit basket becomes an indoor scene with a person (c97). Scene and count together: two red vases become a room with two people (c563). Count: a crowded race field becomes a single rider in a forest (c331). Direction: a walker under a red umbrella becomes a frontal standing figure (c264). Columns: seen image, low-level input, Brain-IT enhanced, NeuroRefine.

Figure 4: Same generator, different conditioning. Qwen-Image-Edit conditioned on the fMRIdecoded caption, on the ground-truth caption, and on the fMRI-derived low-level image with the head content prompt.

Figure 8: Low-level versus semantic factor across arms. The factors are not redundant: the blurriest arm is high on PixCorr and low on CLIP cosine, and the sharp arms spread along the semantic axis; no single arm dominates both axes.
Figure 10: Causal lesion test. Change in head logits when the top-5% salient vertices are zeroed, relative to a random 5% (dots: individual subjects).

Figure 13: Retrieval semantic stage. The retrieved photograph (4th column) is a real image with the right content but a different arrangement; the edit refiner (last) keeps the retrieved content and recovers some layout from the low-level input.
Figure 12: Qualitative comparison (1/2): 14 of the 28 concepts used in the main figures. Columns are the seen image, the low-level input, Brain-IT enhanced and NeuroRefine.
Figure 12: (continued) Qualitative comparison (2/2): the remaining 14 concepts.
Figure 7: Where does subject data go? (a) CLIP image cosine of the readout against the number of subject-1 images, with and without cross-subject initialisation; (b) retrieval top-1.

Table 1: Quantitative comparison. Top block: prior numbers as reported by Brain-IT (Beliy et al., 2026) for methods trained on the full 40 h of NSD data, averaged over subjects 1,2,5,7. Bottom block: NeuroRefine, measured by us with the same compute_metrics code on the identical 930 shared-concept ground truth for subject 1 (LPIPS is omitted by the released code). The two blocks therefore differ in subject coverage: the prior numbers are four-subject averages as reported by BrainIT, whereas our row is a single-subject measurement and should be read as such. The panel is multifactor (low-level: PixCorr/SSIM/Alex(2); semantic: Inception/CLIP/EffNet/SwAV); we report both factors and do not collapse them into one number (Sec. 5.1). Best per column in bold, second best underlined; arrows give the direction of improvement.
Table 2: Identity versus layout. CLIP image cosine and layout correlation on the shared concepts, subject 1.

Table 3: Per-subject reconstruction results on the 930 shared concepts, selector rule per subject (CLIP image cosine decides which arm supplies each concept). Sharpness is the mean gradient magnitude of the 224× 224 output: an edge-energy proxy, not a perceptual-quality score. Rows for subjects 2 and 5 are measured with the earlier edit arm; their head-prompt renders are in progress.

Table 4: External check on BOLD5000 (n-way CLIP identification, %). “Frozen” is an NSDtrained readout applied without BOLD5000 training; “trained” fits the readout on the target subject; “transductive” pools three subjects and normalises at test time. MindLoop is the published number under its own protocol. BOLD5000’s low SNR limits every arm.

Table 5: A definition check, not a ranking proof. Blurring the ground truth raises PixCorr but lowers CLIP cosine; recolouring does the opposite. The perturbation shows that the two metrics respond to different factors; it does not by itself rank real reconstructions.
Table 6: Data efficiency of the semantic readout on subject 1. “Transfer” initialises from subjects {2,3,5,7} and fine-tunes with early stopping. One NSD session is ≈250 images (≈1 h of scanning).
Table 7: Repeat-trial reliability of individual vertices (split-half, Spearman–Brown corrected). The fMRI ceiling is the upper bound for any readout trained on three repeats.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a refinement method for fMRI decoding using a VLM (Qwen) with six-head MLP conditioning, fitting Multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: NeuroRefine: Six-Head MLP Content Conditioning and Qwen Refinement for Faithful fMRI Decoding
papers.tldr: NeuroRefine improves fMRI image reconstruction’s semantic fidelity by using MLP-predicted content prompts to guide a frozen Qwen image editor, while trading off some layout agreement.

papers.abstract: Model merging combines fine-tuned experts into one model that serves many tasks without retraining, but merging many experts this way substantially reduces accuracy. Grouping offers a middle ground: at every layer or weight matrix, the $N$ experts are divided into $K<N$ groups, the experts in a group are merged into one shared module, and a task uses the module merged from its expert's group. Natural choices are to keep the same partners across layers or to group similar experts. Surprisingly, we find that randomly changing partners at every layer outperforms both. We call this Balanced Random Regrouping (BRR): it independently partitions the experts into $K$ equal-sized random groups at each layer (BRR-layer) or weight matrix (BRR-matrix) and merges each group with an existing method. With validation-selected merge scales, both BRR variants outperform reusing one grouping across layers in all 24 CLIP settings, by 1.0-6.8 points, and BRR-matrix also outperforms the similarity-based FlexMerge in every setting. A first-order analysis explains this gain. At each layer, merging a task's expert with its partners shifts the task's output features; when the partners are the same at every layer, these shifts tend to point in similar directions and add up, whereas with new partners at every layer they vary independently and add up less on average. A series of experiments supports this analysis, which further guides a grouping search that can outperform BRR.
authors: Kaiyang Li, Shaobo Han, Shihao Ji
bullets: Problem: Merging many fine-tuned experts into one model can substantially reduce accuracy; fixed or similarity-based grouping may limit performance.
Method: Independently partition experts into equal-sized random groups at every layer (BRR-layer) or weight matrix (BRR-matrix), then merge each group with an existing method.
Result: With validation-selected merge scales, both BRR variants outperform fixed grouping across all 24 CLIP settings by 1.0–6.8 points.
Result: BRR-matrix also outperforms the similarity-based FlexMerge in every reported setting.
Analysis: Changing partners makes feature shifts vary across layers, reducing their average accumulation; this insight also motivates a search strategy that can outperform BRR.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Shared grouping versus BRR (schematic). (a) Four tasks (T1–T4) and three units (layers or weight matrices); at each unit, the experts are merged in two equal-sized groups. Shared grouping reuses one grouping, whereas BRR draws one independently at each unit; the red line follows the modules selected by T1. The accuracies shown are those of shared grouping and BRR-layer on 100 ViT-B/32 tasks (TSV-M, K=10, α=1). (b) Under a first-order approximation, each red arrow shows the shift that merging at one unit adds to T1’s final output features, and the dashed arrow is their sum. In this illustration, fixed partners give shifts in similar directions that accumulate, whereas new partners give shifts in different directions that accumulate less.

Figure 3. Predicted versus measured accuracy gain over shared grouping for 27 groupings on ViT-B/32 (five-seed means). Predictions were fixed in advance and calibrated on the measured gain of BRR over shared grouping, so the shared-grouping and BRR endpoints match by construction; the dotted line marks equality.

Figure 2. Ratio of measured to predicted feature-error gaps (shared minus independent grouping, summed over 100 ViT-B/32 tasks) against the scale ϵ of the merging-induced weight changes; ϵ = 1 applies the full change to the grouped weights, and ϵ = 1.5 extrapolates beyond it. A ratio of 1 means agreement. Bars: 95% task-bootstrap intervals.

(a) 95% intervals for gains (points) and counts of improved tasks at validation-selected scales. (b) Mean test accuracy (%) and gains (points) at selected and fixed scales. Independent grouping draws a partition per matrix. Unequal group sizes are 25, 18, 14, 11, 9, 7, 6, 4, 3 and 3.

Each of three passes tested all methods and batch sizes in random order, with five warm-up and 20 timed forward passes per condition and seed. We report the median of the 60 timed forward passes for each seed, averaged over three grouping seeds (Channel Merging: three clustering seeds; FlexMerge: its single deterministic grouping). Channel Merging gathers each task’s rows per matrix; all other methods route samples to stored modules.

papers.title: Change Partners at Every Layer: Balanced Random Regrouping for Model Merging
papers.tldr: Balanced Random Regrouping improves model merging by randomly changing each task expert’s merge partners across layers or weight matrices, reducing accumulated feature shifts.

papers.abstract: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) posits that AI models converge toward a shared representation of the world, even when trained on different data modalities. Previous work has found evidence for the PRH in the activations of vision and language models. In this work, we ask whether vision and language models also converge in how they act on these representations: precisely, in how these internal representations affect the models' output. At a chosen layer of a transformer, the Jacobian lens gives every word in the vocabulary (or class in an image classifier) a vector in the hidden state: the vector that most increases the model's tendency to generate that word, at that position or later, or to predict that class. Collectively, these vectors make up what is referred to as the model's J-space. We find evidence of the PRH in J-space across vision and language models, and furthermore, we find that J-spaces mostly converge up to a rotation. That is, a single rotation, fitted on a subset of words, approximately maps one model's J-space onto another's, and so applies to words and classes it was not fitted on. A word's vector, rotated from a text-only language model's J-space into the visual patch tokens of a vision-language model, changes the object the vision-language model says is in the image (and only in the image region where it is added). Rotated into an image generator's text conditioning, a word's vector changes the object in the generated image. Rotated into an ImageNet classifier (trained without text), it raises that object's class score above almost all others, and vice versa. This suggests that models converge not only in how they represent the world, but also in how they act on it.
authors: Ross Murphy, Gabriel Brostow
bullets: Extends the Platonic Representation Hypothesis from internal activations to how models act on those representations.
Represents each output word or image class by a Jacobian vector in a model’s hidden-state space, called J-space.
Finds that J-spaces across vision and language models approximately align after fitting one rotation on only some words.
Rotated vectors transfer semantic effects across modalities, altering image understanding, generation, or classifier scores in the corresponding concept.
The evidence suggests cross-modal convergence in both world representation and model behavior, within the tested models and tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Explores convergence in Jacobian space between vision and language models, a core topic in multimodal foundation models and representation learning.
papers.title: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis in Jacobian-Space: Language and Vision Models Agree Approximately Up to a Rotation
papers.tldr: Vision and language models appear to share similar Jacobian-based output representations, which can often be aligned across models with a single rotation.

papers.abstract: Today, a core pipeline of artificial intelligence systems is pretraining on a broad range of text corpora and then fine-tuning on specific tasks or desired behaviors. Yet we still have limited understanding of how fine-tuning on a restricted data distribution modifies representations acquired during pretraining. In particular, it remains unclear whether surface behavioral suppression happens together with the erasure of latent representations that support it. In this work, we study supervised fine-tuning (SFT) by pretraining transformers on a controlled context-free grammar with hierarchical latent structure, the Random Hierarchy Model (RHM), and fine-tuning with a restricted subset of its generative rules. While during pretraining the model's ability to generate with the correct grammar rules coincides with building the internal representations of the corresponding latent, we find that SFT exhibits a very different dynamics: (i) the generation of deleted rules changes on a fast timescale inversely proportional to the magnitude of the token-latent correlation; meanwhile, their corresponding representations stay intact; (ii) the hidden representations of the deleted rules become forgotten on a much longer timescale, associated with a slow drift of the network parameters. Finally, we observe analogous results in a realistic setup with natural language, suggesting that this timescale separation in forgetting is a more general phenomenon of fine-tuning language models.
authors: Yilin Luo, Jin Hwa Lee, Andrew M. Saxe, Antonio Sclocchi
bullets: The study examines whether fine-tuning removes latent representations or merely suppresses their observable behavior.
Using transformers pretrained on a controlled hierarchical grammar and fine-tuned on restricted rules, it identifies two forgetting timescales.
Generation of excluded rules changes rapidly, with the rate linked to token–latent correlation, while their representations initially remain intact.
Representational forgetting occurs much more slowly as network parameters gradually drift.
Similar dynamics appear in a natural-language setting, suggesting the phenomenon may generalize beyond the controlled model.

papers.selection_reason: Studies forgetting timescale separation in LLM fine-tuning, relevant to continual learning and language model behavior.
papers.title: Two Timescales of Forgetting in Fine-tuning of Language Models: Fast Behavioral Suppression and Slow Representational Drift
papers.tldr: Fine-tuning suppresses previously learned behavior quickly, while the underlying representations persist and are forgotten only through much slower parameter drift.

papers.abstract: Attention over long sequences is a major computational bottleneck in video generation, which can be alleviated through sparsity and low-bit quantization. We propose JetDiffusion, a video generation system built on trainable Video Sparse Quantized Attention (VSQA), with custom inference kernels that combine native NVFP4 computation and kernel fusion. At 90% sparsity, VSQA accelerates attention by 8-29x compared with FlashAttention on different hardwares. To further accelerate video generation, we combine VSQA with NVFP4 linear quantization and step distillation. Although each technique can individually preserve generation quality, jointly adapting to all three remains challenging, particularly under aggressive NVFP4 quantization. Through empirical studies, we develop an effective staged training recipe that enables stable adaptation to quantization, sparsity, and few-step denoising. On Wan2.1-14B, the resulting model achieves 273x end-to-end video generation speedup on the RTX 5090 while maintaining comparable video quality.
authors: Yulun Wu, Zihan Min, Minshen Zhang, Kaiqin Kong, Ji Xie, Will Lin, Junda Chen, Wenxuan Tan, Aryan Kumar, Loay Rashid, Qingyu Yin, Hao Zhang
bullets: Targets attention’s long-sequence computational bottleneck in video generation.
Introduces trainable Video Sparse Quantized Attention with fused native NVFP4 inference kernels.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes sparse quantized attention for video generation, combining efficiency and video diffusion.
papers.title: JetDiffusion: Pushing the Speed Limits of Video Generation with NVFP4 Sparse Attention
papers.tldr: JetDiffusion combines sparse attention, NVFP4 quantization, and step distillation to dramatically accelerate video generation while preserving comparable quality.

papers.abstract: The growing use of large language models (LLMs) for mental health support raises important safety concerns. Existing guard models primarily identify categories of harmful content, often overlooking the context needed to determine an appropriate response. We introduce a clinically grounded taxonomy that characterizes harm along three dimensions: what the harm is, who is involved, and when it occurs. It further separates harm characterization from intervention decisions, thus enabling safety policies to be specified outside the model weights through explicit, clinician-curated instructions that can be updated and audited. We validate the taxonomy with expert clinicians and validate a panel of LLM judges to scale annotation. Relabeling public benchmarks in this taxonomy shows that they rarely contain harm directed at the user, which accounts for nearly half of the harm in real conversations. We then train MindGuard2, a 35B-A3B reasoning-based guard model using supervised fine-tuning on short reasoning traces followed by reinforcement learning with a reasoning-length penalty, to minimize inference overhead while preserving the benefits of reasoning. On two public benchmarks and real-world conversations, MindGuard2 achieves balanced accuracy comparable to the substantially larger GLM-5.3 at approximately 10x lower median latency, advancing the accuracy-latency Pareto frontier. Furthermore, it achieves low false-positive rates at high recall, helping balance the need to detect unsafe situations against the risk of unnecessary interventions that may disrupt support and undermine user trust. We release a safety guardrail model with SOTA performance trained on synthetic data, together with synthetic conversations and annotations of public benchmarks in our taxonomy.
authors: Catarina Botelho, Ant\'onio Farinhas, John Mendon\c{c}a, Areti Vassilopoulos, In\^es Gon\c{c}alves, Maya D'Eon, Hugo Pitorro, Laura Cabello, Carrie Spadine, Nuno M. Guerreiro, Ricardo Rei
bullets: Frames harm by what occurs, who is involved, and when it occurs, separating harm assessment from intervention policy.
Uses clinician validation and LLM judges to support scalable annotation, and finds public benchmarks underrepresent harm directed at the user.
Trains MindGuard2 with supervised short reasoning traces and reinforcement learning that penalizes excessive reasoning length.
Matches the balanced accuracy of a substantially larger model at roughly 10× lower median latency across public benchmarks and real conversations.
Reports low false-positive rates at high recall; releases the guard model, synthetic conversations, and taxonomy-based annotations.

papers.abstract: Abstract interpretation can certify properties of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), but precise analyses remain expensive. General implementations repeat work when analyzing the same architecture under different inputs and properties. Interleaving this work with numerical operations limits GPU utilization and restricts how much of the analysis a tensor compiler can process together. We present Scepter, a framework for specializing DNN abstract interpreters through structural semantics. The semantics determine the structure of intermediate abstract values while deferring their numerical evaluation. Structural computations from successive operations can therefore be performed together before certification, generating an executable tensor program. With the abstract interpreter and DNN architecture fixed, the program can be reused with different weights and input regions. We prove that it computes the same bounds as the general interpreter in exact arithmetic. The generated program also exposes operations and their dependencies for tensor compilation and memory planning. We implement Scepter for the tensor programs that Neuton generates from ConstraintFlow specifications. We evaluate Scepter on eight abstract interpreters and 44 DNNs against six baseline systems on GPUs and CPUs. Scepter handles networks with up to 153x as many neurons as the largest completed by the corresponding baselines. It completes DeepPoly on ResNet50 and VGG-16, whereas none of the evaluated DeepPoly baselines completes either network. On configurations completed by both systems, GPU geometric-mean speedups over Neuton range from 11.9x to 44.4x across eight analyses, with a 2.60x geometric-mean reduction in peak memory. In an input-splitting case study, Scepter proves 68 properties for which the baselines time out. Code: https://github.com/uiuc-focal-lab/constraintflow.git
authors: Avaljot Singh, Dushyant Bharadwaj, Yasmin Chandini Sarita, Heng Zhong, Charith Mendis, Gagandeep Singh
bullets: Abstract interpretation can certify DNN properties, but repeated numerical work and limited GPU/compiler utilization make precise analyses expensive.
Scepter separates structural computations from numerical evaluation and fuses successive operations into executable tensor programs.
Programs can be reused across different weights and input regions while preserving the general interpreter’s exact-arithmetic bounds.
Evaluated across eight interpreters and 44 DNNs, Scepter scaled to networks with up to 153× more neurons than corresponding baselines and achieved GPU speedups of 11.9×–44.4×.
The approach completed DeepPoly analyses for ResNet50 and VGG-16, and proved 68 input-splitting properties where baselines timed out.

papers.abstract: Linear attention compresses historical context into a fixed-size recurrent state, reducing the computational and memory costs of long-sequence modeling. From the perspective of test-time regression (TTR), the state matrix can be viewed as an online-learned regression model, where keys and values serve as inputs and targets respectively, and queries are used to read from the model. From this perspective, the effectiveness of state learning depends not only on the update rule but also on how the key-value learning pairs used for state updates are constructed. While existing work has largely focused on how the state is updated and organized, we investigate how the learning pairs used for state updates are constructed. To this end, we propose Sliding-Window Gated DeltaNet (SWGDN), which replaces short convolutions in Delta-Rule linear attention with sliding-window attention to perform content-dependent local aggregation of projected queries, keys, and values. Our experiments show that SWGDN makes the key-value pairs used in consecutive updates more similar in both GDN2 and KDA. In SWGDN, carrying information from the same token across updates can help the recurrent state reinforce a previously learned association. The local mixing strategy can be incorporated into any Delta-Rule-based linear attention architecture without changing its state update equations or chunkwise parallel algorithms. We apply this strategy to two Delta-Rule variants, GDN2 and KDA, and experimental results demonstrate that SWGDN outperforms the original Delta-Rule baseline across multiple benchmarks.
authors: Yuchen Song, Yangbin Chen
bullets: Linear attention treats its recurrent state as an online-learned key-value regression model, making update-pair construction important.
SWGDN replaces short convolutions with content-dependent sliding-window aggregation of queries, keys, and values.

It applies to both GDN2 and KDA while preserving their state-update equations and chunkwise parallel algorithms.
Experiments report improvements over the original Delta-Rule baseline across multiple benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Safety-critical interactions are rare in recorded driving data, leaving end-to-end driving planners with limited exposure to evasive behaviour during training. This lack of critical supervision can lead to unsafe behaviour and, in rare instances, collisions. To address this gap, we introduce CriticalScenes, a reconstruction-based framework that transforms ordinary recorded driving scenes into photorealistic safety-critical interactions with corresponding collision-avoidance supervision. Across 53 reconstructed source scenes, 979 of 1,060 attempted interactions yield feasible threat trajectories (92.4\%), while the inserted threat actors remain detectable in more than 95\% of non-occluded observations within 5--35\,m. Experiments with two structurally different end-to-end planners show that the generated supervision improves critical-scenario planning, while closed-loop transfer varies across planner architectures. SparseDrive achieves a 46.5\% relative reduction in collision rate on an independent photorealistic closed-loop benchmark, whereas UniAD shows only a modest closed-loop improvement despite substantial open-loop gains. The results further highlight the importance of closed-loop evaluation, as improvements in open-loop trajectory prediction do not necessarily translate into equivalent safety gains.

papers.abstract: Full fine-tuning of large pretrained models is expensive, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) is the standard alternative. Most PEFT methods use low-rank updates, whose rank lies far below that of full fine-tuning and is the same for every input. Input-adaptive variants vary the capacity per input but remain within the low-rank bottleneck, and whether a task benefits from input conditioning is not known before training. This paper introduces Kronecker input-gated rank adaptation (KiRA). Instead of the conventional low-rank product, the update $\Delta W$ is the Kronecker product of a frozen random $p\times p$ matrix $A$ and a trainable factor $M(x)$, which overcomes the rank ceiling: because rank is multiplicative under this product, $A$ multiplies the rank of $M(x)$ by $p$ without adding trainable parameters. The factor $M(x)$ is further decomposed as $B_1\,\mathrm{diag}(g(x))\,B_2$, where the input gate $g(x)$, computed once per sample by a network shared across all adapted layers, adjusts the rank of the update to each input in steps of $p$. Where input conditioning is unnecessary, the gate is folded into $B_1$ at deployment. Because the gate changes the rank only in discrete steps, the benefit of input conditioning can be predicted before training from a few hundred labeled inputs. Across six medical imaging and language benchmarks, KiRA attains the highest mean score against five published baselines with 8.7--9.7 times fewer trainable parameters than low-rank adaptation, and the pre-training criterion agrees with the measured benefit of input conditioning on all six tasks.
authors: Akil Ahmad Taki, Shaikh Anowarul Fattah

Across six medical imaging and language benchmarks, KiRA achieved the highest mean score among five published baselines while using 8.7–9.7× fewer trainable parameters than low-rank adaptation.
A pre-training criterion correctly predicted the benefit of input conditioning on all six tasks.

papers.abstract: We seek to learn discrete skill abstractions to facilitate long-horizon, goal-conditioned reinforcement-learning (RL) tasks. Recent approaches have shown success by quantizing actions via clustering or reconstruction. However, these objectives lead to skills that are not directly related to what the current state affords or what the goal requires. Instead, we argue that goal-directed skills should be driven by \emph{how they affect the state} of the agent. To realize this, we introduce a novel quantization method for action chunks that optimizes next-state predictions conditioned on the current state and action. This objective encourages skills to be distinguished by the future states they lead to, resulting in a vocabulary that spans diverse outcomes reachable from a given state. Our framework can easily be paired with common offline RL methods by replacing their continuous actor head with a discrete one that selects among the learned skills. We can execute these skills in the environment by converting them back to continuous actions using a trained low-level controller. Experiments on benchmark navigation and manipulation tasks largely show substantial and consistent improvements over both the continuous-actor baselines and reconstruction-based discretizations. Our project page can be found at: https://burcukilic.github.io/projects/effect-driven-skill-abstractions/.
authors: Burcu Kilic, David Drexel, Emre Ugur, Justus Piater
bullets: Existing clustering and reconstruction objectives may produce skills unrelated to current-state affordances or goal requirements.

A low-level controller converts selected discrete skills back into continuous actions for execution.
Experiments on benchmark navigation and manipulation tasks show substantial, consistent improvements over continuous-actor and reconstruction-based baselines.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for biomedical question answering, but plausible incorrect answers remain a safety risk in clinical settings. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can ground responses in medical literature, while confidence-based adaptive RAG retrieves only when the model appears uncertain. We evaluate this routing strategy on three biomedical QA benchmarks of increasing difficulty and compare models across a broad range of parameter scales. The results reveal a paradox: confidence is well calibrated (AUROC 0.78--0.89) on standard medical exam questions where retrieval adds little value (+2.4\% to -1.4\%), yet becomes \emph{near-random} (AUROC 0.506) on specialist-level questions where retrieval helps most (+11.2\%). Five uncertainty signals---first-token probability, margin, entropy, consistency-based sampling, and verbalized confidence---show the same failure pattern. Five post-hoc calibration correction strategies, including density-ratio reweighting and rank-preserving transformation, do not recover a useful routing signal on hard questions (best AUROC: 0.507). Cross-model comparison shows that larger parameter scale and higher base accuracy do not guarantee reliable confidence-based routing under specialist-domain difficulty shift. These findings challenge the premise of confidence-based adaptive RAG: in high-stakes biomedical settings, defaulting to always-retrieve is safer and more accurate than confidence-based routing when calibration on the target domain is unknown.
authors: Chengying She, Siyu Deng, Haiyan Ge, Lizhuang Liu
bullets: Evaluates confidence-based retrieval routing across three biomedical QA benchmarks with increasing difficulty and models of varied parameter scales.
On standard exam questions, confidence is well calibrated (AUROC 0.78–0.89), but retrieval offers little benefit (+2.4% to −1.4%).
On specialist-level questions, routing becomes near-random (AUROC 0.506) even though retrieval improves performance by 11.2%.
Five uncertainty signals and five post-hoc calibration methods show the same failure pattern; the best corrected AUROC is 0.507.
Larger models and higher base accuracy do not ensure reliable routing under specialist-domain difficulty shifts.

papers.abstract: AI configuration tuning searches for settings that improve the performance of AI systems under a limited budget. Existing tuners use different sampling and search policies, making the choice of decision strategy central to both tuning quality and cost. We investigate whether general-purpose decision models can guide tuning, using Jev as a deployed representative that returns structured choices and numeric scores across diverse tasks. To assess where it helps, we compare its use as an optimizer, performance predictor, and region guider against conventional methods and a large language model (LLM) on eight AI tuning tasks. Conventional optimizers attain rank 1 in six of eight comparisons. Similarly, established predictors outperform Jev in seven. Through region guidance, however, it finds configurations with lower perplexity than those selected by the native tuner, offering a quality gain when additional decision time and API fees are acceptable. These findings yield actionable recommendations on selecting the decision role, retaining conventional predictors, and balancing tuning quality against cost.
authors: Jingzhi Gong, Jie M. Zhang
bullets: AI configuration tuning must balance performance gains against limited search budgets and decision costs.
The study evaluates Jev as an optimizer, performance predictor, and region guider across eight AI tuning tasks, comparing it with conventional methods and an LLM.
Conventional optimizers rank first in six of eight comparisons, while established predictors outperform Jev in seven.
As a region guider, Jev identifies configurations with lower perplexity than the native tuner.
Using Jev can improve quality, but only when extra decision time and API fees are acceptable.

papers.abstract: Safe-mode events causing thrust outages are common in missions with electric propulsion. To demonstrate mission feasibility in such an event, missed-thrust margin studies are performed where thousands of outage scenarios need an exact re-plan solved. We train a neural operator that maps a nominal trajectory with an outage profile to a re-planned trajectory and to the probability that the recovery exists, for 270 low-thrust near-rectilinear halo orbit (NRHO) to distant retrograde orbit (DRO) transfers, at an allowed slip of up to 10 days. On unseen transfers and zero slip, its median control error on the severe half of outages is 1.20% compared to 14.0% for the best cheap re-planner benchmark. With the arrival slip as an input, the error is 1.67% against 23.2%. It also predicts the recoverability of an outage for a given arrival slip with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.997, while the minimum recoverable slip prediction is optimistic by more than half a day on only 6 of the 84 checked outages needing slip. At the original arrival, the ensemble spread of an operator variant with solver inputs has a rank correlation of 0.91 with the actual error, and performing exact solves on the 31% most uncertain severe outages reduces the 90th-percentile error from 8.5% to 2.3%. A query takes milliseconds without a solver, making this a useful tool for large outage studies where the cost of thousands of exact solves outweighs the time to train the operator.
authors: Selim Olgu Pilav
bullets: Addresses mission-feasibility studies requiring thousands of exact re-plans after electric-propulsion outages.

On unseen transfers, median control error was 1.20% at the original arrival and 1.67% with arrival slip, outperforming the reported cheap re-planner benchmarks.
Recoverability prediction achieved AUC 0.997; uncertainty-guided exact solves reduced the 90th-percentile error from 8.5% to 2.3%.
Millisecond queries support large outage studies; results are demonstrated for 270 low-thrust NRHO-to-DRO transfers and the stated slip range.

papers.abstract: Agentic benchmarks report a success rate that confounds distinct causes of failure: misreading the environment, never working out how components of the environment operates, operating the components in the wrong order, and failing to recover from a mistake, each of which calls for a different fix. We present an early preview of MultiNet v2.0-Gridworld - an interactive maze environment built for attribution rather than ranking. Four different types of mechanisms, namely key-door pairs, switch-gate pairs, distractors and decoys, and ordered combinations of these mechanisms, can be added, modified, or removed independently while the renderer, the action space, and the scoring function stay fixed. A breadth-first search over the joint state of position, facing direction, inventory, and mechanism state gives every instance an exact optimal action count, which sets its difficulty and grades unfinished episodes. We fix the evaluation protocol on 15 held-out mazes over 540 episodes, then evaluate three vision-language models on 50 mazes. They solve 6 of 150 episodes, 45 of the 50 mazes were not solved by any model, and no episode containing a switch-gate mechanism was solved.
authors: Pranav Guruprasad, Sean Rivera, Helen Lu, Arushi Jain, Hangliang Ren, Harshvardhan Sikka
bullets: Agentic success rates can conflate perception, mechanism learning, action ordering, and error recovery failures.
The benchmark independently varies key-door pairs, switch-gate pairs, distractors/decoys, and ordered mechanism combinations while keeping evaluation factors fixed.
Breadth-first search computes exact optimal action counts for difficulty setting and grading unfinished episodes.
Across 540 episodes on 15 held-out mazes and 50 evaluated mazes, three models solved only 6 of 150 episodes.
No episode involving a switch-gate mechanism was solved; 45 of 50 mazes were unsolved by every model.

papers.abstract: Many failures of deployed AI arise not from weak inference but from a mismatch between the state a task depends on and the context available when the system acts. Relevant user state, repository revisions, tool traces, sensor readings, or environment changes may be unavailable, distorted, or poorly selected. We call the effort to reduce this bottleneck context scaling. We frame a model as $P_\theta(d\mid c)$ within a system governed by three budgets: training $B_\theta$, decision-time $B_d$, and context-infrastructure $B_c$. Pretraining scaling invests in $\theta$; decision-time scaling searches, refines, or verifies decisions under supplied context; context scaling improves the system's capacity to acquire, represent, deliver, evaluate, and persist deployment state for model use. The three programs interact, but only $B_c$ targets what the system can make available before a decision. This view makes the model-infrastructure pair the unit of analysis. We define effective-context value as a task- and intervention-dependent attribution, separate deployment state from model-visible context, and identify availability, fidelity, selection, and utilization failures. We then organize current mechanisms through a five-operation context lifecycle and propose controlled budget interventions and utility-cost curves for evaluation. The resulting agenda centers on grounded reporting, interaction-data and full-cost infrastructure, and safety and governance for persistent, adaptive systems.
authors: Xipeng Qiu
bullets: Many failures stem from missing, distorted, or poorly selected context rather than weak inference.
It distinguishes three budgets: training, decision-time computation, and context infrastructure.
The model–infrastructure pair is the key unit of analysis, with context failures categorized by availability, fidelity, selection, and utilization.
A five-operation context lifecycle and utility–cost curves are proposed for evaluating context investments.
The agenda emphasizes grounded reporting, interaction-data and infrastructure costs, and safety for persistent adaptive systems.

papers.abstract: Composing frozen Vision-Language-Action (VLA) skills under an agentic planner promises scalable long-horizon manipulation without long-horizon demonstrations, yet strong atomic skills routinely fail at seams even under a correct plan. Standard remedies reset the robot's pose or draft entry conditions in language, missing the physical cause we uncover via causal interventions: even after re-homing, a frozen VLA rigidly retraces its habitual trajectory and collides with displaced scene residue, whether or not it can see it. We propose the Skill Envelope, a policy-measured 3D geometric precondition capturing the volume a frozen skill sweeps during successful executions. Exploiting the insight that the rigidity making a frozen skill fragile at seams also makes its trajectory predictable in advance, we expose each envelope as two classical 3D tools (CHECK to detect blocking residue and FREE to locate safe placement regions), establishing a division of labor where VLAs execute in-distribution manipulation and code repairs out-of-distribution states. On LIBERO-Goal with frozen $π_{0.5}$, our zero-failure envelope predicts collisions at 0.946 AUROC (0.944 from one RGB-D view) and beats frontier VLMs on seam readiness (0.902 vs. 0.793); using it for skill ordering and code repair lifts success from 82.8% to 92.3% on two-step seams and from 29.7% to 93.8% on drawer-bearing 3-4 step chains, matching privileged world reset. Together, these results show that reliable VLA composition hinges on measuring a policy's physical workspace rather than guessing preconditions in language. Ongoing work closes the loop with autonomous LLM orchestration, synthesized free-object recovery, and cross-policy evaluation on cluttered benchmarks and real hardware.
authors: Jiajie Zhang
Yankai Xiang
Changhao Chen
bullets: Frozen VLAs can collide with residual objects because they rigidly retrace habitual trajectories, even after re-homing or when residue is not visible.
The method models each skill’s swept volume as a 3D geometric precondition and exposes it through CHECK for collision detection and FREE for safe placement.
On LIBERO-Goal with frozen π₀.₅, envelope-based collision prediction achieved 0.946 AUROC, or 0.944 from one RGB-D view.
Using envelope-guided ordering and code repair improved two-step seam success from 82.8% to 92.3% and 3–4-step drawer chains from 29.7% to 93.8%.
The approach is evaluated in simulation and remains limited by ongoing work on autonomous orchestration, cluttered benchmarks, and real hardware.
