papers.abstract: World-action models combine action generation with future prediction, allowing visual transitions to serve as supervision for policy learning. Our controlled study of prediction spaces shows that spatially structured semantic features support better overall generalization under visual perturbations and make motion information more readily recoverable from learned predictive representations. Building on these observations, we introduce PreWAM, a world-action model that organizes future supervision around state changes in a prediction space defined by pretrained DINO features. Specifically, Residual World Prediction jointly learns source-relative changes and their resulting future states to emphasize dynamic information while preserving future-state semantics. Temporal-Scale Prediction conditions world queries on temporal distance to capture both short-term local motion and longer-horizon state evolution. These predictive objectives jointly shape a shared vision-language backbone with action supervision during pretraining and downstream policy learning. Experiments across the LIBERO benchmark family, SimplerEnv, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world robotic manipulation demonstrate strong manipulation performance and improved generalization and robustness under diverse distribution shifts.
authors: Wan Chi
Sen Li
Zihang Cui
Chuqin Huang

bullets: A controlled study finds spatially structured semantic features improve generalization under visual perturbations and preserve recoverable motion information.

Temporal-Scale Prediction models both short-term motion and longer-horizon state evolution.
Experiments on simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation show strong performance and improved robustness under diverse shifts.

papers.title: PreWAM: Exploring the Design of Latent Future Prediction for World-Action Modeling
papers.tldr: PreWAM improves robotic manipulation by predicting future state changes in a structured DINO-feature space, strengthening generalization and robustness to visual distribution shifts.

papers.abstract: Robots operating in the real world must often adapt when user instructions change mid-execution, yet current instruction-conditioned robot policies, including Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World-Action Models (WAMs), are largely evaluated under fixed-instruction episodes. We study mid-execution instruction switching and identify trajectory hijacking as a key failure mode, where the policy fails to redirect sufficiently toward the switched target, with its post-switch behavior remaining fully or partially drawn toward trajectories associated with non-target tasks. We propose Counterfactual Action Steering (CAS), a training-free, model-agnostic inference-time method that identifies interfering non-target tasks, queries the same policy with corresponding counterfactual instructions, and uses target--counterfactual action differences to steer execution away from interfering trajectory priors. Experiments on LIBERO-Goal-Switch and CALVIN-Custom-Switch across five VLA and WAM policies, together with real-robot evaluation, show that CAS consistently improves switching success; for example, on CALVIN-Custom-Switch in the $[15,21]$ switching range, CAS improves $π_{0.5}$ from 5.8\% to 54.6\%. Successful CAS-guided rollouts further provide higher-quality self-training supervision than vanilla successful rollouts with the same number of trajectories, yielding stronger policies that generalize to unseen later instruction switches. Code will be made publicly available.

bullets: Mid-execution instruction changes expose trajectory hijacking: policies remain influenced by non-target task trajectories after a switch.
Counterfactual Action Steering (CAS) queries the same policy with interfering alternative instructions and uses target–counterfactual action differences to redirect behavior.
CAS is training-free, model-agnostic, and evaluated across five VLA/WAM policies, two benchmarks, and real-robot settings.
On CALVIN-Custom-Switch for switching times 15–21, CAS raises π₀.₅ from 5.8% to 54.6%.
CAS-guided successful rollouts provide stronger self-training supervision and improve generalization to unseen later switches.

figures.caption: Figure 5 provides an overview of our approach. CAS is a training-free, model-agnostic inferencetime method for mitigating trajectory hijacking during mid-execution instruction switching. Beyond inference, successful CAS-guided rollouts can be used for self-training, providing de-hijacking supervision and enabling iterative improvement of the underlying policy.

Figure 4: Visualization of trajectory hijacking and instruction-conditioned action contrast. Colors denote four tasks: put the wine bottle on top of the cabinet, put the bowl on top of the cabinet, put the cream cheese in the bowl, and turn on the stove. Colored curves show demonstration trajectories, and same-colored arrows show the corresponding 3D end-effector translational actions projected onto the 2D camera plane. Panels (a,b) show two forms of trajectory hijacking in bowl-tostove switching rollouts, with the first frame at ts and subsequent frames after the switch. In (a), the policy completes the non-target bowl task; in (b), it partially drifts toward the bowl trajectory. Panels (c,d) show instruction-conditioned actions predicted from the same observation under the four task instructions: they nearly overlap in (c) but remain clearly distinguishable in (d).

Figure 1: Illustration of trajectory hijacking and the intuition behind CAS. The robot is first instructed to pick up the red block and starts moving toward it. The instruction is then changed to pick up the blue block. Without CAS, the policy may fail to redirect sufficiently toward the blue block; instead, its post-switch behavior can remain drawn toward the red-block trajectory, a failure mode we refer to as trajectory hijacking. In (c), the dashed red arrow denotes the action predicted under the red-block instruction, and the dashed blue arrow denotes the action predicted under the blue-block instruction. CAS contrasts these two actions, and their difference provides a corrective direction, producing the green corrected action that steers the robot away from the interfering trajectory prior and toward the switched target.
Figure 2: Success rates of OpenVLA-OFT, π0, π0.5, Fast-WAM and LingBot-VA at different switching steps. Performance generally degrades with later switches.

Figure 6: Real-world comparison of mid-execution instruction switching. The instruction switches from picking up the red block to picking up the blue block. Without CAS, insufficient redirection leads to an empty grasp; with CAS, the robot successfully picks up the blue block.

Figure 3: Visualization of attention persistence after instruction switching. We visualize actionto-vision attention in OpenVLA-OFT at the last language-backbone layer (layer 31), averaged over attention heads and action-token positions. At an intermediate execution state, we switch only the instruction while keeping the visual observation unchanged. In both examples, attention remains concentrated on the gripper and the previous target object (red), rather than shifting toward the new target (green), suggesting that visual attention can remain biased toward previously relevant objects despite instruction changes.

Figure 5: Overview of CAS. (a) Under mid-execution instruction switching, strong visual priors can cause the policy to remain drawn toward a non-target trajectory, resulting in trajectory hijacking. (b) Inference-time CAS identifies interfering non-target tasks, uses target–counterfactual action differences to determine where to steer, and trajectory proximity to determine how much to steer. In the red-to-blue block example, the hijacking task happens to coincide with the source task, but this need not hold in general. For clarity, the arrows show a single action from the predicted action chunk. (c) Successful CAS-guided rollouts can be used for self-training (CAS-ST), and this process can be applied iteratively. The blue-boxed comparison illustrates the effect of CAS-ST: given the same observation, the policy produces more task-distinct actions after self-training.

Figure 10: Representative rollout sequences for π0.5. Under instruction intervention, the first grasp attempt is slightly misaligned, but the policy still approaches and interacts with the correct target. Under vision intervention, the policy instead exhibits erratic motion without a clear taskdirected manipulation pattern.

Figure 8: Representative rollout sequences for OpenVLA-OFT. Under instruction intervention, the policy behaves similarly to clean inference and successfully grasps the correct object, whereas under vision intervention the gripper repeatedly translates toward the right without exhibiting a recognizable manipulation behavior.

Figure 9: Representative rollout sequences for π0. Under instruction intervention, the policy still reaches and grasps the correct object, although it does not complete the lift. Under vision intervention, the gripper moves slowly toward the right with substantially reduced motion magnitude.

Figure 12: Representative rollout sequences for LingBot-VA. Under instruction intervention, the policy still executes a coherent manipulation behavior but grasps an object corresponding to a different task. Under vision intervention, the gripper instead drifts toward the right and slightly downward without exhibiting comparable task-like structure.

Figure 11: Representative rollout sequences for Fast-WAM. Under instruction intervention, the first grasp attempt is misaligned, but the policy continues to approach the correct target. Under vision intervention, the robot repeatedly moves toward the basket while rotating, substantially degrading the recognizable task-like manipulation behavior.

Figure 13: Representative mid-execution stop failure after explicit training on the “remain still” instruction. The source instruction is “put the bowl on the plate.” At the switching state, the instruction is changed to “remain still” (left). Despite the updated instruction, the robot continues to move substantially over the following 100 environment steps (right), resulting in a cumulative end-effector path length of 30.74 cm and a final displacement of 23.81 cm from the switching state.

Figure 21: Successful rollouts for a switch from put the bowl on the stove to push the plate to the front of the stove. Both rollouts ultimately complete the target task. Without CAS, the policy remains more affected by the source-task trajectory prior and approaches the plate from a less suitable interaction position. As a result, one side of the plate lifts during the push, making the manipulation less smooth. With CAS, the gripper redirects toward a more suitable position for interacting with the plate and pushes it more smoothly toward the target location. Thus, although both rollouts succeed, CAS yields a cleaner post-switch manipulation trajectory.

Figure 22: Successful rollouts for a switch from push the plate to the front of the stove to put the cream cheese in the bowl. Both rollouts eventually complete the target task. Without CAS, the initial post-switch redirection toward the cream cheese is insufficient, causing the first grasp attempt to miss. The policy must then re-approach the object and perform additional corrective motions before succeeding. With CAS, the gripper redirects more effectively toward the cream cheese and succeeds on the first grasp attempt, yielding a cleaner trajectory with fewer unnecessary intermediate actions.

Figure 23: Successful rollouts for a switch from push the plate to the front of the stove to put the bowl on the stove. Both rollouts ultimately succeed. Without CAS, the policy does not redirect sufficiently toward a favorable grasp configuration and awkwardly catches the front edge of the bowl before lifting it. With CAS, the gripper is redirected toward a more suitable grasp pose and stably grasps the side of the bowl, resulting in more direct progress toward the updated task. Despite identical binary success outcomes, the two rollouts therefore exhibit clearly different post-switch manipulation quality.

Figure 14: What the policy sees when robot-state cues are preserved or altered. Each panel pairs third-person and wrist inputs at rollout start. A uses current views; B freezes both views to the initial images; C hides the robot in the current third-person view and freezes the wrist input; D retains only the robot and bowl. A–D share a physical starting state. E5/E10 instead raise the default initial pose by 5/10 cm and use normal images. Views are re-rendered from recorded starts (configuration 10), upright and before policy preprocessing.

Figure 26: Another example of instruction-conditioned action predictions at the same robot state. Colors correspond to wine bottle, bowl, cream cheese, and stove tasks. The base checkpoint predicts very similar actions across all four instructions, whereas the two-round CAS-ST checkpoint produces clearly separated, task-dependent action directions.

Figure 28: Instruction-conditioned actions in a state where the base checkpoint confuses a subset of task instructions. Colors correspond to wine bottle, bowl, cream cheese, and stove tasks. In the base checkpoint, the wine-bottle and stove actions are biased toward the bowl region. After two rounds of CAS-ST, these actions shift toward directions more consistent with their respective tasks.

Figure 25: Instruction-conditioned actions for the same robot state before and after two rounds of CAS-guided self-training. Colors correspond to wine bottle, bowl, cream cheese, and stove tasks. Under the base checkpoint, the four actions nearly overlap and point toward the wine-bottle region. After self-training, the actions become clearly separated and point broadly toward their corresponding task-relevant regions.

Figure 27: Instruction-conditioned actions in a state where the base checkpoint already exhibits partial task-dependent separation. Colors correspond to wine bottle, bowl, cream cheese, and stove tasks. While some base actions are task-consistent, others remain misaligned. After two rounds of CAS-ST, all four actions become more clearly separated and better aligned with their corresponding task directions.

Figure 7: Action-level illustration of Counterfactual Action Steering. The robot switches from the source task put the bowl on top of the cabinet to the target task turn on the stove. Since the current end-effector position pt is close to the demonstration trajectory distributions of the bowlrelated tasks, CAS selects put the bowl on top of the cabinet (green) and put the cream cheese in the bowl (yellow) as hijacking tasks based on their small KNN distances, while excluding put the wine bottle on top of the cabinet (blue) due to its larger KNN distance. CAS contrasts the targetconditioned action atgt with the selected counterfactual actions ahj and aggregates the weighted directions atgt − ahj to produce afinal (red), which steers the robot away from interfering trajectory priors and toward the stove knob. For clarity, the arrows visualize the translational components of a single action from each predicted action chunk, taken at the same horizon index.

Figure 15: Task differences persist in the language backbone but are weaker in the action expert near the source object. We compare early (t = 10) and late (t = 25) states on the same wine-source trajectory. (a) Task separation persists across the language backbone: solid lines show object-token averages and dashed lines the shared final text token. (b) At the first flow update, all instructions start from identical action noise. Task separation grows through the expert in both states, but much less strongly in the late state. Axes show relative separation D (Eq. 6) with different scales. Curves precede final normalization; Table 13 reports module outputs after normalization.

Figure 18: Steering-weight sweep for CAS variants. We vary the fixed steering weight w ∈ {0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8} for Source-only CAS and All non-target Fixed. Every tested setting of both variants outperforms the base policy. Source-only CAS achieves its best Switch SR of 35.4% at w = 0.6, while All non-target Fixed peaks at 23.3% at w = 0.4. Dashed horizontal lines show the base policy and full CAS for reference.

Figure 19: Hyperparameter ablations of CAS on CALVIN-Custom-Switch for ts ∈ [15, 21]. Starting from the default setting K = 30, δ = 0.1, and λ = 0.03, we vary one hyperparameter at a time while keeping the other two fixed: (a) steering strength λ, (b) number of nearest neighbors K, and (c) KNN distance threshold δ. The dashed line denotes the base policy without CAS.

Figure 17: Scene appearance variants used for evaluating robustness to visual train–test mismatch. D0 is the original CALVIN-Custom-Switch scene used for training in our main experiments, while D1–D3 progressively darken the background appearance. The task semantics, object layout, and scene geometry remain unchanged across variants.

Figure 16: Visualization of task trajectory distributions under different object-pose regimes in CALVIN-Custom-Switch. In narrow, medium, and wide, object poses are sampled as perturbations around fixed nominal centers, with progressively larger perturbation ranges producing increasingly dispersed trajectories. The random regime instead samples object positions over a broader workspace region without fixed nominal centers, resulting in a qualitatively different trajectory structure.

Figure 20: Effect of the steering strength λ on CAS with π0 on CALVIN-Custom-Switch (K = 30, δ = 0.1) in the three switching ranges (a) ts ∈ [9, 15], (b) [15, 21], and (c) [21, 27]. Base denotes the base policy without CAS. Over a broad range of λ, CAS clearly improves over the base policy in all three switching ranges.

Figure 24: Official demonstration trajectories for the four LIBERO-Goal tasks used in our action visualization: put the wine bottle on top of the cabinet, put the bowl on top of the cabinet, put the cream cheese in the bowl, and turn on the stove. The trajectory colors are consistent with those used in the action visualizations and provide visual references for the corresponding task-consistent motion directions.

Table 21: Comparison of full CAS with alternative action correction strategies on LIBERO-GoalSwitch and CALVIN-Custom-Switch. We evaluate direct scaling of the target-conditioned action with different scaling factors α, random counterfactual selection with adaptive KNN-based or fixed steering weights, reversed counterfactual correction, and final-action norm matching. We also compare against random counterfactual action interpolation with β = 0.5. All methods use the π0 policy architecture and the corresponding benchmark evaluation protocol, with the switching step set to ts = 20 on LIBERO and ts ∈ [15, 21] on CALVIN. We report target-task success rates (%); higher is better.
Table 1: Simulation results for inference-time instruction switching. We report target-task success rates (%) on LIBERO-Goal-Switch and CALVIN-Custom-Switch.
Table 3: Real-world switching.

Table 6: Average LIBERO success rates (%) under reported clean evaluation and inference-time modality interventions. Results are averaged over LIBERO-Spatial, LIBERO-Object, LIBEROGoal, and LIBERO-Long.

Table 38: Finetuning settings for the main one-round Vanilla-ST and CAS-ST comparisons. Settings are matched within each policy–benchmark comparison; reported checkpoints are listed as LIBERO / CALVIN.

Table 14: Local positional robustness and trajectory proximity. Original-task completion (%; 50 trials per cell) after random end-effector translations of magnitude r, with orientation preserved. Tasks are opening the middle drawer (0), placing cream cheese in the bowl (6), and turning on the stove (7). “Remain still” is the literal post-prefix instruction. KNN distances (K = 30) are medians over original-instruction trials, in cm; bold marks the source task.
Table 2: Evaluation of CAS-guided self-training. We compare CAS-ST with Vanilla-ST using equal numbers of successful trajectories at the data-collection setting and an unseen later switch.

Table 5: CAS variants and design ablation. We compare full CAS, its lightweight Source-only CAS variant, and All non-target Fixed. Source-only CAS requires no trajectory data and achieves 35.4% Switch SR. Full CAS achieves the highest success rate of 45.4% with state-dependent task selection and adaptive steering across relevant hijacking tasks.
Table 7: Suite-level LIBERO success rates (%) under reported clean evaluation and inference-time modality interventions. Each suite contains 10 tasks with 50 evaluation episodes per task.
Table 28: Success rates after 10,000 fine-tuning steps, without test-time CAS. Each switching time has 90 episodes per method; Overall pools all 360 episodes. Gains are computed from unrounded rates.

Table 36: Action statistics of successful post-switch trajectories. Each entry is an equal-weight mean over trajectories; the original and paired datasets contain 148 and 223 trajectories per method, respectively.

Table 35: Switching-point proprioceptive distribution tests on the original π0.5 self-training data (148 trajectories per method). Reported p-values use the aggregate statistic across ten source tasks.

Table 40: Comparison with released AVA-VLA and OpenVLA-OFT+ models on LIBERO-GoalSwitch. CAS improves both OpenVLA-OFT and OpenVLA-OFT+ at every switching time without additional policy training. The average is taken over the four switching times.

Table 24: All source–target pairs where CAS-ST has more retained self-training trajectories than Vanilla-ST. CAS-ST improves six pairs and ties one, with no observed regression. ∆ Traj. denotes the difference in retained trajectories (CAS-ST − Vanilla-ST), and ∆ Succ. denotes the success-rate difference in percentage points.

Table 10: Early manipulation across 20 initial configurations. A–E10 use “remain still”; REF uses the original instruction. Approach: EEF-to-bowl distance decreases by > 5 cm. Lift: bowlcenter height increases by > 2 cm at any step in the 60-step window, a proxy for the lifting stage. ∆d: final minus initial EEF-to-bowl distance.

Table 16: Success rates (%) of π0 on CALVIN-Custom-Switch under different levels of trajectory concentration. The narrow setting corresponds to CALVIN-Custom-Switch-Fixed used in the main experiments.

Table 32: Self-training performance (%) on the 42 trajectory-biased initial states under different finetuning budgets. CAS-ST is substantially more finetuning-efficient: with only 10k finetuning steps, it already outperforms Vanilla-ST trained for 50k steps.

Table 11: Wrong-task completion as a percentage of all switching episodes. Each switchingrange column reports the percentage of all 240 episodes in that range for which the target task fails but a non-target task is completed. Overall aggregates all four switching ranges.

Table 12: Wrong-task completion as a percentage of target-task failures. Each switching-range column reports the percentage of target-task failures in that range for which the robot completes a non-target task. Overall aggregates target-task failures across all four switching ranges.
Table 29: Success rates (%) from trajectory-biased initial states on LIBERO-Goal. CAS consistently improves all evaluated VLA policies and outperforms PCD where applicable.

Table 22: Self-training performance (%) of Fast-WAM on CALVIN-Custom-Switch under different finetuning budgets. CAS-ST with only 4k finetuning steps already substantially outperforms VanillaST trained for 20k steps.
Table 18: Switch-only success rates (%) under scene appearance shifts for π0. Each variant contains 600 episodes covering 12 ordered off-diagonal source–target pairs with 50 repetitions per pair.
Table 31: Self-training performance (%) on the 42 trajectory-biased initial states on LIBERO-Goal. CAS-ST consistently outperforms Vanilla-ST across all three evaluated VLA policies.
Table 34: Self-training data collection and dataset composition for the main one-round results. Vanilla-ST and CAS-ST use matched numbers of retained self-training trajectories.

Table 17: Success rates (%) under the random trajectory regime on CALVIN-Custom-SwitchRandom. Object positions are randomized over a broader workspace region rather than sampled as perturbations around nominal centers.

Table 42: Comparison of ReSteer and CAS-guided self-training at later switching times on LIBEROGoal-Switch. ReSteer results use our adaptation of the authors’ public code. All trained policies are evaluated without inference-time CAS.

Table 8: Post-switch end-effector motion after switching to “remain still” following explicit remainstill training. Results are aggregated over 50 rollouts across the ten LIBERO-Goal source tasks and five switching steps.

Table 33: Prediction horizons and actions executed per policy query in the Observation 1 online evaluations. For LingBot-VA, 12/16 denotes 12 actions in the first chunk after a reset and 16 actions in subsequent streaming chunks.
Table 41: Inference-time CAS and our adaptation of ReSteer’s SteerGen on LIBERO-Goal-Switch. CAS matches or exceeds SteerGen at all four switching times without additional policy training.

Table 23: Pair-level cases where CAS-ST uses fewer retained self-training trajectories than VanillaST but achieves higher evaluation success. ∆ Traj. denotes the difference in retained trajectories (CAS-ST − Vanilla-ST), and ∆ Succ. denotes the success-rate difference in percentage points.

Table 13: Task separation along the language-to-action computation. Values are D for the early/late state pair in Fig. 15. Ratios compare states within each row. Language and expert measurements follow final normalization.

Table 36 shows consistent patterns across both datasets. Relative to Vanilla, CAS increases mean translational magnitude by 13.6%/15.6% and rotational magnitude by 21.9%/18.8% in the original/paired datasets. Adjacent translational- and rotational-command changes increase by 36.9%/39.6% and 44.5%/43.3%, respectively. These larger changes may reflect more pronounced corrective adjustments and redirection under CAS; they describe commanded actions rather than physical motion smoothness.

Table 15: Inference-time efficiency on CALVIN-Custom-Switch with π0. We compare the base policy, CAS, and PCD over the same 240 episodes for ts ∈ [15, 21] on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU, with a maximum episode length of 180 environment actions. CAS is evaluated using serial counterfactual policy queries. Avg. Inference Latency per Replan sums the wall-clock time of all policy queries issued within one replan. Values in parentheses denote the inference latency relative to the base policy.
Table 30: Success rates (%) from trajectory-biased initial states under different OpenVLA-OFT checkpoints and observation configurations.
Table 27: Training data for the paired self-training comparison. All selected trajectories and frames are retained without truncation or downsampling.

Table 39: Comparison with CAG-TF on LIBERO-Goal-Switch. Each policy is evaluated without steering (Base), with CAG-TF, and with CAS. CAS achieves higher target-task success rates than CAG-TF across all three policies and all four switching times.

Table 39 shows that CAG-TF improves π0.5 at every switching time, while its effects on OpenVLAOFT and π0 are mixed. CAS outperforms CAG-TF in all 12 policy–switching-time settings. These results support the value of contrasting against state-relevant competing tasks in mid-execution switching, beyond the gains available from a language-grounding intervention alone.

Table 19: Robustness to inference random seeds on LIBERO-Goal-Switch. We evaluate π0.5 at ts = 25 over five random seeds. Each seed contains the same 90 ordered source–target task pairs. CAS consistently improves over the base policy across all evaluated seeds. Seed 7 corresponds to the setting used in the main evaluation.

Table 9: Instruction-induced attention changes are smaller during execution. Mean last-layer TV across all 12 directed task pairs. Each comparison changes only the instruction at a fixed state. The initial baseline contains six unique unordered pairs reused across directions.
Table 37: Mean successful post-switch trajectory length, measured in executed target-action steps. All retained trajectories are used in full, without truncation or downsampling.

Table 35 shows no statistically detectable overall difference in switching-point proprioceptive distributions. The position-only source-level analysis identifies a localized difference for opening the middle drawer (p = 0.00403, corrected q = 0.0403): the group centroids differ by 0.81 cm, compared with a pooled within-group RMS pairwise distance of 4.53 cm. The paired experiment in Appendix F.7 directly controls switching states and task composition when comparing the training value of the trajectories.
Table 26: Self-training results on CALVIN-Custom-Switch-Random in the [15, 21] switching-step range. CAS-ST substantially improves π0, while Vanilla-ST does not provide a meaningful gain.

Table 25: Self-training performance (%) on LIBERO-Goal-Switch at unseen later switching steps. All self-training trajectories are collected at ts = 25. The ts = 30 results are also reported in Table 2, while ts = 35 provides an additional evaluation farther beyond the self-training regime.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free inference-time steering for instruction-conditioned VLA/WAM policies under mid-execution instruction switching, with real-robot evaluation.
papers.title: DeRail: Escaping Trajectory Priors via Counterfactual Action Steering for Mid-Execution Instruction Switching
papers.tldr: CAS helps robots switch tasks mid-execution by steering actions away from trajectories associated with outdated instructions, substantially improving switching success without retraining.

papers.abstract: A legged robot can learn to walk inside a learned simulator: a neural network that predicts the robot's next state and is run forward on its own predictions. They are usually trained and checked one step ahead, although a policy uses them for a hundred steps or more. We audit one published system end to end, without a GPU: the dynamics model of the Robotic World Model (RWM) for the ANYmal D quadruped, and the uncertainty estimate of its follow-up, RWM-U. We rebuilt the model to match the released code's outputs, losses and gradients exactly, measured 101 trained simulators, 200 compressed copies and 38 simulators of three other architectures, and trained policies inside simulators that we tested in a hand-built MuJoCo model of the robot. Training on the model's own rollouts beat one-step training at 368 steps on all ten held-out episodes (registered), although one-step training was better one step ahead. One-step checks therefore misjudge design choices: pruning 30% of the weights kept 90% of the model's skill one step ahead and 39% at 2 s. Ensemble disagreement ranked rollout error well (Spearman +0.90 at 100 steps), yet covered 4.6% of outcomes at one sigma, against 68% for a calibrated estimate, as each network's own variance collapses under the implemented loss. Two checks that need no recorded future ranked some pools of simulators well, but neither was shown better than 8-step error in a primary test. At the robot level, accuracy has not predicted walking: all 18 fine-tuned copies we tested predicted better than the released model one and eight steps ahead, yet 13 gave failing policies, and registered tests of whether any check ranks simulators by their policies were not settled. In a secondary test, running the authors' policy inside each simulator ranked them well. We also report nine of our own claims that we withdrew. Scope: one robot, one gait, simulated data, no hardware.
authors: Joyjeet Singh
bullets: Reconstructed the Robotic World Model (RWM) and its uncertainty variant, evaluating many trained, compressed, and alternative-architecture simulators.
Training on the simulator’s own rollouts outperformed one-step training over long horizons, despite worse one-step accuracy.
Pruning preserved much more short-horizon than 2-second performance, showing that one-step evaluations can misjudge design choices.
Ensemble disagreement correlated with rollout error but was severely miscalibrated, covering far fewer outcomes than expected.
Simulator accuracy did not reliably predict policy success: most fine-tuned models produced failing walking policies, though a secondary policy-in-simulator test ranked models well.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Error at each forecast step on the 20 held-out trajectories of the five splits, with models averaged within each trajectory. The teacher-forced model first exceeds the floor at step 29, and the 30%-pruned copy at step 57. The vertical line marks the 100-step horizon that RWM and RWM-U imagine.

Figure 1. Checks are run on the simulator; what matters is measured on the policy. The stages this paper follows. Sections 4 to 8 measure the simulator on recorded data. Section 9 measures policies trained inside it, in a physics model. Whether the first kind of measurement predicts the second is the question of Sections 7 and 9.

Figure 4. Growth rate against the training horizon, for a history of 32 steps and three seeds each. Triangles mark models trained one step ahead. Above zero, a small error grows; below zero, it dies out.

Figure 6. Calibration of each network’s own predicted standard deviation, for four models: our rollout-trained model with the released loss (‘faithful Arm A’), the same with the likelihood loss (‘corrected Arm A’), our teacher-forced model (‘Arm B’) and the released checkpoint. The data are the four held-out trajectories of the main split, which may be in-sample for the released checkpoint. (a) Observed against predicted coverage; a calibrated estimate lies on the diagonal. (b) Coverage at one sigma against forecast horizon; a calibrated estimate gives 68%. (c) Mean absolute error over mean predicted standard deviation; the dashed line is where the two are equal. Every model is far too confident.

Figure 8. One-step error, growth rate and kinematic residual (left to right) against 100-step error, for the 97 simulators of the main pool. Models trained one step ahead (triangles) have low one-step error, high 100-step error and positive growth rates. Compressed copies (squares) spread mostly up and down. The dashed line is the floor.

Figure 2. Teacher forcing’s error minus rollout training’s at 368 steps (relative L1), for each of the five splits. Each red dot is one held-out episode, and every dot is above zero. The black diamond is the difference pooled over all 20 trajectories, with its 95% interval.

Figure 5. The collapse during training, in 75 logged runs of 2,500 iterations: 70 with the released loss (blue) and 5 with the likelihood loss (green). (a) The lowest (solid) and highest (dashed) standard deviation the head can output. Under the released loss both fall; under the likelihood loss both rise. (b) How fast the gap between the two bounds changes, in learning rates per iteration, beside the optimiser’s typical and largest step. The likelihood loss flips the sign.

Figure 11. Speed against skill on the 2017 laptop CPU (exploratory). Horizontal: speed-up of a one-robot, one-thread step over the ordinary 32-bit model. Vertical: skill retained at 368 steps against the original 32-bit model, first seed, with 95% intervals. Filled markers are ordinary PyTorch, and open markers are compiled with TorchScript. Models trained from scratch are placed at the speed of the pruned model of the same width. The reference also credits the fine-tuned narrow models with fine-tuning’s own gain.

Figure 13. The walk test ranked the 19 simulators by walking best, at +0.84 and +0.79. Error one and eight steps ahead ranked them partly in reverse. How each check ranked the ladder’s 19 simulators, the released model and 18 fine-tuned copies of it, against the mean walking score of their policies, as Spearman’s rank correlation. Lower errors, residuals, growth rate, imagined falls and disagreement count as better, so a point right of zero means the check orders the simulators as their policies walk. Whiskers are 95% intervals; the registered analysis computed them only for these four rankings, and for the others only for the differences in the table above. The walk-test rows are secondary results; the attitude residual was registered as exploratory, without a decision rule.

Figure 7. Error over spread against forecast horizon, for the released checkpoint and for our five-split ensembles (20 trajectories each). Solid lines use the released evaluation’s rollout, which feeds the ensemble mean back in. Dashed lines roll each member out on its own predictions, which the release does not do. A calibrated estimate lies on the line at 0.80.

Figure 12. Policies stop walking after 20 fine-tuning steps, or 160 at a tenth of the learning rate. The adaptation ladder. Each point is one copy of the released model fine-tuned on data from our MuJoCo robot for the given number of steps, placed at the mean walking score of its two or three policies; lines join copies saved from one run. Filled points: the simulator did not fail. Open points: at least two of its policies failed, so the simulator failed. The open point at 0.15 and 20 steps is the run with one-step windows: its mean rounds to the threshold, but two of its three policies scored below it. The band marks the released model’s own two policies. Descriptive.

Figure 9. Error at 368 steps relative to re-synchronising on a fixed schedule (the line at 1), against the number of re-synchronisations allowed per rollout. The triggers are the kinematic score computed during the rollout (circles), the calibrated ensemble disagreement (squares) and their average (triangles). Every point lies above the line: no trigger beat the schedule. Bars are 95% intervals. papers.title: Auditing a Learned Simulator for Legged Robots: The Robotic World Model on ANYmal D

papers.abstract: Frontier large language models (LLMs) deliver the strongest response quality but carry per-token prices often more than an order of magnitude above those of smaller, task-adequate models. Smart model routing addresses this mismatch by assigning each query to the cheapest model expected to answer it adequately, rather than sending every request to the most capable, most expensive endpoint. This paper develops a formal cost-quality optimization framework for routing -- including a derived optimal threshold-policy structure, a calibration-versus-discrimination distinction, a cascade breakeven condition, and a sensitivity analysis over price ratio and traffic skew -- situates that framework against the principal routing architectures and the signals used to estimate query difficulty, and works through a numerical example showing how a calibrated router can reduce blended inference cost by roughly an order of magnitude relative to an always-frontier deployment under specific, stated pricing and traffic assumptions, reporting both the gross reduction from routing policy alone and the net figure with the router's own overhead priced in. We situate this figure against the range reported by published routing systems (roughly 2x to frontier-level accuracy at one-fifth the cost), and close with the practical risks -- under- and over-routing, aggregate quality constraints masking segment-level harm, calibration without discrimination, calibration drift, prompt injection into routing signals, and operational failures such as tier outages and multi-provider price variation -- that determine whether the savings materialize in production. The analysis is primarily analytical, complemented by a GSM8K evaluation of the cascade framework (Section 5), validated (Section 5.2); extending the evaluation across tasks and model families is future work.
authors: Hesham Elbakoury
Deep Shah
Ankur Sharma
bullets: Frames routing as a cost–quality optimization problem and derives an optimal threshold-policy structure.
Distinguishes router calibration from discrimination and analyzes cascade breakeven points, price ratios, and traffic skew.
A numerical example reports roughly 10× lower blended cost than always using a frontier model under stated pricing and traffic assumptions, including router overhead.
The cascade framework is evaluated on GSM8K; broader evaluation across tasks and model families remains future work.
Production savings can be undermined by misrouting, calibration drift, segment-level quality harm, prompt injection, outages, and changing provider prices.

Figure 1. Sensitivity of the cost-reduction factor R(φ, ρ) to the price ratio ρ and the frontier-tier traffic share φ, per Equation (4). The red contour marks R = 10x; the combinations that reach a 10x reduction lie below it (frontier share small enough for the price ratio), combinations above it cannot reach a 10x reduction regardless of router quality, and no combination with a price ratio below 10 reaches 10x at any traffic share.

papers.abstract: Transformer architectural modifications frequently measure a statistic on internal representations, observe that it is large, remove it architecturally, and report an improvement. Interpreting that sequence requires evaluating whether the statistic exceeds its noise floor, whether it survives a geometric null, and whether the training gain requires the specific direction removed. We formulate these requirements as three reusable checks and apply them to self-attention removal, which deletes the component of an attention head's output aligned with its own value vector. Across nine multi-head pretrained models (5,408 heads, 124M to 6.9B parameters), an earlier-position causal null accounts for 48% to 63% of the head-value cosine alignment, with no monotone scale trend. Under grouped-query attention, this alignment is specific to each head's own key-value group and reverses across groups (+0.24 to +0.27 within-group, -0.11 to -0.19 across-group). Split-half reliability demonstrates that the per-head intervention effect is resolvable in GPT-2 ($r_Δ= 0.80$) but attenuated in Pythia-160M (0.42) and Pythia-410M (0.53), whereas structural self-cosine reliability is near-perfect in all three ($r_{\text{stat}} > 0.99$); which statistic predicts its own intervention is model-dependent. In a pre-registered 3-arm by 8-seed paired factorial at $4.0 \times 10^8$ tokens per run (399,900,672 tokens), a fixed arbitrary rank-one direction does not differ from baseline (+0.0011 nats, $p = 0.197$), while self-directed removal lowers validation loss (-0.0029 nats, Holm-corrected $p = 0.0023$) and outperforms the fixed arbitrary control directly (-0.0040 nats, $p = 0.0018$). At 50.9M scale the training benefit requires the own-value direction rather than a fixed arbitrary one, but a large cosine alignment alone does not establish redundancy in frozen models.
authors: Basavaraj R M
Aryan Bharat Kumar
bullets: An earlier-position causal null explains 48–63% of head–value cosine alignment, with no consistent parameter-scale trend.
Under grouped-query attention, alignment is specific to each head’s own key–value group and reverses across groups.
Structural self-cosine is highly reliable, but intervention-effect reliability and predictive validity vary by model.
In a preregistered factorial experiment, self-directed removal reduced validation loss, while a fixed arbitrary rank-one control did not.
Large cosine alignment alone does not prove redundancy in frozen models.

papers.title: Sanity Checks for Attention Surgery: Null Models and Matched Interventions for Representation-Motivated Design
papers.tldr: Three sanity checks show that attention-removal gains must be evaluated against null structure, geometric controls, and matched interventions: self-directed value removal helps training, whereas arbitrary-direction removal does not.

papers.abstract: Low-bit post-training quantization reduces language-model memory but can sharply degrade downstream task accuracy. Calibration usually relies on generic text, but when task-informed data recover accuracy and which quantizers benefit remain poorly understood. We introduce FragCal-DC, which supplements generic text with training documents from task families with low retention of full-precision accuracy in a two-bit scan. We use a two- to four-bit sweep to locate functional regimes and four-seed calibration comparisons to evaluate six data-dependent methods across six dense models (1.7B-8B) and ten tasks. At their lowest tested functional bit widths, iterative SignRound V2 and OmniQuant improve at two bits, whereas single-pass GPTQ and AWQ show small mean responses at three bits. At two bits, SignRound V2 gains 1.83 percentage points in mean ten-task accuracy over generic-text calibration across six models. At 70 billion parameters, GPTQ and SignRound V2 both improve at two bits, with functional generic-calibration baselines. For two-bit SignRound V2, task-level controls show that recovery concentrates on families included in calibration, while incorrect answer designations retain about 90% of the mean accuracy gain. Changes in reconstruction error do not consistently track accuracy gains. These findings support task-informed calibration as a design principle for preserving downstream accuracy in low-bit quantization.
authors: Yehong Jiang
Yen-Kuang Chen
Xinmin Tian
bullets: Generic-text calibration often loses downstream accuracy at very low bit widths.
FragCal-DC adds training documents from task families that retain little full-precision accuracy under two-bit quantization.
Across six dense models and ten tasks, SignRound V2 improved mean accuracy by 1.83 percentage points at two bits over generic-text calibration.
Benefits depend on the quantizer and bit width: iterative methods improved at two bits, while GPTQ and AWQ showed small mean responses at three bits.
Accuracy recovery concentrated on task families represented in calibration, and reconstruction error did not consistently predict gains.

papers.selection_reason: Low-bit quantization reduces model memory footprint; task-informed calibration is a transferable efficiency technique.
papers.title: When Calibration Data Matter in Sub-4-Bit Language Model Quantization
papers.tldr: Task-informed calibration can substantially improve two-bit language-model quantization, especially for methods such as SignRound V2 and OmniQuant.

papers.abstract: Reproducible evaluation, verifiable inference and on-policy reinforcement learning (RL) need an LLM engine to give a request the same output bits whichever requests share its batch. Batch-invariant kernels exist, but engines still select each kernel and its parameters from the batch. Two kernels that compute the same sum can round it differently. The engines' deterministic modes remove the choice by keeping one conservative kernel per operator and pay for it in latency. Many fast kernels are batch-invariant by themselves, so it is enough to fix the few batch-dependent values that kernel selection reads. Detent expresses kernel selection as a program that the engine executes. It finds the fewest values in this program that must be fixed and tunes them for the workload before deployment. On multi-GPU deployments of Llama-3.1-70B and Qwen3-30B-A3B in vLLM and SGLang, Detent is batch-invariant. Tuned per load, it serves at 1.04-1.17x the latency per output token of Stock (each engine with its standard settings), against 1.67-10.3x for the deterministic modes. In SGLang it matches the GSM8K accuracy of SGLang's deterministic mode. Detent covers multiple deployment combinations, including multiple engines, GPU generations, tensor-parallel degrees, and dense and MoE models. Seeded RL rollouts of models up to Llama-3.1-70B replay bit for bit under other batches and cache splits. A trainer on Detent's kernels and values matches every rollout logprob bit for bit at 1.03x Stock's rollout time per token. BF16 GRPO then stays stable where Stock's run collapses.
authors: Peixu Xin
Runchuan Feng
Jiazhen Guo
Kan Wu
Ming Yin
bullets: Batch-dependent kernel selection can change floating-point results, undermining reproducible evaluation, verifiable inference, and on-policy RL.
Detent represents kernel selection as an executable program, identifies the minimal values requiring fixation, and tunes them per workload before deployment.
Across Llama-3.1-70B and Qwen3-30B-A3B deployments in vLLM and SGLang, it achieves 1.04–1.17× Stock latency per output token versus 1.67–10.3× for deterministic modes.
It reproduces seeded RL rollouts bit for bit across batches and cache splits; training logprob computation runs at 1.03× Stock rollout time per token.
BF16 GRPO remains stable with Detent where Stock collapses, while SGLang matches its deterministic-mode GSM8K accuracy.

papers.abstract: Large language models can generate motion graphics from static images and natural language requests, but it remains difficult to evaluate how well models follow requests that combine spatial, appearance, and temporal requirements. We introduce MotionGraphicsBench, an expert-curated benchmark of 100 instances for animating an input static SVG with a motion edit prompt. By supplying all required visual elements, our editing task reflects a designer-like workflow and isolates motion generation from graphic generation. Derived from real-world Lottie motion designs, our benchmark contains diverse combinations of spatio-temporal animation behaviors. Each benchmark instance pairs its model input with a deterministic, human-readable verification program that accepts different valid implementations and reports which prompt requirements pass or fail, rather than comparing against a reference animation or using a VLM judge. We construct these programs with a multi-agent pipeline using human-labeled animations and synthesized test cases. On a balanced test set of 180 animations, our programs achieve 93.3% raw agreement with human judgments, outperforming frontier VLM judges by 4.4%-12.8% while achieving at least 90% recall for both human approvals and rejections. Across 47 configurations from 32 LLMs and 12 providers, pass@1 ranges from 5.0% to 68.0%. Across 15 models at their highest reasoning effort, additional attempts improve every model, but pass@32 still ranges from 38.0% to 95.0%. Our analysis of verification programs reveals that generated animations often fail to match reference poses, follow requested motion trajectories, or coordinate related events. We fine-tune Qwen3.8-27B with group relative policy optimization (GRPO) using our verification programs as rewards, improving pass@1 from 30.31% to 52.19% on held-out instances. Our project page is at https://motion-graphics-bench.github.io/.
authors: Jiaju Ma
Ashvini Kumar Jindal
Chuhua Wang
Sumithra Bhakthavatsalam
bullets: Introduces an expert-curated benchmark of 100 static-SVG motion-editing instances derived from real-world Lottie designs.

Across 32 LLMs and 12 providers, pass@1 ranges from 5.0% to 68.0%; common failures involve poses, motion trajectories, and event coordination.
Using verification programs as GRPO rewards improves Qwen3.8-27B pass@1 from 30.31% to 52.19% on held-out instances.

papers.abstract: Imitation policies inherit the operator's pace, and re-timing the demonstrations to run faster works only until success collapses at two to three times demonstration speed. Recent methods attribute that collapse to distribution shift and answer it with finer rules for which segments may be sped up; we show it has a mechanical cause that segment selection cannot address. A low-level controller realises only a bounded displacement per control period, so merging consecutive commands produces sums outside that bound: training pairs that promise a transition the plant cannot deliver. The share of such pairs in the re-timed data, which we call the exceed share, tracks where the retrained policy collapses. The rule that follows has a single parameter: merge greedily while the sum stays realisable. Every command is then realisable by construction, the demonstrated geometry is preserved, and the speed-up lands only where the demonstrator left slack. On four simulated robomimic tasks, 200 held-out seeds per cell, a merge cap of two is at or above the frozen policy's success on all four, by 14 points on Square, and shortens the successful episodes. At matched tempo, uniform re-timing loses 9 and 16 points on Can and ToolHang, is within noise on the other two, and reaches zero on the hardest at 2x. Placement also matters: no shuffled, entropy-guided or speed-conditioned alternative beats the rule on three of the four tasks, by margins the exceed share alone does not explain; on the fourth, at a tempo the task absorbs, every placement lands in the same band. The same principle carries to a simulated humanoid whole-body tracker: re-timing 429 reference motions within its velocity envelope succeeds on 71% of clips at 2.3x, against 51% for uniform time scaling at 2x.
authors: Zongtan Li
Tianming Liu
Ye Zhao
bullets: The study identifies a mechanical failure mode: merging commands can exceed the low-level controller’s per-period displacement bound.
It introduces exceed share, the fraction of unrealizable re-timed training pairs, which tracks where policy success collapses.
A one-parameter greedy rule merges commands only while their summed displacement remains realizable, preserving demonstration geometry and using available slack.
Across four simulated robomimic tasks, a merge cap of two matches or exceeds frozen-policy success, improves Square by 14 points, and shortens successful episodes.
The approach also transfers to simulated humanoid tracking, achieving 71% clip success at 2.3× speed versus 51% for uniform scaling at 2×.

papers.abstract: Guidance methods are essential tools for steering the generation process in diffusion models, improving the generalizability of stochastic robotic controllers and enabling high-quality controlled image synthesis. Despite strong parallels between flow-matching and diffusion, integrating guidance into flow-matching models remains quite challenging. Recent work has proposed general guidance frameworks for flow-matching, however, they are direct adaptations of diffusion guidance methods and can prove unstable. In this work, we conduct a theoretical analysis of guidance in flow-matching and show that a naive translation of diffusion-based guidance to flow-matching breaks the coupling distribution used during training, resulting in weaker control over sampling accuracy. Building on this insight, we propose Coupled Guidance, a flow-matching-specific guidance mechanism derived from a geometric perspective that leverages the coupling structure inherent to flow-matching training. To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we conduct extensive experimentation on a custom robotic collision avoidance task using ManiSkill3, four robotic dexterous manipulation tasks from the Adroit benchmark, and three image generation tasks, namely inpainting, super-resolution, and deblurring, using the ImageNet-128 and CelebA-HQ-256 datasets. Our findings show that our framework improves sample quality and guidance stability across all tasks, without imposing any additional overhead.
authors: Mateo Clémente
Léo Maxime Brunswic
Rui Heng Yang
Amir Rasouli
bullets: Naively adapting diffusion guidance to flow matching can break the coupling distribution used during training, weakening control and causing instability.
The proposed method derives guidance geometrically from flow matching’s inherent coupling structure.
It is evaluated on robotic collision avoidance, dexterous manipulation, inpainting, super-resolution, and deblurring tasks.
Experiments across robotics and image generation show improved sample quality and guidance stability without additional overhead.

papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D semantic maps have emerged as a key spatial memory representation for long-horizon robot autonomy, enabling robots to reason about objects, their spatial relationships, and past observations across time. However, existing object-centric semantic maps are primarily designed for static environments and rely on an append-only point integration strategy, where newly observed points are accumulated but previously integrated points are rarely reevaluated. Consequently, perception errors accumulate over time, and outdated points persist after objects move or disappear. Although recent dynamic mapping methods update object-level representations in changing scenes, they do not explicitly revise noisy or obsolete points within each object. We propose an online refinable semantic mapping framework that continuously refines object representations through probabilistic point-level confidence updating. Each object point maintains a confidence score that is updated online using multi-view temporal evidence: consistent observations reinforce reliable points, while inconsistent segmentation masks, depth measurements, and visibility cues suppress spurious and outdated points. Combined with object tracking and re-identification to preserve instance identities under motion and relocation, our framework enables object-centric semantic maps to be continuously refined rather than monotonically accumulated. Experiments demonstrate improved mapping accuracy over the previous method by 3.46% on Replica and 2.55% on ScanNet, show robustness in dynamic environments and under perception noise, and provide an effective spatial memory for object navigation and embodied question-answering with success rates of 82.4% and 76.7%.
authors: Taimeng Fu
Yi Du
Zitong Zhan
Qiwei Du
Shaoshu Su
Zhipeng Zhao
Chen Wang
bullets: Addresses error accumulation and stale points caused by append-only mapping in dynamic scenes.
Updates each point’s confidence using multi-view temporal evidence from segmentation, depth, and visibility consistency.
Combines point refinement with object tracking and re-identification to maintain identities through motion and relocation.
Improves mapping accuracy over the previous method by 3.46% on Replica and 2.55% on ScanNet.
Supports downstream object navigation and embodied question-answering, with reported success rates of 82.4% and 76.7%.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of the proposed dynamic semantic mapping framework. Given posed RGB-D observations, openvocabulary detections are generated and associated with object instances in the 3D semantic map. For each association, we perform a visibility-based point confidence update. Points supported by current detections, such as the green points on the table, receive higher confidence. In contrast, inconsistent outlier points, such as red points mistakenly fused into a bed instance due to previous segmentation errors, are down-weighted when later observations identify them as pillows. Points belonging to removed objects are identified through visibility reasoning, assigned lower confidence, and eventually pruned. Unobserved points in the current frame, shown in gray, remain unchanged until more evidence is collected in later frames. The semantic map is updated online in this frame-by-frame manner, while periodic instance-fragment merging reduces duplicate instances and re-identification preserves object identities when objects are relocated and re-observed at new locations.

Fig. 6: Example of handling under-segmentation. A pillow is initially fused into the chair instance due to undersegmentation. Once the pillow is correctly segmented in later frames, our method adds it as a separate instance and gradually removes the corresponding points from the chair instance through confidence updates.
Fig. 7: Example of in-view object tracking. Our method tracks the moving bowl in images and updates its location in the semantic map while preserving the same instance ID.

Fig. 5: Example of object fragment merging. A table is initially reconstructed as two separate instances due to temporally disconnected partial observations at 1s and 10s. As more observations become available at 12s, our method merges the fragments into a complete object instance.

Fig. 1: Dynamic open-vocabulary semantic mapping. Our method maintains a refinable object-centric 3D semantic map through point-level probabilistic updates. It handles dynamic objects that newly appear, move within the robot’s view, or are relocated out of view and later re-identified.

Fig. 9: Examples of object navigation and EQA tasks executed on the Spot robot. Our semantic map serves as an online memory that helps the LLM localize target objects, plan embodied skills, and answer questions.

Fig. 4: Example of handling incorrect detections. A plastic bag is mistakenly detected as a pillow, creating a false instance in the map. Our confidence update mechanism accumulates positive evidence for consistently detected objects and negative evidence for unsupported instances, eventually removing the false pillow while preserving the true one.

papers.abstract: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) generate sequences by progressively unmasking tokens, but errors introduced during decoding are typically irreversible. Recent work has shown that iterative correction can improve sample quality, yet existing theory fails to explain this given a learned, imperfect denoiser model. We re-formulate MDM inference as a Markov chain on the clean sequence space, defined by a remask-denoise kernel that randomly re-introduces masks and then denoises. This helps us analyze the actual denoising trajectory towards the data distribution. The analysis motivates Random Remask-Denoise (R$^2$D) inference, a purely test-time, finetuning-free, reward-free procedure. To further improve performance, we propose Trajectory Correction Training (TCT), a denoiser-training procedure that exposes the model to its own errors along the generation trajectory. On logical tasks, our approach exhibits a striking near-log-linear test-time scaling, achieving over 97% accuracy on hard Sudoku puzzles and over 99% accuracy on 3-SAT. Our approach also applies to pretrained models on actual language tasks, beating iterative correction baselines and the official Q-mode accuracy of LLaDA2.1-mini on HumanEval+.
authors: Zhaoyi Zhou
Frank Wu
Andrea Zanette
bullets: Masked diffusion decoding errors are usually irreversible, limiting generation quality.
The paper models inference as a Markov chain using a remask-denoise kernel that randomly re-masks tokens before denoising.
This analysis motivates Random Remask-Denoise (R²D), a finetuning-free, reward-free, test-time method.
Trajectory Correction Training (TCT) trains denoisers on errors encountered during their own generation trajectories.
On logical tasks, the approach achieves over 97% Sudoku accuracy and over 99% 3-SAT accuracy, and improves pretrained-model results on language tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Inference scaling on Sudoku-Hard and 3-SAT. R2D and ReMDM are run on standard training checkpoints, both using the standard variant; ProSeCo has its own training method. R2D scales near-log-linearly on both tasks and stays above ReMDM at every budget, whereas ProSeCo plateaus after a handful of correction steps.

Figure 2: HumanEval+ accuracy with the off-theshelf LLaDA2.1-mini (16B). The three colored bars are inference methods we run ourselves, and the two grey bars are the model’s own published Q-mode and S-mode results. R2D achieves the top accuracy, surpassing the official Q-mode performance.

Figure 4: Inference scaling on Sudoku-Hard (top) and 3-SAT (bottom), under standard training (left) and TCT training (right). The y-axis reports task accuracy and the x-axis the per-token correction budget M on a logarithmic scale; error bars are one standard deviation across three training seeds. The horizontal dashed line marks each panel’s own no-correction baseline. R2D scales near-log-linearly in all four panels and stays above ReMDM at every budget. Protocol details are in Section E.

Figure 3: Averaged number of function evaluations (NFE) per sample at the budget of Table 1 (lower is better), with accuracy in parentheses (TCT checkpoint for R2D and ReMDM). R2D exits early, whereas ReMDM and ProSeCo spend their full budget.

Table 1: Accuracy (in %) on Sudoku-Hard and 3-SAT, organized by training method and inference method. ReMDM, R2D and ProSeCo use the same compute budget (256 steps per token for SudokuHard, 32 steps per token for 3-SAT). R2D is the primary driver for inference-time scaling, and TCT cooperates well with R2D to further raise performance.

Table 2: Compute-normalized comparison on Sudoku-Hard and 3-SAT. Each inference method is reported with its accuracy (in %), averaged NFE, and per-sample wall time at batch size 1 on a single NVIDIA GH200 GPU. R2D is the only method that exits early: on Sudoku-Hard it reaches 97.5 in 49.4 s/sample where ReMDM reaches 92.3 in 187.9 s/sample — 5.2 points better at 3.8× less wall time. Measurement protocol in Section E.
Table 8: Denoiser architecture for Sudoku-Hard and 3-SAT. The two share a Qwen2-style backbone and differ only in vocabulary size and maximum position, which are dictated by the input encoding.

Table 3: HumanEval+ accuracy, averaged NFE and averaged wall time (in minute per sample) for the three iterative correction methods of Figure 2, all evaluated with the off-the-shelf LLaDA2.1-mini. R2D reaches the top accuracy while spending roughly half of ReMDM’s compute.

Table 5: Token preservation of the TCT-trained denoiser: The fraction of correct revealed tokens that survive a single forward pass without carry-over, averaged over three training seeds. On Sudoku-Hard the correct grid is an exact fixed point of the denoiser at every masking ratio; On 3-SAT it is not, and preservation is weakest precisely when the sequence is nearly complete, which is why carry-over is essential there and not on Sudoku-Hard.

Table 4: ReMDM implementation variants on the TCT checkpoint, comparing carry-over denoising against the sampling operator, at M = 256 on Sudoku-Hard and M = 32 on 3-SAT. Accuracy is in %, mean ± standard deviation over three training seeds × three inference seeds. The sampling operator dominates: argmax is the operator TCT trains under. Carry-over is close to free on Sudoku-Hard but decisive on 3-SAT. The standard checkpoint is not ablated; there we run the official carry-over + stochastic configuration.

Table 6: R2D (correction) inference design on Sudoku-Hard under TCT training. Each row changes one design element of Algorithm 1 relative to Default. Each cell reports accuracy (in %, mean ± standard deviation over three training seeds) with averaged NFE in parentheses. Low-confidence remasking almost removes the scaling effect; Removing early exit preserves scaling but at markedly higher NFE; Stochastic sampling in place of argmax costs accuracy at every budget while spending more NFE.

Table 7: Reveal rule in TCT training (Algorithm 2) on Sudoku-Hard, replacing the argmax reveal of Line 9 and the top-k confidence reveal of Line 11. Position selection is the load-bearing choice, while argmax reveal is a minor lever; Both approximations help rather than hurt.

papers.abstract: A planner using a learned world model can improve its predicted outcome while choosing a worse action. We study when expected free energy (EFE) can help decide how much computation to spend on a plan. An EFE-inspired objective combines goal distance with disagreement among stochastic predictions. We test candidate scoring, stopping, and online predictor updates separately. Stopping when elite cost stalls reduces refinement on tasks whose success plateaus with depth, with mean success close to fixed-depth references. At the larger tested weights, rewarding disagreement lowers success with a frozen model. Penalizing it helps at some task and weight settings but harms others. When training data omit a region needed to reach the goal, online updates recover part of the resulting loss. The tested cost-stall rule can fail when further optimization exploits model errors, because predicted cost keeps falling after task success peaks. Cost progress can guide computation on a plateau, but protecting performance after a peak requires information about the consequences of the chosen actions.
authors: Tong Zhang
Zhiyuan Shi
Yun Peng
Tao Xie
bullets: Problem: A learned world model may predict improving outcomes while selecting worse actions, making test-time compute allocation difficult.
Method: Separately evaluate EFE-inspired candidate scoring, cost-stall stopping, and online predictor updates during latent world-model planning.
Stopping on stalled elite cost reduces unnecessary refinement on plateauing tasks, with mean success near fixed-depth references.
Rewarding stochastic-prediction disagreement lowers success with a frozen model; penalizing disagreement is task- and weight-dependent.
Online updates recover part of the loss caused by missing training data in regions needed to reach the goal, but cost-stall stopping can fail after success peaks.

papers.abstract: Under matched conditions, classifier-head fine-tuning (\textsc{cls}) paradigm consistently outperforms the LLM-as-Judge sequence-to-sequence (\textsc{s2s}) on binary hallucination detection. We trace this gap to the representations induced by the two objectives. Static analysis shows that \textsc{cls} learns a task-specific discriminative direction, pushing hidden states into a clear two-cluster geometry with stronger class separation and linearly decodable label information. By contrast, \textsc{s2s} relies on the pretrained language-modeling head to make decisions. This minimizes the pressure to reorganize representations, leaving the hidden states much closer to the pretrained backbone. Our analysis also reveals that the \textsc{cls} signal saturates before the final layer, after which upper layers form a plateau of statistically interchangeable and largely redundant representations. However, endpoint redundancy alone does not show whether these layers are dispensable during training. Further training-dynamics analysis reveals 1) a lower pretrained substrate, 2) a narrow upper-middle \textbf{InfoWindow} where task information emerges, and 3) a later-synchronizing upper plateau that mirrors this signal. This mechanism motivates us to remove layers above the InfoWindow. Truncating 31\% of the network leaves accuracy unchanged within seed noise on Qwen3-4B and 8B and cuts latency by $1.4\times$. The same depth fraction, fixed before any analysis of the target models, transfers to Llama-3.2-3B and Mistral-7B-v0.3, and the layer structure behind it reappears there and on QNLI and SST-2. We hope this helps guide efficient task-specific LLM design.
authors: Kaiyang Wan
Forrest Sheng Bao
Amin Ahmad
Yuxia Wang
bullets: Classifier fine-tuning forms clearly separated hidden-state clusters with more linearly decodable labels, while sequence-to-sequence fine-tuning leaves representations closer to the pretrained model.
Task information emerges in a narrow upper-middle-layer InfoWindow, followed by a redundant upper plateau that synchronizes with and mirrors the signal.
Removing layers above the InfoWindow cuts 31% of the network while preserving accuracy within seed variation on Qwen3-4B and 8B.
The same fixed depth fraction transfers to Llama-3.2-3B and Mistral-7B-v0.3, with similar layer structure also observed on QNLI and SST-2.
The analysis is based on matched comparisons and training dynamics; the reported efficiency scope covers the evaluated models and tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Layer-wise analysis of fine-tuning objectives for LLM hallucination detection enabling efficient layer truncation.
papers.title: How Fine-Tuning Objectives Shape Layer-Wise Information in LLM Hallucination Detection
papers.tldr: Classifier-head fine-tuning detects hallucinations better than sequence-to-sequence prompting because it creates a localized, discriminative information window that enables substantial upper-layer pruning without accuracy loss.

papers.abstract: We investigate how humanoid robots can learn a series of motor skills defined by human infant motor development scales, and we evaluate which scales are comprehensive enough to serve as self-contained guides for developing gross motor skills up to standing and walking. We represent each motor development scale as a developmental graph that guides the training of a humanoid robot. We then apply this graph within a reinforcement learning framework so that the robot learns skills following the natural phases of human motor development described by the scale. Our work demonstrates that graphs derived from three out of four popular pediatric motor scales can successfully guide humanoid robots to develop these skills. The fourth scale misses some intermediate milestones that the other scales have, which causes some failures. After adding a missing milestone in its graph, it also enables the robot to develop those skills successfully.
authors: Fanxing Meng
Jing Xiao
bullets: Evaluates whether pediatric motor-development scales can serve as complete guides for robot learning through standing and walking.
Converts each scale into a developmental graph and integrates it with reinforcement learning.
Three of four evaluated scales successfully guide skill development.
The fourth scale fails because it omits intermediate milestones; adding one enables successful learning.
Scope is limited to gross motor development up to standing and walking.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon human-scene interaction requires coordinated spatial reasoning, physical feasibility, and the ability to recover from compounding execution errors. Text-driven motion models are largely scene-agnostic and lack closed-loop correction, while geometry-conditioned approaches depend on paired scene-motion training or explicit 3D preprocessing that limits generalization to novel layouts and open-vocabulary goals. We present InteractAgent, an agentic multimodal LLM system for long-horizon human-scene interaction that plans, executes, observes, and reflects in a closed loop, using a single MLLM as both planner and evaluator and a frozen MotionLLM as the executor. InteractAgent integrates Online Observation for step-wise recovery decisions (continue/redo/replan) and Memory-Augmented Reflection for multi-round plan refinement with adaptive stopping. On UniHSI, InteractAgent improves task success and reduces penetration compared with training-free baselines. Code: https://github.com/AIGeeksGroup/InteractAgent.
authors: Senhe Zhang
Tao Zhang
Yujia Zhang
Zeyu Zhang
Dong Gong
bullets: Addresses scene-agnostic text-driven motion generation and error accumulation in long-horizon interactions.
Uses one multimodal LLM as planner and evaluator, with a frozen MotionLLM executing motions.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video generative models have enabled flexible conditional generation and editing pipelines, such as text-to-video, image-to-video, and reference-guided synthesis. However, these workflows are inherently one-directional, mapping conditions to videos without providing a mechanism to invert this process. In complex media production settings, the ability to recover controllable textual conditions from a given video is highly desirable, yet remains underexplored. While inverse prompting has been studied for image generation, directly extending these approaches to video is challenging due to the need to capture temporal dynamics beyond static appearance, as well as the substantial computational cost of per-video optimization. In this work, we propose the first practical framework for efficient video inverse prompting. Specifically, we formulate inverse prompting as a meta-learning problem and introduce Meta Video Inverse Prompting (MVIP), which learns a meta-prompt optimized over temporal dimensions to enable fast and effective prompt inference. Our approach amortizes the inversion process, eliminating the need for costly iterative optimization at test time. Experimental results demonstrate that MVIP recovers higher-quality inverse prompts with significantly improved reconstruction fidelity compared to image-based inversion and iterative captioning baselines, while achieving substantial gains in efficiency. Code and video results are available at https://ueriniuno.github.io/mvip-page/.
authors: Yerin Jung
Jongheon Jeong
bullets: Addresses the lack of methods for inverting video-generation pipelines to recover controllable text conditions.
Introduces Meta Video Inverse Prompting (MVIP), which learns a meta-prompt optimized across temporal dimensions.
Amortizes inversion, eliminating iterative per-video optimization at inference time.
Reports higher-quality inverse prompts, better reconstruction fidelity, and improved efficiency than image-based inversion and iterative captioning baselines.
Focuses on capturing video temporal dynamics beyond static appearance.

The task-adapted prompts are then used to update the shared initialization, which can be directly applied to unseen videos.

papers.abstract: This work demonstrates the use of a fast simulation-based training framework to learn control policies using reinforcement learning. The hardware requirements are minimal and the simulation-learned policies transfer reliably to the real world. With this setup, we show that a quadruped robot can learn to traverse diverse real-world terrains reliably---including in a lunar-analog facility---after less than 20 minutes of training on a single consumer-grade GPU. These results provide a glimpse of a future where reinforcement learning is a crucial tool in developing more capable and robust space robotic systems. Video demonstrations are available at https://youtu.be/vUFJiZdJaQ0.
authors: Abhishek Naik
Michael Wu
Michael O'Sullivan
Colin Bellinger
Yunli Wang
bullets: Motivation: make reinforcement learning practical for capable, robust space robotics.
Method: train control policies in fast simulation with minimal hardware requirements, then deploy them on a real quadruped.
Result: the robot traverses diverse real-world terrains reliably, including a lunar-analog facility.
Training uses less than 20 minutes on a single consumer-grade GPU.
Scope: demonstrates promising real-world transfer for quadruped locomotion in space-robotics-relevant environments.
