papers.abstract: High-resolution Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) preserve critical, fine-grained visual details by encoding a global thumbnail alongside multiple local crops. However, the resulting thousands of vision tokens introduce severe computational bottlenecks during Large Language Model (LLM) inference. Existing token pruning methods rely primarily on query-agnostic visual saliency, while current query-aware approaches either operate at a coarse crop-level resolution or compute token relevance too late, after vision tokens have already entered the heavy LLM layers. To address this, we propose a training-free, hierarchical token pruning framework that utilizes query guidance prior to executing any LLM blocks. Our top-down hierarchy first operates at the instance-level, dynamically scaling the vision token retention ratio of each sample based on its visual complexity. Next, at the crop-level, we distribute this sample budget across local crops using sentence-level cross-modal similarity. Finally, at the token-level, we exploit projected vision tokens alongside textual query token embeddings in the shared space to measure fine-grained alignment, applying a text-debiasing normalization to produce high-fidelity query scores. These query-guided budgets and scores are fused with local and global visual saliency metrics to select the most critical vision tokens. Extensive experiments on LLaVA-NeXT-7B demonstrate that our plug-and-play framework retains 98.0% and 94.8% of unpruned performance at 25% and 10% vision token retention, respectively. Notably, at 25% retention, our method delivers a 2.0x inference throughput speedup and even surpasses the unpruned baseline on POPE by 0.7 points.
authors: Luther Wei
Ling Zou
Kang-Yang Huang
Yu-Syuan Xu
Wen-Huang Cheng
bullets: Addresses the computational bottleneck caused by thousands of vision tokens from global thumbnails and local crops.
Dynamically allocates retention budgets across samples, crops, and tokens using visual complexity and query-aware cross-modal alignment.
Combines query-guided scores with local and global visual saliency to select critical tokens before any LLM blocks execute.
On LLaVA-NeXT-7B, retains 98.0% and 94.8% of unpruned performance at 25% and 10% token retention, respectively.
At 25% retention, achieves a 2.0× inference throughput speedup and exceeds the unpruned baseline on POPE by 0.7 points.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: Overview of our training-free token pruning framework for high-resolution LVLMs. An input image is processed into a full-image view and multiple sub-images, which are passed through a Visual Encoder and Projector to produce visual tokens (V ). A text query is tokenized into embeddings (E). The pruning process consists of three main stages: (1) Adaptive Budget Allocation: A two-level budget is computed. At the Sample-level, a token retention ratio (Rj) is dynamically set for each image based on its visual token diversity (Hj). At the Crop-level, this budget is distributed among the sub-images based on the query-crop relevance. (2) Query Score Algorithm: A fine-grained relevance score is computed between the query embeddings (E) and the visual tokens (V ). Raw cross-modal similarities are standardized using a text-debiasing z-score to produce a robust query score (qsi) for each token. (3) Fuse & Select: The final token selection score is calculated by fusing the Query Score with two visual saliency cues: a local score from the sub-image’s own [CLS] attention (ai) and a global score derived from the full-image view (gi). The top-bi tokens are selected and fed to LLM for inference.

Fig. 2: Adaptive per-sample budget allocation on POPE examples. Our query-aware framework dynamically scales token retention according to scene complexity. The visually redundant snow scene (left) retains only 516 of 2,880 visual tokens, whereas the cluttered baseball scene (right) dynamically allocates 860 tokens to preserve fine-grained details needed for accurate question answering.

Fig. 1: Pruning masks on a POPE sample at a 25% retention ratio. GlobalCom2 uses an image-only mask that is unchanged by the query; for the chair question shown here, it removes most chair evidence before the LLM and answers incorrectly. Our query-aware mask retains the relevant chair tokens and answers correctly.

TABLE I: Comparison with existing methods on LLaVA-NeXT-7B. The retention ratio R is defined with respect to the 2,880 token positions including padding. Avg. is the mean score relative to the unpruned model. Baseline results without a mark are taken from GlobalCom2 [11]; ∗ denotes results obtained by running the released code. The best and second-best results among pruning methods are in bold and underlined.

TABLE V: Inference efficiency of LLaVA-NeXT-7B on POPE at R = 25%. TFLOPs: LLM prefill FLOPs. Memory: peak GPU memory. Throughput: questions per second. Performance: average relative score in Table I.
TABLE II: Module ablation on LLaVA-NeXT-7B at R = 25%.
TABLE III: Ablation on α at R = 25% (β = 0.5). α = 1 uses only the global score; the default is underlined.
TABLE IV: Ablation on β at R = 25% (α = 0.7). β = 0 uses only the query score as the local score; the default is underlined. β = 1 removes the query score.

papers.title: Hierarchical and Query-Aware Visual Token Pruning for High-Resolution LVLMs
papers.tldr: A training-free hierarchical method prunes high-resolution LVLM vision tokens using query relevance and visual saliency before LLM inference, substantially reducing computation while preserving performance.

papers.abstract: Radio-frequency (RF) and wave-based imaging systems play a critical role in sensing under adverse conditions, but are fundamentally constrained by a trade-off between collection speed and spatial resolution. Reducing measurements to enable rapid collection of fragment geometric information across sensing dimensions, leading to highly non-injective inverse problems that destabilize conventional image-domain reconstruction and super-resolution methods. Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) exemplifies this challenge in sparse-aperture sampling. We introduce SPIRIT, a physics-informed inverse rendering framework for sparse-aperture SAR. Rather than enhancing formed images, SPIRIT reconstructs an explicit three-dimensional surface. By adopting an optimization strategy and explicitly modeling visibility, phase coherence, and wave propagation, SPIRIT aggregates distributed geometric features across sparse aperture views into a coherent reconstruction. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate that SPIRIT recovers accurate geometry and signal under extreme sparsity, reducing data collection by over 90% while achieving low geometric and signal error and consistently outperforming baselines.
authors: Yimeng Liu
Maolin Gan
Jingkai Lin
Jialuo Du
Mi Zhang
Zhichao Cao
bullets: Targets the speed–resolution trade-off and ill-posed reconstruction caused by sparse-aperture SAR sampling.
Optimizes a 3D surface representation rather than enhancing a preformed image.
Models visibility, phase coherence, and wave propagation to combine geometric evidence across aperture views.
Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show accurate geometry and signal recovery with over 90% less data and lower errors than baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of SPIRIT. Sparse coherent measurements are encoded into an explicit surface representation and evaluated through a differentiable RF forward model. The renderer produces predicted measurements at observed and unobserved aperture locations; consistency with the observed sparse measurements constrains the recovered geometry, while the learned structural prior regularizes unobserved components of the scene.

Figure 3: Held-out synthetic reconstructions under extreme 1-scan sparsity. Columns correspond to representative test objects excluded from the training split; rows show (top to bottom) groundtruth point clouds, SPIRIT-predicted geometry, sparse SAR observations, and predicted renderings. These examples visualize geometry recovery in the controlled synthetic setting; held-out physicalmeasurement results are reported separately in Appendix F.3.

Figure 5: Real-world SAR observations of a metallic digit 9 under different aperture configurations. Black boxes mark radar aperture locations, and the red marker denotes the active position. From left to right: full-aperture, single-pass sparse aperture, upper-aperture subset, and lower-aperture subset. Full-aperture integration produces the most complete formed image, whereas restricted aperture subsets emphasize different portions of the target. The comparison illustrates viewpoint-dependent scattering and the loss of angular/spatial-frequency support under sparse acquisition.
Figure 1: SPIRIT formulates sparse-aperture SAR reconstruction as physics-informed inverse rendering.

Figure 4: Real-world SAR data collection and signal propagation illustration. (a) Physical scanning setup and Z-shaped raster trajectory used for planar SAR collection, consistent with the simulator configuration. (b) Conceptual illustration of wave propagation and angle-dependent scattering, highlighting that while the beam covers the entire region of interest, different aperture locations emphasize different geometric components of the target.

Figure 6: Geometry collapse under unconstrained Stage 2 fine-tuning. The top row shows ground truth, while the bottom row shows Stage 2 full fine-tuning without geometric constraints. Despite improved image appearance, unconstrained optimization leads to geometric drift and collapse.

Figure 7 visualizes the effect of retaining different amounts of aperture support. A single scanline provides only a restricted subset of the spatial-frequency and angular observations available in the full aperture. Adding scanlines introduces additional viewpoint-dependent measurements and reduces, but does not eliminate, the ambiguity of the inverse problem. The experiment therefore illustrates complementarity among retained aperture positions; it should not be interpreted as evidence that sparse sampling preserves all scene information.

Figure 7: Reconstruction under increasing aperture coverage. Rows correspond to 1-, 3-, and 6-scan inputs. Additional scanlines provide complementary angular and spatial-frequency measurements, reducing ambiguity relative to the 1-scan setting. Sparse sampling nevertheless leaves unobserved support and does not uniquely determine the scene.

Table 4: Quantitative comparison on the object-disjoint MITO real-world test split after residual-only Stage II adaptation on the disjoint real training split. The listed methods are matched controls under the common evaluation pipeline rather than claimed faithful reproductions of every recent radar system. CD is computed against the common registered reference geometry; signal and image metrics use the corresponding measured/reference radar products. Lower is better for CD and signal error; higher is better for PSNR/SSIM.

Table 1: Scope comparison of representative reconstruction paradigms. Entries summarize the published input domain, scene representation, forward model, and primary reconstruction regime; the table is descriptive rather than a performance ranking.

Table 2: Controlled synthetic comparison under 1-, 3-, and 6-scan sparsity. CD is reported in millimeters; PSNR/SSIM use backprojected magnitude images. SPIRIT is mean± standard deviation over three seeds; controls use fixed schedules.
Table 3: Core 1-scan ablation. Full unfreezing without the refiner causes geometric drift; the final joint configuration gives the best tested joint result.
Table 5: Noise robustness analysis under varying SNR levels. Each entry reports Chamfer Distance (mm) / Signal ℓ1 error. Lower values indicate better geometric fidelity and signal consistency.
Table 6: Sensitivity to the identity-regularization coefficient λid.

papers.title: SPIRIT: Sparse Physics-Informed Inverse Rendering for SAR Imaging
papers.tldr: SPIRIT reconstructs explicit 3D surfaces from extremely sparse SAR measurements by combining inverse rendering with physics-based modeling.

papers.abstract: Real-world egocentric videos capture multi-step household procedures, but their recorded trajectories leave alternative actions and recovery from the learner's own mistakes largely unexplored. We introduce EgoVine, a post-training framework that turns a fixed demonstration set into interactive experience for long-horizon planning. EgoVine operates in executable symbolic environments compiled from real-world video annotations, where an agent must coordinate object manipulations under partial observation and account for delayed consequences. Restoring a decision state allows the learner to explore alternative actions and compare their eventual outcomes. Union jointly trains action generation and consequence prediction in one model, using the same executions to supervise candidate comparison and recovery. Verified repairs add recovery targets from failed attempts, while comparisons among sampled continuations guide policy updates. The updated planner then returns to the environments, with its own decisions and mistakes shaping the next round of experience. On a shared benchmark, EgoVine-1.5B achieves 81.8% success on Main planning tasks and 66.7% on longer task compositions, outperforming all evaluated Flash LLM baselines on both. EgoVine connects real demonstrations to an iterative learning process that trains compact planners on choices and futures beyond the recorded trajectories.

papers.title: EgoVine: Post-Training with Branching Experience Compiled from Real-World Videos
papers.tldr: EgoVine post-trains compact planners by branching from real-world video demonstrations to explore alternatives, recover from mistakes, and improve long-horizon household-task planning.

papers.abstract: Generating 3D-consistent novel views from 2D diffusion models remains a fundamental challenge in computer vision. In this work, we introduce a framework that enhances geometric alignment for monocular view synthesis under drastic camera changes by jointly generating a target view and its corresponding depth map. By conditioning the diffusion pipeline on the single source image, source depth, and target camera rays, our approach forces the model to inherently reason in 3D space even under extreme viewpoint shifts. To guarantee spatial fidelity, we propose a novel per-pixel depth consistency constraint, which verifies and enforces 3D consistency across generated views. Our framework establishes a robust pipeline for geometrically consistent view synthesis, yielding superior visual accuracy and spatial alignment compared to current state-of-the-art methods. With this work, we pave the road towards robust 3D world models capable of understanding complex environments from a single view image.
authors: Ge Ya Luo
Daniel Severo
Brian Karrer
Christopher Pal
Adriana Romero-Soriano
Michal Drozdzal
bullets: Addresses ambiguity in 2D diffusion models under large camera viewpoint changes.
Conditions diffusion on a source image, source depth, and target camera rays to encourage 3D reasoning.
Introduces a per-pixel depth consistency constraint to preserve spatial fidelity across views.
Reports superior visual accuracy and spatial alignment compared with existing state-of-the-art methods.
Targets robust single-image understanding for future 3D world models.

figures.caption: Figure 3 ESC Framework. The framework extends Qwen MM-DiT with depth information and Plücker rays conditioning by leveraging LoRA adapters and a Ray ControlNet. At inference time, we leverage PCC-based sampling to enforce improved generated scene geometry.

Figure 2 PCC computation pipeline. The source view (a) is from the original scene, while the target view (f) has been modified: a red sphere is added and a yellow sphere is removed. Top row (∆t, detectingmissing geometry): the source depth (b) is unprojected to 3D and reprojected into the target camera frame (c); black regions indicate pixels outside the reprojection coverage. Where the yellow sphere was removed, target camera rays pass through and hit the cubes in the back instead of striking the sphere surface, producing large positive ∆t values. These inconsistent pixels are highlighted in red (e), with nf = 13703 pixels exceeding the error threshold δ. Bottom row (∆s, detecting hallucinated geometry): The modified target depth is reprojected back into the source frame (h). The added red sphere reprojects into a region with no corresponding geometry in the source perspective, yielding large positive ∆s values and nb = 8581 inconsistent pixels (j). The final PCC score of 0.0232 quantifies the overall geometric disagreement between the two views.

Figure 9 Effect of frame gap onmodel performance. Performance consistently degrades across all models as the frame gap increases. Nevertheless, our method outperforms all baselines at every frame-gap setting on all metrics except PSNR and SSIM, for which LagerNVS achieves the best results.

Figure 1 Novel view synthesis highlights. Given a single input view, its corresponding depth map, and Plücker ray conditioning, our method generates novel views that remain 3D-consistent with the target across challenging datasets (DL3DV, RealEstate10K, T&T) and selective in-the-wild scenes. For the datasets, we illustrate a single novel view generation alongside the ground-truth target, whereas for the in-the-wild setting, we demonstrate two distinct novel view generations.

By projecting the point cloud derived from each image into the other view, the PCC-based procedure identifies points whose projected geometry is inconsistent with the modified scene. Figure 7 Sensitivity of the DA3 PCCmetric to controlled scale perturbations. Starting from a clean reference scene, we re-render each object with a random per-object scale jitter of 1–40% and measure (a) PCC, (b) pose AUC@3, 5, 15, 30, (c) relative rotation error (RPE-R), and (d) relative translation error (RPE-T), with depth and cameras predicted by DA3 and FG/BG-split affine alignment (no top-% pruning). With one exception, all evaluated metrics track geometric error monotonically alongside increasing jitter magnitude. Specifically, PCC rises from 0.07 at 0% jitter to 0.62 at 40%, AUC@30 falls from 0.84 to 0.51 (with AUC@3 collapsing from 0.67 to 0 by the 20% mark), and RPE-T increases from 0.77 to 12.35. RPE-R is the only metric that fails to reliably reflect the introduced noise, remaining largely stagnant and breaking monotonicity at 2%, 7%, and 30%.

papers.selection_reason: Joint generation of target view and depth with geometric constraints for 3D-consistent novel view synthesis, relevant to spatial reasoning and 3D vision.
papers.title: ESC: Escaping 2D Diffusion Ambiguity with Geometric Constraints for Consistent Novel View Synthesis
papers.tldr: ESC improves 3D-consistent novel-view synthesis by jointly generating target images and depth while enforcing per-pixel geometric consistency.
